An all-time favourite in your Christmas collection, this is one of the best renditions that you could possibly possess of traditional carol singing. The Choir of Trinity College & the soprano & descant voices in particular, are exceptionally superlative in their interpretation of each carol - each one carefully chosen to make a fantastic collection of festive music. It is beautiful & exquisite when played softly whilst reading before nodding off to sleep & outstanding when blasted out loud for the sheer joy of music in itself.

The immaculate packaging, excellent clarity & depth of sound, very reasonable pricing and the best selection ever of univerally-loved carols make this set of 2 cds stand out phenominally from all the many drab & often boring Christmas music cds avaliable in the market nowadays.

As the "Greatest Hits" Disc cover states this is "The most comprehensive, single disc compilation of adventures of pop-rock singer-songwriter Todd Rundgren's brillient work, this collection is the first-time that the cream of his solo & Utopia material have appeared together!" "Includes several /Billboard Top 40 pop hits & "Hello it's Me", a #5 smash." It's like going back in time, to the early seventies. I use to have all his early albums.

What I really like about this compilation CD: It contains the original, studio/radio versions, of these wonderful songs. It takes me back to my teens & early twenties. I use to have every one of these songs, on vinyl or on an 8 track tape, but somehow they got lost along the way. Now, I get to re-experience this great music.

The song set is as follows:

1. We Gotta Get You a Woman ("We gotta get you a woman, and when we're through with you, we'll get me one too"!!!!)

2. Be Nice to Me

3. I Saw the Light ("I walked out before, but I won't do it anymore, cause I saw the light in your eyes...")

4. Hello It's Me (One of the greatest songs ever!!!! "Its important to me, that you know you are free, cause I'd never want to make you change for me...Think of me, you know that I'd be with you if I could...")

5. Couldn't I Just Tell You

6. Just One Victory

7. A Dream Goes On Forever (One of the Greatest Songs of All Times!!! "So Long ago, and so far away, but a dream goes on Forever, How much I love you, you'll never know, til you follow me in my dreams")

8. Real Man

9. Love of the Common Man

10. Love is the Answer (with Utopia) - This was originally written by Todd Rundgren & Utopia, but was covered by England Dan & John Ford Coley, back in the 1970's, and became a huge pop hit for them. However, I like Todd & Utopia's version better.)

11. Love in Action (with Utopia)

12. Can We Still Be Friends

13. The Very Last Time (with Utiopia)

14. Band on the Drum All Day ("I don't want to work, I want to bang on the drum all day")

15. Something to Fall Back On

16. The Want of A Nail (with Bobby Womack)

This is one "super-outstanding" compilation cd of the very, very best of Todd Rundgren & Utopia, all on one disc. This is very good smooth, progressive rock at its very best. The use of musical instrumentation, is awesome, in some of these songs, especially on "A Dream Goes On Forever".
I highly recommend this one. Thanks!!!!

reviewText: Throughout the 1980's this adult-oriented pop outfit from Zealand developed a large and loyal fanbase throughout their homeland and Australia. They achieved a few hit singles in the U.S. and then in the early 90's found success in the U.K. Then in 1996, they called it quits. This best-of compilation comes with three brand new studio songs but they're clearly not in the same class as the time-tested hit singles. Even after a decade, Crowded House are a breath of fresh air, clearly a testament to the exceptional songwriting talents of singer Neil Finn and his brother Tim. 'Into Temptation' and 'Pineapple Head' are equal to if not better than well-known songs 'Weather With You' or 'Don't Dream It's Over'. For a band that released just four studio albums, their back catalog is mighty impressive and this disc proves it.
label: positive

reviewText: You can throw away every other album you own.  If you are stranded on an island this would be the only album you would need.  It has the best start to an album ever.  The first six songs flow better than any other album I have heard.  They are catchy yet original.  The lyrics are so interesting that it draws you to stay focused while dancing your heart out.  Recovery is a little poppy for Frank but still a quality song.  Plain Sailing Weather is my favorite Frank song to date.  It beat out I am disappeared from England Keep my Bones which I also highly recommend.  Losing Days and The Way I tend to be are also very catchy yet have this serious tone to them.  Four Simple Words back to back with Polaroid Picture is also another magical combination.  I heard Polaroid Picture several years ago and it is better than I remember.  I could detail each song as I have in the past but I do not want to spoil your Frank Experience.  This album is absolutely amazing.  This seals the deal for me that makes Frank one of the best singer songwriters ever.  His backing band, the sleeping souls, seems to get more rocking and they have an amazing time when you see them live.  Frank is also an awesome human being.  I have met him three times when I saw him live and he always spent time talking with me and his other fans.  Anyways, go buy this album.  I think it appeals to all types of music fans.  It is part folk, part rock, a little country, and a whole lot of awesomeness.

reviewText:
Several years ago in Aspen, Colorado, I  heard, for the first time, Julia Fischer perform and was very impressed.  Now, she has hit "the big time" recording for Decca some "biggies"--Chausson "Poem" and Vaughn Williams' "Lark Ascending."  She along with the Orchestra Philarmonique of Monte-Carlo led by Yakov Kreizberg perform the aforesaid works with great beauty and feeling -really lovely renditions.  However, for me the two (2) unknown, to me, compositions that are on this disc are really what make this album called "Poem" worth owning.

Ottorino Respighi's very atmospheric "Poema autunnale" was previously unknown to me and I guess it would be called a "Program Piece" that depicts the "Autumn Season" beautifully.  Fischer plays it beautifully with great intonation and great feeling--I love the work. The other featured composition that was also unknown to me is the very dramatic Josef Suk composition "Fantasy". In that work Julia displays her great technique playing very brilliantly as does the orchestra.  All are outstanding.  I really enjoyed  this recording.  The sound is also very fine indeed.
label: positive

reviewText: The feelings that wash over me when I hear Sigur Ros play, when I hear Jonsi's voice, are almost indescribable.  Their music, this music, taps into a deep core that passes through intellect directly into my heart.  I listen to this soundtrack several times a day recently.  It passes me off to dreamland, it fills my mornings with pleasure.  It is worthy of full attention, but is also happy to provide your background.  This soundtrack is so sublimely beautiful, of course, but the feelings of hope, of joy, of sorrow, of regret, and of hope once more that are evoked by the melodies are simply overwhelming.  All the things that you would hope for from a Sigur Ros release are here--surging strings, beautiful and otherworldly vocals, and that magic that seems to make each of their records a special event.  I cannot say how much I have enjoyed and loved this wonderful album but to say this: Gently, gently, this music inhabits your soul.

reviewText:
Okay, there is no way I am going to rehash what you have already read, and this review will likely disappear soon in the morass of reviews to come (there are already 127 of them inside a week of it's release), but to be sure, you have been reading reviews that touch on the history of this project, on the contents of the CD/DVD, and on the controversy we all knew it would spark the moment we learned of it.

But let's talk about how this music makes us FEEL!  Further down you will or have read a review by a "professional musician" (and others) who take a machette to the whole concept that this album is.  I for one am a Beatles "purist".  I am also an engineer.  I know technology, I know electronics, I know systems and processes and the cutting edges of our technological growth.  But...I fixed the hole in head where the rain got in a long time ago.  Do these (so called) purists, and experts, and critics have NO imagination?  What were The Beatles all about there folks?  If you are a Beatle fan, old or new, young or aged, jaded, faded, or just born, surely you have been fixing that hole and allowing for the love and introspection and imagination that was the driving creativity of The Beatles and Sir Martin.

Just listen to this, have fun, it is an immense undertaking and don't let the detractors sway your impulses that this is simply what the boys were all about.  "Love" is a masterpiece.  If you listen to this and just enjoy it for it's creativity and ingenuity, as well as it's perfectly polished sound, and realize that this is created from masters that are 35 to 40 years old, pieces of products that were taken from a vault, the dust blown off, and set into motion on digital engineering equipment; if you have IMAGINE-ation, and Love The Beatles for what they were, a driving force in revolutionary music, and "a little band that just wanted to sing about love", if you can just enjoy something without over-analysis, then you will truly consider this a masterpiece.

This is NOT a cash cow pulled out just in time for Christmas shopping, this is NOT a whim designed to part you from your money (just look at the Amazon and Walmart prices of the CD), nor is it a contrivance like so many "best of" compilations.  It was a labor of love on the part of Sir George Martin, his son Giles (George declares this is his last project and he is turning the reins over to Giles), and fully blessed by Olivia Harrison (George wanted to make this and started planning it with Cirque Du Soleil before he died), Yoko Ono, Ringo Starr, and Paul McCartney, none of whom have any need for more pocket change.

This is music that feels good!  I wish more artists had left the legacy and the creativity that The Beatles did, but they were one of a kind and this "soundscape" album is a one of a kind.  So fill the cracks that run through the door, that keep your mind from wandering where it will go because it really doesn't matter, if you're wrong, you're right!

reviewText:
Pros: great songs, clever lyrics, wonderful arrangements

Cons: Im still confused by the different sides to the story concept; someones rapping (?)

 I have been a fan of Extreme since Ive heard their songs within the first Bill & Ted movie. Their mix of hard rock, funk and guitar god is, in my opinion, attributed solely to Extreme. I admit that while I state that I am a fan, I really only gave any attention to their first two albums. Two discs full of fun, easily digestible sounds that make me want to listen over and over. I bought their III Sides to Every Story, and probably like most people, never listened to it. I found this CD sitting in a box with other CDs in my basement, and decided to give it a listen. This 1992 follow up to their biggest album Pornagraffitti is a lot to take in. There are fourteen songs, the CD is nearly 77 minutes in length, and there are social-political statements all over the place. Then to make things even more confusing, the songs are split up into three sides, Yours, Mine & the Truth. Who is yours, is this me? By listening to the songs I cant tell. All I know is that guitarist Nuno Bettencourt and lead singer Gary Cherone have drawn up sides. They look serious and kind of pissed in the CDs photos. I don't want to be on different sides than Extreme, I like the band. Yet here they go bringing up two subjects that Brian Epstein always told the Beatles to avoid - politics and religion, a whole albums worth! Yet even though these guys broached the subjects themselves, I still cant make heads or tails where they stand on these subjects, and I guess ultimately this is a good thing. Now that I can or never will be able to tell if I am on opposite sides with Nuno, I can just sit back and enjoy the music. What else is there to do?

 The Yours section sounds like the Extreme we have all come to know. We have six songs of fast, upbeat funk metal with lighting fast guitar solos, nig horn sections, and Gary Cherone attempting to jam in as many lyrics into a small space that it will make your head spin. Warheads opens up the CD with a sergeant barking out orders to a young boy, this gives way to Nuno showing off to the background noise of an air raid alarm going off. The track is terrifically Extreme, and thats a good thing, despite this, its the weakest song on the album. The sound effects tend to get a bit corny for me, yet its a fun song to sing along to. Almost immediately, we break into a string quartet intro for the song Rest In Peace. The hook of the song is the chorus, and what makes it magical are the background vocals. Nuno and bassist Pat Badger have voices that blend together so well, that even in live situations it sounds like more than just two voices. They have really honed this strength and used it throughout this album, and its better because of it. There are some Beatles and other 60s references to this and other songs. Rest In Peace has the lyric Someone said Give peace a chance and thats all that were saying while were sitting on a fence.  Obviously a heavy nod to John Lennons Give Peace a Chance anthem. Some of the licks Nuno uses are very Jimi Hendrix-esque; Rest In Peace is son of Voodoo Chile at some points so much that Nuno even plays it for a second note for note. The next song Politicalamity has some Hendrix in there as well. The songs title is another new word made up by the band, something they do almost on every album (ex. Pornagraffitti, Americocaine). Color Me Blind asks the question Why do we dream in black and white? Color me blind I don't dream in black and white, do you? Although the lyrics do not directly address race relations, you can kind of tell that this is where they tried to go with it.

 With Cupids Dead, again they utilize a classic Beatles lyric, I read the news today, oh boy, which makes me wonder if this is actually making the bold statement that III Sides is actually on par with anything that The Beatles have done including Sgt Pepper. Theres some great drumming by Paul Geary, and I kind of like the song despite the quick rap session from guest star John Preziosa Jr. Peacemaker Die is my favorite track out of the Yours section. Until this song I couldn't be absolutely sure that all the lyrics from the Yours section are sung sarcastically. Yet, if this is so, which Im sure that it is, the continuity doesnt make sense when it comes to songs like Color Me Blind or Rest in Peace, there seems to be a severe case of schizophrenia here. It doesnt matter, lets just enjoy the songs and deal with the fact that whatever kind of point of view they hoped to make was tragically lost amongst the (originally) 15 songs.

Mine starts off sounding different in style and lyrical content. Seven Sundays is a piano power ballad, without even a guitar solo. The song is repetitive, but moving. The lyrics are basically saying that if the person had one wish, it would to have seven Sundays occur in a row because this is the day they spend with God. Tragic Comic is my favorite song from the whole album; its all acoustic guitars, Hammond organ and a lot of bass runs. The lyrics are amazing, and the melody is so dang catchy.  This track was never released as a single, which is a tragic error on the part of the band and the label. Our Father has the Boston band rockin pretty hard again, especially for the Mine section. The vocal harmonies are so alluring, and they are used for the majority of the song. Its hard to tell if the lyrics are talking about God or a more personal plea for an absentee father. For my taste, its too vague, as their lyrics for Rest In Peace, get off the fence and make a choice. Stop the World is the second best song from this section. Its hard to pinpoint a specific genre for the track although it kind of feels familiar at the same time. Its keyboards mainly with some guitars lead and rhythm. The lyrics talk about a yearning for the afterlife, living in the place where there is love, contrasted to this place where love is lacking. God Isnt Dead is more of a question than a statement. The lyrics start off by quoting The Beatles Eleanor Rigby with Ah look at all the lonely people. Not only this, but the opening piano chords sound almost too much like the opening to Let It Be. This emotional soft piano ballad is a great way to end the Mine section, as an orchestra is used much in the same way that The Truth section will utilize an orchestra arranged by Mike Moran.

 While there are only three songs in this truth section, the tracks are all quite long. Rise N Shine sounds very Broadway musical to my ears. This isn't demeaning the song, I like this genre, yet this description is way too simplistic. The song is epic with apocalyptic lyrics paraphrasing The Bible here and there. The lyrics go so far to name one of the major prophets, Daniel Dream Daniel dream for whats yet to come. The lyrics then move to the New Testament paraphrasing Jesus giving the answer when his disciples asked him about the end times and when it will come. They do not mention Jesus of course, but His words come through loud and clear for me - And in the West a cloud appears for shadows of a coming shower near, oh so near. Hypocrites, you analyze the earth and the sky, I ask you why you cant analyze the signs of the present time? See Luke 12:54 for a comparison. Am I Ever Gonna Change is slightly longer than Rise N Shine, and perhaps slightly less ambitious as the song is not changing from genre to genre but is a more straight ahead rock ballad. Yet, the Biblical theology continues, this time with the book of Romans. The title of the song itself is a lesson straight from Romans 7, the war within our own bodies. We want to do good, but sin is a constant while we are in the flesh. I can feel the frustration from Gary Cherones vocal. Somewhere in the middle heard in the background a priest can be heard reading aloud the Peoples Confession in Latin. For those of you (like myself) who cannot understand the Latin language, here is the translation:
May our Lord Jesus Christ absolve you; and by His authority I absolve you from every bond of excommunication and interdict, so far as my power allows and your needs require. Thereupon, I absolve you of your sins in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost. Amen.

Who Cares ends the CD, a tremendous song coming in at over eight minutes in length. Conductor Mike Moran really got to sink his baton into this track. I know Mike Moran from his Queen connections; he is present on their Innuendo album as well as Freddie Mercurys masterful Barcelona solo effort. The song is operatic in nature vocally; the soft piano and the harsh strings set the tine for the CDs climax. The best lyric here, in fact for the whole album is here; So many children losing time / Walk in darkness, looking for a sign / Chasing their rainbows, the future looks bright / Slowly were losing sight of the Light I am convinced that this song is Queen-influenced as Nuno even gives his best Brain May impersonation during the guitar solo. Lyrically, the song reminds me of George Michaels Praying for Time. The song is ultimately a downer, despite the last line promising a new day coming. The song keeps asking who cares that I lost my way? Again, I feel the schizophrenia, this runs rampant throughout the album. My advice to all who are interested is to please don't try to figure out the underlying message; it may keep you up nights. I am still trying to get past the plot of these three stories. Enjoy the music; its easy as just about every song is simply amazing. I love that its so varied in styles, the lyrics are very clever here and there, and theres glimpses of true inspiration within this deep sea of self delusion. Who cares if its cuckoo, its Extreme, and its great!

reviewText: There was no sophmore slump to be heard on Barry White's second album,following up his classic debut Ive Got So Much to Give with another album of elongated,romantic slow funk symphonies that even further bettered those featured on his previous outing. From "Girl It's True,Yes I'll Always Love You" on you'll realize that not only has White really beefed up his sense of rhythm but on the crawling,implicitly sexual "Honey Please,Can't Ya See See","You're My Baby" and "Hard To Believe That I Found You" that he'd officially mastered the James Brown derived technique of spinning off melodic,rhythmic and harmonic ideas from one song and spinning them off into another,for all intents and purposes creating new moods and flavors from different ones. One of the most fascinating aspects of this album are his extended monologues. Here Barry White comes off as a reflective yet plain talking kind of guy who wishes to let the lady he's speaking to that he not only loves them but respects their love as well. Sure there's plenty of sexual machismo behind it all but there's a mildly unrehersed quality to these monologues that totally erases any possible corniness that could've easily derived from yet. Yes I realize over the years that's become one of his signitures and is often lovingly spoofed but no matter how you cut it Barry White delivers make out funk that not only gets you in the mood but also think about the many twists and turns of love before you pull back the sheets. This is all reflect in his honeyed baritone voice,the honeyed strings and.....even the honeyed rhyhtms if you can imagine such a thing. Again in the spirit of spinning off songs into new ones "Never Never Gonna Give Ya Up" completely re-harmonizes and re-arranges the layored midtempo funk of "I'm Gonna Love You Just A Little Bit More Baby" from his debut and makes a terrific follow up. There are many people who cound this and his debut as sort of two halfs of his masterpiece and taken apart they're both masterpieces of the genre. This along with that newly reissued debut would also be the perfect albums to pick up together and listen to back to back if your just getting into Barry White's music.

reviewText:
"Road Between" is the debut album by Lucy Hale, country music singer but probably best known as actress; she plays Aria on ABC's "Pretty Little Liars." But forget about that as this is not one of those hurriedly produced cash-in attempts from an actress who's a wanna-be singer. Hale, who grew up in Memphis, has been singing from a very young age. This country-pop album, which was produced by Mark Bright and Mike Dailey, has been nearly two years in the making and is a return to her first love: singing and making music.

The fun, up-tempo "You Sound Good To Me" has a very catchy chorus and your feet will be irresistibly tapping along with its upbeat melody. The title of the mid-tempo ballad "From The Backseat" might suggest something else, "But you learn to love from the back seat" is a nostalgic love-song. It's about watching your parents ("Dad was a Superman stick shift driver, Stay at home Louis Lane beside him") interact in front, before moving up to "...Sitting shotgun" on prom-night. Lyrically, one of better songs on this album. Another standout track is the emotional ballad "Nervous Girls," with lyrics that really tug at your heartstrings. The line: "I'm beautifully strong and tragically confused," sums up the way girls (and women) all struggle with their insecurities, even though they may have dissimilar problems and dreams.

This is followed by the up-tempo ballad "Red Dress," a duet with Joe Nichols that has a somewhat melancholic undertone, and in which they show different sides of a relationship as he sings with his baritone voice: "It is you I remember dancing with your red dress on," in counterpart to hers: "It is you I remember every time I hear that song." Then we get to the sassy rock-country of "Goodbye Gone." Hale really rocks it up on this one, the hardest rocker on the album, and a real foot-stomper of a revenge ballad. Next up is "Kiss Me," a very catchy pop-country track, which is followed by the emotive power-ballad "Road Between," in which she sings about trying to find herself but that she is "Still learning the road between."

 "Lie A Little Better" is one of those catchy tracks that has "potential single" stamped all over it, just like "That's What I Call Crazy," another radio-ready country-pop track, about how love can make us do crazy things when the relationship has ended. It's a direct counterpoint to "Love Tonight," a quirky song about ill-advised hook-ups, but "Let's call it love tonight," the handclaps giving it a fun vibe. Hale co-wrote the album closer, the poignant piano-ballad "Just Another Song." It's about how a song can evoke powerful memories, good or bad: "Maybe to you, it's probably just another song, But to me, it's a bullet out of a gun." It shows a lot of potential for this budding singer-songwriter.

Final verdict: the eleven tracks on her debut album are a nice mix of catchy, powerful pop-country songs and emotive ballads, all of them well-written (with "From The Backseat," "Nervous Girls" and "Just Another Song" being outstanding examples) and a good showcase for both Hale's vocal capabilities and her range of musical styles. She shows a lot of promise, so I can't wait to find you how she'll develop as a singer-songwriter in the future!
label: positive

reviewText:
I have been listening to these concertos for years. I cut my Brahms teeth listening to these Cleveland pcs. The first is still among the better ones. The second is still among the first two or three best I know. I adore these Brahms concertos above all other piano concertos. I have heard a lot of performances. I own a lot of them. And I have given away even more performances of them out of disgust. I do not know where Hurwitz gets his thrill from the Jochum/Gilels 1st (which I own, and is so slow I can cook breakfast between the notes, and even my best friend won't take it from me as a gift! However, maybe the 2nd is the very best ever!) If all we had was the 1st by them, we'd all be in rest homes before they got through. (I like really like broad, slowly, sensitively played Brahms, but their 1st is so abjectly slow it detracts from the great 2nd concerto, which, again, may be the best ever!)

These Brahms concertos are challenged only by one other set I know: the Haitink-Askenazy recordings on Decca. The first is with the Royal Concertgebouw and the second with the Wiener (Vienna) Philharmoniker. The Haitink-Askenazy team fielded many concertos (e.g. the Rachmaninoff cycle) and sustained a lengthy relationship. Their first is my first choice for that concerto, the Szell-Curzon-London Symphony performance second, and the Fleisher third. But that's great company.

For the best second concerto, the Szell-Fleisher-Cleveland is neck and neck with the Haitink-Askenazy-VPO performance and the Gilels/Jochum. To still be that good after all these years is quite a recommendation and a good reason to purchase these cds as a set. (The Barbirolli-Barenboim-New Philharmonia and the Abbado-Pollini-Vienna sets are quite decent, but quite less thrilling than these other two.)

Yes, Get the Szell-Fleisher Brahms PCs. They are as good a set as one is likely to find. (Avoid the Giulini-Arrau, the Jochum-Gilels, Reiner-Gilels, Szell-Serkin, Ormandy-Serkin, etc. and a whole host of others.) Get these Cleveland cds and the Haitink-Ashkenazy through Amazon.com and be glad you can get them.

reviewText:
9 Dead Alive opens much softer than the two previous solo studio releases (self-titled Rodrigo y Gabriella and 11:11), selecting a sound that allows the two guitars to blend more smoothly than ever. Their taste expands beyond the Flamenco twirls and Metal Irish Bhangra speed strumming that defined and exhilarated their previous works. They play with many moods, veer into blues and test out new grounds.

Rodrigo y Gabriella has been one of my favorite musicians to listen to, as their virtuosity, unique guitar-defined beats, and pure instrumentalization make for perfect car trip, writing and studying music. That remains true on this album from start to finish.

Because it lacks the pounding energy of the previous albums, I like it a bit less, but far more than most other bands. The always swirling solo work of Rodrigo now curves back as they work harder than ever to blend the two guitars into one sound.

This album brings to mind a weight-lifter; when he first begins, he goes from 150-180 with a massive energy push, amazing all around him. Now that he's at 180 and he pushes to 185, he's still working hard and producing awesome results, but it comes out a bit less awestruck.

One dislike: The added soundbites from Richard Dawkins and others in Sunday Neurosis disrupts my flow without fail and cuts into the album like a screaming baby on a tired night. The musical aspect of the song is bluesy goodness.

Summary: Another great album by Rod & Gab, beautiful compositions and fusion of styles and genres stripped to bare essentials with two guitars.

Steve Perry is at his very best vocally here, and that is saying a lot. The harmony vocals on all tracks are also breathtaking. Every tune is absolutely killer, with no "Back Talk" incongrously shoved in to remind you they're human...a great album that deserves a far greater reputation.

reviewText:
Awww Yeah!...I came across this band's cd while I was working at my college's radio station. This band makes some wonderful pop music,staying away from the glam and over-produced sounds of today's "top" pop culture acts. More importantly,as I have said twice now,this group is a band and not some choreographed fluff,so you can really hear the musicianship and songwriting depth contained in Friend I Once Had. For starters,the vocalist,Karolina Komstedt,has a wonderful voice. Second,I absolutely love the band duo's quaint range of emotional lyricism. They really do create some beautiful songs.
'Spending Sundays in your apartment / is like a holy day for me,' Karolina sings on "Holiday"--  a song flooded with imagery of trying to combat loneliness while only really having one person to sort of turn to for company,which becomes the brief period for a languid holiday,before the coming anxieties of the week,take their toll again. On "The End of The Affair," Karolina bluntly acknowledges a break-up,singing 'I found / I can replace you / yes I found / your just a habit that I can get rid of.'  What a way to phrase the end of a relationship!"Better Days" is beautifully done,with just a backing acoustic guitar,a snyth-keyboard,and of course,Karolina's longing vocal inflections. The soft acoustic aura of this song is so compelling because it emotionally moves you. When Karolina sings,'You think I just need someone / but I need you / just a moment every day / and I can't see it changing', my heart beats along in agreement."Missing You" is a slightly up-tempo dance song,probably somewhat encapsulating the sound of the current Sweeden dance/club scene. Club 8 is not afraid of experimenting a little,and that proves to be very beneficial to the listener.
And there are many..many..many other cool pop songs on this album. This is one of the best albums of all-time. At least,that is how I feel about it,even though it has gotten an "underground-inde" type of treatment and not too many people have become familiar with the band.
You must buy this album,and then go put it on for your friends and see them get the same chills and smiles that you got,when you heard Club 8's album for the first time! This album is also a great mood setter OR...lol....mood relaxer (you'll see what I mean,after you finish listening through it).I'll sometimes listen to it in the evenings and just lay back and zone out.
Come to think of it,I do that with a lot of my records,tapes,and cds!! :-)

reviewText: This was just a solo project done on the side for fun, not a serious solo album done in competition with The Who like EG and CE were, so it's not going to be as finely-crafted as they were, but for what's on it, it's great.  These songs reflect Pete's devotion to Meher Baba in particular and his deep spirituality in general.  It took awhile for the album to grow on me precisely because of the abovementioned descriptions, but once it had, I really began to love it.  My faves are "Content" (wish it were longer!), "There's a Heartache Following Me," "Pure and Easy" (slightly different from the band's version), "Nothing Is Everything" (a million times better than The Who's version, what with the different lyrics and interpretation; this song was not written for Roger at all), and the beautiful original closer "Parvardigar."  The final song was adapted and set to music from Meher Baba's "Universal Prayer," a gorgeous piece of non-sectarian and spiritual religious poetry in addition to just a prayer.  It really demonstrates the unfathomable and indescribable nature of the Divine, and uses many different names for him/her towards the end.  Who wouldn't want to say Amen to such a beautiful universal prayer set to music?

reviewText:
I loved this one when it was released in its original vinyl format, and I still love it, almost 4 decades later.

At this point, Brian was still contributing to the group ("Sail On Sailor" from "Holland," which I've always considered the last "great" track he penned for the group, and "Marcella" from "Carl And The Passions - So Tough," and album Warner Brothers thought had to be packaged with a copy of "Pet Sounds" in order to sell).

This isn't an album from the squeaky-clean coordinated striped shirts Beach Boys. These are the guys who were hanging out with Charlie Manson and his clan, the guys who blew off a major opportunity to cross over from the "pop" to "rock" audience when they canceled their show-closing set at the 1967 Monterey Pop Festival...they've picked up a few ragged edges by this point and they only add to the charm of this period piece set.

The album-closing "Fun, Fun, Fun" isn't sloppy, it's...oh, I don't know, maybe "elegantly wasted" is the term. Carl launches into the opening Chuck Berry riff in a style that's a lot close to Keith Richards' Berry covers with the Stones than it is to the original BB single. Eventually they ramp up the tempo but it's more of a bad attitude version by a great cover band. That's the point. The touring band of this era had not yet succumbed to the "oldies roadshow" ennui that would later follow. They played the hits, to be sure...but they really wanted you to listen to the deep album tracks from "Holland," "Carl & The Passions," "Surf's Up"...

In many ways, The Beach Boys flamed out as a recording act after "Holland." It would be three years before the "Brian Is Back" P.R. campaign and the hit-and-miss "15 Big Ones." That's not to say that the albums released over the decade that followed were without the occasional standout track. But they were scrambling around, trying to construct some form of modern-day relevance that eluded them in the wake of their questionable early-to-mid 1970s choices.

So celebrate this one for what it is...2 Wilson brothers, Mike Love, Al Jardine and South African pick-up musicians Blondie Chaplin and Ricky Fataar...pounding out a mix of hits and new material with a loose, engaging sense of joy.

Pop/rock started taking little twists and turns, the funk got a little funkier, the anti-war songs got quite a bit louder, and the new dance beats started filtering in - it's all here on this nice CD, with great sound too. "American Woman" is one of the last great protest rock hits and it requires careful mastering. The fine guitar segues are smooth and clear here. I have to admit that when I first saw that Rihanna was coming out with yet another new CD so fast I thought it was going to be a quickly thrown together pile of crap. In my opinion her first 2 releases had MAYBE a handful of decent songs and then the rest were very weak.

Rihanna's third effort: 'Good Girl Gone Bad' is without a doubt her best CD and quite possibly one of the best CD's I have heard this year so far!

It is remarkable! It has great beats, catchy hooks, a few guests, no entire song samples (think SOS  LOL) and her voice seems a bit better than in her previous efforts.

The CD starts off with a bang with the melody driven, smash hit: "Umbrella". Great summer song to jam to. I do not think there is a single person that does not know this song.

The CD keeps with the pace and takes us into the slammin' "Push Up On Me" that uses a very slight sample of the classic Lionel Richie tune "Running With The Night" in the beat. Very good use of that sample. Just an awesome song.

Next it gets kicked up a few notches with an already club friendly: "Don't Stop The Music". VERY infectious beat. A great sample (in the deep background) of Michael Jacksons "Wanna Be Startin' Somethin'. This song is so infectious - has you wanting to hit the nearest dance club to tear up the floor.

"Breakin' Dishes" keeps with the energy with the beat but she steps the attitude up about 20 notches! Talking about how she is sick of waiting on her man and "breaking dishes all night and I am not stopping until I see police lights". Very good beat and lyrics.

"Shut Up And Drive" is another great uptempo song with a nice rock edge to it. Very catchy - you will be singing this and tapping your toes after about 3 listens....guranteed!

From here the CD slows down a bit. Not a boring, snooze-fest slow but a good mid-tempo slow. Some really great R&B jams. The most noteworthy are "Rehab" (no, not the Amy Winehouse's culy hit) and "Question Existing" - a very sensual and sexy slow jam with a good beat.

This CD is EXCELLENT! A must purchase! I can tell there are going to be a lot of hits that come off of 'Good Girl Gone Bad'. They are all so melodic and radio friendly and the beats are off the chain!!  A 5 star release all the way!!!

reviewText:
Faure is a master of creating cool, delicate, elegant melodies that progress in complex, unexpected, and, often, achingly lovely, ways. "Ravishing" might be nearly the right adjective for these  quintets, but that adjective calls a bit too much attention to itself, and  Faure's music never does that. These piano quintets, like virtually all of  Faure's chamber works, are nothing if not subtle, and, though certainly  "French", they don't sound like anything else, before or since.
This interpretation by Domus/Marwood is all that any admirer of this  music could hope for. The performers here do a lot more than get the notes  right--they seem sensitive to the atmosphere these works can create when  played with insight and concentration. The recording itself has to be  perfect to capture all the necessary nuances of the music and intricacies  of the performance, and it is. The end result is about as beautiful as  music can be.
If you admire Faure's Requiem, but are not familiar with  his chamber works, well, you have a lot of catching up to do. This CD is a  great place to start.

reviewText:
The music of Slightly Stoopid makes you wish you'd kept playing that instrument your mom wanted you to learn when you were 10. It's music that makes the most anxiety-ridden among us relax. It's lyrics and sounds formed by exceptional musicians who embrace diversity. These guys are a tight, music-loving fraternity; paying their dues in the beginning was probably fun for them. Inclusivity is embraced by Slightly Stoopid -- exotic sounds for the common man.

The band is a dichotomy of end-of-the-world CD covers influenced by Iron Maiden and good-time Bob Marley-like haze; reggae tunes occasionally interspersed with a completely different vibe like country or speed metal. I discovered this group on Palladia. The video "Top of the World" came on immediately following an episode of "Live from Daryl's House" (featuring the Dirty Heads, another interesting, reggae-influenced group), and I was immediately drawn in. Interestingly, most of the songs that follow "Top of the World" on the album of the same name don't have the same hook-heavy sound. Overall, this CD settles into an easygoing string of flowing reggae and soul tunes that transport you to the sunny location of your choosing, drink in hand.

That's not to say there aren't curveballs along the way. Just when you think you've got Slightly Stoopid figured out, the band throws in a breezy instrumental, some ska or an old Bruce Springsteen ditty to keep things inventive. It's refreshing to hear musicians straying mightily from the formulaic. Miles Doughty and Kyle McDonald switch up the smooth-singing and bass-playing duties, and each is a tremendous vocalist and guitar player. Complementing them are congas, keyboards, a trumpet, saxophones, drumming with some bounce, and plenty of guest artists to keep the band's music on "Top of the World" exceptionally lively.

Is he the most macho singer in the world? No. Is he one of the most fearless, gifted and soulful singers of all time? Yes. Is he as great as his father? No, but he was definitely on his way and given enough years would have been. Are the lyrics a little immature, a little too lovesick, too sensitive and simple? Yes but the music and the soul behind the music is much more mature than the actual words of the lyrics if you bother to listen and the lyrics do not get in the way of the music even if they might soften its impact a little bit more than it otherwise would have been if Jim Morrison or Peter Sinfield wrote the lyrics. How did this happen? No one knows but often people, especially artistically gifted musicians, are in their inner soul as mature as anyone has or ever will be at a young age and this does not necessarily come out in their daily lives or in their actual words but only when they freely express themselves through music. There are hundreds of musicians whose music is much more poetic and infinitely deeper than the mere words of their lyrics by themselves will ever be. Basically it's the music that counts and the lyrics are problematic only when they stand in the way of the music coming out or ruin the music by pigeon-holing it into certain limited perspectives.

The best way to listen to this album is from beginning to end as one work and keep playing it 3 or 4 times on repeat until you become used to it. All the songs are excellent and work better as part of one extended work or little sketches that complete the puzzle of the Buckley soul. Don't judge it too harshly on first listen when you spot a couple of things here and there you can criticize. The whole is much greater than the parts. Let the music grow on you and by the third or fourth listen all your criticisms will start to disappear and you'll start to really like and even love this album and when "Lilac Wine" comes up you might even be surprised to notice a few hot tears making their descent down your cheeks. reviewText:
Steve Gunn makes music that is simple sounding on the surface, but underneath theres a complexity hiding under the breezy sway and summertime shine. Hes an incredible guitarist that shows he can handle pretty much anything that comes at him. On his latest, Way Out Weather, its all about southern jangle with an east coast sophistication.

When I heard last years excellent Time Off I wasn't aware that Steve Gunn played in Kurt Viles live band The Violators. Now that I know that I can really hear that Vile laid back drawl in Gunns music. While Vile is firmly planted in the rock and folk camps in his songs, Steve Gunn sticks with a more earthy, organic sound. Though, he can kick it up a notch as well. Drifter is a hard-driving tune with some great Allman Brothers-like guitar. And Atmosphere has an almost psychedelic vibe to it with Gunn singing through a Leslie speaker. Steve Gunns voice is a smoother version of Califones Tim Rutilis crackling, whispy voice. And Steve Gunns music does bring to mind that Chicago bands rustic and at time acoustic-driven sound, though Gunn is more subtle and intricate. Hes a clever songwriter in that he hides his prodigious playing under simple, pleasing music. Way Out Weather brings to mind Allman Brothers Brothers and Sisters and the Deads Workingmans Dead. The latter showing a band in their prime taking it easy while still dropping jaws at their musical proficiency. Wildwood has a nice shuffle rhythm and some great guitar run through a Leslie speaker. Millys Garden is a mover and a shaker. Its a breezy track that could soundtrack a million road trips and don a thousand mix tapes. It will please fans of the Dead and Real Estate alike. It even has a little bit of the Stones in there with the great lap steel guitar. Shadow Bros is the blues, but of a different shade than what were used to. The acoustics crackle and jangle as Steve Gunn sings along to the beautiful waltz-time track. Fiction keeps that easy feel flow going with a touch of melancholy just underneath. Tommys Congo closes the album out on an almost tribal note, with a mantra-like guitar line that keeps repeating.

There seems to be a mantra-like feel to Steve Gunns music. It repeats itself over and over, lulling you into a meditative state till you almost forget theres music playing. It transcends from just a song to something much deeper.

Way Out Weather is a record from start to finish that effortlessly flows and moves like a river in the country or a subway in the city. Its one of those rare records that will appeal to many that cant see eye to eye normally. Its an album that brings folks together and lets them nod their heads together in unison. Simple and sophisticated.

When asked to pick the best AC/DC album, it's a tough call for me between POWERAGE and LTBR.  Although POWERAGE is my personal fave, LTBR is right on it's heals.
No other AC/DC album has the same loud, obnoxious, nasty guitar sound that LTBR has.  Period.  It's evident from the very first track "Go Down" to the very last track, the classic "Whole Lotta Rosie," and on everything in between that Angus and Malcolm just plugged in, turned it to 11, and went for the jugular.  If there's every been a good argument that AC/DC are a heavy metal band (which they whole-heartedly deny), LTBR (both the album and song) is that argument.
Not only is the guitar sound great, but the songs on a whole are magnificent.  Bon's writing continues to grow from the earlier albums, combining sex, drugs, and rock n' roll with a good dose of humourous storytelling.  Again, "Whole Lotta Rosie" is a prime example, as is the title song.  Who else but Bon could pull off a shag story about a 19 stone woman so eloquently!?!  To quote Angus, Bon truly was a "gutter poet!"  In addition to the lyrical content, the hooks on this album are HUGE!  The title track and "Dog Eat Down" are excellent showcases of the boys ability to work out some of the catchiest licks in rock history.
Bottom line, this is an essential album for any AC/DC fan (or any rock fan in general).  If you're just starting out, you can't go wrong with this one.  If you're an old timer, like me, this remaster brings the sound to an even better level, so even if you have other copies of LTBR, it's well worth the effort to get this one!

reviewText:
Little Walter was the greatest Chicago harp player ever.  To be even more accurate, he created the Chicago style of blowing the harp into a harmonica cupped in your hands (as shown on the cover of this CD).

There are claims that others played in this style before Walter, but I've never heard any recordings that substantiate that claim.

Walter's greatness is such that all other Chicago-style players are forced into a second-rank that needs to be broken up into good/better/best.  I'd put Walter Horton in the "best" category, for example, James Cotton in the "better", and Junior Wells in the "good", though if you listen to different recordings you might be inclined to reverse my listing.

Too bad Walter became a low-life drunk.  A friend saw him playing in England in the 1960s and said he stank of cheap wine, though he played very well--and my friend being a good harp player himself, he was in a position to judge.  (Of course, Walter Horton was a drunken wreck too: fortunately, Cotton and Wells avoided this fate).

MELLOW DOWN EASY has to be one of the most exciting and accomplished harmonica blues ever recorded.  And Walter excels when he's playing both complicated licks (ROLLER COASTER) and relatively simple ones (BLUES WITH A FEELING).

Too bad he wasn't a better vocalist, though I doubt he would have done any better if he had been; you listened to Walter for that stunning harp playing--period!

He died of a heart attack after a street brawl: what an ignominious ending for a master musician.  Makes you think of Mozart being dumped into a public pauper's grave ....

But weeks later he was recovering and in front of his drum set again. The sound and content of this album is affected very greatly by the events of September 11 and the following issues that arose from it. As lead singer Fran says "I can now see how fragile the world is." It is by far a more somber and melancholy album than their other three. The album includes tweaked versions of two tracks that have been released on compilations since their last album, The Invisible Band. Those tracks, Love Will Come Through and Beautiful Occupation, are a good gauge as to how you will react to the album. The mellow and hypnotic tones of Love Will Come Through are reflected in the albums stand out tracks "Walking Down Hill" "Somewhere Else" "Quicksand" and the first single "Re-Offender" about Domestic Violence. The political vibes of "The Beautiful Occupation" are reflected in tracks like the aforementioned "Re-Offender" and the in your face track "Peace the F**k Out." Being a fan of Travis' previous works won't guarantee that you enjoy 12 memories. But it is a great album in on its own rights that will get under your skin after a couple of spins.

reviewText:
In the end, it may all depend on taste and on mood. There are many recordings (of about 40 existing total) of Mahler's Eighth Symphony which are considered almost automatically as 'the best Mahler Eight' by ever so many different people. (My favorites would be Abbado and Nagano, by the way...)

Aside from many other 'big' names like Haitink, Gielen, Kubelik, and Sinopoli, we have the 'early' classics like Horenstein (1959) and Mitropoulos (1960), the classic favourites of Bernstein (especially 1966 and 1975) and Solti (1971), (somewhat) more recent favourites like Tennstedt (1986) and Abbado (1994), and the 'latest additions' to the catalogue like Chailly (2000) and Nagano (2005) and now this, maybe to top it off, the recording on Naxos by Antoni Wit conducting the Warsaw National Philharmonic Choir and Orchestra and soloists. (We can only wait to hear what Pierre Boulez and Michael Tilson Thomas will have to say in the matter, but could it get much better than all that has gone before or that which has now been reached with, for example, Abbado, Nagano and Antoni Wit...?)

ABOUT THIS RECORDING. This specific recorded performance has - I believe - many, many virtues (which outweigh any of its possible 'defects'), of which the most important is - at least to the ears of this particular listener - a sense of coherence and overarching vision.
First of all, there is coherence in the music-making, as it is being nicely held together - in the aspects of tempi and phrasings - by the conductor, ever moving along purposefully, never sagging or revelling in the music for beauty's sake.
Antoni Wit seems to have a clear sense of the need for stressing the drama behind the music. The conductor doesn't seem to want to relish in the beauty perse, bringing with it the danger of making it sound (overly) sweet or sentimental. Nonetheless, there ARE recordings out there that DO relish more in the gorgeous multicoloredness and deep sentiment of this music than this specific recording, but without succumbing to sentimentality, and which are IMHO an even finer success as the recording under review here - I especially think of Claudio Abbado and Kent Nagano.
But please don't get me wrong, while Antoni Wit keeps tight enough rein on the proceedings to make all of the music sound 'of a piece', there is enough pure sentiment here, nonetheless, to keep 'both sides of the field' happy: there is sweet beauty and sentiment, held in balance with clarity and purposefulness.
In line with - to my ears at least - his 'purposefully going forward' Antoni Wit doesn't stress the differences in tempi as much as other conductors might do here and there in the piece, especially Part II. This is a good thing in that it keeps the sense of forward momentum, of dramatic flow, inevitably towards 'das Ewig Weibliche'. But the playing here never sounds rushed or self-consciously '(micro)managed' by the conductor, which would IMHO be intolerable. (And there are of course such recordings out there - by much more 'renowned' conductors - which are held in high esteem by many. I will not name any names. But then again, many people also consider the rest of Antoni Wit's Mahler-cycle for Naxos as quite unremarkable ...)
There are other reasons why this recording/performance sounds so wonderful, aside from coherence and tautness and balance between 'head and heart'. There is more, such as nice ensemble-playing: the whole orchestra sounds appropriately grand and massive, but at the same time, all the individual instrumental voices (be they groups or solo) are made to sing their lines within the orchestral textures, never being drowned out. A perfect sense of orchestral balance where every instrument is given full opportunity to shine when his time is there. (Is that which we experience/feel as 'sentiment' a result of just the 'right' amount of instrumental coloring and phrasing within a harmonious textural balance ...?)
This sense of 'finely balanced ensemble' may also have to do with the recording-balances and the sound picture as such, in which the orchestra sounds 'cushoned' within a deep and wide soundscape, and as a result a bit 'woolly' sometimes (maybe too much so, compared with Solti, Chailly or Nagano?). Although, in tuttis, the sound never becomes congested, but always stays open.
The choirs and (most of the) soloists are Polish, and while their pronunciation of German is sometimes a bit odd, they are all quite up to the task. The soloists are no A+ or 'star-voices' altogether. This does probably have the advantage that there is - to say it in the words of the previous reviewer - no 'operatic grandstanding'. But the singers are mostly just fine, some better than others. I am not going to compare with other recordings here - this performance must speak for itself, which it does eloquently enough, I believe. Only the Gretchen by Izabella Klosinska sounds just a bit (too) course/rough to really please the ears of this particular listener, which is a pity, but not so much as to cause a distraction, because, happily, her high notes are agreably natural and sweet enough. Timothy Bentch's Doctor Marianus to my ears has to struggle sometimes just a bit too much reach the highest notes, making them sound a little strained now and then, as if shouting. But although his singing is accomplished enough, in the end, I would not trade him in for likes of, for example, Rene Kollo (for Solti), Peter Seiffert (for Abbado), or Ben Heppner (for Chailly)?

While there are many more 'high-profile' recordings out there that are maybe more 'distinctively accomplished' in specific aspects of conducting, music-making and singing, this is really only a matter of details (maybe even tastes) and as such would amount to nitpicking (even for Izabela Klozinska's not very 'beautiful' Una Poenitentium and Timoty Bentch's 'shouting' his high notes, when very specifically, a low volume is asked for in the score).
There are not many recordings (even 'great' or 'classic' ones) which are consistently beautiful or artistically accomplished 'across-the-board'. And maybe, not many great recordings are better than this specific one of the forces from Warsaw conducted by Antoni Wit on Naxos. From beginning to end, in this recording, when one is susceptible to it, the listener's imagination and feelings are held captive in a compelling and ecstatic vision that is so wonderfully sustained from beginning to end, that, by the end, the final chorus mysticus really lifts the mind to higher spheres of emotion and ecstacy.
Surely, there are even better recordings of Mahler's Eighth Symphony around. I would never like to be without my Abbado and Nagano performances, for example. But this is a nice recording in itself. At least 4 stars, then, for this sympathetic performance.

reviewText:
I love this album, and it is a must have for any fans of 1980's rock music or Madonna in general. This just may be my favourite album she has done in the 80's and the 80's is the era when Madonna was at her best. Madonna showcases herself as a Rock chick with this album, and that feel is very present on the record. Madonna had plenty of commercial appeal and that is very present on this album, even the cover art looks great. The album was recorded with Sire in 1983. Madonna had five singles from the album,
"Lucky Star", "Borderline", "Burning Up", "Holiday" and "Everybody". all the singles are the best tracks on the album, so it is a good buy just to get them all on one disc.
The album is short with only eight original songs on. The other three were not singles and are "I Know It", "Think Of Me" and "Physical Attraction". Two great bonus tracks were added to this Remastered version of the album, "Burning Up - The 12 Version" and "Lucky Star - The New Mix".
The new edition of this album sounds like it was just recorded yesterday and has the quality of not the original 80's recording but that of any of todays records. It is great if you want to experience some music from the early 1980's.
Below is the Track by Track rating.
1. Lucky Star.
This is my favourite song on the album, and oppitimizes 80's pop music with it's electric guitar strings and synthizisers. Madonna talks about a lover as sort of a good luck charm, and she feels lucky when they are around."You must be my Lucky Star, cos' you make the darkness seem so far, and when i'm lost you'll be my guide. I just turn around and your by my side". The song is also about her early ambitions and lust for stardom. This is a classic Madonna song and remains so because it has stood the test of time. This album version is not the radio edit. It is the extended version and runs at 5:37.
Some people call this a Pop song, but I feel it is more Rock then pop. Brilliant track. 5/5
2. Borderline.
This song grew on me. I didn't find it as good as Lucky Star or Burning Up, but it wasn't too bad. It sounds very much 1980's,and has a good little intro, and then the beat comes on and you know its going to be a good song. It talks about a guy that Madonna wants but he won't open up to her and is pushing her love away. This version is an extended version of the radio-edit and runs at 5:20. It is quite catchy once it grows on you. 4/5
3. Burning Up.
I like this song quite a lot. It ranks right up there with her other classic 80's hits like Lucky Star, but the 12 In version is much better then this original album version because it has more feeling to it. The chorus to this song is great and the best part of it is when the electric guitars come in. It has a good bridge too. "Do you wanna see me down on my knees, abandoned over backwards, now would you be pleased." She repeats the phrase "C'mon let go !". This song is good and very effective. Enjoyable listen. 4/5
4. I Know It.
Even though this song was not a single it is still quite effective, and catchy. The synthisizers sound good on it and you may find it stuck in your head. 3/4
5. Holiday.
This was one of Madonna's biggest singles ever and this album version sounds great. It runs at 6:10 so it is not the radio-edit version that runs at 4:04. This version sounds a little slowed down but you will still find yourself bobbing your head to it. The synthisizer parts sound cool, and it has a jazz type ending. Very good track. 5/5
6. Think Of Me.
This song has a good beat, and is fairly catchy , but nothing special. It does seem quite filler, but is worth a listen. There are some good guitar bits in it though.  3/5
7. Physical Attraction.
This song was very catchy I found. It sounds a bit lame in parts but it is fun. I couldn't get it out of my head after hearing it a few times. There is some good instrumental parts in this song and it sounds very funky, bordering between 70's and 80's disco. 4/5
8. Everybody.
I liked this song. This is her closest 70's sounding song, and is pure disco. I didn't like it as much as other tracks on the album but it wasn't bad. The middle part which is instrumental is a good part in the track. Overall this song is worth a listen. 4/5
9. Burning Up - The 12 In Version.
This is one of the albums best tracks. This is my Second favourite after Lucky Star. This is 80's music at its best.
This song was one of the most enjoyable on the album. Warner Bros made the right choice including this as a bonus track on the Remastered edition of "Madonna". This version of the song sounds a little bit like a New Order track, and is a great Rock song. I already had the 8 track version of this album, but I went out and bought this version of it because I heard the sound clip of this song on Amazon.com's music sampler.
I did not regret this buy, and this track alone made the buy worth it. 5/5
10. Lucky Star - The New Mix.
This remix sounds a lot like the original version except it echoes a lot which makes it sound more 1980's. This version is better then the original version, and makes the Remastered edition of this album worth the buy. 5/5
...So what are you wating for ?. Buy yourself a copy from Amazon.com

reviewText: Even though he was around only enough to release just one record , Jeff Buckley was undeniably one of the most important artists of the 90's . His tragic death some years ago gave to his , full of passion and anger debut an extra sentimental value . You can't help but feeling moved when you hear him singing " ... and the rain is falling and i believe / my time has come " on Grace . Sketches For My Sweetheart The Drunk gives us a taste of what he was up to for his following . This release includes two cd discs with ten and eleven songs each . The artwork besides photographs of the singer includes some of his personal handwritings and also a message to Buckley's fans written by his mother . Although we are informed that all these songs haven't taken the final form Buckley would want them to , it's actually really difficult to understand that this is half-finished work . Jeff displays once more his rich vocal talent on " Everybody here wants you " while on " New Year's Prayer " he strikes a weird chord of the listener's soul by commanding him to " feel no same for what you are " . From the second disc the song which eventually stands out is " I know we could be so happy if we wanted to be " , a touching ode to a decomposing love . He describes the relationship and the feelings with all the details . "... there's no easy answer / none to blame or forgive / we were two cripples dancing / to the bitter and we live " he sings almost sounding in pain . What makes his work so affecting is that everything came 100% from his heart . He actually said once that " they will accuse me of stealing from my father . They already stand in baited judgement " probably reffering to the press and music journalists . He was so wrong ! His genuin love for music and his talent would never allowed them to.

reviewText:
Whoa. Okay, I liked CunninLynguists enough have bought one of their albums in the past but this is a sharp departure from their earlier works. In a word, this album is best described as Melancholy. Gone are the joking metaphors, uptempo beats loopy beats and exchanged for rich sonic textures, drawling half sung vocals, and more serious matters. While I'd compare this albums sonically most closely to older Outkast, the immediate comparison that comes to my mind is to Little Brother, two great MCs and a truly gifted producer. I'm not the first to reach this conclusion but both groups are representing the South while earning the respect of hip hop heads without being cliche dirty south.

Interestingly enough, Kno only spits one verse on the album and Deacon let Kno take the boards for all 16 tracks. While Deacon is a good MC and alright producer, the Kno is the star of the show from the opening chant to the long downtempo instrumental gaps. The interludes are as compelling as the songs themselves, Damnation is compete fire and the only thing missing from perfection Remember Me is a verse or two. Its a complete and plays out as an album, rare for a rap record. Its apparent Kno does know (for lack of better words) that he's great... one of the best. In the album credits, Kno takes time to thank the musicians he sampled as he feels they are the the artists. In some way, its a strange admission that the art of sampling is only secondary to the art of being the originator.

Also CunninLynguists take some needed time to defend the South from what they feel as unjust attacks from the rest of us. While its stated plainly on the album, actions speak louder and words and they back every bit of it up. Its a shame kids aren't running to Target to pick this album up instead of Young Jeezy.

I'm not one to go around rating 5 stars for much, but seriously this is top choice. QN5 seems to be on a roll as Tonedeff's Archetype was one of the best albums of 2005. Only downside is that CunninLynguists put out candidate for album of year so early but even in 2007, it should still be on the tip of people's tongues.

reviewText:
I have to admit that I'm a late arriver to the Radiohead scene.  I purchased "Pablo Honey" when it first came out, mainly because I had heard "Creep" on the radio.  I listened to the entire CD and soon realized that this band was truly unique, but little did I know they would soon be making what is undoubtedly one of the greatest works of musical art ever produced.
Where to start in the praise for "OK Computer"?  The lyrics are superbly crafted, perfectly suited for audiences craving real insights into modern problems.
Radiohead as a band could not be tighter in their understanding of what sounds work perfectly to evoke just the right emotions.  Incredibly skilled musicians, they also surpass the usual drivel of what one hears in modern music.  One of the most overlooked instruments on "OK Computer" is Thom Yorke's voice, which sweeps in and out, wrapping delicately around his fully realized view of society, technology, hope, hate, and our most hidden desires.  One need only listen to "Let Down" to feel the almost symphonic reach of Yorke's voice.  Listen carefully to the double tracking of his voice as he sings "You'll know where you are" (heard best with headphones, where the line builds on the right side of your hearing) and then is mixed with "One day I am gonna grow wings/Chemical reaction."  Both build to a sonorous and chillingly beautiful crescendo as Yorke takes his voice higher and purer than anyone else in rock music.
The best way to review "OK Computer" is with single words: brilliant, phenomenal, amazing, perfect, lingering, unforgettable, haunting, pure, and OK.  OK, indeed!  This is the best record of the 90s, hands down.

reviewText:
Set in the 1960s and 1970s, BROKEBACK MOUNTAIN presents the tale of two emotionally conflicted gay men, a painful love affair, and the emotional wreckage visited upon them and their families over the course of two decades.  A remarkably complex and serious film, it is greatly buttressed by Gustavo Santaolalla's quietly effective score, which includes several haunting instrumentals, a few original songs, and a number of songs from the period.

Santaolalla's most effective work for the film occurs in the pure guitar instrumentals: for the most part these are simple chords, sometimes echoed as if from a great distance, extremely evocative of the vast physical and emotional spaces on which the film dwells.  Simple, elegant, and painful, they were powerful additions to the film and they stand alone well on their own.

Equally effective are "A Love That Will Never Grow Old" and "No One's Gonna Love You Like Me," both of which were specifically written by Santaolalla for the film.  The first is performed by Emmylou Harris, and she gives a typically flawless vocal that bespeaks of quietly simmerly passions; it has, I think, become one of my favorites among her work, and the Bernie Taupin lyrics are memorable for their great simplicity and sincerity.  In the context of the film, "No One's Gonna Love You Like Me" is a low-key honkytonk song, something of a musical throwaway--even so, Santaolla nails the period sound; it sounds very much like something Patsy Cline or Kitty Wells might have performed, and vocalist Mary McBride gives it full period charm.

The remainder of the soundtrack is a mixed bag of period music, some of it drawn from the jukeboxes of the day.  Linda Ronstadt is an always welcome voice, and her version of Buddy Holly's "It's So Easy To Fall In Love" is well-selected for this particular story; Steve Earle's "The Devil's Right Hand" is a classic of it's kind.  Willie Nelson contributes a nice rendering on Bob Dylan's "He Was A Friend of Mine," and the Roger Miller standard "King of the Road" gets a notable overhaul courtesy of Teddy Thompson and Rufus Wainwright; Wainwright also offers the darkly powerful "The Maker Makes."

Like most film soundtracks, there is little in the way of a unified musical statement--after all, the purpose of the music is to support specific moments in the film--but the score for BROKEBACK MOUNTAIN not only recalls the film extremely well, it does strike an overall mood that bespeaks of love, loneliness, and loss without drifting into cliche.  Fans of the film will find it indispensible.

GFT, Amazon Reviewer

reviewText: WHAT ABOUT NOW is yet another great Bon Jovi album. I know I'm playing devil's advocate here, but their first four albums, while great (with the exception of, ironically, SLIPPERY WHEN WET, which was average at best), were NOT at all representative of what the band was truly capable of, musically or lyrically. The band really started to grow musically when, during the writing of KEEP THE FAITH, they started taking such influences as the Allman Brothers Band, Lynyrd Skynyrd, the Marshall Tucker Band, the Outlaws, and Bruce Springsteen, started plugging them in where their Aerosmith/Loverboy leanings had been, adopted a pro-law-enforcement stance, became more hawkish in support of people wrongfully imprisoned in countries other than their own, and began writing deeper lyrics about the struggles and the triumphs of the human spirit. Since then, every album except for CROSS ROAD (a skimpy best-of) and THIS LEFT FEELS RIGHT (featuring terrible acoustic versions of their hits) has been wonderful. It appears that they've learned lessons from such great CDs/cassettes as U2's WAR, Marshall Tucker's THE BEST OF THE CAPRICORN YEARS, Springsteen's DARKNESS ON THE EDGE OF TOWN, the Outlaws' BEST OF THE OUTLAWS: GREEN GRASS AND HIGH TIDES, and Bob Seger's NIGHT MOVES, taken them to heart, and used them to create a new sound equally rooted in hard rock, heartland rock, new wave, and Southern-fried country-rock, with all of those elements all present in equal portions on every album from CRUSH onward. I was at first reluctant to buy this CD, but my realization of how sincere these guys were in their beliefs made me change my mind yesterday. This album may not be your cup of tea at first, but if you're patient with it, you'll really enjoy it.

I've had this album since it came out 4 years ago.  I still listen to it at least once a month.  That should say something about the longevity Blind Guardian's A Twist in the Myth album has.  Many fans have complained that the songs don't stick in your head as much as some of their older music.  In comparison to A Night at the Opera, this album has less orchestrations and more "metal" aspects.  The songs have an average length of 5 minutes or so.  I do feel this cd is missing the long epic song that ANATO had in it's finale.  My only other complaint on this album is that there are no dynamics.  Everything is so compressed and punchy that there is practically no way to listen to this album without making your ears hurt after 20 minutes.  That is a sad thing because the music on this album is incredible and keeps your attention for its entire length.  Some of Blind Guardian's best songs are on this album.  My personal favorites are:  Turn the Page, Otherland, Straight Through the Mirror, Lionheart, Skalds & Shadows, and Fly.  All these songs are extremely catchy and have interesting lyrics that fit the music perfectly.  There are a few weaker songs on here, but keep in mind that a weak Blind Guardian song is equivalent to most bands' most epic song.

If you are new to Blind Guardian, this is as good an album as any to start with.  I can't choose a favorite BG album come to think of it.  They are like adopted children that I love equally yet differently.

reviewText:
Flashback: I bought this album on cassette outside of Dallas on a church choir trip in the summer of 1991. One of the most poignant memories of my youth was listening to "Jade's Song" and the opening to "Winter's Call" in the dead of night riding through Dallas with those lit-up skyscrapers. It lasted only a couple of minutes, but that moment has been burned into my memory ever since then...So, almost 20 years later I'm surfing around on Amazon and it just hits me: "Why don't I look up Badlands?"  Of course, it's a 25-dollar selection.  No matter, I bought it anyway. When it comes to perfection, money is not an obstacle.

In it's most basic description, Badlands is a blues-rock band. They can (roughly) be compared to Whitesnake, Blue Murder, Black Sabbath, and Led Zeppelin. The first Badlands line-up was formed with guitarist Jake E. Lee (of Ozzy Osbourne fame) and vocalist Ray Gillen (RIP 1993). Add to that duo the drummer Eric Singer (who will join KISS later), and bass player Greg Chaisson. They managed to eek out a second album, "Voodoo Highway", and then Gillen was supposedly fired and Eric Singer soon left. The "Dusk" album was released posthumously in 1998.

But on to the freshman eponymous album. It's a sleek and sexy piece of art with all the right trimmings. The opener, "High Wire" is a fast-paced rocker with a groovy middle eight. The next cut is Badland's commercial hook and single, "Dreams in the Dark." As far as 80's hard rock singles go, it is actually quite catchy and addictive. It's one of those songs you catch yourself humming in the elevator. The real one-two punch of the album is the instrumental ditty "Jade's Song", which I think serves as an intro to "Winter's Call". This is one of my personal favorite songs in my entire music library. Haunting and sensual, it is the cornerstone of the entire album. "Dancing on the Edge" and "Hard Driver" are two more stompers in the vein of the opening track. Listen closely and you can hear Ray's zippo flick in the opening bars of "Dancing on the Edge"..."Rumblin' Train" is a gritty, raunchy, Howlin' Wolf-inspired example of whiteboy blues. Jake E. Lee really shreds it here. "Devil's Stomp" is the age-old story of making a deal with the devil (gotta have this on a blues album - it's a staple). This song also has Ole Scratch's famous quote, "It feels so good to be so bad." The album closes with "Seasons", a 6-minute long mid-tempo number about aging and loss. The "Bonus Track" (which even the 1991 cassette I have includes) is "Ball & Chain" (great line: "The girl has got a chain wrapped around my heart; Help me, Jesus, to the promised land...Gimme that Ball and Chain"). Great syncopation on rhythm guitar during the solo.

The album cover is simple, but effective. It's a black and white band photo topped by the band's name in crimson. The image exudes one word: Attitude. Produced and managed by Paul O'Neill (Savatage guru), the sound is pretty clear.  Thanks to whichever music industry exec thought reissuing this was a good idea.  You should get a huge bonus.
label: positive

My biggest gripe is that I would have mixed the CDs a bit better. Most of the music is the beautiful, haunting melodies of the Jackie Gleason Orchestra and then all of a sudden a couple broadway/showtunes style songs play out of nowhere. I have to say though ... Gleason was a true genius. He really knew how to create a mellow 'Hollywood' sound. This to me sounds like vintage Hollywood ... you can just imagine sitting there with a glass of whiskey and a (ugh) cigarette and hearing this in some glamorous lounge or restaurant.

For the price, if you are new to Jackie Gleason music or just need to set the mood ... it's cheaper to buy the 6 albums in this set, even if the audio quality lacks a bit. If you really get into Gleason music, you can always replace them with better mixes later. However, on most home stereos, it doesn't really make a big difference.

reviewText:
Although the production is pure late-sixties crankage, the addition of jazz-influenced Phil Collins on drums (after the rest of Genesis fired third drummer John Mayhew for having to constantly pre-produce John's drums) and resident extra-terrestrial Steve Hackett on lead guitar (after original Genesis guitar genius Anthony Phillips locked himself in the practice-shed and swallowed the key) gives this 3rd album by Genesis proof to their fans and detractors alike that they had truly reinvented themselves.

Except for the Peter's escalatingly over-the-top eccentricism, Phil's brilliant fusion drums, and Steve's wild tone (and technique that would soon influence a young Eddie Van Halen) steal the show. Tony Banks even gets in on the guitar wars with some 12-string action, and Phil's vocal stylings would alter the history of Genesis for years to come. Turn up loud at a really bawdy English Comp Lit or drama major house party, and check all the girls for adam's apples.
