reviewText:
This disc combines the 9th symphony recorded in 1958 with the LSO with the 8th and the VPO recorded in 1969. Both are very well matched as sound and both sound far better than their respective ages would suggest. Decca recordings were particularly renowned for their fidelity at that time. The two orchestras are equally responsive to Krips' Viennese style of performance heard here.

For many years after these recordings were first issued their readings were referred to with something approaching awe. They were renowned for being essentially 'Viennese' in spirit, a spirit that even then was seen to be something of a vanishing art. That remains true but even more relevant today as that special Viennese ambiance as preserved here has become even rarer. That may also be to do with the increasing internationalism of orchestras worldwide with technical prowess achieved at the cost of national identity.

The recorded sound is as truthful and freshly minted as if made very recently. The detail of the performances is allowed to come through with complete ease and naturalness. In effect the music is allowed to glow and sing in a most unforced way. In addition, instead of drive and drama such as in the final movement of the ninth, we get a dancing lilt and the total effect is one of joyousness. The question may be asked if this is a Viennese speciality - or just finely skilful and lyrical music making directed by Krips and delivered by the orchestra both collectively and individually? Whatever the answer the sum total is the same - a breath of Schubertian fresh air.

In conclusion, I would suggest that this disc is really quite special and unique among recordings of these much recorded works. As such it deserves to be included in any short-list of discs being considered for purchase.

reviewText: It's hard to believe that Iggy has been cranking out great rock 'n roll for going on 4 decades.  Enough has been said about the Stooges (truly one of the great US rock bands), but the middle of Iggy's career has been largely forgotten and dismissed as his "Bowie" period.  However, while the Bowie influenced albums may not be rockin' enough for diehard Stooges, "Lust for life" and "the Idiot" (as well as the Soldier and New Values) are good to great albums regardless. Even "Party" and "Blah, blah, blah," in my opinion the weakest Iggy albums are OK. However, following these albums, Iggy has put out nothing but strong, solid (Brick by Brick, Zombie birdhouse) and at times essential (Instinct, American Caesar) records. Following the reflective "Avenue B," I thought that the last thing we would see was a ferocious, hard rockin' piece of art such as "Beat 'em up."  This album is so good and strong, it's hard to believe that you are listening to a 54 year old man!  Almost all of the tracks on this disc are standout, but Mask, Howl, Savior, Death is certain, Drink new blood and ugliness are particularly great.  A couple of lines from mask, sum up the state of music today and why this is such a spot on record. "Irony in place of balls, balls in place of brains, brains in place of soul.  Where is the soul?  Where is the love? Where am I? Which mask are you?

This  CD opens with 3 songs steeped in world weariness. The lyrics of the first song, Palmistry state: "You can see by the lines on my hand, I've been carryin a heavy load." The simple repeated lyrics of "Everything is Moving so Fast" follow the same theme. Similarly, my favorite song on this CD is "Pulling on a Line.", with the chorus. "pullin on a line, pullin on a line and sometimes it pulls on me."

This is a CD that features stunningly beauiful vocal harmonies throughout, based on what band's website aptly describes as "the singular voice of (lead singer) Tony Dekker, a voice that summons ghosts from times past. (and) It's a voice that is capable of conveying heartache and comfort all in the space of a single phrase." The vocals in "Everything is Moving so Fast" and "River's End" are especially beautiful. The vocals are reminiscent of  folk-style Crosby, Stills, Nash and Young songs such as "Teach Your Children".

Listening to the songs in order the additional themes are estrangement (Concrete Heart) and separation (She Comes to Me in Dreams). This is followed by unexpected sources of hope and beauty such as "The Chorus in the Underground" and the simple bells of "Singer Castle Bells". Further songs such as "New Light" and the last song: "Unison Falling into Harmony" convey a sense of hope and peacefullness though still suffused with sadness.

I continue to be intrigued by the lyrics and drawn in by the beautiful music after repeated listens.

I commented on my own review to give links to a great CBC News interview and album review and also to the band's website where you can listen to full tracks of several of the songs. Enjoy.

reviewText:
. . . but dragged down by a few gratuitous moves.  The big question for me is why couldn't've Ramsey Lewis resisted the urge to bring in some crowd-pleasing elements and just stuck with the glorious piano trio sound he conjures for most of this disc?  After all, fellow fusionista Bob James stayed the course on his latest, as did Harvey Mason, and the results were pretty great.  Alas, Mr. Lewis just couldn't seem to untether himself from the safety net of sweetening.
It must be admitted that sometimes the inclusion of additional musicians lifts the proceedings onto a higher plane, esp. when they are subtly deployed as on "Wade in the Water," featuring some very tasty guitar (by Buddy Fambro) and B3 organ (courtesy of Kevin Randolph) as well as the soulful vocals of Ronald McCowan.  But on the two gospelized numbers, "Open My Heart" and "Hosannah," the aural signature ventures so far from the established vibe as to be distracting, the main offenders being The Chicago Gospel Voices, who, in other circumstances, I'm sure, are perfectly wonderful.  It doesn't help that Lewis himself succumbs to the cheese by engaging in some rather gratuitous pianistic grandstanding on these numbers.
Still and all, there are so many great moments on this disc that I'm of a mind to forgive Ramsey Lewis his excesses, and not even subtract a half star.
Really, there's no reason to grouse.  The moments of sheerly glorious beauty (esp. the two classical numbers) far outshine the deficiencies.
With quite a wide variety of material, mostly thoughtfully--even ingeniously rendered--everything from Bach to Brahms to spirituals to pop to folk--this disc is easily recommended.

reviewText:
I am what one could call a Beatles purist, with a preference for all-analog original UK vinyl LPs and 45rpm singles. So, why am I reviewing this "soundtrack" to a typically Las Vegas Cirque du Soleil event?

Because it is fantastically musical, with the Beatles' early through late period songs mixed and EQ'ed into a coherent album. This is indeed a conceptual album- let's say a trip- into the heart of stereo workmanship that only Martin and family can make.

It is a fascinating listen: the bells and whistles, to put it lightly, of the Beatle's spirit of musical innovation is preserved and indeed continued as Martin and co. mixed the songs for maximum, but not overbearing, stereo effect. What I mean is the following: you hear instruments and vocals that were either mixed low in the original songs and albums. Is the music "new"? The song "Because," shorn of its instruments, gleams brightly as a successful "remix"- the vocals are naked, leaving the listener in Beatles harmony heaven and, a propos, the classical influences of the mixing are brought to bear. Individually, the songs are really neither new nor old, just a re-expression of what was already there in the original groove.

As for the ordering of the album, the inclusion of early Beatles with middle and late period makes for a fascinating exercise in taking the listener on a journey in which the humble beginnings of the Liverpool lads are intertwined with the sonic brilliance of the latter-period. It is truly a trip into the core of what made the Beatles so intriguing. The entire length of their growth from lads to riches to put it simply is here to listen to on these two LPs.

Note that this isn't a truly analog LP- the source master "tape" is really a collection of remastered 24-bit digital files.

But that doesn't detract from the effortless beauty of the record. So give it a spin and hear the Beatles again.

Oh, and I never saw the Vegas show.

reviewText: This edition of the 1999 album Ecstasy includes a second disc, a live album recorded at a festival in London. The mid-tempo rocker Paranoia Key of E opens the album, closer to his talking than his singing style, a love song of dreams & nightmares. On the next, Mystic Child, he sings! Impressive guitar work with stylistic shifts, an urgent beat and passionate vocals make it great. Mad, about domestic strife, has an interesting, jazzy arrangement, whilst the title track, contrary to its title, is a subdued number in slow tempo, giving impressions of New York with some personal reminiscences. Another song in this style is Tatters - poetic lyrics but not much of a tune. Modern Dance is a ballad, mostly tender but containing highly melodic segments with driving guitars over a lilting beat. As the song progresses, lovely backing vocals join in to make it sublime. The fierce Future Farmers of America blazes like a comet over the hitherto mostly quiet landscape. Once again Lou sings, the guitars roar and the melody is gripping and memorable. Then comes one of Reed's most delicate and melancholy songs, Turning Time Around. This one is in the league of Perfect Day and Satellite of Love. What a magical composition with its tender tune, stirring lyrics and sensitive delivery! O by the way, it's about how to properly designate love & mentions Harry, family, lust and the heart's hieroglyphic. Rock Minuet is a tour de force, a sort of short Street Hassle for the late 1990s. Laurie Anderson contributes electric violin on this sordid biographical tale of woe. After that, Baton Rouge is a welcome return to normality even though it deals with marital strife, whilst Rouge is a melancholy one-minute instrumental with Laurie again on electric violin. Like A Possum is something else - all 18 minutes of it. Perhaps, like the aforementioned Rock Minuet, it's an updated Street Hassle. The guitars groan, wail and whine as Lou sings of the hole in his heart as huge as a truck. The disc concludes with the roaring rocker Big Sky. The second disc is a semi-acoustic live set where he employs an unusual device on his guitar. The sound tends to the subdued side and the song selection is refreshing, including some delightful obscurities. There's the The Velvet Underground classic I'll Be Your Mirror and early Reed like Perfect Day plus a determinedly grim version of Vicious. The Kids & Berlin from the album of that title stand out, as do the powerful Dirty Boulevard. Other remarkable performances are New Sensations, The Original Wrapper, Coney Island Baby and a song previously unknown to me, titled Into the Devine. Ecstasy is a five-star album whilst the live one merits four. These two albums are highly recommended for fans of Mr. Louis Reed, debonair New York poet & musician.

reviewText:
I am a major Van Morrison fan.  I have many CD's by this great man.  Moondance, Astral Weeks, Common One, Tupelo Honey, Too Long in Exile, and Hymns to the Silence for starters.  I would love to collect all the albums he's ever done.  I decided to buy this one because my intuition said "get it now".  So I bought it a week or so after it came out.  It's one of my top five Van Morrison CD's.

I knew I would like this album, but I just don't like it, I REALLY love this album.  I think it's one of Van's best albums ever.  It's immensely soulful, gentle, moving, spiritual, and quite uplifting.  It's also spare (for a Van album).  In other words, Van is keeping it simple (though not simplistic).  There are a few songs when Van complains about the machinations of the music business (School of Hard Knocks, for example), but the lyrics of this song and others don't detract from the overall beauty of the album.  This album contains two of my favorite Van songs ever in That's Entrainment and Behind the Ritual.  They're both so simple in their instrumentation, yet work so beautiful in their own unique ways.  As for Van's "blah blah blah" chorus on Ritual (which some reviewers have complained about), it doesn't bother me.  Van repeats phrases like that for effect his whole career, and it works wonderfully here.

The instrumentation is wonderful.  Van plays a beautiful saxophone here.  On many past albums, his playing was off in the background with other sax players.  On this album, he's the only saxophone player.  The organ playing is superlative as usual (by John Allair).  And Van's voice sounds as deep and as majestic as it did on Astral Weeks a mere 40 years ago.  This album shoots through you like a gentle, forgiving breeze.  This is one of Van's most beautiful albums ever.

I won't lie and said I've been listening to Trae since he came out, because the truth is I haven't. Infact I regret that I'm not too familiar with any Trae, Z-Ro, ABN material, but I was told that this was a great album so I decided to give it a listen. What I really like about this album is that it has a dark vibe to it that makes it sound great. The production matches Trae's deep/scratchy voice almost perfectly. And you add guest appearances from well known rappers, and you have this album.

The album is chalked full of a lot of guests that really don't dissapoint. Although most are big name artists on the album, Trae doesn't allow them to outshine him. The ones that don't have any guests, he holds his own as well. The production here has a dark emotional vibe on many songs, that adds the suspense of Trae's rhyme style. A lot of tracks here really stood out to me as a first time listener of his music. The very first was "Inkredible" that also appeared on a Jadakiss mixtape earlier this year that also features Rick Ross. Following that is the lead single "Gettin Paid" featuring Wiz Khalifa that comes with a smoked out vibe. Immediately after that is "I Am The Streets" featuring Rick Ross, The Game, and Lloyd bringing an R&B sound to the song. "Thats Not Luv" with Lil Wayne, and "Life" with Jadakiss are both dark emotional vibe tracks that are strong lyrically. The latter song has a dark piano loop done by V-Don. Wyclef makes a suprising appearance on "Slum Religion". "Not My Time" is a lyrically strong song done by Trae and Linzie Kent singing at the end. Later on in the album is what I believe the strongest song is the title track, a Trae solo with deep heavy sample for the hook. reviewText:
One day I was in Best Buy shopping with the missus for a new fridge.  One fridge had a TV screen in it.  I saw it and did a double take.  Hey, that's Jack Bruce... and that's... that's Clapton and there's... Baker!  What the hey?  I stood open mouthed in front of the fridge.  My missus had no idea why I was so enthralled with that fridge!  I had no idea this wonderful reunion had occurred.  I had to pinch myself. (I didn't buy that particular fridge though).

So this is Cream, but it ain't the Cream you heard in the 60's.  That Cream was full of youthful vigor and uncontrollable fire.  This Cream is full of aged wisdom and measured fire.  Anyone who reports their playing has not changed is dead wrong.  Today's Cream is far more skilled, more accomplished. If the old Cream was a wildfire, this Cream is more like controlled bursts from a flame-thrower.

The tunes are basically the same tunes you heard 36 years ago on the Lps but the playing more closely resembles the actual studio sides of that band rather than the live sides - and that's ok.  Recently I picked up Cream Gold (which has all but one of the live tracks - Train Time - from Wheels of Fire).  I was amazed at the sheer volume of that incarnation (6 Marshall Stacks between Bruce and Clapton) and while I really enjoy the music I couldn't help but notice it had something of a sameness from track to track on the live disc.  Oh yeah, it's incredible, thunderous jamming, but one gets easily lost in the furious maelstrom!  Funny, it didn't sound that way when I was a teenager...  Anyway, you don't find that sameness from track to track on this release.  It's controlled, measured bursts from the flame-thrower and it is hot hot hot.  Stormy Monday, previously uncovered by this band is the high-point for Clapton here.  Lord have mercy!  Baker is more restrained with his double bass drum pedals and doesn't continually sound like an army of African drummers. Precision bursts from the flame-thrower - Baker's drumming on Deserted Cities of the Heart is thunderous at the right points and otherwise in a steady groove.  Bruce's voice is almost as good as it was way back when (Bruce has always been one of my favorite singers) and  the lines he plays on his bass (sans the "fartsy" fuzz sound") on this new disc are just tremendous - the perfect complement to Baker and Clapton.

It's so good to see/hear these guys back together again as seasoned, mature players.  It's sweet Devonshire clotted cream.  Pass me a scone and some jam.  I just love it and so will you.

oh, and to all the nay-sayers that want this band to sound exactly like it did 36 years ago... that's just plain stupid - and insulting to these musicians.  Real artists never stand still, they are always changing.  It is only natural that the re-united band will sound different. There is no denying that they are far more skillful - you want them to unlearn everything they've learned in the past 36 years just so they can sound the same for you?  Then go put on your tie-dyed t-shirt and harachi sandals, pull out the Live at the Fillmore sides of Wheels of Fire, crank up the volume, and close your eyes and pretend you are still 17.  Geeze!

reviewText:
None of the ex-Beatles achieved the same level of success as solo singers that they had achieved while together but Paul's solo career was very successful by any other standards. Paul recorded mostly ballads but he could rock too, as he showed bwith songs like Jet and Band on the run.

It is not possible to include all of Paul's hits on a single CD but all the tracks here were British top ten hits. Eleven of them made the UK top three including three number ones (Mull of Kintyre, Pipes of Peace, Ebony and ivory),while others peaked at number two. Uncle Albert / Admiral Halsey topped the American chart but, like Maybe I'm amazed, didn't chart in Britain so isn't included here.

Some UK top ten hits were left out for lack of space, including Mary had a little lamb, With a little luck (a top five UK hit and an American chart-topper), Goodnight tonight, Wonderful Christmastime, Waterfalls and The girl is mine (with Michael Jackson). Also missing are Paul's top twenty UK hits including Give Ireland back to the Irish, Helen wheels, Junior's farm and Take it away.

So it would have been easy to fill a double CD with Paul's hits but his more recent compilation, Wingspan (a double CD) missed that opportunity, instead containing one hits CD and one CD of mostly album tracks with a few hits. Nevertheless, the hits selection on Wingspan is different and the most obvious omissions from this set can be found there.

Of the tracks that are here, my favourites are Mull of Kintyre (complete with bagpipes), No more lonely nights (a superb ballad), Let `em in, Pipes of peace, My love, Another day and his duet with Stevie Wonder, Ebony and ivory. Also worthy of note are Say say say (with Michael Jackson), Silly love songs (possibly an attack on those who criticize Paul for doing mostly ballads?), Band on the run and the James Bond theme, Live and let die.

Considering the many great tracks that have been omitted, some people will be disappointed at the inclusion of We all stand together (complete with frog chorus) but although it's not one of my favourites here, its place is justified - it was a British top three hit, after all, so a lot of people DO like it - and it's not meant to be taken seriously anyway.

Originally released in 1987, this compilation provides an excellent overview of Paul's solo music. Although he has made some interesting music since 1987 (even including classical music), it is the music he made prior to 1987 (especially with the Beatles) that ensures his place in history.

One of the majuscule virtues of this outstanding director resides in the fact he has reached golden peaks around two well distant composers in conception, intentions and approaches as Bruckner and Mahler.

If you carefully realize, you will infer that, far beyond of the seductive, enraptured and deceitful consequences of the late Romanticism, was the visible tendency toward evasion and the search of refuge in the warmth of the matrix-memory. And the three most important composers who fell in this conception were Schumann, Mahler and Shostakovich.

Bruckner `s main concerns were totally different. He was not interested in the past that could have been and was not (by the way, this is the essential dramatic premise of the tango), Bruckner `s music has to do with the universe . That is what explains the enormous resonance and transcendence of his intentions. So when Horenstein directed Mahler did it with Brucknerian lenses, which enriched, enhanced and revaluated the Mahler's symphonies.

That's why listening Horenstein' s Mahler, you understand the rue dimension of the inner demons and the inspired noblesse of his Adagios. And the cheerful vital expression at the end of a Mahler' s  Symphony under Horenstein `s baton has nothing to do with self indulgence, neurosis or fears that many directors have found in Mahler. I think on the contrary, this has been a clever pretext to use Mahler as a vehicle of the contemporary unbalanced anima state. That is a Manichean use of the art.

It's very easy to use the music as a sharp metaphor of our surrounding world, but that vision pitifully diminishes, the scope of the artistic fact; due the grandness of the art resides precisely in its lack of temporality. The art must not be neither indulgent nor anecdotic.

reviewText:
.
"The weather is frightening, the thunder and lightning seem to be having their way,
but as far as I'm concerned, it's a lovely day." -Irving Berlin, "It's A Lovely Day."

Five "WONDERFUL" Stars. What a marvelous tribute! On the album "Bennett-Berlin", the Hall of Fame "Best in the Business" (to quote Frank Sinatra) jazz and popular music singer pays tribute to the songwriter who is one of the greatest of all times, Irvin Berlin. Berlin wrote hundreds of inspiring songs which include the likes of "God Bless America", "White Christmas", "Easter Parade", and many more that some may have thought were "traditional"  with unknown authors lost in time. Tony Bennett brings his inestimable talent and the fabulous Ralph Sharon Trio to the celebration, with longtime associate Sharon on the Bosendorfer piano, Joe LaBarbera on drums, and Paul Langosch on double bass. Special guests are three other Hall of Fame musicians: Dizzy Gillespie on trumpet (2 songs), Dexter Gordon on tenor sax (2 songs), and George Benson on guitar (1 song). Bennett mixes in some more obscure Berlin songs, including "Russian Lullaby" pointing to Berlin's country of birth before arriving stateside at the age of 5. Berlin's popular music songs have long been considered "made to order" for jazz adaptations by singers and musicians, and the heart of the Great American Songbook.

Kicking off with a joyous version of "They Say It's Wonderful" Bennett swings the lyrics and Sharon shows the value of swinging repetition with a quote from Thelonious Monk's "In Walked Bud" infused within his solo. "Isn't It A Lovely Day" extols the power of love and positive thinking, as Tony sings, scats, and whistles through a rainy day. The salutary "All Of My Life" has Tony and 'Long, Tall, Dexter' joining forces for an evocative performance. Dizzy goes muted as he joins Bennett for a jaunty "The Song Is Ended". "When I Lost You" is Tony singing completely solo with one emotional pass thru the lyric and a Sharon punctuation mark at the end. George Benson joins the proceedings playing and scatting with Tony and the group on "Cheek to Cheek" done at a blazing tempo. Bassist Langosch plays the beginning and weaves in and out of a delightful "Let Yourself Go" and then solos nicely. Bennett and Sharon do an excellent duo performance of a slow-tempo "Let's Face The Music and Dance". The hip "Shakin' the Blues Away" features Bennett and the nifty brush work of LaBarbera. Dizzy inserts "Volga Boatman" at the beginning of "Russian Lullaby" and plays a sizzling muted solo to go with Bennett's soaring ending to the lyric. "White Christmas" is a fitting end to a great all-Irving Berlin session with Bennett's heartfelt reading and Gordon's obbligatos and solo. Produced by Danny Bennett. All songs arranged by Tony Bennett. Highly Recommended. Five INSPIRED Stars. (Columbia Records. 12 tracks. Time-30:30.)

reviewText: This is Melvins' best work. A session of music that sets a higher standard for what is a hardcore, rough and relentless sounding type of hard rock. For this session, Lorax (Lori Black) is not the current bass player. They got a musician named Joe Preston, who has proved himself to be one of the heaviest and hardest-hitting bass players out there. They start the record leading through what has got to be the most interesting and listenable piece of drone metal that there ever could be: "Hung Bunny". Leading up to a song called "Roman Dog Bird", which is impressive for their ability to stay 100% in sync with each other. There are some pretty interesting note changes in the song that I think would be very inspirational to future hard rockers. The third song is a Flipper Cover titled "Sacrifice", which Melvins bring a whole new sound of dread and seriousness to. An AMAZING idea for these guys to do a cover of. If you don't believe that this is better than the original version played by the original band, than it is at least noteworthy till the end of history. And what is more impressive than that are the next two songs. An expert group of musicians picking a somewhat forgotten pair of Alive Cooper songs. First is an instrumental "gesture" resembling Alice Cooper's "Second Coming". Also, like Alice Cooper, leads into "The Ballad of Dwight Fry". Melvins bring a new light and a new dark sorrow to it that is too good to be true. Covering these two Alice Cooper songs is a LEGENDARY rock star move for a band, that at the time, had only made 3 LPs. The last song on this record is an original Melvins song called "With Teeth". The song's verses feature blaring guitar chords that sound so good, you want to rock out to this for as long as you can. Even if you don't appreciate the artists that made this record, it is among the highest of exemplary works.

I must agree with many of the other reviews of this dvd. Fantastic look into how to make the most of something you love to do with no money.  It takes effort and hard work, with a lot of creativity to make it in any business, let alone the music industry, and this documentary gives you a small look at how one of the founding members of OVERKILL, Rat Skates, contributed to his band.  It also gives you a cautionary woe at the end with making sure all priorities are in order when you get to where you are going.  Rat admits he left due to "burn out" and his wanting to start a family, which was not in the lifestyle the band had made at the time.

Sure, this is a skewed point of view of how one band made it, and it would have been nice to have the rest of OVERKILL's input, but the message still gets across.  Rat loved what he was doing, still is proud of his work and the band, reguardless of where they are now, and wants to share his story so that others can identify with it, much like how Thrash was founded. This is a must have for any thrash fan, and a must for any OVERKILL fan.

reviewText:
BRNS debut full length album. BRNS songs are like imagery poetry, lyrically they are amazing. I came across this artist on Spotify when he had just a few songs that was then put into a small EP (all of which are on this album). Combined with the video for Electric Love, and I fell in love. He's a modern day hippie/psych rock artist. His sound is more on the dreamy/happy/trippy side rather than the darker bass driven rock side, but that just makes me love him more. Think more Velvet Underground, Lou Reed and less Hendrix. As a fan of psych rock I really dig his sound, and lyrically he blows my mind. The images and emotions he invokes when you listen, it's definitely a trip you have to take.

What I love is I am trying to find someone current to compare him too, and I can't. There are some that are a little like his sound, but he is so uniquely himself from his sound to his voice to his lyrics that I actually can't really compare him. It's like the pacing of The Japanese House (for pacing) mixed with the songwriting of the old Glamrock artists, and the ethereal sound and feeling of like Lana Del Rey's voice. Even the slow songs have enough pep that will get you swaying.

Favorites: 10,000 Emerald Pools, Electric Love (naturally), American Money, Dopamine (one of the standouts as it's a bit faster tempo and the writing is pushing his comfort zone. Makes a great standout song).  I love the whole album, but I find myself always coming back to these.

I've seen reviewers say not to get this on Vinyl, that it does not sound right. This is absolutely not the case. I bought this on vinyl, and I have a regular midrange turntable (audio technica bluetooth wireless), and the sound is great. Either they were playing the wrong speed or they were messing with the sound settings on their sound system and don't understand Bass and Treble. Reading the reviews sounded like they had no idea how to properly set those for this type of album and screwed it up. After getting the vinyl and checking it out, I found that I was right, nothing wrong with how this music sounds on Vinyl. User error.

reviewText: It is unfortunate that the Cardigans only have a small North American following, because this is a band that has produced throughout their career. "Long Gone Before Daylight" is a haunting journey, guided by the perfect voice of Nina Persson, through love and loss, war and tragedy. Nearly every song on this album is brilliant, and the highlights include the very sad "No Sleep", "You're the Storm", "Communication" and "Good Horse". A big fan of the Cardigans, I was hoping they would continue to explore the electronic experimentation they began on "Gran Turismo", but was more than happy to hear the mellow, loungy sounds of "Daylight". Be warned, this may not be a CD that will lift your spirits, because the lyrics are often dark, making this disc even more personal and influencial. Most slow albums like this are only good for one or two listens, but "Daylight" has found it way into my CD player hundreds of times since I bought it. This is a musical maturation for this band, a step forward in songwriting, and another lyrical leap forward.

reviewText:
Barbra's powerful presence in the music industry is felt once again with the release of her newest album Guilty Too. This album has much much exceeded my expectations. Her voice remains lush, creamy and powerful, is still able to reach those amazing high notes and can fade into an audible whispers, revealing her fabled golden tone and unique timbre. I refuse to be unkind anymore to these younger generation of singers who claim themselves as "Divas", so ubiquitous in mTV (and incredibly annoying), I call on to everyone who appreciates the art of music that here is this Grand Dame, Streisand who is 63, still has the power to astonish. Madonna, Britney, Jlo, Celine and a host of other female packages should lock themselves in a dark room for several months without food nor drink and should listen to this album incessantly, then perhaps could develop even a fraction of Barbra's enormous and amazing talent. Barbra rules!

  While Barbra is still alive, no one but no one could claim to the title of being the Best Female Vocalist of the Century. Hers is the Voice that has been heard for four decades now and has touched the lives of so many millions of people. Her art remains alive and is the beacon of perfection in singing. Barry Gibb captured it right. There are the Top 10 Female Singers and there is Barbra Streisand.

  What truly amazed me is how Barbra's depth and range appears to be limitless. I haven't heard the entire cd yet (It was just released today in the UK.) Everyone knows that Barbra is at her best with ballads and love songs, but in the cd is also a disco tune "Night of My Life" and it is absolutely amazing. The much younger generations who perhaps isn't familiar to Ms Streisand's music would definitely love this. It has been remixed and would surely be popular on dance floors all over Europe and America.

  The dualdisc contains also 4 videos (more like music sessions.) The moment she uttered her first note, she sounded so fresh, you wouldn't believe this was her 61st album. This is what true talent is all about. Being timeless and able to survive changes in musical times. This is what Barbra Streisand possesses (also the likes of Aretha Franklin.) A voice that doesn't just sing but a voice that breathes life to the listener, a voice that nurtures, a voice that yearns. Barbra's voice exactly does that and more.

 This dualdisc is so so beautiful and reminds everyone what a true star and diva is all about.

reviewText:
I have been inspired by Deuter's music ever since I heard his album Ecstacy in the early 80's. All of his music puts me in touch with my spirit. And this one is no exception. Once again Deuter enfolds with his enchanting embrace. All nine selections are infused with the feeling tones of joy and upliftment. If this music was a wine I would have to say it is champagne -- pure sparkling golden effervescent bubbly.
Each of the nine vignettes makes me feel as if my spirit has taken a holiday to a lush and idyllic tropical island where the sun shines all day long while little billowing white clouds float along in the sky. Then at night I sense the full moon casting is silvery rays off of the calm ocean waves, shimmering and iridescent.
Apres La Pluie, track 4, is one of my favorites. Opening with the beat of tabla drums, as if waves are rhythmically lapping the shore, it sets the stage for the entrance of Deuter's recorder flutes. At first, one magical songbird starts singing while the sun's rays poke over the horizon at dawn. In a little while more birds join in with their songs. Then, as if a warm gentle breeze is rising up off of the ocean, the synthesized strings add their lush texture.
Whether you want to relax or daydream or take an inner journey, I can only give this work my highest recommendation. You won't regret it.

By the time you get to Barely Legal and Someday, you're tapping your feet and you're into the groove. The best song on here is probably "Last Nite" which is what hooked me.

If you can get the imported copy of "Is This It", do it! New York City Cops is definitely the 2nd best song on the album, but was left off of the US version because it was being released around Sept. 11th and the Strokes didn't want to offend or confuse anyone with the song (it's really about a story Julian's aunt told him from the 60's). reviewText:
This is a fun soundtrack. If you're expecting it to be a Nine Inch Nails album, you will be disappointed, though there are two tracks that are remixes of tracks found on NIN Ghosts. For that matter, if you didn't like Ghosts, you probably won't like this. For me, though, this really hits the spot. The spot that craves the sonic work done by Trent Reznor (and Atticus Ross). If you're a fan of soundtracks AND enjoy later NIN works, give this a try. If you're a collector and BIG FAN of Trent Reznor, this is a no brainer purchase.

There is a definite influence of "game sounds" in this soundtrack, which is sort of appropriate considering the film is about a computer product fad and the geeks and social misfits that created it. So, along with the usual Reznor sound mixture of synths, guitar and lovely piano pieces, you will find some bubbly arpeggiated simple synth chords, as you would find in mid to late 80s and early 90s computer games (such as on Amiga and C64 computers). Some people like this sound and some people don't. i don't. However, it's kept to a much more subtle extent than actual game music, and doesn't hurt my appreciation of this soundtrack. Some of the arpeggiated chords are used in a quite fun and energetic way, without feeling dated whatsoever. It's really only one track where it's a bit heavy, but the rest of that track is excellent anyway.

The soundtrack is a mixture of moods, but on average, The Social Network is far more upbeat than the Reznor/Ross soundtracks that followed it. This is "the fun one". The other two (as of December 2014) are the emotionally heavy ones (but also excellent).

reviewText:
Full disclosure: I LOVE Journey to the Centre of the Earth. The book, the movie, the record. It was probably the book that introduced me to sci-fi, the movie probably showed a hundred times on WGN's "Family Classics", and Rick Wakeman's LP was one of the first prog albums I even bought. So I have a soft spot in my heart for the workmight as well call it an oeuvre, it is all of a piece.

When I read that Rick had recovered the original conductor's score for Journey and he was going to re-record it, I couldn't help but be excited. Any work by "Wakey" is to be celebrated so far as I'm concerned. Besides, I was looking forward to seeing if he was actually going to correct the one serious flaw in the work: referring to the volcano via which the party makes its exit as Mt Etna rather than Stromboli as is related in the book. So much for that; Wakeman sticks to his guns. Mt. Etna it is. Artistic license, I suppose, and I'm good with that.

So all that said, what do I think of the music? Well, it should come as no surprise to find that I love it. All of it. Even Hayley Sanderson sitting in for the late Gary Pickford-Hopkins worksshe has a lovely, strong voice that works very well with that of the inimitable Ashley Holt, whose cast-iron pipes seem only to have improved with age. The "new" tunes, "Echoes" and "Quaternary Man", fit so nicely that it's hard to see them as wedged into the original work. They are, in fact, part of the original, cut so that the work could be squeezed onto an LP. My only regret so far as these pieces are concerned are that had they been contained on the 1974 recording, I could've been enjoying them so much longer

The blips and duff notes are gone. Of course, the original was a live version, and recorded in one go (financial constraints, fans know the story) so much had to be left in situ. It added to the charm, I thought. The studio version heard here is at once warm and immense. If anything Wakeman seems to allow the orchestra to take the bigger part of the grunt work, adding keyboard runs where he deems it appropriate. It's a little odd after having listened to the original for 40 years, but it works. And of course there is the drumming of Tony Fernandez and the booming voice of Ashley Holt to anchor it all.

So here it is 2014--well, 2015 tomorrow--and I finally have the whole thing in my hand and I've listened to it four or five times already. I must add that it comes complete with a magnificent Roger Dean cover and a complete set of liner notes courtesy of the Caped Crusader himself. The album was a Christmas gift from my wife, along with the re-release of "Return to the Centre of the Earth", which is just as magnificent. Could life get any better? I find it hard to imagineeven without the proper labeling of Stromboli.

Sit back, turn the lights off and light some candles, pour some wine, and listen. Listen, Bold Traveller. You shall find the Centre of the Earth. I have done this.

In addition to the stupendous opening, the seondary theme is wonderfully felt, and the brass playing is noteworthy: powerful and hair-raising without being overwhelming. The other sections of the orchestra show similar traits as well.
The second movement, more flowingly done that usual, is very beautiful indeed and is handled so well that it hardly seems to rush at all. the scherzo is very steady in its rhytmic pulse and the horns are magnificent in the trio. The last movement had always puzzled me...not anymore.
this is essential for any klemperer fan (one of his finest recordings), bruckner fan to have in their collection.

reviewText:
Well, as for the Beethoven 9th, I'll mention that I have one particular favorite, the "Reiner/CSO" on RCA Gold Seal.

I will say that I have 8 recordings of it by the likes of Celibidache, Giulini, Bernstein, Harnoncourt, Hogwood, Norrington, Wand and the aforementioned Reiner.  In their own way all are excellent, except perhaps for the Celibidache, which is so slow, it sounds funereal.  On my rating scale of 1-11 most get an "11" for sound (corresponding to a "5" on Amazon's scale of 1-5.  As far as performance I find the Hogwood too plain and the already mentioned Celibidache too religious for me.  Hell, it's supposed to be a joyous piece, not a requiem mass.  (If you're a Celibidache fan you can beat me over the head with a wet 2X4, but it's only his Beethoven I find fault with.  I love his Schumann, Brahms, and Bruckner).

But, before going more into the Reiner, a bit about me.  I'm no spring chicken anymore.  A Baby Boomer I was in college at the height of flower power in the late `60's.  I'll hit the big 60 this Memorial Day.  I'd read quite a bit on the better qualities of pharmaceuticals and herb.  I'd already started smoking grass in my sophomore year and along with that my interest in classical music grew.  (Those of you in the know realize that one of the great things about herb is that you become more attentive and appreciative of good music.)  Well, I wanted to read more about LSD and hit the books by Aldus Huxley.  Their detailed descriptions of a trip on acid sounded fantastic and right up my alley.  Yes, I wanted to be the first person in the dorm to drop.  All my friends smoked so the idea of doing acid came naturally.  Anyway, I wanted to make my first trip picture perfect and I bought the LP version of Reiner 9th especially for the occasion.  I knew that I enjoyed classical music, but there were still many things I couldn't make sense of in it; like how do 4 disparately sounding pieces of music go together to make up a single work, a symphony.  So, my hope was that I would realize that and come to a greater understanding of classical music while listening to not just this LP, but Mussorgsky's Pictures, the Beethoven 3rd "Eroica" and 5th, and don't forget a bit of acid rock.  Well, I dropped sometime after sunset.  From the beginning friends from all over the dorm dropped in to check on me and ask questions like, "What's it like?"  Many, of course, brought joints to help celebrate this momentous occasion.  The 2 guys across the hall kept taking turns watching me the entire night.  Of course, I listened to the music and a whole new world opened up with me in the form of classical music.  The Beethoven 9th, 3rd, & 5th all made perfect sense to me.  I got a good feeling of how everything fit together.  The Mussorgsky was a total delight.  I came to realize that one of the things needed to get into a work was great sound and all my LP's had it.  Even today the Reiner 9th in cd format still has great sound and stands at the top of the small mountain of 9ths that are in my collection.  Well, needless to say, I was hooked.  Not on drugs, but on music, both pop and classical.  I would listen to the radio for as much classical music as they programmed.  I would check the record bins and ask questions of the clerks as to what might be the best version of this or that particular work that I thought might make an interesting addition to my slowly evolving collection.  My main interests seem to be in classical and pop or acid rock.  I remember a friend came to my room to tell me he'd gotten the new Moody Blues LP and a group of us went to his room to give it a spin.

Well, back to the Reiner Ninth.  From the very first listen I thought everything made total sense musically.  The first movement allegro was dramatic, the scherzo just bowled me over, the adagio was just perfect in everyway, something every other recording may approach but never attain; Fritz Reiner and Margaret Hillis (choral director) made the final movement the point at which all the other three movements pointed towards.  Heck, I'm listening to this cd right now and, to be honest, listen to it a few times a month, more than any other Beethoven 9th.

Fortunately, by the time I moved to Chicago I had stopped acid but will remain in it's debt forever for helping me get over the hump with classical music.  Right now I have more Beethoven than any other composer, but to be honest Gustav Mahler is soon to take over the spot that Beethoven now holds.

If you want a truly great Ninth I cannot urge you strongly enough to add this cd to your burgeoning collection.

Mark Zimmerman - the Bipolar Bear!

This is a top 25 rock album for me and clearly Genesis' best. Phil Collins was never better and the instrumentals never more focused, elaborate and creative. Their later albums like Abacab and Invisible Touch had tracks that got more radio play, but were not better albums, with a lot of silly material that hasn't aged as well today. No so here. Just listen to tracks Behind the Lines, Misunderstanding, Turn It On Again, Dukes Travels/End. All of these tracks are on a level considerably higher than any other albums from the band. The rest of the album is solid as well. Duke sounds better with each listen and, taken as a whole, is one of the greatest rock albums of all-time. It still sounds amazing, even today.

** Note - For the small portion of Genesis fans out there who think their early stuff was the best and the departure of Gabriel brought the band down, I will just say this: Phil Collins wrote/co-wrote every song on Duke, sings all of them, and plays the drums on all tracks. If that isn't talent I don't know what is. He's amazing. No, they didn't miss that oddball Peter Gabriel at all here. 5 Stars. Highly Recommended.

I'm a big believer that most concert DVDs are wastes of money.  Honestly, how many times will anyone watch the same concert, with the same songs, and the same stage show, etc.?

Every rule has its exceptions.  For me, `Operation : Livecrime' is that exception.

The extras are nice additions, but this DVD is all about the performance - THE performance.  Queensryche were hitting on all cylinders at the time of this recording, and it showed.  The album being presented here in its entirety is nothing less than an underappreciated masterpiece, and the stage show underlying this performance, with it's animated characterizations of the album's key players, as well as an on-stage appearance by Pamela Moore (performing as 'Mary') accentuates an amazing story.

If you were fortunate enough to have caught this tour, as I was, this will bring back some incredible memories for you.  If you weren't, and are discovering Mindcrime for the first time, then this will only enhance your experience.

I reviewed Operation : Mindcrime for Amazon, and stated that the album belongs in every music lover's collection.  While I don't believe that true of this DVD, it is a definite must-have for anyone who loves the Mindcrime album.

2010 was a year that bands tried their hardest to achieve a pinnacle in their music. Taproot is one of the bands that accomplished this. With past efforts, Taproot seemed like a band that could do well musically and lyrically, and succeeded in every single aspect. But, honestly, Plead the Fifth is their strongest record to date, strong enough to tie with Diamond Eyes by Deftones for Best Album of 2010.

All of the tracks are lively, as they all have their own appeal and artistic value to them, not to mention exceptional use of Drop A guitar tuning. Now Rise kicks off the CD with a BANG and does not stop its intensity and thrills at all. The other tracks also intend to do the same thing, and there is no failure. There is not one track that I consider to be a bad one. The album's peak is reached as the melodic 9.1. Lost kicks off, which is the best song on here in my opinion. This is a great song that has an awesome beat and amazing guitar work. One thing I have to point out about this song is the whispering around the second/third verses is executed very well. I also like Fractured, Now Rise, Release Me, No View Is True, Left Behind, and Trophy WiFi.

Thanks to Taproot for having a great release from 2010. The Episodes, Taproot's next record, will be released in April 2012. Let's hope that Taproot can give us their second consecutive home run in a row and improve further.

reviewText:
I think this is a fabulous recording.  Rachmaninov's music is, of course, utterly beautiful and Paul Hillier and the Estonian Chamber Choir do it proud.

This is a deep expression of faith and spirituality and is some of the loveliest, most affecting choral music of the 20th Century in my view.  Rachmaninov employs the full depth of the traditional Russian bass which adds genuine profundity both literally and metaphorically and can be a technical challenge for some choirs.  Not here; these singers are excellent and sound as though they have been singing in this register all their lives  which they may well have been, of course.  The effect is stunning and Paul Hillier's experience, intelligence and scholarship makes this something really special, I think.  It is technically excellent, expressive and beautifully balanced, and the effect is quite spellbinding.

The recorded sound is excellent.  It is sufficiently resonant to bring out the wonderful sonorities in the music but never blurs into an over-echoey mush.  The presentation is very attractive and the notes are good.  This is an all-round excellent disc and I can recommend it very warmly indeed.

reviewText:
I was in my local CD store browsing for something else in the E section when I ran across Eluveitie. Who? Then again, when Im cruising the metal section, I don't give much thought to bizarre names. What attracted me to the band was that they played folk/Celtic type metal, or something to that effect, according to a sticker on the cellophane wrapping. Hmmm. Most of the metal I have to screen because truthfully, Im pretty sick of the screaming, shouting and harsh vocals thats all the rage in the genre. Dont get me wrong, I love heavy music, but so much of it is just plain brutal to be brutal and having been into heavy music since Blue Cheer turned air into cottage cheese back in 1966, yeah, Im THAT old, I appreciate some form of musicality to my metal.

Usually, when theres folk or Celtic influences, the vocals can go either way, gruff like Finntroll or clear like a few of the others I cant recall at the moment (yeah, they're rare) with either female vocals or a male vocalist who is for the most part clean or gruff in a style that isn't grating or annoying. They can be symphonic also, like Nightwish or Epica which mixes the two genres, at least to my ears.

To be blunt, the singer(s) is/are another instrument in the band, a very important one. I could care less what the lyrics are. Their candyrock psychedelic profundities go right over my head along with all poetry. My forte is reading, not poetry, at least when it comes to words. However, theres something musical about lyrics as well, in the pattern of the syllables. In that regard, I like to at least understand them even if I don't pay attention to their meaning. The vocals are as much a sound as guitars, bass drums or whatever.

Thats one reason I don't get off on screaming, shouting and gruff vocals unless theres something musical, lyrical or rhythmic about them that contributes to the rest of the instrumentation.

I bring this up because when I first put on this album, it started with old man narration. I thought, aha! This sounds pretty cool. The music was Celtic/folk flavored with whistle and string accompaniment. Made me think of fantasy, Ireland, etc. Then the second song kicked in and the screaming started. I cringed at first and went Oh no, not again!

HoweverI just bought the darn CD so I decided to stick it out. Though the annoying gruff/screaming/growling vocals were a bit much, the music was pretty good and I did my best to adapt to the sound. Strike one was the obnoxious sound of the vocals. Strike two was I couldn't understand a thing he was singing. I couldn't distinguish any syllables, or hardly any.

On to the next and then the next few songs and things started to change. The music continued to be excellent and then the female vocals kicked in and the pattern started to change. After a while, and a few listens, I adapted to the male screaming and given the female interludes, the mix started to work.

After repeated listens, I came away with a better and more positive feeling of Origins.

However, when I went to watch a few performances of the band live on the net, I was left cold. As soon as the band started a set, the band leader played whistle for a few moments then kicked in with a high-pitched screaming and it went downhill from there. I don't think I could watch this band live!

On the other hand, Origins is an excellent album. There are some outstanding songs, but of course, the one with the lead female vocals is the standout. You already know why. The male singer is barely present! The Hall Of The Mountains is a clear winner here and one I cant get out of my head. Other favorites include Celtos which is sung partially in ancient Gaulish. Its also at least partially sung by Anna Murhpy, the hurdy gurdy player and the female relief vocalist.

Other standouts are Virunus, Vianna, The Silver Sister and King, among others. While I have to tolerate the gruff male vocals, once in a while they aren't so annoying that I can enjoy everything about these songs.

Ive listened to this album enough now that Ive adapted to the vocals and can say I enjoy it enough to give it five stars, though its really four and a half. Im sure a lot of metal fans would love this while others may not think its harsh enough. Oh well, cant please everyone. Still recommended.

reviewText:
Gimme Back My Bullets is generally considered the least successful of the original Lynyrd Skynyrd albums, but it has always been my favorite.  I rate it just slightly ahead of the essential "Pronounced".  I remember staying up late as a teenager, to hear its midnight debut on the local radio station (WDVE, Pittsburgh), and buying it ASAP after that.
"Bullets" is a transitional album for Lynyrd Skynyrd.  Most obviously, it features a 2-guitar line-up, coming after the departure of Ed King, and a few months before Steve Gaines joined.  The 2-guitar sound is a bit leaner that previous albums, but Collins and Rossington are more than capable of carrying the load!  But it's also their first production with the legendary Tom Dowd replacing Al Kooper who had produced their first 3 albums.  And it has the debut of the Honkettes, the female backup vocal group consisting of JoJo Billingsley, Cassie Gaines and Leslie Hawkins.
Gimme Back My Bullets is very much Allen Collins' record.  Over the first 3 Skynyrd albums, the songwriting was spilt pretty evenly between the 3 guitarists (along with Singer Ronnie Van Zant, of course).  Allen Collins co-authors 8 of 24 songs, Gary Rossington and Ed King each co-author 7.  But Allen wrote many of Skynyrd's best songs, including "Freebird", "Gimme 3 Steps", "Tuesday's Gone" and "Needle & The Spoon".  On "Bullets", Allen has songwriting credits (along with RVZ) on all 8 of the original songs (Rossington is also part of the team on 3 of the songs).
Musically, "Bullets" didn't have any big hits, but does include several Skynyrd standards.  All of the songs are great.  The title track, "Double Trouble" and "Searchin" are all Skynyrd standards, along with the acoustic-ish "All I can Do Is Write About It".  "Roll Gypsie Roll" is a reflective piece about life on the road, and one of my all time favorite songs.  "Every Mother's Son", "Trust" and "Cry For The Bad Man" are all solid songs.  There's also a cover of J.J.Cale's "Same Old Blues" that has a great, almost funky, feel.  Trivia note: Lynyrd Skynyrd only did 2 covers on their first 4 studio albums, both were of J.J. Cale songs.  The other was "Call Me The Breeze".
If you're a casual Skynyrd fan, start with "Pronounced", or the original band's live set "One More From The Road".  But if you want to get deeper into the spirit of the band, this album can't be beat.

reviewText:
When my brother first introduced me to Thick As A Brick in the early '90s (he had an LP) I was captivated by it. Sometime later I bought it on CD and one day, on my way to work on the train, decided to listen to it through my earphones. A special bond was about to be forged.

This will sound melodramatic, but I mean it: I tell you that album was made for that train trip. The first three minutes of the music and the train ride are calm and easy. Suddenly, both music and train become loud and frantic. At various times throughout both, the speed and energy rises and falls in close synchronisation. Although it's far too difficult and lengthy to go into all the details, I must say it was quite uncanny how well the music in my ears was so appropriate to the vision in my eyes.

I will always remember those days fondly, and Thick As A Brick will forever occupy a very special part of my heart and mind.

It's a very pleasant, positive sounding album in many respects, thanks to the chord progression and the use of flute, xylophone (or glockenspiel?), acoustic guitar and the synthesiser of the day (was it the Moog? I'm not quite sure). At the same time, if one examines the lyrics, one finds them to be less than positive and very metaphorical, as they are concerned with society and its often absurd rules and ways, and there is an inferred criticism towards these rules.

Instructions for listening:

You must not put this on in the background and do other things that distract you from the music: you absolutely must give it your undivided attention. It deserves nothing less, especially if you want to get the complete feeling and imagery it delivers. Immerse yourself in this masterpiece and you will be richly rewarded.

This album went to number one in the US and number five in the UK. It's widely regarded as perhaps Jethro Tull's finest work - their magnum opus - THE concept album. One of my favourite albums, closely followed by their next album "A Passion Play", an album that polarises people, but that's another story.

In many ways, I miss the simple purity Lizzy had with these early records, something that was lost when they hit it big.
Shades of a Blue Orphanage is an extension of their first album; storytelling, poetic lyrics, musical experimentation with blues, rock, folk and prog elements. There is no real formula to any of it; These tracks would be right at home in a live jam, and I can only imagine some of the great shows Lizzy must have put on in the early days.
Listeners looking for classic Lizzy hard rock will be scratching their heads at hearing this album. Listeners without an appreciation for lyrical imagery and experimentation will be prone to dismiss what they don't understand as "awful". Shades is an original recording filled with verve and genuine emotion. It's too bad most modern music can't say the same thing.

Though most people only know Scaggs through his blockbuster "Silk Degrees", he had a very devoted following that began with his self-titled album on Atlantic featuring the classic track "Loan Me A Dime" with Duane Allman. Both this fabulous set and the previous 2 cd set on BGO are prime examples of his stylish and sophisticated take on R&B, blues, and rock 'n' roll. While "Moments" and "Boz Scaggs & Band" sold reasonably well, his audience began expanding as FM radio came to the fore in the 70's. Radio play for "Dinah Flo" and several other tracks introduced many new listeners, who were very likely to introduce friends to his subtle charms. He was definitely a word of mouth artist. His earlier albums were also ballad driven but on "My Time" he seems to weave pop into a mix that never weakens or denigrates the soul/blues foundation of his music. I was aware at the time that several of the tunes were covers, but it's a tribute to his own singular and elegant phrasing that it can be difficult to tell originals from covers.  If it seems as though these albums might be too laid back, I don't mean to give that impression.  Boz knows how to rock, but his voice is such a great vehicle for ballads that one tends to overlook the equally entertaining uptempo numbers. Plenty of them here as well, but due to his approach, even edgy smokers like "Full Lock Power Slide" never seem impulsive and out of control.
  On "Slow Dancer" you can sense an artist bursting at the seams, ready for the next step, and in full control of his artistic abilities. Opening with what should have been his first big hit "You Make It So Hard (To Say No) this album never takes a wrong step, and remains to this day, my personal favorite. It would be over two years before we had another album by Boz.  Although his following was expanding, the pieces didn't really fall into place until "Silk Degrees." Musically, however, Boz was in a class by himself as early as his first recorded work with the Steve Miller Band. His work on "Sailor" especially stands out from that period, but his solo material showed such incredible maturity and direction from the beginning that I can easily recommend any of his early albums with complete certainty that they will fulfill expectations. BTW, his newer material has been uniformly excellent, and also comes highly praised. Don't be limited by "Silk Degrees", there's much more to hear.

Denying that Radiohead are one of the most influential, interesting and innovative bands in music's history is like denying that you don't need oxygen in your lungs - quite frankly - it's a fact of life.

It's often said that radiohead are depressing - I can see the point, but Radiohead songs aren't all doom, gloom and 'the end of the world is nigh' - you can save that for Muse. Infact, closer inspection of their back catalogue reveals intricate, beautiful melodies, riff laden,stadium filling rock anthems and satirical, meaningful and consistently brilliantly sung lyrics (courtesy of singer Thom Yorke) - EVERY SONG ON OK COMPUTER is a gem.

Now, this album won't be for everyone - but it bloody well should be - it's essential, it's avant garde, it's one of the best albums ive ever heard. I don't like everything Radiohead have produced, but this offering draws me back time after time after time without a doubt. It's the most life changing album ive ever listened to - and what you get from this album depends on how willing you are to actually listen to it.

Very few of the songs are about depressing subjects or even sung depressngly - on the contrary - Thom Yorke's vocals add a character, emotion and life into each song that ranges from down trodden and heart broken to world beating and all knowing. This is a fine album from one of the greatest all time bands.

reviewText:
Even before I put this CD into my player, I had to pause and reflect on the unlikely fact that Iron Maiden are still releasing albums in 2003. 'Brave New World' was an accomplished and extremely competent comeback, with only a few minor flaws to drag it down. Could 'Dance Of Death' really perpetuate a run of form and prove beyond doubt Maiden are truly back for good? Despite some wildly varying opinions I've seen in the reviews on this page, I'd firmly assert the answer is a resounding yes.
A number of factors contribute to making this Maiden's most complicated, and certainly best produced, album since 88's 'Seventh Son'. The double impact of the album openers,'Wildest Dreams' and 'Rainmaker' does very little to hint at what lies ahead. As two potential singles these songs will carry out their purpose very well: 'Wildest Dreams' is a distilled slice of classic Maiden, with a chorus that, instead of being supremely infectious, slowly begins to take shape with every listen, until it comes into its own. I prefer 'Rainmaker', with its gorgeous guitar melodies and equally catchy chorus and bridge.
My major criticism of 'Brave new World' was that some of the epic tracks, while being of the highest quality, were simply dragged out for far too long, almost as If they were merely showing that they could. 'Dance of Death' contains four songs exceeding the seven minute mark, and each packs in a lot of technical skill and reams of fantastic songwriting. 'No More Lies', the only song Steve Harris penned alone for this album, is the first of these, and is of the quality I's expect from a songwriter of his prowess. A twisting Harris riff gives way to a melodic verse, only bulding to a thunderous chorus. It's a perfectly formed and supremely catchy epic, and its position on the CD ensures we are reminded of the formidable talent of each and every musician in the band. The title track took a bit of getting used to on my part. It intially seems repetitive, but repeated listens reveal a moody epic, with classical influences and off kilter melodies contributing to a sprawling centrepiece. 'Paschendale' is my standout track from 'Dance of Death'. Indeed, I'm fast coming to consider it a metal masterpiece. Kind of like a 2003 cousin of 'The Trooper',it deals with war in a surprisingly sensitive manner, urging us to 'tell the tale of paschendale' and evoking images of blood soaked trenches effectively. I love the slow build up being offset by the first of many thunderous riffs, the lurching, up tempo guitar sound before the first solo, the middle eight, and the triumphant, inevitable chorus. I cant think of any prevoius Maiden song to compare it to, as their are none comaparable. I would say that the explosive dynamics, powerful lyrics, supreme musicianship, multi sectioned nature and a restrained vocal preformance from Bruce make it one of the best Iron Maiden songs.
Journeyman, the closing number, is a departure for Maiden, with chilly strings and acoustic guitars dominating. I believe it will alienate some fans, but i think it a gorgous, perfect parting shot, rounding up the album by reminding us that Maiden are and always have been so much more than mono brain celled headbangers.
Nicko's contribution,'New Frontier' is great, with a killer chrous. With so many talented writers in the band its unlikely he will get beyond one song per album though: how about a solo album Nicko? 'Montsegur' has lyrics that sound like 'Seventh Son' and 'Piece of Mind' esque music, while 'Face in the Sand' and 'Age of Innocence' are up tempo classic Maiden.
'Dance of death' certainly requires repeated listens, but it will reveal its secrets and exhibit numerous qualities which make it the bands most consistent and original album in well over a decade. Kevin Shirley's production is superb, ensuring the strings don't drown out the gutitars, and somehow letting three guitarists each have their own place in the mix.
Most Maiden fans will have picked this up already, but if you're on the brink, I higly recommend 'Dance Of Death'. Maiden haven't ceased to meke challenging and compelling heavy metal.

This disc has been substantially improved on grounds of sound alone thanks to the 24 bit remastering. The Glagolitic Mass dates from 1963 and Taras Bulba from 1961. The playing and performances are both idiomatic and authentic, the Glagolitic Mass having additionally received the Grand Prix du Disc award in 1964 to underline the point.

The main work on this disc is probably therefore the Mass which was written and based on the Old Church Slavonic version. Furthermore Janacek made it clear that his intention was not to write a mass that was primarily Christian in its focus but rather that it should, as he himself put it 'capture faith in a nation, not on the basis of religion, but on the basis of morality and strength, to which God alone is held as witness.' Other worthwhile quotes to emphasise his focus are 'The fragrance of the damp Luhacovice forests was always an incense. A temple arose for me in the gigantic greatness of the forest with an arching sky, concealed in mist, extending into the distance; and the ringing little bells of a herd of sheep. I hear in the tenor solo a great priest, in the soprano a girl - an angel, in the chorus our people. The candles - the needles of the tall fir trees lit up by stars; and in the ritual, somewhere, there is the prophesy of saint Wenceslaus. And the language of the missionaries Cyril and Methodius.'

In this performance, all these clues become reality in a way that is aided by performers sharing the original language and concept base. This disc has an authenticity that would be close to impossible for non-Slavic performers to emulate, let alone improve upon.

The Taras Bulba piece focusses on three episodes in the life and death of Taras Bulba, the legendary Cossack freedom fighter. In that sense it is programme music while neither being a suite nor a symphonic poem. originally this very fine and compelling recording was coupled with the equally fine and compelling recording of the Sinfonietta by the same forces. Both that and this Taras Bulba have been transformed as sound by the remastering but have been split up, the Sinfonietta being coupled with pieces by Martinu. (reviewed under that coupling).

This is a compelling and authentic disc of high quality which many will consider to be authentic. The Slavonic nature of the sound produced by the orchestra and the singers add enormously to the effect of both pieces. The distinctive Slavonic woodwinds, string and brass timbres of these players is now sadly a thing of the past as a result of internationalism - a feature of orchestras worldwide. This disc therefore has the added invaluable extra attraction of being a record of a cultural past not likely to be repeated in the future.

I would suggest that this disc is arguably an indispensable part of any serious Janacek follower and worthy of serious consideration as a purchase.

reviewText:
Anyone who thought 2009's uneven "Together Through Life" showed signs that rock's poetic mastermind was losing his edge as he neared 70 can rest easy now with the release of "Tempest," his best work since 2001.

The 10 songs on "Tempest" boast fascinating lyrics, intricate, well played arrangements and a Dylan who, at 71, is at the peak of his interpretive powers, even with his voice undergoing signs of decay. As with "Modern Times," most of the songs are dark, with little levity throughout. The opening "Duquesne Whistle," with a jumpy swing arrangement taken right out of 1933, and the gorgeous closing John Lennon tribute "Roll On, John," offer something close to relief, and even the former track contains images of lowdown women and fear that the titular whistle is "gonna tear my world apart." The album's very best songs, "Pay in Blood" and "Tin Angel," are also its darkest. "Pay in Blood" boasts one of his finest musical accompaniments in years, and the lyrics, which paint Bob as an executioner "sworn to uphold the laws of God," are loaded with delicious dark humor. "Tin Angel," a nearly 10 minute tale of lust, revenge and murder, is simply astonishing, an accomplishment worthy of the same ranks as "Blind Willie McTell," "Mississippi," and similarly lauded works from Bob's post-1975 career. "Long and Wasted Years" is spoke-sung in a manner many compare to 1987's classic "Brownsville Girl," and is a bittersweet, endearing ballad, as is "Soon After Midnight," which begins tenderly enough but gets progressiveley more vicious, with Dylan vowing to "drag his corpse through the mud" in regards to a competitor for his heart's object of affection. "Narrow Day" is a down and dirty shuffle sung with grit, and "Scarlet Town" is bone chilling with its sparse arrangements and images of despair. "Early Roman Kings" is a "Together Through Life" sounding blues shuffle taken from the Muddy Waters handbook, but the lyrics elevate enough, including the biting "I ain't afraid to make love to a bitch or a hag."

Much anticipation has been given tot he album's nearly 14 minute title track, a blow by blow account of the night the Titanic sank, and it happily is a success; while certainly not an original subject matter or as good an epic as "Desolation Row" or "Visions of Johanna," it's a charming, lilting tribute to the famous event, and Bob draws much sympathy for the characters he envisions on their doomed voyage.

"Tempest" is an essential entry into the Dylan catalog, proof that in his twilight years, he still has a lot to say about the state of our being and where we're headed.

reviewText:
How exciting it must have been to be of age in Britain in 1980 and part of the burgeoning underground hard rock/heavy metal scene.  '80 arguably saw the NWOBHM movement at its absolute peak, with debut LPs being released by the scene's top contenders, most notably Iron Maiden, Def Leppard, Diamond Head, Tygers of Pan Tang and Girlschool.

With the exception of Iron Maiden, none of those groups however, not even Def Leppard, would chart that year as high as Barnsley's Saxon.  Their breakthrough LP (and second overall) "Wheels of Steel," released in March of '80, peaked at #5 in the U.K. national charts, an astonishing feat in itself, but even more astonishing is that they would unleash its follow-up a mere seven months later.

And the amazing thing is that October's "Strong Arm of the Law" LP didn't suffer a bit from the usual sophomore slump and was actually even MORE rockin', even FASTER and overall better than its predecessor.

This record is chock full of mini metal masterpieces, not the least of which is opener "Heavy Metal Thunder," yet another of Saxon's odes to their legions of headbanging fans.  The mere title indicates that here was a group that wore their metal colors with pride at a time when many of their peers were trying to distance themselves from that label.  From there, the title track is another monster of a rocker, and the group's record company seemed to agree at the time, as it was released as a successful single from the LP (singles were a big thing at this time).  And who could forget that Saxon were arguably one of, if not the fastest band to exist in heavy metal in 1980.  Just listen to the velocity of stand-out speed metal scorchers like "20,000 Ft." and "Sixth Form Girls" for proof.  You just did not find tempos this rapid in music at the time without crossing over into hardcore punk.

And finally, in 2009, nearly 30 years after Saxon's peak, their early albums get CD releases that actually do these essential recordings justice.  Because if you ask me, the poor mixes of previous pressings all but stripped the music of its original rawness and power.  I am happy to report to you that you can in good confidence replace any previous Saxon CDs in your collection with these remasters, as I did.  The mere term "remaster" is ambiguous when dealing with music made long before the digital age dawned, as it usually involves replacing the original mix with something presumably "cleaner" and more up to date (read:  sterile) that all but ruins it.  To me, the best remaster of an album from 1980 is one that attempts to replicate the sound of hearing a brand new copy of the original vinyl.  These 2009 Saxon remasters do just that, so much so that I've officially retired my worn old Carrere LP pressings of these albums.

If that weren't enough, each reissue contains expanded liner notes with input from frontman Biff Byford himself, along with various clippings from the day and reproductions of the back covers of each LP, making them essential for collectors.

To summarize, mandatory NWOBHM album, and remasters that give these 30 year old recordings a new lease on life.  Highly recommended.

Here we finally have Jennifer Hudson's second release.  It's been a while since her first which won her a Grammy and life has dealt her a great many obstacles over that time.  There are some gems here and also some filler but the obvious thing that smacks the listener in the face with the first song till the end is that Jennifer has truly found her voice.  She has always displayed superb vocals with amazing range.  It showed at its best with her DREAMGIRLS songs.  On other material, though her vocals were gold, she wasn't always focused.  Now she has matured to a true artist and performer.  She has learned how to take her special gift, her voice, and use it to its fullest potential.  She knows when to reign it in and when to let it loose holding amazing notes.  The control she has over her beautiful instrument is awe inspiring.  And with this is a much more advanced ability to put strong emotions in all her songs.  Each note sung here is from her heart and it adds so much to her raw talent.

For me the second track I GOT THIS personifies the whole cd experience.  It is a true r@b anthemic performance where Jennifer stands strong and tall as a person with all she's walked thru starting quietly and building to a powerhouse raw emotion finale.  WHERE YOU AT is of course a great track.  Alicia Keys worked with Hudson a lot here and those tracks are the true standouts.  EVERYBODY NEEDS LOVE and DON'T LOOK DOWN are upbeat dance tracks where Jennifer soars flawlessly.  ANGEL is reminiscent of a Teena Marie track and a gift to the strong vocals of Hudson.  I REMEMBER ME, STILL HERE and WHY IS IT SO HARD are the ballad type tracks here and they go from middle of the road to true r@b and totally showcase Jennifer.  The only two filler tracks are GONE and the final gospel tinged BELIEVE.  A true highlight that will gain Jennifer even new fans is her interpretation of FEELING GOOD.  So many have recorded it and she adds new flavor and purpose to this great song.

Bottom line is listeners have always known that Jennifer Hudson was vocally gifted.  So far she has been known as the underrated AI contestant and the DREAMGIRLS queen.  On this cd she now shows herself as an r@b diva in the Aretha Franklin school.  This cd shows much promise for the career of Jennifer Hudson.  She owns each song and controls her beautiful voice with inspiring range and emotion.  Those notes she reaches will send shivers up and down your spine.  The inner strength and conviction the listener hears shows a woman who has found her place.  Even the lackluster tracks here become magic with the touch of Hudson's vocals.  Kudos to Hudson.  Highly recommended.
