reviewText:
The Beatles are undoubtedly the most important band in rock history. Ask any music to name another band that has had as big an impact on the world of popular music, and you'd be very hard pressed to find an answer. Sure, you can say bands like Led Zeppelin (who I personally consider superior), The Who and The Rolling Stones who achieved similar commercial and artistic achievements, but it's unlikely any of these bands would've achieved these scales had it not been for The Fab Four.

To commemorate their arrival in America in 1964, Capitol Records has released "The Capitol Albums, Vol. 1", containing four Beatles albums digitally remastered in both steroe and mono, with the tracks initially featured on the original American releases. These albums are "Meet The Beatles", "The Beatles' Second Album", "Something New" and "Beatles '65".

I must say, for Beatles fans, this is a dream come true. Whether you were around when John, Paul, George and Ringo first hit the United States, or you're a younger fan who wants to experiecne just what it was like when that first wave of Beatlemania conquered the world back then (such as myself), this collection is a must have. Classics like "I Wanna Hold Your Hand", "I Saw Her Standing There", "All My Loving", "I Wanna Be Your Man", "She Loves You" and "I Feel Fine" sound better than ever, not to mention that there are many songs here that have not been available stateside on cd, so that's reason alone to purchase this set. The liner notes are also very insightful and make for a great read.

As other people have mentioned, the packaging for the set is incredibly poor. Best to keep the cds in a cd holder as to avoid dropping and / or scratching them.

Still, that should not stop you from buying this fantastic collection of early Beatles albums. It is an absolute must for all fans of great rock and roll music, as performed by the most important band the genre has ever spawned.

reviewText:
"Illmatic" is the perfect rap album. This is the one album ever made that bridged the old school to the new school, the best producers to the greatest MC, real world lyrics to straight fun. Nas introduced himself as the world's greatest rapper here, and although he would defend this title for years to come, he would never match the quality of "Illmatic". He paints stories of life in Queensbridge, his beloved project, makes philosophies on the state of the world, reminisces over his younger days, and obviously has a lot of fun. What's so beautiful about "Illmatic", however, is that Nas could never have done it alone. It's totally a group effort, because Nas recruited only the greatest producers of 1994 for this album. Put it in the CD player and treat yourself to the productions of Large Professor, Pete Rock, Q-Tip, L.E.S., and DJ Premier. "Illmatic" is probably the only hip hop album ever to have immortal lyrics matched by such immortal production, which is why it is widely considered hip hop's bible.

The album starts with an intro, where Nas and his friend AZ have a conversation about the state of current rap and life over a dope beat. If it weren't for "The Genesis", I doubt that albums would have intros like they always do today. "NY State of Mind", Primo's first track, is the first song that Nas paints a ghetto portrait for the listener. "Life's a B**ch" is one of the greatest hip hop collaborations of all time. AZ leads in with one of my favorite verses ("Visualizin' the realism...") and they give their young philosophies on life. Large Professor produced that excellent beat. "The World Is Yours" was revolutionary, and is the reason Nas is regarded as a ghetto prophet. The piano and bass beat is done by the one and only Pete Rock, and Nas is still recycling lyrics from this song to this day. "Halftime"'s technique changed hip hop for good, and it's jazzy beat only enhanced it. "Memory Lane" might be my favorite song on "Illmatic". Primo's toned down beat with keyboard and vocals is perfect, and Nas takes time to reminisce and think. "One Love" is Nas's classic talk to a friend in jail, produced by Q-Tip. "One Time 4 Your Mind" and "Represent" are both legendary storytellers with great beats and hooks. "It Ain't Hard to Tell" is one of my favorite songs ever, with it's ultra-jazzy and souled-out beat, it's the most purely old school track here. The 10th anniversary edition is definitely worth the extra $2 because it provides a second disc of remixes which complement the originals nicely, plus a newer classic, "Star Wars".

"Illmatic" was successful in melding the quickly progressing hip hop world to its early nineties styles, and in so revolutionized rap in itself. There aren't too many albums that I would call perfect, but "Illmatic" is an unduplicated legend in itself.

reviewText:
Julius Rntgen was nothing if not prolific, especially in his later years, and cpo is slowly making their way through at least his most important orchestral works. Of course, with an output like his (some 650 works, most of them in multiple movements, including some 24 symphonies, 18 of which were written between 1930 and 1932) the quality may be bound to be variable, and it is hard to know for a newcomer where to start to explore such an enormous oeuvre. This disc of his fifth, sixth and nineteenth symphonies is probably as good a place as any  the sixth may be the best still among those I have heard (competing, in my view, with the wonderful eighth).

Stylistically, Rntgens music is harmonically traditional and conservative, with Grieg and Brahms being perhaps the most obvious models, but with a much more classical temperament. With respect to form, however, Rntgen does not appear to have felt particularly bound by tradition, and many of his works are unusually structured  the musical argument, however, is consistently clear and usually rather uncomplicated; perhaps no wonder when you are composing at such a tremendous rate (the nineteenth symphony was apparently written in a mere two weeks), yet many of the ideas are arresting and rarely less than interesting.

The sixth (subtitled 'Rijck God, wie sal ic claghen), from 1928, is scored for chorus and orchestra. Cast in a single movement, it nevertheless goes through a variety of moods and characters over its 16-minute span, including a rapturous slower section on a Dutch 16th century tune and a gloriously captivating finale. The nineteenth symphony is based on the familiar BACH theme. Cast in four movements but lasting for a total of only some 16 minutes, it is overall a rather low-key work  reflective but transparent and nimble and elegant; compared the relatively powerful fifth and sixth it may perhaps initially strike one as somewhat unremarkable, but it grows on the listener and the character of the work is, if anything, even more individual than in the fifth or sixth. The far more ambitious fifth symphony, for tenor, chorus and orchestra (though tenor and chorus only join in intermittently in the final movement), was completed in 1926, and is a sort of memorial to World War I  the finale sets a poem from the Thirty Years War, and is also the most compelling movement; everything before seems really to work mostly as a set-up for the undeniably powerful finale.

The performances by the Netherlands Symphony Orchestra under David Porcelijn are predictably excellent and they are joined by a very good Consensus Vocalis and, in the fifth symphony, a fine solo performance by Marcel Beekman. The sound is first-rate. Strongly recommended.

reviewText:
For the 40th anniversary, Jethro Tull's "Aqualung" gets a face lift. The cover artwork looks like it has been sitting on a shelf undisturbed for forty years with aged discoloring, but the sound is new. Previous CD releases of this classic have suffered sonically being thin and edgy, much tape hiss, an incomplete track, added reverberation, etc. Most of what is heard here is from 16 track analog tapes circa 1970, which were transferred to 96k/24 bit at Abbey Road by Kris Burton, then remixed by Steven Wilson (of Porcupine Tree fame) via Logic Audio 9.1.4. Steven did a great job! The new mixes really don't sound new, just revived. By using emulators of original period equipment, reducing tape hiss and paying close attention to the original mix, many, many veils have been removed. The sound is much fuller, present and personal. For example, the drums have more "whack". In general, everything has more body and better dynamics. In spite of these improvements, you'd be hard-pressed to notice many changes in individual instrument levels, effects or pans from the original '71 vinyl release. Great work for a great work!

Note the 62.4dBC dynamic range of the new mix of the title track, an improvement of 2.9dB. On average the song is louder (82.5dB vs, 79.6dB), yet still offers more range. The song's quietest passage is 30.2dB, while it's loudest is 92.6dB, versus the 1984 version of 32.2dB and 91.7dB respectively.

Included in the 40th anniversary edition is a 32 page booklet with many color photos of the band, etc., and interviews with Ian Anderson and Steven Wilson.

The second CD contains fourteen 1970 and 1971 recordings made just before and after Aqualung. Five of these tracks have not previously been released, and another three of them have been remastered. This double cd* is a steal for the $17.95 retail price!

*There is also a deluxe 40th Anniversary Collector's Edition, which includes; a 12'x12' 48 page booklet, a 180 gram vinyl pressing, the two cds, a DVD and a Blu-ray. The DVD and Blu-ray have the two cds plus a few extra tracks in 96/24 LPCM stereo, plus a 5.1 remix by Steven Wilson, and the original Quad mix, both in DTS-HD Master Audio and Dolby Digital.

Mr. Band and Mr. Kamin are back!  This time they're out to show they're not just one hit wonders (which so many believe though it wasn't true of the first CD) but they can capture all our hearts again...and they did!

'Two' is a lot more 'postive song' filled then 'Camino Palmero'.  Hey when your biggest hit is along those lines why go away from it?  Sadly this leads many to confuse them with 'similiar yet not' Christian band Lifehouse which tends to scare away a lot of people. So yes this CD will make you feel good but religious messages aren't really here...

'Two' kicks off with 'One by One' a song that might make you question what I just said about positivity.  'One by One' was written about the school shootings and brilliantly shows off Alex's ability to make you think about such things.

'Our lives' picks up the positivity vibe though.  This was the first single and a minor hit in the US (also played at the Olympics if that tells you anything!)  For surely a song to pick you up when your down and a definite Graduating class favorite.

'Things will go my way' continues the trend with a bit more of a cynicaler start.  This was the second single and not as big a hit *but* it was never really given the chance.  I find it quite inspiring myself!

'Chasing the sun' is the first 'Im married now and your gonna listen to me go on about how much I love my wife' song.  Bitter people might just wanna skip ahead a to 'If only'...consider yourself warned!  Its actually a very sweet song and a lot of people think it had great single potential.

'Believing' goes back to the positivity vibe and though inspiring is one of the 'not as great but still great' tracks on 'Two'.

'Anything' is by far one of the greatest The Calling songs EVER!  Written for his wife its a very sweet fast paced love song that if RCA didn't suck so much would have been bigger then 'Wherever you will go'...sadly thats not to happen as it was just announced this single wouldnt be released and 'Two' is done for.  *Sigh* This is one of the best tracks to check out if your a new The Calling fan!

'If only' is a left over from the Camino Palmero era but it might be hard to notice.  Its a sadder song kinda like if you meshed 'Could it be any harder' and 'Unstoppable'...which also means its one heck of a brilliant song!

'Somebody out there' makes me wanna cry every time I hear it.  Its a song about Alex's struggle with being sexually abused at a young age.  Now that you know that you'll probably be like me and have a hard time enjoying it because its so dang sad!

'Surrender' is a bit 'Unstoppable' meets 'If only'.  A good classic The Calling song.  'Dreaming in red' is an odd song about nothing...kinda up there with 'Believing'.  Two finishes up with 'Your hope' a song about simply keeping the faith in yourself no matter what.  One of those tracks that could easily mistake them for a Christian band and a beautiful way to end Two.

Overall a BRILLIANT Sophomore release by The Calling!  A lot of artists fall flat on their faces with the second album but The Calling did no such thing...check it out for youselves and see how brilliant these musical minds are!

reviewText:
It was an employee at the local "wreckastow" Bull Moose who put this in my hand saying I really needed to hear this album. No sales pitch there. Just recommending music based on my taste. Knowing Wes Montgomery's earliest albums as a leader didn't arrive until 1959? The liner notes to this album tell the same story as the man who recommended this. There's little precise data as to where and exactly when they were recorded outside the years. The bass player on two songs is even unknown. That being said? I was curious to know if these near mystery of a recording session would live up to it's tremendous promise. Now I know.

  "Diablo's Dance" starts things off with spicy salsa rhythm while "Round Midnight" takes Wes and organist Melvin Rhyne right back to church. "Darn That Dream","Misty" and "Body And Soul" all take on a slow swinging ballad number that Wes works like a musical Picasso-taking his melodic solos at all musical angles at once. "Straight No Chaser" really brings out the discordant melodies of Thenonious Monk's original to the next level while "Nica's Dream" revisits that Brazilian Salsa vibe to fabulous effect. "Take The A Train" beefs up Billy Strayhorn original with a heavily soulful atmosphere while "After Hours Blues" takes on a slow grinding,Juke Joint style lowdown blues stomp at the very hand.

  The wonders of this music come primarily from it's attitude. Everybody involved here are basically just seeing how thick they can make the melodies and often Brazilian inspired rhythms of this music be. It surely takes on the Dizzy Gillespie styled end of the hard bop/soul jazz approach that was right at home in the mid/late 50's. And the interplay between the musicians is extremely impressive. Each song leaves a lot of room for Wes himself to solo. And therein lies where this album is historically. This album marks the moment when West transitioned out of the Montgomery Brothers trio,with his two siblings in pianist Buddy and bassist Monk,and onto being a leader on his own. From ensemble style playing to full on soloing? The roots of Wes Montgomery's music are already right in place on these nine excellent numbers!

Like many of the other reviews here, this CD, along with Kind of Blue, was the first jazz CD I purchased.  I do remember that my parents owned a copy of Time Out as well, but I was too young to appreciate what a masterpiece  it truly is.  Where to begin?  Take Five deserves every bit of its  reputation as the best-selling jazz song of all time.  From Joe Morello's  sly and understated opening drum licks, to Brubeck's steady rocking piano,  to THE absolute greatest sax lines ever, as blown by the inimitable Mr.  Paul Desmond (I don't want to sound too much like a teenager here, but  Desmond rules!), the song is a pleasure from beginning to end.  It is so  wonderful that it almost brings tears to my eyes every time I hear it.  Every time I play the CD (which is often), I play Take Five first, then  play the whole CD, basically because I just can't wait to hear the song.  It's that good.
Not to be overlooked, Three To Get Ready is a lovely  tune, one that makes my two-year old son sway with pleasure in his high  chair.  I find myself humming Brother Dave's melodious intro. all the time.  Kathy's Waltz is equally wonderful, and is all the more special to me, as  a father, knowing that Dave wrote it for his daughter.  Then...(why am I  wasting space--every song on the CD is great!!)
It thrills me to know  that Mr. Brubeck is still with us, at almost 80 years of age.  I recently  read that the marvelous Joe Morello is now totally blind but still teaches  drums and plays (!) too.  I don't know what has become of Gene Wright, but  his fine bass playing should not be overlooked.
The only sad part for me  is knowing that the incredible Paul Desmond has been dead for more than 20  years.  I haven't had the opportunity to hear all of the great sax players  (yet), but Desmond will always be at the top of my list, especially for  alto players.
BUY THIS CD!!

Verdict?  This is an awesome album!  No old people around here; these guys sound incredible.  The beautiful multi-layered harmonies are present, and so are the hooks.  I just can't stop singing and humming, especially the title cut.

Several reviewers have stated that they felt the Beach Boys were too old to be singing some of the material on the cd.  I guess they want to hear songs about enlarged prostates and hip replacements.  Judging by the reviews and the sales of "Radio", it seems that most of us are enjoying this delightful record.  If the Boys are having fun, and they sound great, then why are their ages relevant?

I know a lot of people have been impressed by the last three songs of the album, but I love it all. From the opening harmonies of "Think About the Days" and "That's Why God Made the Radio", the album starts with a bang (not a loud one)and keeps going.

I am happy for these guys because this album is a real triumph. "Radio" is not just a good record for a group the age of the Beach Boys; it is a  great record for anyone.  The album just has that wonderful classic sound of their former hits.  I honestly can't believe how good they sound.  If you close your eyes, you can almost imagine that they (and we) have never aged, and that the world is still somehow like California was just a few decades ago...

I hope that the Boys will release more music, but this album adds to their legacy and is a really nice way to celebrate the upcoming 50th anniversary of the band.

Nice job, guys.  Thanks for making my radio sound sooo good!

EDIT:
June 22, 2012.  I love this album so much I bought "Sounds of Summer - The Very Best Of The Beach Boys".  It has 30(!) songs, about half of which were new to me.  I made a playlist for my ipod of "Radio" and "Sounds" mixed together, and it is amazing how well the new stuff fits right in with the hits.  I was impressed by the continuity over 50 years.

Finally; if you liked the Beach Boys songs you have heard on the radio, you will love "Sounds Of Summer."  If you don't already own it, buy BOTH.

reviewText:
CCR is high on the list of bands that made me glad I saved all my old records.  As was the case with most bands from the pre-CD era, the first CD reissues of their albums had sound quality that seemed thin enough to tear, so you were better off with the pops and skips on the original vinyl.  That finally changed a few years ago with the remastered versions of all their albums, and this collection features all of those (including liner notes and pictures) plus a bit more.
With nearly every note the four guys from El Cerrito are known to have recorded under their various band names from 1961-1972, this is about as close to a complete collection as we're ever likely to get.  (The infamous "lost" 1962 single of "Yes You Did" and "Now You're Not Mine" is still lost, but everything else appears to be here.)  So unless you bought all the remastered CDs individually, this collection is well worth the price tag to any serious fan.  Creedence was all but unique among singles-oriented bands in that most of their album cuts have aged just as well as their hits, and it shows here.  If anything, relatively obscure songs like "Wrote a Song for Everyone" and "Ramble Tamble" sound fresher than "Proud Mary" and some of the other classics which oldies and classic rock stations have done their best to play into the ground.  Even the much-maligned "Mardi Gras" album proves not to be the disaster it was once made out to be (although it is still their weakest link).  Stu Cook's "Door to Door" actually rocks pretty convincingly, and most of the other selections have their moments as well.
One word of advice:  If you're thinking about buying this collection only for the pre-CCR songs, I wouldn't recommend it.  Some of the early sides are quite good ("You Better Be Careful" and "Fight Fire" would have sounded at home on their first album) and even the weaker efforts are an interesting look at the roots of one of rock's all time greatest bands; but bottom line, there is a reason why they didn't become famous until 1968.  But if there are any other holes in your collection, this is the perfect addition to it.

reviewText:
If you're a lover of Blues-Rock and a lover of Walter Trouts immersion into this legendary art form  he puts his veritable  body and soul into a proclamation that screams and pounds out to the listener that Walter may have been to the absolute precipice of life itself but with a blessing from above and a soul that never forgets where it came from Trout presents a performance here that would blow any formally needed life support equipment out the window!

This CD is a demonstration of how a musical axe can be used like a top-of-the-line pile driver! The fury that Walter booms  through his axe makes the listener believe Walter could use it to blast through the thickest vault door at Fort Knox without a key or a combination. Happily Walter doesnt cheat you on the length of the songs either  Disc 1 is 8 songs (I don't count the two short intros that are listed as disc cuts) and is approximately fifty-five minutes of excitement. (Im rounding off here because the electrical pile driver makes it hard for me to add up the seconds!) Disc 2 is 6 songs for approximately forty-six minutes. Personally when it comes to the blues in addition to length lyrics are quite important and after being at deaths door" and/or heavens gate Walter shares everything from fear to thankfulness so make sure to listen closely.

Some specific highlights that really affected me was the classic electric blues song Say Goodbye To The Blues ten-minutes-40-seconds of absolute blues the way they were meant to be and it was dedicated to B.B. King. Another cut Rock Me Baby though recorded by many people over the years this is by far the most road-house-blues sounding performance Ive heard. It was also heart-warming when Walter would bring his son Jon on the stage to play some guitar. To hear him proudly say. PLAY THE GUITAR SON. THATS MY BOY! added to the overall joy of Walter being back.

One thing I have to add to be straight-forward to the people who read my reviews is to share something I read that another reviewer once wrote a number of years ago and is still true today.  The reviewer said that a long drum solo when you're in person half drunk or loaded may be fun but when you're home listening to an album or CD and hear one its not too exciting and there is one on this CD.

But to finish on a very high note Thank the good Lord for Walters healthy recovery not only is his axe wielding powerful but his voice is smooth silky and strong. And if you had seen how emaciated and weak Walter had become before his life-saving transplant you wouldnt have thought it was possible. Thanks to the glory of the Lord and the continued advancement of medical science Walter is back AND TRULY SOUNDS BETTER THAN PERFORMERS HALF HIS AGE!

reviewText: Dark Passion Play was the beginning of a new era of Nightwish, but the scattered nature of the album's tracks and the disappearance of the original female lead was a turnoff to most older fans. Comparatively speaking, Anette Olzon's first works seemed a bit unpolished across DPP, as if two music styles were butting heads on the tracks. This was not particularly bad, per se, but for a purist it can be a heartwrenching turn of events. For the rest of us, it was an interesting development, and not cause to write off Nightwish at the drop of a hat. Any such pretense of mixed styles or mixed messages died by track two of the newest Nightwish album. Imaginaerum takes all the strengths of the new female lead and plays them for every ounce of power possible. Anette proves she can do the slow operatic pieces that made Nightwish stand out under Tarja, and she can do the powerful pieces in a more upbeat mood as needed for the faster tracks. I gauge her flexibility to be at least equal to the original female lead, but on a different range of vocal pursuit than Tarja. This is not a bad thing, but a different application and the rest of the band has duly compensated to make it work very well. (NOTE: Marco can still do the power metal vocals in his typical fashion, and the rest of the crew are still in top form. No complaints whatsoever for they.) More to the point, the entire album plays on one long story from end to end, and not an entirely happy or dark story at that. Listening to it straight through will give a listener an acute case of mood whiplash, especially going from track by track throughout essentially the whole album. The entire track 12 is a four-part mood whiplash in one movement, with some interesting social commentary at the end. Opinions will be mixed on the accuracy of such things, of course. Two instrumental tracks (7 & 13) give a good occasion to listen to the major instruments without vocals for those who like the lack of lyrics. Effectively, this album is something for everyone for the Nightwish non-purist. If anything, I would say that Tarja moved farther away from Nightwish in her own pursuits (Her solo albums My Winter Storm (U.S Version) and What Lies Beneath) than Nightwish departed their own selves in their new albums.

I have been anxiously awaiting this CD since I saw 3 of Hearts live almost a year ago!  It is well worth the wait!
The album kicks off with "Love is Enough", the single which, in my opinion, did not get enough radio play!  Next up is the Shaye Smith ("Single White Female") penned "It Happened to Me", a song about falling in love. "6, 8, 12" is an awesome cover of the Brian McKnight tune.  "Over the Edge" is another slow song, destined to be a single.  "Sugar and Daisies", co-written by Holly Lamar ("That's the Way"), is an up-tempo, catchy tune that makes you want to dance.  The new single "Arizona Rain", is a change of pace from "Love is Enough", but has a great message about starting over after heartbreak. The first time I heard "The Hard Way" I liked its toe-tapping beat and message of life's lessons.  "Wash Away this Kiss" shows the ladies range, it is a great ballad. "You Break Me" is a phenomenal song by the hugely talented Troy Verges' ("I Would've Loved You Anyway"), the chorus is super catchy and it leans towards the pop genre with is slick beats.  "Is It Love" is poses the question 'Is it love?'.  "Baby That's the Way" closes the CD with a soaring ballad about how being with the one you love fills your heart.
All in all, this is a stunning debut effort by the group, it makes you happy and makes you want to dance!! I look forward to hearing a lot from Katie, Desi and Blaire in the future!!

reviewText:
Hats off the the Heliocentrics crew for hooking up with Mulatu Astake.
Hats off to the production on this recording.
My hat is off and i am getting sunburnt.

If you are a jazz head you might know of Mulatu and his Ethiopetes jazz series (from the 1960's and 70's) and their unique melodic phasing on the horns. I was quite a fan of one of the several issues with the Ethiopetes but i found the others quite difficult to listen to.

The Heliocentrics have one foot firmly rooted in Funk and it works really well on the 'one' and brings back some simple groove to what can sometimes be quite complex ethio jazz arrangements.

This Heliocentrics recording is EASY listening, with some infectious electric bass, brilliant percussion ad all layered up to showcase the unique phrasing of Mulatu Astake's style which is rooted in Ethio jazz.

I don't know why i would mention 'St germain', but for some reason it kind of reminds me of that stuff, but with a lot more creativity, but that same easy listening feel about it.

I enjoy this album very much, even more than the old recordings of Mulatu Astake and I am now a convert of the Heliocentrics and greatly look forward to their future recordings.

This album is one for the jazz head, as it is different, new and fresh....but also a really nice one for anyone on the fence wondering about the world of jazz....i guess it would classified as 'jazz' but it seems a bit too funky, too many twisted fusions to be called straight 'jazz'.

reviewText:
After a long seven year wait Sarah Mclachlan finally came back with an album, and I have to say that the wait is definitely worth it.
With this album, Sarah went with the time and made her album darker and more leaning towards rock and Fumbling Towards Ecstasy sound than her mellower albums such as Surfacing. Some of the songs (Awakening, Love Come, Out of Tune for e.g.) sounded a little bit like Depeche Mode's Precious in that gorgeous techno-rock way. Her lyrics are much better than Afterglow. Her voice is just as good and expressive as before. Her melodies are much more complicated, like Fumbling. I believe it is a great improvement of her last album. But then again I would need to listen to it a few more times before I can completely decide. Because Afterglow grew on me a great deal. But all I can say as of now is that, fans don't worry, it sounds just like her; her style hasn't changed, it's still Sarah, which means no matter what you should at least like it if you are her fan like I am. So go buy it with confidence :)

Now I have to complain a few things about this album:
1. doing a cover of Susan Enan's Bring On the Wonder. Don't get me wrong, her version is great, but the thing is that the song is too well known (especially for those Bones watchers) and Enan's version simply cannot be topped. So some can see this as kind of leaning toward laziness because this is the first time I can recall that Sarah is covering a song on a studio album as a main track that wasn't written by her.
2. Putting two songs she's already released before on Closer Don't Give Up On Us and U Want Me Too on her album. I'm just thankful that I didn't buy Closer and waited so they are still fresh for me.
3. The album is slightly overproduced in that many of the background vocals were obviously not hers. Sorry I tend to have a qualm about "helping vocals" I tend to like it better if the background vocals were also the singers. There are exceptions, of course, but in this case I think I would like it better if the male background vocals weren't there.

But these are just little things, and I understand her obligations towards her family more than music. Overall it still deserves 5 stars. Thank you Sarah!!!

P.S. Awakening really should be the first single; it is an absolutely gorgeous first track!!!

reviewText:
After listening to Can't Slow Down for several days now, I have become a convert. Honestly I was not that impressed the first time I heard it, but it definitely has grown on me. Yes, I still believe Foreigner will never be the same without Lou Gramm's vocals (see my review of Insider Information). What it was before it is no longer. I said I could not imagine liking anything but the original line-up of the group. However, this new incarnation is surprisingly high quality. I am actually glad to have to eat my words because I truly enjoy this album. More than just enjoying it, I find myself coming back to it again and again. The album has an integrity and a consistently smooth sound, which again is different from the Lou Gramm days. Yes, it does have hints of the old Foreigner sound, and Kelley Hansen is a good fit on vocals, but it really is a new band.

Once I stopped comparing this to the Foreigner of the 80s, I could appreciate it for what it is. What if I just picked this up and listened to it simply as a new album by a new band? While this admittedly this is impossible, I believe I would find myself drawn into to the hooks and harmonies. Mick Jones' composing is up to modern standards and sounds fresh even while it echoes the past. Especially fine are "I'll Be Home Tonight," "As Long as I Live," and "Angel Tonight," but there are really no filler tracks here. Production is top notch, and the tunes are catchy. Unlike another reviewer, I like the mix of ballads just fine. I believe you will find, as I did, that this new Foreigner has truly struck a good chord.

reviewText: This is the first Elias album I ever heard and was instantly smitten by her musicianship and voice. It was only later that I delved into her larger body of Brazilian material. She practically channels Bill Evans on piano, but it's her vocals that make this album special to me. Having her husband Marc Johnson on bass and Joey Baron on drums round out the experience. Although I knew Johnson actually played with Evans, for some reason I kept imagining he and Baron as Scott LaFaro and Paul Motian - my favorite Evans trio line-up. Perhaps it is merely evidence of my mind going in my old age, since both Johnson and Baron have their own musical styles, but I caught glimmers of LaFaro and Motian in their playing the same as I could clearly hear Evans himself in Elias' playing. Sadly there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review, but you can run through them on this page: Something For You MP3. Let those and your ears guide you because you can hear enough of each track to make up your mind if this album is for you. I mention this because I notice that some of Elias' fans are not as enchanted with her when she steps outside her Brazilian heritage. For me, it's the standards and tributes that I most love (although I love her Bossa albums too.) One final note: this and I Thought About You (A Tribute To Chet Baker) get a lot of play in my home, but I think that a tribute to George Shearing would be a natural for her and an incredible gift to music in general. One can only hope.

reviewText:
It's the Eighties, so be prepared to have fun listening to some excessive axework in this great live record. Yngwie plays here with the intensity you expect from a guitar hero of his magnitude, up to burning his guitar out. His performance is passionate and brilliant, even when he missed out some notes here and there - but I love that: he didn't hide his errors in order to retain the actual "taste" of the live show, and I think that's a very honest attitude.
The guy unarguably is one of the greatest guitar players of all times - yes, he is; in spite of any critic, any rumor (or fact) about his ego, any repetitive playing or anything else. :-) This album demonstrates how good he actually is, as Yngwie proudly shows all his abilities off, from the purely neoclassic shredding in "Black Star" and "Trilogy Suite", to the explicit quotes to Paganini, Bach, Beethoven and the likes all the way along, to the frantic riffing in any of his own songs with vocals, to the bluesly soloing in the Hendrix's song "Spanish Castle Magic" and in "Spacebo Blues" - at whose end he also amuses the crowd with some great feedback and guitar effects.
Furthermore, the choice of sung pieces is great. This CD contains many of the best vocal tracks of Yngwie's early solo career - mainly from "Trilogy" and "Odyssey". Joe Lynn Turner's mellow vocals seamlessly fit into Yngwie's style, yet doing far better than Mark Boals when singing those songs from the "Trilogy" album. The production honors his voice, and that's fair to his amazing performance.
Lynn is a great songwriter too. "Odyssey" (the studio album to whose tour this gig belongs to) includes a bunch of amazing material. That material is showcased in "Trial by fire" in a clean manner. I still think that the Yngwie/Lynn combination was a killer one from the songwriting point of view - just tell me: do you *really* believe that those cheesy and ridiculous love lyrics are specially worst than those others lyrics about warriors, dragons, knights, swords and kings? C'mon! :-)
By the way, going back to Joe Lynn Turner, I'd want to point out some few things about him in this review. This vocalist has been widely criticized because he aims commercialism too much, because he's mellow, because he's not aggressive enough, because he doesn't like wailing, etc. Maybe all that is true, but he has one of the greatest, cleanest, most perfectly tuned and most melodic voices ever heard in the rock genre. He also has a superb tone and a truly wide vocal range - listen carefully to his interpretation of "Liar". Isn't it GREAT? In addition, he is a master of dynamics - the enormous load of feeling that he delivers in "Dreaming" says it all! And he doesn't miss a single note in this album! This album witnesses that he can perform live as a genuine vocal god. Honestly, I believe he deserves much more recognizance for the flawlessly job he does here and in every band where he has performed (including Rainbow and Deep Purple).
Back to "Trial by Fire", this album contains an excellent choice of Yngwie Malsmteen's "hits" (if so can be said) and astonishing guitar pyrotechnics complemented with vocals of the highest quality. I strongly recommend this CD even for Yngwie newbies. Hard rockers will appreciate it too. So, go for it NOW, put it into your CD player, fasten your seatbelts and enjoy! The trip will pay off, I guarantee you that.

Well it just doesn't get much better then this for Chuck Berry. The Great Twenty-Eight is really THE greatest hits. Spanning one decade from 1955 through 1965 chronicling Berry's greatest period in music, and arguably his most influential time, really it was the most important time in music all around.

Containing virtually everything the casual Berry fan would want to own, The Great Twenty-Eight is really as good as it gets. Whether it's the guitar classic 'Johnny B. Goode' or the fun 'Roll Over Beethoven' it doesn't matter because it is all here. This is the collection of songs that inspired a thousand guitar players from Joe Perry and Ted Nugent to Keith Richards and Eric Clapton.

The king of Boogie is represented perfectly here and no other collection comes close to this. Berry was the singles kind and this proves it.

reviewText:
Two shining stars join to create a fresh and vital performance of the beloved Tchaikovsky Piano Concerto No. 1 in B flat minor. Danil Trifonov is highly respected for his virtuosity both on works for the piano alone and for concerti. Here he collaborates with Valery Gergiev and the Mariinsky Orchestra is a brisk and sparkling approach to the often times lugubrious concerto.

Everything sounds fresh and almost spontaneous in conception  tempi are a bit on the fast side, but Trifonov balances that aspect with his pulling on the heartstrings in the other sections.

In all this is a fine performance of a favorite that renews interest in the piece. With the entire recording Trifonov is at his finest in his solo performances of Un poco di Chopin, the Chopin Barcarolle, and the Schubert/Liszt Erlknig, Frhlingsglaube, Die Forelle, Auf dem Wasser au singen, Die Stadt, and Liebeslied. Grady Harp, August 17

reviewText: Lemon Records (U.K.) is the first label to pair up these classic BTO albums and has done an excellent job remastering them. No longer do you hear hiss from the second or third generation tapes that were used in the U.S. releases. Also, the enclosed bookelet includes the original artwork and informative liner notes by Malcolm Dome. "Not Fragile" was released in 1974 and immediately spawned the band's most popular hit ever "You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet" with it's stuttering vocals courtesy of Randy Bachman. But quite frankly it wasn't that song that blew me away as much as it was "Roll On Down The Highway", the self titled "Not Fragile", "Sledgehammer", "Free Wheelin'" and the jazzy rocker "Rock Is My Life, And This Is My Song" with it's infectous guitar solo. The following year BTO released "Four Wheel Drive" which was a good album but not quite up to par as it's previous release. The hit "Hey You" was all over the airwaves in 1975 and "Four Wheel Drive" also recieved a good amount of airplay. Other songs on the album I remember playing over and over were "Flat Broke Love" and "She's Keeping Time". BTO continued to release albums ("Head On", Street Action", Rock N' Roll Nights" etc.) but in my opinion their best stuff was from 1972-1975. Hopefully Lemon records will released the self titled debut BTO along with BTO II on one cd and remastered. Snag this one up before it goes out-of-print.

reviewText:
A moment before the phenomenal success of "Born To Run"(BTR) , came "The Young The Innocent and the E-Street Shuffle", several months after his advent with "Greetings From Asbury Park NJ " . The latter two albums together are considered and heard as something young, fresh, new and full of happiness . Springsteen, at the dawn of his career, sounds enthusiastic and thrilled to get started and try to reach nationwide distribution and recognition .
As with all his later albums, it seems like he invested every inch of talent at his disposal to achieve his very best , and did he achieve it , pale ! I have to emphasize that what I'm saying here stands for both albums, since they are much alike in sound , atmosphere and the feeling they generate in me. Listening to them you don't have to wonder why Bruce was considered from the very start as the "New Dylan" , and as a big promise on his own . Almost every song in these albums is special and remarkable, and as with his later works, some songs are rhythmic and represent the `Rock and Roll' side, and the others are unique ballads only a few others can compete with .
Now, as mentioned, "Born To Run" brought the major success and the big bucks . From that point on the man has grown up , a fact that made his songs more and more serious and even somber now and then, a fact that was distinct in "Darkness On the Edge Of Town" after the quarrel he'd had with the record company. "The River" was also not an entirely jolly album , just listening the song "The River" confirms . In "Born In The U.S.A" he protested against the government , while in "Tunnel Of Love" he mourned his ruined marriage , and so forth . My point is - you're left with these two (maybe Three, including "BTR") albums as a witness of a worries free, innocent , happy and youthful Springsteen . More precisely, only the two first ones embody the maiden style, before the transformation he has gone through in "BTR" to the Springsteen we know to date, a fact that make them even more desirable .
Switching solely to "The Young, The Innocent And The E - Street Shuffle" , if you're a serious fan you can't let this one go by : all the above is revealed from the very first song --- "The E - Street Shuffle"--- What a song ! All the excitement of a young man from the life he's discovering is wrapped up in this song . You actually hear and feel Springsteen's will to devour the world and everything it offers in the composition and in each and every word written . Then, you cannot fall in love, on first listen, with the beautiful `Sandy' a delicate longing song, probably for his former girlfriend . Bruce sings like he's telling a story in some parts , and in other parts he sings almost in the pace of talking, a twist that adds a lot to the impact of the song . Long after I'd heard it(fot the first time !) I couldn't stop humming the chorus `Hey Sandy girl, my, my, my, my ,my baby ...".

The next song I wish to discuss is "Incident on 57th street" . This is so relaxing creation - just hearing the line "Good night it's alright baby..." produces a pleasant feeling of peace and tranquility I can't stay indifferent to . And if I dare dozing off, the Boss returns to the funky rhythm and wakes me up with the fervent "Rosalita" that really rocks . Lastly, we're introduced to the grandest epic in this album - "New York City Serenade" - a poem that delivers everything its name implies ; This is the longest song in the album (up to 10 minutes), consisting a few musical genres that integrate wonderfully in one another , making it a fitting closure to a great album .
I can sum it all up by saying that the 5 stars consensus here in Amazon says it all -  no way are you going to be dissatisfied with this terrific album !

It's just great songs after great songs. Basically this cd gets better and better everytime I listen to it, and I find myself constantly tapping my feet or nodding my head, and in general, this CD makes me smile whenever I hear it. It would be a HUGE mistake not to buy it, and I think anyone could enjoy it, whether you're a killers fan or not. reviewText:
Laura Branigan really honed her style in her sophomore effort, which firmly established her in the ranks of 80's pop/rock women like Pat Benatar and Sheena Easton.  Chalk up another winner for one of the 1980's best pop/rock goddesses.
Branigan 2-the Sequel, begins with the single "Solitaire" on a woman who's alone now after a bad relationship and it falls under reflective/breakup song.  "Solitaire, it got so lonely/Solitaire, no one to hold me/Where were you when I played solitaire?"  The melody reminds me of Sheena Easton's "Long Distance Love Affair" and has the same pace, although it rocks as hard as any of Benatar's material.  A big highlight here!  Getting this is not akin to playing poker--you'll hit the jackpot anytime.
"Deep In The Dark" features a monologue and is a forerunner to "Self Control" is rhythm and the chorus.
"Close Enough" is actually a positive love song that Journey could have tried to do, given the searing keyboard synthesizers.  However, it's Laura's song hands down.  She sings "Close enough to make it last/Now there's no turning back/We'll do it together." And to finalize the moment, she says, "And now, now the time has come/To keep the love we found just close enough."
"Lucky" tells of the woman's necessity to leave someone unfulfilling who was oblivious to her pain.  The chorus and keyboards are akin to a muted version of "Gloria."  It goes "Lucky, I said I hope you try and understand/Lucky, guess it's not like we planned/Lucky, you know I really really love you so/But Lucky, I still have to go."  This could easily become a country song, given the right singer.
Then comes her cover of the Who's "Squeeze Box," tastefully done in the mid-paced Branigan style pop.  And now, to set the record straight, comes a lovely song that may have been a hit for Michael Bolton but was covered beforehand by Laura-"How Am I Supposed To Live Without You."  She's got the better voice too.  The ultimate Branigan heartbreak song is right here-"Tell me how am I supposed to live without you/Now that I've been lovin' you so long/How am I supposed to live without you/And how am I supposed to carry on/When all that I've been livin' for is gone."  Good going, Laura!
"I'm Not The Only One" is a dance number akin to Self Control's "Satisfaction."  "Mama" is a daughter-to-mother letter proving the daughter right, that yes, she did become a bad girl, but the guy she fell for made it worth it and they're still together.
The narrator in the soaring pop ballad "Find Me" displays a great vulnerability and emotion, wanting the shelter of someone's arms.  That's the opposite case in the fierce, bitter rocker "Don't Show Your Love," extolling loneliness and freedom.  A key lyric spells it out:  "Loneliness lives out in the world/People afraid to give/Better off free, out on your own/Living your life alone."  She's definitely talking about the capitalist 80's, where people loved money."
No, she did not call her next album Branigan 3, because she had Self Control-sorry, I couldn't resist.

It's amazing that such a lovely, talented and successful singer has been largely forgotten today. With her striking dark looks and haunting voice, Branigan was a fixture in both the pop and dance scenes here and in Europe, transitioning nicely into the world of MTV as well. Perhaps since the music is so rooted in the 80s synth-pop sound (think Flashdance and Moroder) people find it dated or embarrassing. Too bad, because she was a talented vocalist that transcends genres, giving her songs an emotion weight and sincere reading that others just cant achieve.

This, her first LP, is a mixed bag. It's apparent the label is trying to find the right way to market their young charge: the mood careens from dance to ballads to country and rock. In a skimpy 9 track album, that's quite a feat. Here on the remastered reissue the slight offering is rounded out with bonus tracks that, while enjoyable, emphasize the schizophrenic feel of the record.

But you know what? It's all good, and worth buying. Even if it plays like a compilation, with it's array of different producers and writers, Branigan steps up and takes command of each song.

My two faves, the ballads When and I Wish We Could Be Alone were both penned by the singer herself and are stunning. This CD is a must for any Laura Branigan fans, and those getting to know her voice and music.

reviewText:
I discovered Journey a few years ago, while watching VH1's hilarious series "I Love the 80's".  As a fan of 80's music I realized I could not go on without hearing more of this classic band, so I sent my parents on a grand journey to pick up this album.

Immediately, I fell in love with the band.  There's a certain freedom in their songs that feels relaxing, like a cool breeze.  Of course, it can be empowering as well.  What I love so much about the 80's is the huge amount of emotion captured in that decade's entertainment.  Journey - and this album - are a perfect example of that.

The album opens with "Only The Young", a fine example of what the band's capable of.  Steve Perry's optimistic, high-flying vocals accompany strong drums and hopeful lyrics.  This song is exclusive to this CD.

The second song on the album is my personal favorite.  "Don't Stop Believin'" is what the 80's were all about - trying to find romance and grab life the horns, to really feel alive.  Steve Perry is as his finest, and there's some terrific guitar and percussion.

"Wheel in the Sky" sounds to me like a song of regret, and of someone who's trying to keep going in life.  It's lead by great guitar and powerful vocals.

"Faithfully" is about a man's relationship with his loved one and how his travels strain the relationship.  It's one of the more popular love songs of the early eighties.

"I'll Be Alright Without You" is about a man who has just broken-up with someone, who is angry with her and who is trying to forget her, but he can't get her out of his head.

Sixth on the album is "Any Way You Want It", a song that many a fan has rocked out to (myself included).  Moviegoers may remember Rodney Dangerfield dancing to this in the 1980 comedy hit "Caddyshack".  Feel the music and go mad!

"Ask the Lonely" feels like it should be in an inspirational exercise montage in something like "Rocky IV".  Not that that's a bad thing.

"Who's Crying Now" is an easy-going song thought up by Steve Perry while he was driving to San Francisco.  In the pouring rain he went to Jonathan Cain's house and together they finished writing the song.

"Seperate Ways (Worlds Apart)" is one of my favorites.  The synthesizers in the opening transform into heavy percussion and strong guitar.  One of the harder Journey pieces, and I love it.

"Lovin', Touchin', Squeezin'" is one of the band's earlier songs.  It's a blues song, and it stands apart from the rest of the songs on the album because of it.

"Open Arms" is another one of my favorites.  Wondering why the band was one of the biggest make-out groups of the eighties?  This'll tell you why.  It's a powerful love ballad and considered by many to be one of the decade's best.

"Girl Can't Help It" has a great chorus: The girl can't help it, she needs more / He hasn't found what he's looking for / They're still standing in the rain / He can't help it, and she's just that way.

"Send Her My Love" seems to me to be a little more calm than the rest of their songs.  Living in Vermont, the opening makes me feel like I'm driving through the hills in the countryside, and it's a powerful feeling.  The 2:40 mark is my favorite part in the song.

"Be Good to Yourself" is a great way to end the album.  It's a fast-paced, feel-good piece full of joy - and Steve Perry, of course.

For people looking to see what the band's about I'd highly recommend this album; people who already know to expect should probably pick up the 2-CD remastered "Essential Collection" set.  But if, like me, you love the 80's and just wanna give it a try, then this CD is absolutely essential.

reviewText: This album consists of songs from Rick Nelson's last three significant albums. Unfortunately, some of these songs were not even released until 1993. The contents of this album further substantiates the diversity of  Rick Nelson's music and his talent at making a song his very own. This  album shows him at his most comfortable ever as he sings mostly  contemporary country and classic folk tunes. "One X One" is the  most outstanding example of Rick's talent in conveying a powerful mood and  spirit through the lyrics he sings. This folksy, Peter Paul and Mary -like  tune possesses a quality of delightful innocence. I also feel that Rick  sings his best rendition of a Bob Dylan song by way of the classic,  "Mama You Have Been On My Mind." This tune enraptures you from  the very start because of its timeless beauty and innocence. Two other  incredible tunes with a timeless feel are "Stay Young" and  "Conversations"-contemporary country works. Finally, his cover of  "Dream Lover" is by far one of his finest recordings of the  latter part of his career and even surpasses Bobby Darin's original  version. A must album for any true Rick Nelson fan of fan of contemporary  country music!

reviewText:
First thank you to Al and Michael and Bob and everyone else associated with this for the love and respect you give Michael.  I have loved his playing and attitude and other gifts since I bought that first Butterfield album when it first came out.  That, Muddy's best and a Lightnin' Hopkins were my first real blues albums after going through the Stones and Animals to get there.  I'm on my fourth or fifth copy of the first Butter album and own many others featuring Michael.  I'm still on the first Disc and I'm familiar with much to come but want to jump into the early reviews just to pay homage to a hero of mine and to offer a few hints to others, whol like one reviewer here, may only have Super Session.

I did notice the edit on Killing Floor.  That seemed unnecessary but I wasn't there making the decisions.  We're all here because we loved Michael so let's forgive decisions we didn't get to make.

I mostly want to point at my favorites that aren't here.  I read a Bloomer biography a few years ago that had a short disc stuck in the back.  As I remember, without going home and pulling it out, it was playing from Big John's or from that pre-Butter period.  You hear the distinctive Bloomfield phrasing but he is lacking some restraint that came later.  Still great to hear.  I love the Hammond stuff here.  That fast pickin' song, wow!  So if I got to chose my favorite Butterfield cuts not included here they would include: Shake Your Moneymaker, Screamin' (two geniuses at work together), I Got  A Mind To Give Up Livin', and Two Trains Running (who's solos have such beautiful architectture and emotional intensity).  Another Butter cut would be Nut Popper (I think that's the title), an instrumental on the "Lost First Butter album, or whatever its called.  Many great cuts there.  Like others I'd include the Guitar Player Album, If You Love These Blues..., which wasn't available for years on cd but now is.  It showcases some of the breadth of Michael's ability.  I would have for sure included Mama Lion with Nick singing in this set.  Finally, one not many seem to mention is the Woody Herman set, Brand New.  I must have read about it in Rolling Stone when it came out because I had it when it came out.  Just ordered the CD here on Amazon. (Oops, I also forgot Two Jews Blues by Barry Goldberg)

If they started issuing random live sets for Michael like they do with Johnny Winter nowadays I'd be there with my credit card.  I suppose since so much of Michaels prime stuff is in bands with others like the Flag and Butter that it would be hard to get all the permissions you need to release things.  Anyway, I'm at least still hoping for an expanded Live Adventures and glad to see a bunch of that and a couple with Nick at the Filmore and that other recent live one from that period.

What a loss, his passing but thanks again to all for this excellent tribute.  Hopefully it will whet some appetites and people will go out and get some of the original albums to hear more.

OK, I'm just writing to please myself.  Don't slag me, Mr One-star, or any of his friends.  This one was truely A Long Time Comin' and I'm glad it's here.

Just want to check in since I finished disc three.  I sort of thought things might go down a little on the third disc but I'm very happy with it.  That Glamour Girl is just plain incredible and there are lots of other nice ones on there too. Got me to pull out so other stuff.  I've got about a hundred songs on a Bloomfield play list on my Ipod.  Forgot how great Fathers and Sons is, not a ton of Michael but Paul and Muddy are just at their best.  Really like the Dylan cut too.  Now when I get that Woody Herman disc in the mail (only had the LP before this) I'll be ready to go.  I'm also going to get a few more of the 70s discs to round things out.

As I look back on my Bloomer hero worship, I know that for me it was always about those blazing electric leads.  Part of the disappointment of the 70s for me was all his acoustic stuff, just not my bag.  But now that I've grown up to be an old man with a minor bit of guitar playing behind me, I realize what a well rounded musician Michael was.

Final comment: this set is so totally worth it.  If this is all you own of Michael, well you might not have my favorite moments but you will have a good overview of a fine gentleman and a "nice outstanding musician" (as Junior Wells once referred to Sonny Boy 2.  But if you get serious this is a good pointer to many other charms.  Keep searchin'.

reviewText: This album is just absolutely incredible, I really don't even know how else to describe it. While Iron Maiden's 1986 classic "Somewhere in Time" featured the band experimenting with synthesizers, here on their 1988 follow up "Seventh Son of a Seventh Son", they decided to take the progressiveness from the previous album further to an even more epic level of sheer brilliance with a handful of progressive elements on this album, especially on the near 10 minute title track which is a great example. SSOASS is also a concept album that follows the story of a cursed child who is born with special powers and is tempted by both good and evil, meanwhile the band's chemistry and musicianship are completely intact and in full force. Bruce Dickinson's vocals are incredible as always, while Steve Harris delivers excellent basslines that he's so well known for, and Nicko McBrain continues to show his masterful talents behind the drums. And of course, guitarists Adrian Smith and Dave Murray both continue to lash out a series of amazing riffs and solos throughout, unfortunately Adrian would depart from the band after this album, and wouldn't return until 2000's "Brave New World". Every song on SSOASS is a winner, but here are my favorite highlights. The opening song "Moonchild" starts off with acoustic guitars and clean, relaxing vocals from Bruce, until it builds on into a fast, adrenaline pumping headbanger with more aggressive vocals, guitars, and drums. There's also a great use of keyboards in the background as well. Track two "Infinite Dreams" is an excellent melodic number featuring more great vocals from Bruce and awesome soaring leadwork. This song is just perfect. The third track "Can I Play With Madness" is another classic Maiden tune which is followed by another catchy energetic rocker in "The Evil That Men Do", while the epic title track "Seventh Son of a Seventh Son" is a near 10 minute piece of pure musical magic. The band's musicianship is just absolutely wonderful throughout especially with the masterful instrumental section. A brilliant song this is, and one of the best songs on here, I may add. My favorite track on here would definately have to be "The Clairvoyant". It features an excellent bass intro by Harris, as well as a soaring chorus, awesome background keyboards, and more fantastic soloing. A true classic. And then we have the album's grand finale "Only the Good Die Young" which features fast riffs, another great solo, and a powerful chorus. The ending also closes the way that it began on "Moonchild" as well. All in all, SSOASS is another masterful work of pure musical brilliance from one of metal's all time greatest and most dedicated bands. It's truly an absolute must have for any fan of Iron Maiden, believe me, you won't be disappointed one bit...UP THE IRONS!!!

reviewText: The pairing of the 3rd piano concerto and the Choral Fantasy was the one of the original LP, Columbia ML 6016 (mono) and MS 6616 (stereo), so it is understandable that Sony should reissue it as it was, although the 4th piano concerto would have made a more fitting coupling with the Choral Fantasy, since the two compositions were premiered together, at the infamous 22 December 1808, four-hour long concert which also witnessed the premieres of the 5th and 6th symphony, and portions of the C-major mass for good measure (in an unheated hall). If fact, the pairing of the 4th and the Choral Fantasy is such an obvious one that it is amazing that apparently no record label has ever thought about it. Anyway, let's satisfy ourselves with what we get, now and in 1964 (The 3rd Piano Concerto was recorded n January of that year; the Choral Fantasy was done in May 62, during the same sessions with the Emperor). The combination of Serkin's classicim and preference for a dry staccato touch, and Bernstein's heart-on-sleeve passion and involvement may not seem an obvious one, but it has yielded here fine results. In the first movement of the 3rd Piano Concerto they offer an urgent and muscular reading, vehement even, with Serkin always underlining the music's muscularity rather than its delicacy, his dry touch conveying a crispness even in the more lyrical passages. The Largo may not have the hushed and dreamy quality and sensuous orchestral environment of Katchen-Gamba (Art of Julius Katchen 1), and the finale their boisterous dynamism, but they are fine nonetheless, the Largo especially, played with beautiful restraint. The finale is crisp and muscular, if lacking the last touch of forward momentum. While Serkin and Bernstein's reading of the 3rd Piano Concerto is good, their Choral Fantasy is (like their Emperor) outstanding. Many people, even Beethoven lovers, seem puzzled by the Choral Fantasy, presumably because it seems piecemeal and disjointed, and because they cannot categorize it: a piano concerto of sorts that starts with a huge improvisatory cadenza, and ends with a chorus, something like a sketch for the 9th Symphony, that erups only in the last minutes of the circa 18 to 20 minute-composition. I love the Choral Fantasy, not only because it is filled with melodies and touches of orchestration that are equal to Beethoven's best, but also because it follows no other rule than those of Beethoven's inspiration (it was written in great haste). Serkin and Bernstein pull all these strands together magnificently. As befits the composition's episodic nature, it is a version of contrasts, urgent AND lyrical. It starts with an urgent and highly dramatic introductory cadenza, a far cry from the more grandiose and stately approach of Katchen (Art of Julius Katchen 2), Barenboim (Beethoven: Piano Concerto No. 5/Choral Fantasia) or, more recently, Aimard with Harnoncourt (Beethoven: Triple Concerto; Rondo in B flat; Choral Fantasy). The same spirit of menacing urgency imbues the first phrases of the orchestra, first entoned by cellos and double basses (2:51), as well as the "allegro molto" section at at 7:37, which exudes an almost raging energy, and the biting Marcia at 12:18 (track 4). But Serkin commendably relaxes for the more lyrical utterances, as when the main theme is stated by piano alone at 4:12, with the ensuing woodwind chirping conveying a fine sense of pastorale bonhomie, or in the dreamy and delicate Adagio (9:17). The vocal soloists are from the chorus and, while not exceptional, they are very acceptable, and I could hardly detect a trace of American accent in their delivery of their German lines. The final chorus is powerful and triumphant. Other than some important pizz accompaniment figures that are covered by the piano at 1:09 track 4 (13:17), the sonics are great, the soloists sing with utmost clarity, every word can be understood. This is, indeed, a great performance of the Choral Fantasy. The same has been issued on volume 11 of the Bernstein collection, paird with the Missa Solemnis and Haydn's Theresienmass: Beethoven : Missa Solemnis / Choral Fantasy & Haydn : Theresia Mass.

reviewText:
No, this is not Nightwish.... so who gives a sh&t? Because Tuomas is the composer/keyboardist of NW he is restricted to just writing and playing power metal? I  listen to a lot of different music, a lot of Nordic power metal, rock, jazz, blues, yada yada, and this new CD from Tuomas Holopainen could best be described as classical/symphonic with a little celtic thrown in. Regardless, this is some of the most beautiful music I've ever heard, and I've listened to well over 300 CDs in the last year alone.

Now that I've listened to it about ten times I feel that I can say that this music is beautiful, inspiring, amazing, different, and just sensational. I loathe reviews where the reviewer has to rate every track on the album as I view albums as a whole. I am not going to give or deduct points based on how many 'good' tracks are on it, in relation to how many of them  suck, which is how a lot of people review an album. I will say though, that there is no bad track on this CD... each one is superb and beautiful, and Tuomas' keyboard work on it leaves me at a loss for superlatives to describe just how good it is. A part of Tuomas' genius is how he uses several vocalists he's worked with before, including Johanna Kurkela and Tony Kakko of Sonata Arctica. it also features The London Philharmonic Orchestra, the choir group Metro Voices, and several guest musicians including fellow Nightwish member Troy Donockley who plays the celtic instruments Uilleann pipes, Bouzuki and the Mandola.

As others have commented, this CD sounds like a terrific movie soundtrack, and I would not be surprised if it someday becomes the soundtrack to the Scrooge McDuck movie that has not yet become a movie, or some other film. I bet a movie producer could license this work a lot cheaper than hiring Hans Zimmer... he heh.

Bottom line - Tuomas is a genius. This CD is sensational. Go get it now.

reviewText:
On Music of My Mind, Stevie spread his wings. On this album he stretches his genius. This is the first real masterpiece of the numerous Stevie has given us. As I always do in my reviews, let's go song by song.
You Are the Sunshine of My Life: As he did on Music of My Mind, Stevie surprises us here in the first song several ways. First, the first notes heard are actually a progression of minor 3rd chords. This is something that had never been heard in popular music before. The song has become so popular now anyone can hum that very chord progression. Stevie's teaching us as he goes. The next surprise is that the first voice heard is not Stevie's! It is a male voice but it's from someone we don't know! Then, the next voice you hear is....again not Stevie's! It's female now! Why all the surprises? It's Stevie's way of keeping us on our toes. And, a way of making an otherwise regular pop song into something interesting. On the 45 version, Stevie adds horns which makes the song sound a little more upbeat. On the album without the horns, it sounds a lot more solemn. Which leads us to.....
Maybe Your Baby: This song is about the age old question, "Is she cheating on me?" or "Am I losing her?" Stevie has two songs that deal with this subject, the incredible Lately on Hotter Than July and this one. Lately is more like Beethoven meets Ray Charles. Maybe Your Baby is more like Ray Charles meets Johnny Lee Hooker and Eric Clapton. This is gut bucket, heartwrenching, rockin' side to side, cryin' in your beer music, and it's the best example of how someone feels when they think or know they're being cheated on, or for some reason, is losing their lover. The title itself is a stroke of genius. The "Maybe" in it is what keeps us from completely believing the truth, even though it's right in front of our eyes. The song also features a background vocal that continually repeats the phrase, "Maybe your baby done made some other plans" in a very high-pitched voice. It's enough to drive you crazy. Which is exactly the point! The voice represents the thoughts that rage through our minds when we've been jilted by a lover. That's coupled with a very distorted rock guitar that plays in the background. My suggestion is to grab a beer, think about an old lover and put on this song. I garauntee you you'll play it over and over again.
You and I: The second of what would become known as the Classic Stevie Wonder Ballad (primarily voice, bass and piano). This song is about the greatness of every relationship that a person has. Whether it's good or bad we take something from it. That something is generally knowlegde. This song is cinematic in it's sound and great in it's delievery. A true classic.
Tuesday Heartbreak: After two heartwrenching songs, Stevie gives us a little break with this one. It's more upbeat, although it's still singing about the wanting of love. It's a lesser song on the album but still very good.
You've Got it Bad Girl: This song harps back to Girl Blue on Music Of My Mind. Again it's about a person who doesn't see the lover right in front of them. Beautiful chords, melody and a very jazzy drum line give this song a soul.
Superstition and Big Borther: This is a book you know. And like any book you have the main subject (in this case, a break up and it's aftermath) but there are always other things going on around the main story. Stevie separates Superstition and the next song, Big Brother by first, having them start the second side of the original album, and by connecting them musically by having Superstition's ending horns melt into Big Brother's opening clavinet. But what can you say about Superstition that hasn't already been said. It's a great song by an amazing artist and musician. Big Brother is quieter musically but just as loud, if not louder thematically.
Blame it On the Sun: The lyrics to this song were written by Syreeta Wright, Stevie's ex-wife. She is the same ex that this album is basically all about. In this chapter of the book, we're at the "Who's fault is it anyway" point of the breakup. We blame it on everything except ourselve until finally we have to take responsibility. It's a beautiful song with some haunting moog synth work throughout.
Looking for Another Pure Love: This is smooth jazz before it was ever created. In this chapter we're at the stage where we've finally accepted the fact that it's over and we have to move on. We're looking for another pure love. Not just another love but a pure one. There's a nice guitar solo by Jeff Beck that helps bring the song to another level. All this is fronted by a warm lead vocal by Stevie and nice floating backup vocals too. A great warmup, if you will, for what's to come next.
I Believe When I Fall In Love This Time It Will Be Forever: Long title, long song. And another great finale to a great album. It starts slow and wanting, revs up to become a slow rocker and finally explodes with love and sincerity into a full blown rocking/gospel shout. It's Stevie the optimist again basically stating that he's been through a lot (Shattered dreams, worthless years. Here am I encased inside a hollow shell), and yet he knows the next time he falls in love that that will be it. It will last forever.
There is so much going on musically in the last song and throughout the album that I can't fit it into less than 1000 words for this review. Buy this album and listen to it. Don't just put it on and go and paint the house or something. REALLY LISTEN TO IT. Then and only then will you understand the plot of this great book.

reviewText:
The Cars hit a formula right from the very start.  With Ric Ocasek generally taking the lead vocal, The Cars combined wonderfully wordsmithed lyrics with a solid rock beat to become one of the best New Wave groups.  Some people have argued that The Cars, along with Devo and several other groups, created New Wave.
This album is a remarkable debut, with three of the songs released as singles and three others released as flipsides for a incredible 6 of 9 songs appearing as singles - something that few other groups have managed to achieve.  The songs are: "Just What I Needed"/"I'm in Touch with Your World" (5/29/78), "Best Friend's Girl"/"Don't Cha Stop" (10/10/78), and "Good Times Roll"/"All Mixed Up" (2/27/79).
I've always had a great appreciation for The Cars' lyrics.  They are typically artfully evocative and more intended to evoke emotion than to convey a concept directly.  As an example, look at the opening lyrics of "All Mixed Up":
she shadows me in the mirror
she never leaves on the light
and some things that I say to her
they just don't seem to bite
When you read The Cars' (typically Ric Ocasek's) lyrics you feel surrealistic.  Once you understand you are to picture images of feelings, or feel the feelings yourself, you gain an understanding of how the singer/songwriter is feeling.
The Cars insisted they are music performers and not an "act", preferring to be known for their music rather than their ability to look flashy or jump around on stage.  Fortunately for us, the listeners, that desire translates into musical quality and sincerity.  This music has a pop feel to it, but with enough of a hard edge that pushes it towards the boundary between pop and hard rock.
The musical style is somewhat dated, feeling like the late 70s music that it is, but it has aged to the point where it is now classic rock.  This CD is very solid music for anyone a fan of The Cars, of late 70s or 80s music, or anyone looking for something a bit out of the mainstream that has a good solid rock beat.

reviewText: The appeal of this CD for me was mainly the presence of Mozart's Concerto No. 18.  I owned the Casadesus/Szell account of No. 17, but neither Casadesus nor Serkin recorded No. 18, as far as I know.  No. 17 in Perahia's hands is as engaging as Casadesus's, but in rather fuller sound.  Perahia conducts the English Chamber Orchestra from the keyboard in a performance that is energetic and ingratiating and which displays considerable variety of dynamics from both orchestra and soloist.  The sound is good without being exceptional, with plenty of presence for both piano and orchestra and with fine balance between them.  The finale I have always found especially appealing -- its coda is sprightly and humorous, and Perahia does it full justice.  No. 18 is fascinatingly different: it strikes me (especially after 17) as quite dark, and Perahia's tonal palette is appropriately more subdued.  The slow movement is especially powerful -- it seems rather fragmented, with pieces of melodic material that the development never allows to flower into full-blown lyricism.  It seems almost troubled, and Perahia makes no attempt to impose on it a false coherence or glossiness.  There are discreet dissonances in the orchestra too, where the dynamic variety contributes to the troubling effect of the whole.  It doesn't seek to charm but is nonetheless the most compelling movement on the disc.  I haven't heard Brendel or Uchida in this music, but I'll make an effort to do so now.  Recommended

reviewText:
Originally to be titled "Snowblind" this is Sabbath's 4th effort and a bit different from the rest at the time. The album was retitled for fear of drug references. Most of Vol 4 has a dirge-like feel to it. Lots of slow, plodding metal riffs, possibly early stoner metal (?). The lyrics are a little different this time out. Previous, Sabbath warned us of the perils of war, drug abuse, Godlessness, polution, atomic war, and various other cheery subjects. This time out they take a completely anti-religious stance in "Under The Sun" and the "drug reference" in "Snowblind" is actually more subtle that say "Sweet Leaf" pro marijuana anthem. This is to say that if it weren't for the word "cocaine" being whispered at the end of the verse it would almost sound like an ode to photokeratitis or ultraviolet keratitis (a condition caused by by exposure to ultraviolet rays). That is if you're someone who actually pays attention to the lyrics. Most of the songs sound similar in form - starting out extremely slow then changing to double time in the middle and then returning to the original tempo. This tempo change at this time was another characteristic that set them apart from others. Another feature of Sabbath was the ability to build a song on just one or two chords for the most part and their use of drop tunings for even more bottom layer bone crusing riffs. This album to me always had a darker feel to it and a more "personal" feel to it as if it were coming from some introspective point of view.
Mostly slow death metal tunes except for "Supernaut" a heavy upbeat tune, "Laguna Sunrise" - strangely relaxing instrumental. The album's weak spots are for my money: "FX" (effects ?) electronic drums played through echo, and "Changes" is a maudlin piano ballad structured around two chords.
Fairly predictable as usual and pretty raw production, but by this time you probably already know whether you like Sabbath or not and this won't change your mind.
