reviewText: Excellent ! I've always been curious about Linda's albums of 'standards' and I recently took the plunge. I bought the CD that has all of Linda's standard songs, all in one package....and it is great. I tried to think of all the artists' in the 'pop-rock' industry that have produced an album of classic tracks and I came up with a list of "the late great Harry Nilsson, Rod Stewart, Paul McCartney, Carly Simon, Barry Manilow, and I'm sure I'm missing quite a few, but these singers come to mind first. There are many surprises on Linda's "Round Midnight". I never knew she recorded the Disney classic, "When you wish upon a Star". or even "What'll I Do?" , also recorded by Nilsson. Some of the songs will bring you to tears, "My Funny Valentine" and some I honestly wasn't familiar with, such as "Mean to me" and "But Not for me". No, Linda doesn't rock out with this release, but on "Round Midnight", she doesn't have to. It's all about Linda's magnificent voice and Nelson Riddles' arrangements. With two hours worth of music, there's a generous helping of Linda singing her heart out with the great American songbook. If you're looking for her to sing, "You're No Good", and her classic rockers, this is not the collection for you. If you want to hear Linda's beautiful voice and some classic songs, sit back and relax, you'll enjoy the journey.

reviewText:
I can safely say after hearing The Inner Mounting Flame by The Mahavishnu Orchestra, that was truly a remarkable experience.  I've never heard ANYTHING quite like it before, especially from the 70's.  I can see why radio stations wouldn't play this band!  Their sound and style would be a pretty easy way to jump start your day, I can tell you that!

Birds of Fire is a pretty good album, but honestly I feel the album is missing that special something that made the Inner Mounting Flame so incredible.  I love the title song though.  It picks up where the previous album left off with some unbelievable guitar playing, the likes of which I've never heard before on a 70's album (though on repeated listens, it's not that difficult of a song to get into because that one guitar bit repeats quite a lot).  As much as I love it, it DOES feel like the band members just stole some of their ideas from the opening song on the previous album and used them again here, but with updated production values.  Of course those are really good and exciting musical ideas, so I'm not knocking the song.

"Miles Beyond" is a pretty easy-going song.  It's filled with tasty little ideas, sort of like tasty little Halloween treats fill your trick-or-treat bag.  It's funky, and immediately stands out compared to the rest of the album.  "Celestial Terrestrial Commuters" is a hard enough title to say without twisting your tongue all around *and* a hard enough song to listen to the first time you hear it!  It constantly shifts around from guitars and violins, played with lots of furious passion, and it's only 3 minutes long!  It requires more than one listen to fully understand.

"Hope" again features some similar ideas copied from the Inner Mounting Flame (specifically the heavy opening riff of "The Dance of Maya").  It's not really a BAD thing, because the band members are able to put their ideas to good use almost every time.  "One Word" is kind of disappointing.  After hearing a mostly softer-than-usual by normal Mahavishnu Orchestra standards opening half of the album, and after noticing that the song is nearly 10 minutes in length, I was fully expecting this track to *really* pick up the intensity of the guitar and violin work to help make this album the heaviest thing since sliced, um... not sliced bread (sorry, I'm not clever enough to make a joke here!) Unfortunately, it's one of those slow-builder type songs, that just barely seems to progress into other above-average musical passages as it goes on.

The first half of the song is pretty mellow and atmospheric (and perhaps slightly musically twisted) but wastes too much time fiddling around.  The second half features a lengthy drum solo, and in my opinion, this is one band that shouldn't be doing drum solos.  I would have rather had violin or keyboards playing here instead.  I don't mean to complain.  It's like the whole song builds and builds, but in the end when you stand back and look what was built, it's just... something not very useful.  I DO like the song, but it's not what I expected it to be.

"Sanctuary" is pretty awesome, though.  A song that can be moody, dreary, atmospheric *and* intense.  Pay close attention to what's happening in the background and you will have yourself a pretty frightening song.  "Open Country Joy" is probably the only thing on Birds of Fire to indicate we *are* in fact listening to something from the 70's.  The band was just SO innovative and heavy that it's hard to believe this is, in fact, 70's rock (yes, I consider these guys much closer to rock than jazz).  It starts off really delicate and beautiful, and builds into some pretty neat musical ideas.  "Resolution" again reminds me of a song on the previous album with the slow build-up ("Dawn").  In fact, the entire 2 minutes are nothing BUT a build up.  And that's the problem with the album.  Everything builds and builds, but *what* is being built?  I don't know.  Maybe you know, maybe God knows.

I also have a small problem with the crystal clear production.  The Inner Mounting Flame's special charm was that it was pretty rough around the edges, but on Birds of Fire, the sound became more polished.  You could even compare the way these two albums sound to that of Genesis Foxtrot and Selling England By the Pound albums.  One of them is muddy and dreary, the other much brighter and happier.

I love the album.  I really do.  That's why I'm giving the album 5 stars.  The Mahavishnu Orchestra had too many interesting musical ideas to criticize any of their weaker moments.  We're talking an ABUNDANCE of creativity here, folks.  Overall, disappointing compared to the Inner Mounting Flame, but still worth owning because the music really is good, and in the end, that's what matters.

reviewText: If you believe that Beethoven knew what he was doing, then this is the recording for you.  Beethoven wrote precisely the dynamics he wanted, from pp (the softest) to ff (the loudest), and how gradually or suddenly to change them. I think he was the first composer to notate dynamics in such detail, and Vanska follows his instructions exactly.  Like other listeners, i wondered what happened when the sound disappeared on this recording.  So i tried turning up the volume until i could just barely (but distinctly) hear the first place the sound had become inaudible.  The volume on my machine (a Bose Acoustic Wave) goes from 1 to 99, and 85 (!) was the setting at which pianissimo was audible.  The opening chords were startling, but the cello entrance was piano as indicated in the score. The sound is gorgeous at that setting, never raucous. The precision and intonation are uncanny. This is the best Eroica i've ever heard! In fact, i've never heard it before in such exquisite detail and with such a lush sound.

This disc, recorded in 1959, is a good example of the success of the SACD sound as applied to a single sole instrument. The original issue was rather wooden as a recording but that problem has been totally removed in this remastering. We are now left with uncompromised and masterly Chopin playing.

There have been almost countless recordings made of this repertoire over the last 50 or so years, but it is no exaggeration to observe that there have been very few to rival the majesty, the brilliance and the total empathy that Rubinstein displays in this works. Like many other collectors, I am not short of good versions to compare this with, but for me, if I were to only choose one Rubinstein disc to take with me to some distant desert island, it would be this one. There can be no one definitive recording of any music, but this one must be considered as one of very few to choose from.

I would therefore suggest that this disc, in its remastered format, deserves the strongest recommendation to be included in any short-list of desirable recordings of these two sets of works.

Further Note: The 10 disc box set published in 2010 with 24 bit remastering of the whole collection offers a significant improvement on sound in every way on all discs. This can be confidently stated as I own both and have been able to do an A/B comparison. That box set must now be the best possible purchase although this particular SACD disc still remains the best of all. The same performances in the box set are much improved but not as much as this one example.

reviewText:
The liner notes allude to it, and it was certainly true of the boy bands that performed in the high school gym of my high school in 1965-66 (in the High Desert town of Palmdale, Calif).  They covered the Yardbirds like there was no tomorrow.  Youre a Better Man Than I, Shapes of Things and Im a Man were wildly popular and played with a spirit that approximated the originals.  If you weren't around in the mid-1960s, this is important to know because it shows just how popular and influential the Yardbirds were at the time.  And the key to that popularity was Jeff Becks unique guitar sounda rocket-fueled, frenzied fuzz-toned blending of eastern and western sounds that took pop-rock to new, stratospheric heights.  Indeed, psychedelic music begins here, with a series of forward-looking tunes recorded in 1965 and 1966 that made Jeff Beck rocks first guitar hero, and influenced the likes of the Beatles and Jimi Hendrix.

Besides Jeff Beck, the Yardbirds franchise is famous for launching the careers of guitarists Eric Clapton and Jimmy Page.  But on this song collection the star is clearly Jeff Beck.  Clapton performs on the bands earlier tunes with his guitar spotlighted here on four tunes: Too Much Monkey Business, Good Morning Little School Girl, I Aint Got You and the instrumental Got to Hurry.  Jimmy Page was the guitarist on the bands final LPLittle Gamesfeatured here in its entirety, buts its hardly a guitar album, but rather a song collection that emphasizes melody and lyric content.  Page has his big moment on White Summer an acoustic instrumental he wrote that forecasts things to come with Led Zeppelin.  The one cut featuring both Beck and Page is Happenings Ten Years Time Ago, recorded during three sessions in the summer and fall of 1966.  As indicated in the liner notes, this was far and away the most progressive single the band would ever release, and their last certified Top 40 hit.  The bass player is future Led Zeppelin member John Paul Jones.

Also featured in its entirety is the LP Over Under Sideways Down which in England was released as Roger the Engineer (after recording engineer Roger Cameron).  This was the only album to showcase Beck on every song. The stand out cut clearly is The Nazz Are Blue where Becks super-sustained, one-note solo is a marvel to hear.  Another is Jeffs Boogie, a reworked, souped-up version of Chuck Berries Guitar Boogie, and the riotously inventive Psycho Daisies. Other standouts include Lost Woman, the title cut (which peaked at number 12 on U.S. charts), Hes Always There, Rack My Mind, What Do You Want and the echo-laden Turn Into Earth.  While Roger the Engineer was the Yardbirds finest album, Having a Rave-Up was their most popular and features their best-known songs, all on this CD: Im A Man, Still Im Sad, Heart Full of Soul, Evil Hearted You, Youre a Better Man Than I and the rollicking The Train Kept A-Rollin  Interestingly, most of these songs were recorded in the U.S., in Memphis (engineered by legendary Sam Phillips and Roy Halee, soon to become famous as Simon and Garfunkels producer) and in Chicago at Chess Records.

Bottom line: this is hot stuff, a song collection featuring three of rocks greatest guitar heroesEric Clapton, Jeff Beck and Jimmy Page, but particularly Jeff Beckwhere psychedelic music originated and seldom has been surpassed.  The sound is clean but with minimal sound separation not as sharply defined as we have come to expect in the digital era. Whats important to know is the guitar solos are prominent and forefront.  Five stars.

reviewText:
In the 1980's, dance music was the natural evolution of what had been formerly called disco in the 1970's.  The beat was a bit faster and there were more synthesizers in the mix, but it was still disco all grown up.  That said, "disco" was a dirty word in most dance clubs in the 1980's.  The U.S. was rebelling against anything that smacked of disco as the 1980's began.  However, in the dance clubs, disco was now this different, more electric sounding music.  Typically that same music didn't find it's way onto the radio stations around the country.  The reverse was often true, with a lot of the "new wave" music hitting the dance clubs, but ususally not the other way round.  And the hit dance songs followed a strict path to mainstream dance club popularity:  It was released to the gay bars and if it was a hit there, then it went on to the straight clubs - this could often take a year or more for the transition to take place.
Lime was one of those groups that was a staple in the gay bars for many years before they ever hit the straight bar scene.  With a driving bass beat in all their songs and a heavy synthesizer influence, Lime's songs were perfect for moving to.  "Your Love" and "Angel Eyes" were two of the most popular.  However, you'll be hard pressed to find a bad song on this album.
No, you'll probably not find any of these greatest hits on the Top 40, but you'll definitely take yourself down memory lane with these great hit songs from the dance club era of the 1980's!

That's not to say that the radio hits aren't here.  "Holy" leads off the album.  "To Know You," "Fool for You," "Who You Are," and "Brave" are all included.  But we also get some choice songs that might have been overlooked originally like "River God" and "Every Season."

Just like with every other collection I have, there are a couple songs I don't care for.  In this case, I really want to know why "Why?" is here.  While I like the choruses, the verses are some of the most awkward phrasing I have ever heard.  And I've never been a fan of "Is it Any Wonder?" but I do recognize that I'm in the minority here.

We get two new songs as well.  "Sunrise" celebrates that, no matter the trial, God is there with us.  "Finally Free" is about the power of God to free us.  I like the first one, but frankly I find the second one too subdued for the message.  I want it to sound more jubilant.

Still, this is a great collection that will please casual and hard core fans.  I'm certainly glad I added it to my collection.

reviewText:
This 5-CD set contains Rudolf Serkin's complete recorded repertoire of Beethoven Sonatas-just over half the sonatas in Beethoven's ouvre.  These recordings, some of which were not released until after Serkin's death, are now compiled together for the first time.
For those accustomed to hearing Beethoven as played by Schnabel, Kempff, or Brendel, these performances will come as a splash of cold water across the face.  Serkin was unconcerned with niceties of tone, color, or pianistic perfection.  He famously described Arturo Toscanini's interperative philosophy as "architecture with passion," and the same could be said of Serkin's approach.  His vision was to reveal the structure-both emotional and musical-of Beethoven's masterpieces.  To put it bluntly, Serkin could be a little rough: chords are sometimes pounded, scales are occasionally uneven, he hums, grunts, and he stomps on the pedal (once, when playing with the Cleveland Orchestra, he knocked the lyre mechanism right off the piano).  But Beethoven himself was known for brutalizing the pianos of his day, and the composer's fighting spirit is in these performances as is seldom heard elsewhere.
Several of these performances are appearing on CD for the first time, and nearly everything on this set is revelatory.  Serkin is most successful in the "big" Sonatas: The finale of the Appassionata scorches with rage, the last movement of the Moonlight is a blitz, and the Hammerklavier-where the pianist lays out the fugue with remarkable clarity--has never been bettered.  Less successful is the Pathetique, with a questionable interpretation of Beethoven's first movement repeat sign, and some poor chord weighting in the Andante cantabile.  Serkin's performances of Beethoven's last five Sonatas should be mandatory listening for all pianists.
Except for the Les Adieux, all of the performances here are studio recordings.  The sound will be a bit dry and hard for most tastes.  Nevertheless, the remastering is a considerable improvement over earlier issues.

This is my take: The Beatles have an extensive catalogue of great songs (perhaps the greatest catalogue in Music History...) anyway, we all know that half of them are dead and we will never hear a new recording from them ever again. They are gone. Deffinately gone.

And yet, we fans never get tired of them. We always listem to their songs as if they were here. For us, they are not a band with half their members dead. They are very real and living. And deep inside I believe we never really think we'll never hear from them again.

LOVE is an album where several of the Fab Four's greatest songs were remixed, remade and adapted for a great show put on stage by Le Cirque du Soleil. Wisely, this soundtrack was made by George Martin himself... with Paul, George, Ringo and Yoko's blessing. I am sure that, like in everything regarding The Beatles' releases, all the people involved with this are hard working and serious people commited to give us nothing but the best treatment of the greatest material ever composed in pop music.

So, for me, this is a great thing and we'll never have anything better than this. People (like myself) may prefer the original songs... it's ok. But we must also understand that this new album is not meant to replace the older, original recordings. They are a just the soundtrack for a stage show... made by the best people we could think of... and made with the blessing of those could bless it. I was lucky evough to get a copy of this today... and after listening to it back to back... I was very very pleased to hear the great work they made.

All the songs sound beautiful with lots of new insights and several propositions that must work very well on the stage. This album gives a new view at these classic songs. For example... joining ELEANOR RIGBY (my favorite Beatles song) with a transitional use of JULIA is a very interesting proposition that the Beatles never thought of doing, obviously. Or the putting together of BLACKBIRD and YESTERDAY is another example of the experimentations made here.

The treatment of WHILE MY GUITAR GENTLY WEEPS is, I am sure, the thing that would end up happening with the song if the Beatles (in the end) did not go for the well know "heavier" approach we listen to on The White Album... and I'm glad George Martin did it here... because, since the Anthology, I'm sure we all thought of that.

This album is the closest thing we'll ever get to a new Beatles album... and it will certainly bring new fans into our club. I am very happy with it... and I am thankful that more than 35 years after these recordings were all made, people are still fiding in them new sources of inspiration. This album should NOT be mistaken for those hundreds of lousy cover/homage albums made by third rate people (The Beatles Salsa... or the Beatles go Reagge... etc)... or those bootleg albums whose sound quality leaves a lot to be desired.

Like the great Anthology series, the Capitol box sets, the "one" album, and the "Naked" album, Love is an obvious labour of passion, care, taste and love. It is a great celebration of the music we all love... from four musicians who are eternal.

reviewText:
Iced Earth is my favorite band next to Kiss and fear factory. I have been a fan of Iced Earth for nearly two years now, and I have to say, out of ALL the albums that were released of Iced Earth, Burnt Offerings is THE BEST album. This album is the only album where Jon Shaffer has given us his true anger from the three year lay-off.

This is Matthew Barlow's first album, and it is the best album. I originally thought that albums such as Something Wicked This Way Comes, and Horror Show were the best albums when I first got into them. To be honest, you don't know Iced Earth till you've heard Burnt Offerings.

Originally, I was VERY skeptic about this album; when I first heard the song Burnt Offerings, I hated it, same with Last December. Dante's Inferno was NOT bad to me when I first heard it. Do remember, those were my opinions when I first heard Iced Earth when I was listening to albums like Horror Show and Something Wicked This Way Comes.

Over time, It grew on me, I actually wanted to try Burnt Offerings, because of a friend told me it was the best, and I trust him. I got it, and continued to listen to it, and I realize why he said it was the best, and the reason for that is because it simply and truly is THE BEST album. After having the album growing on me, I learned to appreciate and Love songs like Burnt Offerings, Last December and Dante's Inferno.

To start off the album, we get the opening track entitled "Burnt Offerings." The intro to the song in my opinion is VERY epic, and when things get heavy, it gets creepy in some ways, with the guitar melodies. It reminded me of a Thrash Metal version of the "Tales From The Crypt" theme song. This song is about Shaffer being VERY angry with his three year lay off, simply with phrases in the song such as "Every note and every word you hear comes from deep within." AND "A warnining from the sky, F*ck with us and die." This songs riffs are very angry, so it makes you feel angry when you listen to it. A PERFECT 10/10

The next song is what would be sort of considered as a Mini-Epic entitled Last December. Of course SO many people consider it to be an epic of Romeo And Juliet, but when you listen to this song, the lyrics say "Teenage Suicide Our Only Way Out, Together We Might Live, Devided We Must Part... Last December, Mother You Have Forced Us Here." Basically stating that the two lovers in this song kill themselves because their love is forbidden. In Romeo and Juliet, They killed themselves because they thought that their lover was dead. You get the idea. Originally, this song was written by Matt Barlow and his old band called Cauldron Entry Number 161914 Pain. This song would probably considered the single of the album since next to Pierced Spirit, is the shortest song on the album. 9/10

The third song, which is a personal favorite on the album, and is also one of the two songs that start out heavy. Also considered to be a Mini-Epic of Dracula. This song was written by Matt Barlow, and has to be by FAR one of the best songs on the album. It starts out kinda creepy and heavy. It is a slow song, but it is VERY heavy none the less. Very well written too. 10/10

I personally believe that one EVERY single album of any band HAS to have a song that is NOT always considered to be the best. Well folks, this next song, entitled Brainwashed is your basic Throw-away. The weakest song the album. This one is not a mini-epic however, but it does bash Organized Religion *Ahem* Catholic if you wanna get more percise. Matt's Vocals are NOT that great if you ask me, but the Chorus however is KOOL "Lies, Foolish Lies Behind Your Brainwashed Eyes!" I'll give it a 7/10 because I think it is VERY Weak for this album.

Now, time for another Decent song, Burning Oasis. I do like this song, but it's NOT one of the best. It is Creepy though, with the wind intro. This is another Mini-epic about The Garden Of Eden. I personally think this song is NOT as good as it COULD have been. To keep it short, I'll just say It's not the best, but it is good none the less. 8/10

Here is A PERSONAL favorite song of my own, CREATOR FAILURE \m/. This song is scary, and sinister with Shaffer's riffing. I must say that it took me a while to get used to because of it's intro, even though it is the only other song next to Diary that starts out heavy. Hey, it's also written by Matt Barlow. This song is Indeed a mini-epic about the novel Leviathan. One of my favorite parts of the song is where Matt Barlow goes HIGH with his vocals, and it is SO amazing how high he goes. You might say he goes sort of into a King Diamond type mode, but it's VERY impressing none the less. I LOVE this song, even though so MANY DON'T, especially if the version you heard was the original un-remastered version on the original version of the album. The reason I say that is because on the original version, Matt Barlow goes WAY off key at the begining, it's ANNOYING. When the remastered version of it was released, it was fixed, which is good. 10/10

Judging by the Anger, Horror and Hatred on this album, I NEVER expected there to be a more peaceful and more beautiful song by Iced Earth. Well folks, there was, and it is called Pierced Spirit. Matt Barlow sounds AMAZING with this piece, and is in my opinion, the most BEAUTIFUL thing created for a suithing song. This song I do believe is an intro to the epic coming up "Dante's Inferno." I also consider this song to be very emotional and suithing. Even though it is the shortest song on the album, it is still VERY melodic, creative, and beautiful. 10/10.

Ladies and Gentle men, boys and girls, fasten your seatbelts because we are about to take a trip to Hell. This is the song entitled Dante's Inferno!!!! This is ALSO an Epic detailing the Devine Comedy. When you listen to it, you literally feel like you are being taken to hell. It's is VERY creepy, and I advise you to be very aware when you are listening to it. It is 16 minutes long, and is VERY progressive. Lyrically, this song HAS to be Shaffer's best song to date, and is VERY popular. I also believe this is why the album is SO popular to people. A perfect 10/10.

OVERALL: If you are starting off as an Iced Earth fan, I advise you NOT to get this album to start off with. It is VERY different, and if you don't like it, KEEP listening to it, DON'T be skeptic about it, IT WILL grow on you. TRUST ME! TEN STARS **********10 STARS**********

reviewText: I really cannot say enough good things about this album. I could go on and on, but I will be brief. While Up on the Sun and Meat Puppets II typically receive all of the critical accolades (and rightfully so), it is 1987's Mirage that is the hidden gem in the Meat Puppets discography. It manages to combine high-brow intellectualism with off-the-wall silliness. The song The Mighty Zero is a perfect example of this. The music is clever and the words even more so. Lyrical content is devoted to such things as nature, time, and math. Other standouts include Leaves, Confusion Fog, and I am a Machine. It is obvious that the Puppets spent a lot of time creating Mirage (three months, as opposed to four days for 1988's Huevos). This is a whacked-out piece of work that could have only been produced by the collective genius of the Meat Puppets. Listen to it while you think and laugh at the same time.

reviewText:
The first time I ever heard of Ian Matthews, I was an 8th grader who took an instant dislike to his hit song "Shake It" and, thinking he was a newcomer, blew him off as a one-hit wonder in the vein of others who had similar one-strike hits back then (Ian Gomm's "Hold On"--except that song was exponentially better due to slick production and a great hook--Nick Gilder's "Hot Child in the City," which has the dubious distinction of being the worst song of all time in my book, etc.).  It wasn't until I heard "This Fabrication" ten years later on a now defunct jazz/new age format that I took another look at this artist, and that song alone had me running to a certain record chain that is now no longer around either.  The result was a glorious musical tapestry, the likes of which still hasn't gone out of style with my tastes over the years.

Not only is Matthews capable of singing a wide range of material, but he does his best work when his heart is in it rather than when some record label wants to make him a "pop artist," quite similar to what happened with the Moody Blues.  His voice is so pure, clear, and emotive that you get goose bumps just listening to these great renderings of Jules Shears' poetic, folky songs.  The distinction here is that, probably because he was working on this project under the Windham Hill lable, the album comes off as new agey with all the synth embellishments.  At the time, this was a wise move, because the 80s were ripe for this particular sound.  Outside of the dated keyboards, this album really stands the test of time because of the choice of material and the way in which Matthews performs them.  It's a vast improvement over the Bangles' cover of "If She Knew What She Wants" which would also have fit in nicely on here with the right treatment.

Gorgeous tunes abound without a loser in the bunch, but the standouts certainly have to be "Standing Still," the somewhat Beach Boyish "Following Every Finger," a very celtic inspired acapella reading of "On Squirrel Hill," "Shadows Break" with it's great melodic structure, "This Fabrication,"--which is very personal to me--and "Lovers by Wrote," complete with the truest lyric:  "Stupid questions about love are the stupidest questions of them all!"  My absolute favorite, however, is "Alive Alone," another song that is personal for me.  It contains some of Shears' finest lyrics, and Matthews sings the song in such a smoothly gut-wrenching manor that the beauty of it hurts in the best way.

Unlike my old vinyl copy, I was delighted to see the inclusion of two tracks, raggae ballad "Smell of Home" and "Why Fight," in which Matthews projects his Brit accent that is seldom discernible.  This album has brought me years of pleasure on both vinyl and cd, and it is also proof that this man can do more than play good country and folk rock.  If you want something different from his stellar older works and are looking for a Matthews project that is both masterful and not embarrassing, Walking a Changing Line is a great recommendation.  Hell, it was the very first of his albums I ever bought, and I haven't regretted it a single day.

reviewText:
This is like old timey Appalachian style music, electrified, but without losing its roots feel. It's more down to earth than the almost visionary sounds of these guys' first album. On that one, it was hard for me to even talk about individual songs, so strong is the numinous presence of the album as a whole. There is still a gracious quantity of allegorical nuggets here, and ample humor as well, maybe even a bit more.
Their [original] version of "The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down" is far superior to the one made popular by Ms. Baez; and believe me, I truly love the way that young woman sang way back when.
"Whispering Pines" is one of the most beautiful and the most heartfelt songs you'll hear anywhere, at any time; ditto for the tremendous amount of feeling purveyed/displayed by "Rockin' Chair" and "The Unfaithful Servant".
"Across the Great Divide" is one of the most genuinely happy songs ever.
"When You Awake": "Ollie told me I'm a fool . . . so I walked on down the road awhile . . . went to the house that brings a smile . . . sat upon my Grandpa's knee . . . what do you think he said to me?"
Then there are the rollicking numbers: "Rag Mama Rag" where Richard Manuel absolutely wails on the piano, "Up On Cripple Creek", where Robbie Robertson manages to play his guitar to sound like a mouth bow or Jew's harp; and the intensely soulful but still humorous "Jemima Surrender". "Jemima surrender . . . that's all ya have to do . . . I'll bring over my Fender, and I'll play all night for you. There's a bird on my head but his mouth won't talk . . . ya know he laughs just like a bull moose, but he loves like a hawk!"
The two rockers are excellent quality: it's hard to imagine how they come up with such amazing story lyrics. "Look Out Cleveland" is emotionally upbeat, but the subject belies it, creating a dreadfully luscious ambiguity. "King Harvest (Has Surely Come)" has incredible minor melodic feeling in its song line as well as in the lead guitar passages. When just playing the rhythm parts, Robertson plays it funky throughout. Textually, it's a union versus company song, but juxtaposes this with choruses each which shows the power of nature and its cycles still holding sway over the 'other' side of humankind. Nature is presenting herself somewhat outside the bounds of human culture/work, but like a fragrant, fertile ghost, forever penetrating and pervading it.
"Corn in the fields, listen to the sound as the wind blows 'cross the water:
King Harvest has surely come!"
"The scarecrow, and the yellow moon . . . pretty soon a carnival on the edge of town.
King Harvest has surely come!"
"The smell of the breeze from the magnolia trees in the meadow . . .
King Harvest has surely come!"
Back in 1970, when we were first becoming aware of the idea of ecology, this is what it meant.

reviewText:
When it comes down to it, there are very few people that have such an incredible guitar sound. Eric Johnson is definitely one of those people. Voltage sag or no, his sound is almost always perfect, and on "Live and Beyond" he is a lot more raw than his studio albums. Yet, he still has that perfect tone. This is a fun album. One, because it came out a little quicker than the last one, and because of it's rawness. Johnson should be heard and seen live to really appreciate it, and this does a good job of it. He has an amazing bassist in Chris Maresh and Bill Maddox pounds on the skins.
This album is a little different than classic Johnson due to the rawness of being live, but his sound is still exceptional and his speed is still blinding. Solos on "Zenland", "Once a Part of Me", "Last House On the Block" and "Enzo Shuffle" will leave your jaw bouncing off your lap. Malford Milligan steps in to sing a couple of songs including Jimmie Vaughan's own "Don't Cha Know". His voice is a little more fitting for the blues than Johnson's own. He gets a little airy on "Elevator Sky Movie" with long delays and repeats before kicking it into a countrish overdriven speed workout. He segues into "Shape I'm In" which is very classic Johnson sound.
When it comes down to it, Johnson is an incredible axe player. A joy to listen to, and watch (although guitar players find him quite frustrating). His speed and sound are amazing, and he uses both with an elegant ease. After listening to "Trademark" I had to play guitar, and even to this day I still am energized to play after hearing him (I also feel like breaking all my fingers and putting my guitars through the wood chipper as well).

reviewText:
I've been a fan of Emm Gryner for a while now, since 2000 or something like that.  This was the first album I bought and it was truly one of the best decisions of my life.  "Public" is comprised of "stages".  It's like diving into a giant bowl of your favourite dessert and that feeling lasts every single time you play this record.  It's a timeless record (aka one that never gets old, boring or overplayed).
Gryner, who I think is one of the best song writers out there, has a special gift for music.  This little known Canadian artist was named a favourite by David Bowie!  She deserves a hell of a lot more credit than she gets.
As for the songs on "Public", one word sums it up:  BRILLIANCE.  The album starts off with the upfront guitar featurette 'Hello Aquarius', which I find musically inspiring.  Emm goes into her simple yet complex lyric mode with the follow up 'Wisdom Bus'.  'Summerlong' was her single that has a more stripped down version on "Dead Relatives".  It's an upbeat and her most "pop" song on the record.  The first ballad-esque song on the album, 'Death is a New Day' is lyrically amazing.  This will blow your mind . . . seriously.  'Phonecall 45' is a heavier song and one of my favourites.  It's angry Emm.  'Acid' is a slower, piano ballad that is angry, sad and an emotional downslide.  If this song doesn't want to make you cry - you have no feelings.  'The Good You Make' is sort of like 'Summerlong' in that it is a bit "pop" but it's still musically unique.  'Your Sort of Human Being' was my favourite when I got the album, it's distinctive and different.  'The End' is my favourite song now, it's the "who-stole-my-heart" song and her nifty lyrics.  This can leave you feeling chills.  'July' is again like 'Summerlong', it's a feeling of love lost. reviewText:
Destiny's Child have been deemed the top-selling female group. They have garnered massive CD sales, airplay and an abundance of hits, and they have spawned some reasonably successful solo careers for each star although Beyonce is the most successful of all three. This CD is a nice collection that brings together all of their hits from No, No, No to Cater 2 u. Just comparing those two songs, it is easy to notice how Destiny's Child have matured from some young teenagers to young adult women.

The three new songs on the CD are Stand Up for Love (produced by David Foster and Humberto Gatica) it is a big ballad that is about standing up for love, for injustice around the world. It is one of those Whitney Houston type ballads that have been missing from the musical scene for almost ten years. Since the ladies have never done this before, it's refreshing to hear them tackle this kind of song. Michelle Williams turns in a very impassioned performance as she takes the bridge home. It is a hopeful song and an uplifting one; The next new song is Beyonce's Check on It (produced by Swizz Beatz and Beyonce herself). The song is featured on The Pink Panther Soundtrack and solely features Beyonce. It has done extremely well reaching the top five on the Billboard Hot 100 and has propelled the sales of the CD to Platinum status; The last new song is Feel the Same Way I Do (produced by Rodney "Darkchild" Jerkins, Beyonce and Ric Rude and featuring all three ladies with Kelly Rowland taking the first verse). It is a slow jam that is strongly R&B and could make some ends on Urban radio. It is a nice, laidback cut that could've worked well on their 2004 Destiny Fulfilled CD.

It does not take me to go through each of their hits song-by-song because all of their songs have reached the top echelon of the charts and most people already know about them. Their 1999 The Writings on the Wall has been certified for sales of 9 million; 2001's Survivor has sold 4 million units; and 2004's Destiny Fulfilled has sold 3 million copies. Some of my favorite Destiny's Child cuts on this CD are Independent Women Part 1 (the dance to this song and the energy of this song back in 2001 was crazy); Jumpin' Jumpin' (a nice party joint with the frenetic beats and a catchy chorus); Lose My Breath (they came hard when they returned in late 2004 with this joint which helped to also put Darkchild back on the map as a producer); Say My Name (the colorful video was tight, and while the song has not necessarily aged well, it was a good catchy song); and Cater 2 u (one of the best DC ballads and their only single as a ballad next to 2001's Emotions which was a remake of the Bee Gees' classic). I never really cared for Survivor, Soldier, Bug a Boo, No, No, No for some reason. But this is a nice add-on for anyone's collection.

Kool and the Gangs Emergency was released in 1984 as the Gang was in the middle of a hot streak. Their five previous studio albums all went platinum and spun off numerous pop, R&B and dance hits. Kool and the Gang brilliantly combined R&B and commercial pop and the results were mesmerizing. Emergency catches the band at their peak and is possibly a defining moment in their 40 year plus career. Side one (as it was back when the album was released on vinyl) contained 4 back to back Top 10 smashes. The pulse pumping title track, the fourth and final single to be released from the album, has a rock feel but can still pack a dance floor. Fresh is a sexy mid-tempo groove that is irresistible, funky Misled is another groove that will make you want to dance. Side one closer Cherish is perhaps the albums shining moment, a stunning ballad with inspirational tones. The words and the melody weave together perfectly and can still send chills down your spine.

With side one complete, it is almost hard to believe that there is a side two to this gem but there is and it is as strong as side one. Surrender keeps the party going. Bad Woman is a sexy R&B slow burner that should have been released as the fifth single. J.T. Taylor does an amazing job on this sexy midnight groove that is as good as anything Kool and the Gang ever recorded. Album closer You Are The One has killer sax work and is another song that is fun to dance to.

Big Thanks as always must go to Big Break Records for re-mastering Emergency and for doing such a fine job. The liner notes here are very informative and contain an interview with Ronald "Kool" Bell. His reflections are great to read. This double CD re-master is a treasure for the fans as it contains a plethora of bonus material. All the singles from the album as well as the title track are also presented here in their Single versions and in their 12 dance versions, including the rare 12 remix of Cherish. The albums colorful original album cover art front and back is preserved as well. A must have for any R&B lover and collector.

reviewText:
There was a time when I didn't understand Iced Earth.
Or the band's many rabid fans.
I kept hearing and reading "Iced Earth this" and "Iced Earth that." The band's name popped up everywhere. Even my fave reviewer Lord Chimp couldn't stop raving about them. And I figured if he likes 'em, there has to be more to 'em than I can see at face value. Or first listen.
So I kept at it.
IE's album graphics are typical metal horror images, with a logo that's more than a little reminiscent of Iron Maiden's. Since I love Maiden, I immediately took to IE's graphic image.
One day -- after hearing so much about the band -- I went out and bought every single one of their CDs, bought Dark Genesis, bought the 3-CD Alive in Athens set, and went through it all. CD by CD. Read the liner notes. Read the lyrics. Listened to the Jon Schaffer interview on the limited edition version of Horror Show -- the whole nine yards.
And here's what I discovered as I listened to Alive in Athens:
Iced Earth is an extremely serious, intense band that churns out riffs of unrelenting anger and ferocity. Their album graphics are cool. And chief orchestrator (Jon Schaffer) is as focused and driven as anyone I've ever known. He has kept Iced Earth on track for a lotta years, and he deserves credit for sticking to his guns, not giving in to the fickle winds of marketing trends.
Matthew Barlow's vocals sound a little like James Hetfield's, and it still drives me a bit nuts to hear one syllable words stretched into two (for example, "See" becomes "See-ahh"..."Me" becomes "Me-ahh"). Barlow's voice is an acquired taste for me. I'd have to listen to it more before I can get past his unique style. But I'll keep trying. (Just for the record, I prefer voices along the lines of Bruce Dickinson, Russell Allen, Dio, Jorn Lande, Harry Conklin, Paul Rodgers, Steve Perry, and others who have a powerful, clear voice.)
Alive in Athens is an atomic, captivating CD that'll blow you away if played from start to finish (especially the 3-CD version) at a fairly loud volume. The songs are pile drivers and your head is their target.
My favorite genre of music is progressive rock/progressive metal/symphonic metal (or whatever you want to call it), but I used to notice on Amazon that people who bought certain CDs in my favorite genre also bought CDs by Iced Earth. I didn't understand why then. Now I do. Although IE's music isn't the same as, say, Symphony X's, it still offers something to interest anyone with a love of metal guitar riffs. (And that would be me.)
Iced Earth is metal played the way metal should be played. Expect nothing more, accept nothing less.

reviewText:
It's hard to believe that at one time the two most popular musicians in America were trombone players (Miller and Dorsey). Since then the instrument has seen giant strides in the proficiency of its players yet been treated by the public as though it were an accordion or tonette.  The attitude is that it's fine for parades or Dixieland tailgating but not to be taken more seriously.  The only two exceptions I can think of at present are Steve Turre and Robin Eubanks, fine players who still occasionally manage to put out a CD under their own names.

But it's doubtful that any player will equal let alone surpass (Bill Watrous perhaps is closest) Rosolino and Fontana.  Who knows what happened to Rosolino at the end?  It may have been extraordinarily complex or as simple as the unbearable pain experienced by a peerless but poverty-line musician having to face the prospect of being unable to support his family barring acceptance of a minimum-wage factory job. All I know is that I'm not going to judge the man let alone the artist based on his incomprehensible moment of insanity (though it prompts me to increase my donations to the Brady fund).

Fontana is even scarcer on record that Rosolino.  Yet I recall having a conversation with a major, high-profile trombone player (Phil Wilson) back in 1973 when he expressed his admiration of Carl Fontana above the others.  Never has a listener had a better chance to compare the two, as well as appreciate the work of either player, than on this continually absorbing, even headshaking, display by both players. No arrangements--except the "extemporary" ones worked out during the course of play.  (You can hear the two communicating verbally as well as musically.)  To my ears, Rosolino is the flashier of the two; Fontana is crisper and cleaner, yet full of surprises and clever quotes. Rosolino integrates his slide more completely into the production of sound and rhythm; Fontana relies on what must be the fastest tongue possessed by a human being.  Like some of today's tenor players whose altissimo register is so unlimited that the alto saxophone seems gratuitous, both Rosolino and Fontana take the instrument into areas previously thought to be the trumpet's sole domain.

I still love Teagarden, Lawrence Brown, Al Grey, and I consider J.J. Johnson the Miles Davis of the instrument. But these are the two guys who took the instrument to yet another level. I have yet to hear anyone capable of following them.

When this album came out in 1994, you either loved it or hated it. Most of those who hated it did so because they sounded too much like Nirvana (and Nirvana at this time were gods). Regardless of the criticisms, it didn't seem to hurt the album's success. "Everything Zen," "Machinehead", "Little Things," "Comedown," and "Glycerine" were huge hits -- all over the radio. I still hear these songs today on the local modern rock radio station. This is because of one good reason -- the songs are incredible, regardless of their supposed lack of originality.  Bush (along with Collective Soul, Live, Foo Fighters, and others) created what would be called post-grunge rock, which is basically a more polished grunge sound with greater pop-sensibility. This sound dominated the rest of the 90's (for example, Third Eye Blind in the late 90's) until the rise of various metal groups (such as Linkin Park) and emo-punk groups (such as Taking Back Sunday) that dominate modern rock radio today.

This debut album from Bush will forever be considered as one of the greatest albums of the 90's (certainly in terms of success). For those of us who grew-up in that decade, it will forever form the soundtrack of our lives at that time and indubitably will bring back fond memories. Bush was a great band for a simple reason -- they had great songs which nearly everybody loved.

Here's my album recommendations for those interested in post-grunge rock of the 90's:

Bush - "Sixteen Stone"

Live - "Throwing Copper"

Collective Soul - "Collective Soul"

Stone Temple Pilots - "Purple"

Candlebox - "Candlebox"

The Offspring - "Smash"

Foo Fighters - "Colour & The Shape"

Everclear - "So Much for the Afterglow"

Our Lady Peace - "Clumsy"

Hum - "You'd Prefer an Astronaut" (includes their one and only hit, "Stars," which is perhaps my favorite song of the 90's)

Stockdale has certainly expanded his music with this album, but different does not mean inferior.

Granted it took a couple of plays to adjust to the variety, but Stockdale put out an amazing album.

You definitely have your "Wolfmother-esque" tunes on the cd.

Meridian, Of the Earth, Let it Go and She's a Motorhead....these fit right in with both of the first two Wolfmother albums.  All are cut from that mold.

There are bluesy songs, some rockabilly tunes.  Variety and versatility.

You could swear that Long Way to Go was a Zepplin tune and then Everyday Drone sounds like an upbeat Dylan song.  And then Black Swan you could swear was Yes.

There is a lot to like and a lot to listen to with 16 songs.

One song for me that didn't work is Year of the Dragon.  It's more the lyrics than the song itself.

The surprise song for me is Suitcase (One More Time).  It's got a great upbeat feel to it, and would not be what I would have expected from Stockdale, but it is infectuous.  Maybe my favorite on the album.

For me the Top Tunes are as follows:

Long Way to Go
Keep Moving
Somebody's Calling
Vicarious
Meridian
Suitcase
Of the Earth
Let it Go
She's a Motorhead
Black Swan
Everyday Drone

That's 11 songs out of 16 that I continually play over and over again.

The aforementioned Year of the Dragon and Ghetto are the only two that don't work for me.

But Let Somebody Love You, Standing on the Corner and Country are 3 songs that I find myself doing a replay on again and again.

So In the end, I would say 14 of the of the 16 songs are either A or A+ songs and only 2 I don't currently care for.

That's a 5 star rating in my book any way you slice it.

Welcome Back Mr. Stockdale.  Side projects aside, you have been sorely missed.

I'm not joking. Victim of Changes sounds like a stab at Black Sabbath type of riffing, something that dissapeared when Priest got their image together in Stained Class. Dreamer Deceiver and Deceiver are Early Priest at their psychedelic best, and together with Genocide are the standout tracks on the album. So whats the deal with Sad Wings, you ask? Well, its a band searching for an identity. Maybe they didn't know it at the time, but they were succeeding. This is not a party album, and its probably because the band were not successful at the time, had a bum record deal, wore threads that looked like they were salvation army rejects, and had to lug around equipment in freezing cold weather. One interesting note about Priests early songwriting is that emotes a rather dark, brooding type of feeling, and all this minor key stuff doesnt help. Still I can say that while a million bands sound like late 70's till mid 80's Priest, nobody sounds like early Priest, and that includes the better songs on Rocka Rolla. Interestingly, this is the only Priest album that contains a slight Rocka Rolla-ish approach and sound, while including a glimpse of the Monster songwriters that priest would become. This is also evident in listening to SIN AFTER SIN's Sad Wings style epics while furiously riffing STAINED CLASS style. Stained Class is the apex of their early sound, and the end of innocence, because Hell Bent for Leather is the beginning of the proverbial sell out. Alan Moore is a terrible drummer, he chokes all over the album, the drums are SO ameturish on TYRANT, it has to be heard to be beleived. This is what really holds the album back, by the way. Judas Priest disowned this album because it was a GULL release, which means they don't get paid. 2 words: Psychedelic Metal.

reviewText:
Through their first three albums the Mars Volta's career had been somewhat hit-and-miss (though admittedly the hits outnumbered the misses), but with the Bedlam in Goliath they managed to shape their approach into their best album yet.  While displaying their usual ambitious songwriting and instrumental flair they've finally struck the perfect balance between the insanely infectious, groove-laden attack of the their debut "De-Loused in the Comatorium" and At the Drive-In's Swan Song "Relationship of Command," and the spacey progressive leanings that marked "Frances the Mute," while reining in the occasional meandering found on "Amputechture."  The band's usual hallmarks are all present--inscrutable time signatures, out-of-left-field instrumentation, and spastic shifts in tone and genre, frequently within a single song--and for the first time since their debut they manage to get every track over with in less than ten minutes.  With John Frusciante assisting, Omar Rodriguez-Lopez's demented guitar genius is even more evident than usual as they assault listeners with a dizzying, non-stop array of dense metal riffage, screeching feedback, and unrestrained leads.  Thomas Pridgen turns out to be a more-than-satisfactory replacement for Jon Theodore on the drums (just check out his enthusiastic annihilation of his drum kit on Ouroboros), and Cedric Bixler's high-pitched alien wail is as ear-splitting as ever.

The opener Aberinkula sets the tone nicely, firing out of the gate with an electrifying salvo of rifle-shot drumbeats and confrontational wails before a hallucinogenic, acid-jazz sax solo begins an extended instrumental passage that seems to bear little resemblance to what preceded it.  The rest of the album follows a similar pattern, with the band managing to indulge their afro-latin-jazz fetishes while simultaneously rocking hard at almost every turn.  Tracks frequently begin with a somewhat conventional (for this band, anyway) rock-song approach--Goliath boasts an especially anthemic chorus, and "Cavalettas" even gets pretty punkish--before embarking on the sort of free-form, genre-bending explorations for which they've become known.  "Soothsayer" is a notable exception to the pattern, establishing a haunting, ethereal atmosphere that's abruptly rent apart by an eyebrow-singeing guitar solo that would make Hendrix proud.

As with any TMV album, "The Bedlam in Goliath" takes a few listens to absorb (I myself didn't particularly care for it at first), but it eventually coalesces into a richly detailed epic that stands with the best progressive efforts of recent years. From their debut the band established themselves as one of the only outfits out there with a legitimately distinctive sound, and this latest album is no exception.  As usual, those willing to put aside any preconceptions will find themselves amply rewarded.

reviewText: This 180-gram re-issue is, assuming you get a defect-free copy, one of the best-sounding vinyl LPs I've heard from the mid '70s era. The sonics are warm, natural, and emerge from a totally silent background. Columbia/Sony deserves credit for doing this Simon classic justice. BTW - these comments also apply to the debut LP "Paul Simon" and the '73 follow-up, "There Goes Rhymin' Simon" as well. All three LPs boast superb remasters and sound, especially when the 40+ year age of the recordings is taken into account. When compared to the price of the "typical" audiophile vinyl re-issue, they are a relative bargain as well. Of the three LPs I ordered, one had to be returned because of a defect on one track, but the replacement was flawless.

Buy the physical cd- it includes Autorip, so you will get both the cd and digital copy. Highly recommended.

reviewText:
The Good
"Dirty Little Girl" is dominated by meaty guitar riffs and gritty vocals. Driving guitars set the steady pace for "Save Me." Vocalist James Hart delivers an empowering performance here. The chorus hook is sure to draw you in. "Here With Me" is a little more glossy than the tracks that preceded it. It still has that rock edge, but is clearly a song set up for the radio. Hart shows his vocal diversity here. "So Addicted" sound like it was plucked right from the Alice in Chains or Stone Temple Pilots catalog. "Saloon Song" is undeniably catchy, and tells the tale of a bar hook up that lead to a long love affair. Burn Halo comes with all barrels blazing on "Our House." "Falling Faster" is a predominately acoustic ballad with an over-the-top chorus. "Anejo" brings the energy level back up.

The Bad
Nothing notable

The Verdict
Vocalist James Hart said he wanted to go out there and create a straight-up rock record with commercial appeal. Well, Hart hits the nail on the head with Burn Halo's debut. This album is pure modern-era rock with plenty of heavy riffs and melodic vocals. Burn Halo reminds me the current rock sound being put forth by Hinder or Rev Theory. Halo is in great company indeed.

reviewText:
Abba was, from the very beginning, a great singles group.  They matured into great album makers, and their last three full-length studio recordings are all great from beginning to end.  This, their last, proved that they still had a lot to offer, and they went out on a high note.  Especially notable here is the inclusion of "The Day Before You Came" as a bonus track.  It showed that, had they wanted to, Abba could have become a major force in techno-pop, believe it or not.  It is a beautiful song based on a simple keyboard and drum-machine backing, with fantastic vocals by Agneta.

But the whole album is strong, The Visitors, When All Is Said and Done, Head Over Heels, One of Us--all worthy of inclusion among their greatest.  But also tender ballads, "I let the Music Speak," "Like an Angel Passing Through My Room"--gorgeous.  This was the first Abba Remaster that I bought when it came out, and it would be worth it for double the price.

reviewText: I've been a Soul Coughing fan since 1996, when I purchased "Irresistible Bliss." I loved it. Later I bought "Ruby Vroom." Loved it. I finally broke down and picked up "El  Oso" this week and once again, these guys can do no wrong. Their music  can be described by the titled of their second album: irresistible bliss.  It's difficult music to describe, since it's so unique, but my best  description would be Beck meets Devo. M. Doughty has a wonderful gift for  creating oddball lyrics that are never cliches and usually hilarious.  "El Oso" is a bit more instrumentally spare, less dense, than the  band's previous efforts. The bits of unusual sampling are kept more in the  background, only to make room for the vocals and those consistently funky  SC grooves. "Circles" was apparently the "single" from  this disc (I wouldn't know...I never listen to the radio), and it's a  great, catchy little number. So far some of my favorite songs are  "$300," "So Far I Have Not Found the Science" and  "Misinformed," but I'm sure that I will grow to love them all.  This is a wonderful disc with grooves, hooks and lyrics that are impossible  to get out of your head. A bit more accessible that their previous efforts,  but that's certainly not a bad thing. Unfortunately, SC announced their  break-up a few months ago. The good thing about that sad news is that they  split up LONG before their music became boring. I wish all four members the  best of luck. Thanks for the great tunes!

reviewText:
I had heard of Gram Parsons well before I listened to the Burritos' amazing debut lp- but I was an avid anti-country kind of person. I just did not want to know. Yet compilation tape after compilation tape I got from friends managed to include Parsons, the Burritos, "Sweetheart of the Rodeo" era Byrds, or a combination thereof. So, finally, in 1988 (I was 18), I found an old lp copy of "Guilded Palace of Sin" at the Salvation Army and bought it for 75 cents. My life has never been the same.
From the opening strumming of "Christine's Tune (Devil in Disguise)", there was this odd blend of country, folk, and fuzzed out psychedelia (Sneaky Pete's steel guitar) that immediately grabbed me and has never let go. Then there were the vocals. Along with the wonderful sense of harmony that Chris Hillman possessed, Gram Parsons was able to blend blues, folk, country, gospel, and rock in one voice- and do them all convincingly. His charisma was obvious. His love for the music undoubted. He was the focal point for much of what would become the LA country sound- Linda Ronstadt, Eagles, Emmylou Harris. They all emulated him, but could never reach his level of talent.
The songs on the lp are all top rate, in my view. The melancholy of "Sin City," the rockabilly of "Christine's Tune," the tongue in cheek anti-war bluegrass/folk tune "My Uncle," "Wheels," their tribute to motorcycles, the up-tempo "Hot Burrito #2," the satire of "Hippie Boy," complete with gospel ending. All genres of music from folk to country/rock are well represented here, with the Burritos more than able to handle of them competenetly.
The results are glorious! To find this lp at a record store will be difficult, except among indie shops who know the score. Whether as part of the great "Hot Burritos!" anthology or here, this lp should be purhcased and added to your collection with no delay. It is THAT good and THAT pivotal in that it influenced the last 30 years of music. No Burritos- no Eagles, no Emmylou, no Dwight Yoakam, none of the cross-over success that country has today. It's that cut and dry. Get this lp. Get it now.

reviewText:
Pink Floyd singer/guitarist/songwriter David Gilmour released his self-titled solo debut in June of 1978 in the US (was released a month beforehand in Europe).
David Gilmour's self-titled effort was recorded during down time in Pink Floyd's history.
At the same time David Gilmour was making this self-titled solo album, bass player/singer Roger Waters created demos for The Wall and The Pros and Cons of Hitchhiking (which would be his second solo album in 1984) whilst drummer Nick Mason was producing artists as diverse as jazz musician Michael Mantler, punk rockers The Damned and art rocker Steve Hillage. Lastly keyboard player/songwriter Rick Wright was making a solo album of his own Wet Dream.
David Gilmour's album was recorded in late 1977/early 1978 at Superbear Studios in France with David producing and handling all of the guitars, vocals and keyboards. Also joining him were ex-Roxy Music and eventual Foreigner bassist Rick Wills and Quiver/Sutherland Brothers drummer Willie Wilson, whom both had played with David in the power trio Bullet in 1967.
All of the tracks were written or co-written by Gilmour himself (except as noted).
This album kicks off with the great instrumental "Mihalis" which is a great guitar workout for David. The next song is "There's No Way Out Of Here" (written by Unicorn member Ken Baker) and is a laid back classic delivered with the minimum of fuss and overdubbing; Gilmour's voice rarely rising above a breath. This track was originally recorded by the band Unicorn as "No Way Out of Here" and this song was the single off the album doing well on rock radio in the US in 1978. In fact, this was the song that sent me looking for the album in March of 1988 on cassette (I have on CD now). Next is "Cry From the Street" (co-written by Gilmour and Eric Stuart) is a great rocking number with some great playing. "So Far Away" is a nice ballad which has David singing calmly throughout and one of his best guitar solos (the harmony parts at the end of the solo remind one of Queen). Mick Weaver plays some piano on this track.
The rocker "Short and Sweet" kicks off the album's second half and was co-written by David with fellow Harvest labelmate Roy Harper and is a great song. "Raise My Rent" follows and was the second instrumental on the album with more fretwork from Gilmour on the Fender Strat and the riff was inadvertently resurrected in 1994 on Pink Floyd's The Division Bell on "What Do You Want From Me". The bluesy "No Way" follows and has a great Gilmour vocal and superb lap steel guitar work. The instrumental "It's Deafinitely" follows and has superb guitar work from Gilmour. The album closes with the atmospheric "I Can't Breathe Anymore" which sounds like it could have appeared on a Floyd album and rocks out to a collage of Stratocasters and lap steel guitars.
David Gilmour's self-titled effort was a modest success as it peaked at #29 here in the US and went Gold and has held up well over the years.
David Gilmour's self-titled solo debut was finally re-released on September 12, 2006 on Columbia Records with digitally remastered sound thanks to longtime Pink Floyd mastering engineer (since 1979's The Wall) Doug Sax plus fully restored artwork.
The remastering is amazing and many of the tracks have longer fadeouts(Raise My Rent, No Way (now to have a lap steel/Strat duel at the end), There's No Way Out of Here, Mihalis, So Far Away and I Can't Breathe Anymore (now with another lap steel/Strat duel)) and the sound is better than the original CD by a longshot!
David Gilmour's self-titled album is Highly Recommended!

reviewText:
While looking for some new CDs to listen to on a recent trip, I came across Chantal Kreviazuk's "What If It All Means Something" and decided to give it a try. It's my new favorite.
Some female singers scream. Some have raspy voices. Some are soulful, poetic, and have angelic voices. Chantal is in the last category. Her voice is strong and emotional, yet delicate and full of spunk. I've never heard anything quite like it and am sure that I won't for quite some time.
Now for the songs: I'm a fan of artists who are actually that. I like people who write their own material as a reflection of what is actually going on in their lives. This album is a beautiful quilt created out of Chantal Kreviazuk's life. All of the songs are amazing, but I feel like some deserve spotlight recognition:
In This Life: With a catchy melody, easy-to-relate-to lyrics, and an overall great vibe, this will become a quick favorite.
Time: Few songs have described my life so accurately. The tune is about all of the wasted days we spend moping over things that will never be. It seems like this one is everywhere - on ABC Family's "Lucky Seven", in the film "Uptown Girls", etc. It's a great tune that you will find both uplifting and touching.
Flying Home: We've all lost loved ones, but few artists have ventured to write so wholeheartedly about losing a loved one to suicide. The song is touching, heartfelt, and highly emotional - yet not angry or accusing.
Feels Like Home: This is a bonus track not featured on amazon's tracklisting, but it is on this album. As far as love songs go, it's powerful and realistic.
There are so many fantastic tunes on this album that I'd love to go through them all - but it would really better if you could hear them for yourself. Buy this one. You'll have a new favorite.

reviewText:
This typically dark, musically dense MM album is their best yet for me. Add someone of Mr. Marr's quality to already one of the greatest bands to ever come out of America and you've created musical alchemy like none other in the 21st Century to date.

More cohesive and energetic than their last couple of albums combined and definitely more raucous.  If after ten years of ingenious, addictive songs and the building of a solid base of fanatical followers, a lot of bands are crawling up their behinds and looking back and smiling.

Isaac Brock and company, however, still aren't where they want to be and are still sailing that dead ship forward.

Spitting Venom is my favorite track and is an epic by most standards, but nothing is weak on this album.  The quality of the production no doubt has been raised with Johnny in the house but the jangle and schizoid moods MM always evoke are here in force and better than ever.

Dashboard is a good pop start as a single, but songs like Florida and Education show Mr. Brock getting more vocally confident and strong with the years.

Lyrically there are many themes of contemplating your mortality and with the energetic music, such lyrics come across more ironic than anything.

Modest Mouse is a great band and they keep getting better. (Now just keep those New Order dudes out of the mix, and they'll be fine.)

reviewText: 1978 the stage is set for an album to emerge out of the crumbling decay that is the city of  Cleveland. Just like their other fellow Ohion's DEVO, the guys in PERE UBU obviously saw the world in a slightly different way. I have owned this recording in various formats since 1980 and I have never grown tired of this album. I find this album to have an almost timless quality in that even though it was recorded over 25 years ago,  if the original band itself tried to go back into the studio and re-record it, it  just wouldn't happen. There is just a certain magic that they  captured in 1978, as to the music itself I tend to break - up this  album into 2 distinct parts. Side One being the more accessible "drunken" side with more garage style sounds almost punk rock in its leanings guitar wise, but a little too intelligent, just listen to the lyrics. Side 2 is definately the "drug" side like a bad acid trip vocalist David Thomas takes you on a journey thru the seedy back streets of Cleveland(I have never heard smashing bottles sound so creepy or atmospheric) and the rest of the band help to re-inforce this craziness by going off in a million different directions. I could give you a track by track anylisis of this record but suffice to say that music is somethig you should anylize, experience and consume at your own leisure, and then form your own opion of what each of the songs on this album  mean to you. So if you loved things like Throbbing Gristle's song Hamburger Lady then u will surely love Pere Ubu's album the Mordern Dance. As another reviewer mentioned before Black Francis of The Pixies fame must have almost certainly listened to these guys. I also hear there influences in recent  bands such as Portishead and Queens of the Stone Age just to name a few. So if you enjoy bold experimental music that is still as fresh sounding as it was in 1978 then give your ears a chance to have a listen to this album, even if you have to beg,steal or borrow it.

reviewText:
"Heathen" is a sigh of relief for Bowie fans that couldn't attach themselves to all of his more recent style focused albums.  I'm just a novice so I might not speak for everyone.  For my money, I loved Bowie's erratic electronica meets satire on "Earthling" yet didn't fall in love with the mostly adult contemporary rock with middle aged blues of "Hours...".  However, "Heathen" is a much more widespread musical effort that includes spacey electro pop ("Took A Ride On A Gemini Spacecraft") to blistering guitar rock  (his cover of Neil Young's "I've Been Waiting For You").  In fact, Bowie has a lot of success with all 3 of the covers.  He sounds malicious yet passionate while ripping through the Pixies "Cactus", one of Bowie's better sounding alt-rock tracks in years.  The album has a lot of great upbeat rockers like the soulful "Slow Burn" and pop rock of "Afraid", which might have a familiar intro from recent commercials Bowie has done for satellite radio.  The theme of "Heathen" seems to be about needing to be loved, which can be heard in songs like the dark "I Would Be Your Slave" and soothing "Slip Away".  The album is erratic yet it works very well with a strong selection of songs that come from all areas.  Many of the songs are somewhat worldly like the bouncy child-like rock beats of "A Better Future" and the ominous ender "Heathen (The Rays)".
"Heathen", the special edition, features a few good remixes of "Sunday" and "A Better Future".  "Sunday" is stretched out and adds some new drumbeats and guitar while "A Better Future" sounds more melodramatic and electronic.  "A Better Future" was one of the more straightforward pop songs while the album has many strangely beautiful keyboard driven numbers.  While "Heathen" is co-producded by Tony Visconti, who was part of Bowie's Berlin years, it doesn't sound like a campy sellout to that era.  It sounds like a classic return to a feeling of music and not any genre.  The only problem with "Heathen" is that there are so many more songs that could have went on the main disc.  "Conversation Piece" feels like a perfect fit along with the redone version of "Panic In Detroit", but then again those additions could hurt the album by making it sound like a flashback.  If you get a chance to, buy the special edition because it is worth it.  The real special edition disc however is Bowie's import single for "Slow Burn" (sold separately from the disc, of course) which features a wide array of songs that didn't make the cut but fit the wide mold of emotions that "Heathen" displays.  If you liked this album, you will love those b-sides.  Even if you buy the basic CD, you will be in for a treat of many shades of rock, pop, grunge, AC, electronic and even blues that display many human yearnings for lust, belonging, fear and showcases the great struggle that is life.  This one is a Bowie album that everyone will find something they love about it.
label: positive

reviewText:
I got into Rosalia De Souza's voice without really knowing it - when I was listening to Les Hommes and Quintetto X; both artists on Schema's label along with Rosalia. But I really got hooked after she featured on Break & Bossa vol 5, where she opened up a continuous bossa mix with back to back tracks - the classic Canta De Ossanha and then the unique track "Zig-Zag" (it's on her album but without lyrics). Some months afterwards, her debut album was released and it was stunning. Now in 2006, Rosalia's back with her second album. But this time she has the help and production work of the terrifically talented Roberto Menescal instead of the very impressive Nicola Conte.

This is a very good album, although I must warn from the start that the vibe is FAR different from "Garota Moderna". This was recorded in Rio De Janeiro and again, with the expertise of Roberto Menescal. It has a completely different ambiance. From the first song on, I was actually reminded a bit of her work with Quintetto X but with a bit of a 'spark' to it. "Onde Anda O Meu Amor", a classic Orlandivo cut was a pretty classy intro, very smooth. Voz da Lapa is another nice track highlighting Rosalia's voice but with the help from labelmate Toco on vocals. "Que Bandeira" (that flag) features Marcos Valle in a guest role, hmm... nice but not the highlight of the album to me. "Ao Amigo Tom" is a nice tribute to Antonio Carlos Jobim (Tom), nicely laid over a play of one of his classic ballads to close. Other standouts on this to me were "Agarradinho"... what a song. "Nem Que Seja a Nado" was also nice, "Rio De Janeiro" had that sweet Carioca feel to it, "Vivo Sonhando" is a Jobim track that Rosalia does a fantastic job of covering and the album closes wonderfully with "O Que e Amar"... beautiful song with great a romantic guitar.

I certainly recommend this. The album was well put together, is rather deep and sung with care and the musicianship is simple... yet not so simple. To be honest this reminded me quite a bit of Joyce's more recent works on Far Out records but... recorded in Rio. The album is certainly a tribute to Brasil, Bossa Nova and Samba and Toco, Roberto Menescal and of course Rosalia De Souza were outstanding and put togehtre some beautiful songs. I listened to this from beginning to end, but must again warn that if you're looking for a more bossa album or a sound like in "Garota Moderna", you'll be disappointed. If you do like this, definitely check out Joyce's "A Little Bit Crazy" and you'll probably like work by Maria Rita, Rosa Passos and Luciana Souza.

As far as format - I'm unsure if it will have a domestic (USA) release. But it will have a Schema release (this one), which means it'll be available without the two *bonus* tracks on the import from Japan.  There will also be an LP version of this however it will not have "Agarradinho" or "O Que e Amar". Also please note that if you do get the Japan import version instead of the Schema import, the linear notes and information is in kanji.

reviewText: _Time Lost_ is an album consisting of four unreleased _Wounded_-era tracks and three songs from the band's days before _A Blueprint of the World_ debut. The first four songs (all from the _Wounded_ sessions) are, in plain terms, nothing short of amazing. They're easily on par with the best material that album had to offer, and walk all over such songs as "Below Zero", "Hostile World", "Armour", and "Missing", in my opinion. How these four tracks were justified in being left off the album, I'll never know. Seriously, _Wounded_ might have been one of the best albums ever recorded had some of its weaker tracks not been given precedence over these gems. The last three songs (all from the band's early days) are less outstanding in comparison, but are still quite valuable in there own right. "Interact", at nearly 11 minutes, if a little stretched out, is still the longest song the band has ever recorded, with a unobtrusively melodic sound that I think would have fit in very nicely on _Blueprint_. "Standing Ground" is another very nice track, shorter than the band's norm at just five and a half minutes, and written (with more of the brilliant lyrics I've come to expect from the band) about the temptation of selling out in the music business (or life in general?). The finale, "Mettle Man" is essentially an eight minute instrumental (I say "essentially" because there's one short verse recited at the very end). It's quite the progressive piece, which ends up being surprisingly catchy considering its length and complexity. If you've been following along you'll note that I've praised every one of the seven songs on this album. Truth be told, front to back, this grab-bag release is a definite winner that should not only delight any fan of Enchant, but all other fans of prog rock, as well.
