reviewText:
Think of cold, smooth ice. And imagine a warm, shimmering light appearing just under it.

That's what comes to mind with Husky Rescue's exquisite debut album, "Country Falls." The Finnish group reflects their chilly Helsinki winters with equally chilly pop, but filled with sunny warmth, as if on the first day of spring. Basically imagine Sigur Ros playing folk-pop.

It opens with a gentle stretch of shimmering synth, and a mellow little folkpop tune. "Sweet little kitten on the porch sleeps in the sun/The sunbeams climb up on the wall," Reeta-Leehna Korhola sings in a slightly breathless, wispy voice. "Small girls with sun warm hands cuddle bring him milk/then run after make castles in the snow/Jokers juggle in the air rainbow colored fountains of sugar waters flow..."

They dip into psychedelic pop in the kitschy, colorful "Summertime Cowboy," with all those whipcracks and jangling bells. But then they're back to the icy, sparkling sound of the first song -- ambient balladry, glitchy experimental tunes melting into creepy ballads, and little mellow guitar tunes that are smothered in shimmering, sparkling synth.

This edition also comes with an extra DVD, which contains three music videos. "New Light of Tomorrow" is a spare, eerie video, with a young man having a vision of a spacesuited angel, while "Summertime Cowboy" is a kooky, neon playground. And "City Lights" is a shifting video of a young woman carried away by a love song on the car radio (come on, we've all done it), who has a dream of herself dancing in green fire.

Husky Rescue is the brainchild of Marko Nyberg, who apparently wanted to make expansive, warm music to counter the cold up in Helsinki. So he collected around twenty musicians to make the right sound for "Country Falls" -- and the result is so cohesive in sound, it almost sounds like a concept album.

Almost every song is based on a little guitar melody. Sometimes Husky Rescue dip into catchy electric riffs and solid drums (like in the poppy "Summertime Cowboy"), but usually they stick to gentler, folkier material with the odd droning riff here and there, and the occasional burst of murky drumming..

And they're all wrapped in delicate layers of shimmering synth, which sound like a soundtrack for the Northern Lights. Sometimes they're glitchy, gurgly or tinkly, and sometimes they're epic sweeps of sound. And they're interspersed with devilish little laughs, robot voices and ambient sweeps of exquisite sound.

Really, that would be enough to recommend this album in itself. But it's topped with vocals from two artists: Korhola's pretty, slightly breathless voice, and Nyberg's slightly stilted, distant voice. Both of them sing songs of warmth, hope, "cotton clouds," lullabies to a "tiger," and the sweet plea, "Would you treat me right if I am kind/Would you like me more if I can smile/Would you set on tears if I start to cry/Would you take me there last one more time?"

"Country Falls" is an exquisite mixture of folk-pop and electronica, and it sounds like the end of winter when the spring sun starts to shine. Absolutely astounding.

I'm delighted with the accompanying dvd in this package. What a great concept, being able to see the entire album being recorded exactly as you hear it on the cd. It causes me to ponder 'what if' scenerios of similar documentation of any of my all-time-favorite recordings. The upgrade to this duo-disk set is well worth the few dollars more.

Most albums, you can listen to every so often but spend most of their lives in the box.  This one has been spinning on my turntable since it came out, even squeaking through my 8-track (in the seventies) and it is one of the few albums I just never get tired of listening to. If I remember right, this was the most expensive album I'd bought up to that time, and it was worth every penny.  Listening to it, one feels as if they are transported back in time to a seventies rock show, with all its enthusiasm and energy.  Wings was no Beatles, but it was a great band in its own right, and the mix of songs on this album is a perfect blending of Beatles songs, McCartney solo efforts, and Wings classics.  And it all works.

Lovely sounds, the band obviously having a great time, playing well together to an energized audience.  One listen to this live classic will take you right back to the great days of arena rock when one of the greatest musicians of all time came to America and gave it a special show.

reviewText:
The last two and a half years would have made anyone crazy - relationships, the press wanting you to fail and then and needing more press regardless, and then projects and ideas realized then shelved. Luckily Fantasia Barrino is not the kind to lay down even though she's had enough curve balls tossed at her to make the strongest woman give up, and God knows she's endured a lot.

Her new album - let's face it - shows the kind of positive power Beyonce used to have years ago, an independent, a no frills honest-to-God good album that you can play from beginning to end and you'll find a favorite track.

After listening to this album for two straight days, here are my impressions, straight and unfiltered. 13 songs at just over 45 minutes:

01. Supernatural Love (feat. Big K.R.I.T.) - Right of the bat Fantasia goes big and does her best to go hard and soft at the same time. She makes a statement early, too - don't mess with her, but if you do, you'd better know what you're getting into! The song leans a bit towards Beyonce territory, but she still strikes the right notes nevertheless. It's radio ready and it works for me.

02. Ain't All Bad - A mellow jam and once again Fantasia tells her story through her songs. It's a story of heartbreak, but there's always an upside to it. No more tears, and she's grown up and she didn't need your mess anyway...

03. If I Was a Bird - She sings about heartbreak the way a bird flies in the air. She wants to fly above it all and her sound soars in this song.

04. Girl Talk (Interlude) - Some miscellaneous chat with her "girlfriend" Kelly Rowland and playing around, and then goes right into

05. Without Me (feat. Kelly Rowland & Missy Elliott)(Explicit) - The official "put you on blast" version, and boy did she ever. I'm not going to name names, but her recent ex-boyfriend as she recorded this will be shocked to hear confessions on this album. You've been kicked to the curb, you burned me one too many times, and without me you're nothing. Period. Having Missy Elliott help nail the nails in the coffin is just cold, man...! This ranks right up there with Justin Timberlake's "What Comes Around Goes Around."

06. Side Effects of You - When you break up with someone, it's like a part of you gets ripped out, and there's a ghost right next to you, and it's going to suck. Using her breakup as a similar situation for the bad side of just that just shoots for the heart. A ballad that definitely kills.

07. Get It Right (Explicit) - An upbeat number to leave all the stuff behind. It's time to get dressed, go out and forget the heartbreak at home. She's all at once soulful and playful and in charge of the beat. Her voice was never clearer sounding and in better form.

08. So Much to Prove - She challenges herself with this quick uptempo rocker, with her voice soaring and taking you through a real roller coaster. Once again it's kinda Beyonce-like, but her stamp is all over the song regardless.

09. Change Your Mind - A female's thinking in using sex to both heal a relationship and keep a man is as old as the sun rising in the east and setting in the west, but this supercharged attempt goes everywhere at once. It's a bit scattered.

10. Lighthouse (Explicit) - This is her "Umbrella," but her song has the kicks and the beats in the right places - "f*** the b*tches, f*** the fame, I'm gonna be here anyway" says it all. Fantasia's life has been a solid attempt to be more than just a singer, taking advantage of what needed to be done, but in the end of the day she just wants to be a woman who just wants love, as we all do.

11. Lose to Win - This is the song everyone has been listening to for several months now, and there's two camps: one side wants her to stay the soulful balladeer, and one side wants to see her grow as an artist. I'm in the second camp, and when I first heard this song (rapped over an old Commodores song no less!), this was a quantum leap over her 2010 release, and is showing all listeners one thing - she has grown as a singer and (almost the entire album) songwriter. This is proof that her album was going to be big, and it really is. This is one of the better songs on the album, and not just because it was released first.

12. End of Me - In this song she is so in love after a passionate night of lovemaking her head and her heart is going to explode, and every verse is filled with her coming down and her thoughts while laying in bed. This is most definitely her "Love Hangover," and she's not ashamed to describe her almost stalkerazzi style of possession over how much she loves this man, all sung to a heavy beat and even some rock guitar solos make there way in. All I can say is wow!

13. In Deep - How deep are you willing to let a woman go with you? What is she willing to do? Here Fantasia says it all - she wants the bad, the ugly, and every part in between and back again, to show you how much this chick is willing to love every part of you. This song is so simple in lyric but is so honest it blew me away. What a way to close out the album!

(If you are willing to shell out a few more dollars, the iTunes version has two additional songs attached - here they are:)

14. Haunted (feat. Tank, King Los, Al Sherrod Lambert & Jamia) - this song is about choices, plain and simple. She made the wrong choices, and now she's going to pay for it, like she was stuck in a horror movie in her head that just won't go away. Like Fantasia says, Karma's a b*tch,because it will come back and hurt you for sure. Very interesting.

15. To the Heavens - inspiration comes from everywhere, and what you don't see someone else might. Here Fantasia pays tribute to some inspirations in her life - Michael Jackson, Whitney Houston, Jimi Hendrix and Bob Marley, just to name a few. As she sings in her song, we stand on the shoulders of those who made their way for someone else to climb. She makes the argument while the beats kick and the uptempo beat once again gives you pause to understand that you may be the latest, but you weren't the first, and there's nothing wrong with giving spiritual shout-outs to those who made it possible to get you where you are.

What else can be said but this is the album Fantasia tried to make a few years ago but, now injected with more soul and rock and rap and beats from now, not six months ago.

It is mature, it is adult, it has ballads and rockers and soul and makes a very bold statement overall - Fantasia Barrino is an artist that must and will be contended with, and I heard at least 4 Top Tens here - "Side Effects Of You," "Lighthouse," "In Deep" and of course "Lose To Win."

I could be wrong, but if you check out my other recent reviews of artists in the last 5 years, I haven't been too wrong! (On a side note, my DeBarge review from 2 years was mysteriously taken down by Amazon after I predicted what happened to him.)

I give it 5 stars because, really, almost every track can be played on the  radio NOW and she will have hits, hits and more hits. Considering the ones the media have been trying and damage her with, she deserves this, and she probably will have the last laugh.

(Thanks for reading my review, and it helped it any way, please leave a thumbs up or down, and don't forget to leave a comment too!)

reviewText:
To begin with, let me say that I am not a fan of Kiss.  As a matter of fact, I used to absolutely detest Kiss.  Of course, I was familiar with "Rock n Roll all nite," "Shout it out Loud," and all of their other big hits before.  I even bought their greatest hits album in an attempt to try to get into their music.  Needless to say, it didn't work.  In the end, I decided to write them off as a bunch of old, boring farts who played disco rock.  That is....until I heard Alive!
This album had the thing that their studio tracks seemed to lack...Pure Energy!!!  This was not the uninspired, Multi-million dollar corporate Kiss of today.  This is the sound of a young, hungry band that sounds absolutely exhilarated to be on stage.  Sure, it's the same songs that I thought were cheesy before.  But here, those same familiar songs sound fresh and exciting.  These versions of "Strutter" and "Deuce" are bursting with energy.  And songs such as "Cold Gin" and "100,000 Years" have some tasty rock guitar playing by Ace Frehley.  In fact, hearing these live versions of Kiss classics make the studio versions sound pedestrian in comparison.
I believe it says a lot about an album when even a non-fan can enjoy listening to it.  It is a guilty pleasure of mine.  And along side with the New York Dolls debut, Alive! ranks as one of the trashiest, most invigorating rock albums of all time.  I still don't much care for Kiss the band, but Alive! is undeniably a fantastic rock album.  I've heard rumors that this album has been doctored in the studio.....frankly I don't really care.  It's still a blast to listen to when I'm driving in my car.  A great addition to any rock collection......even if you hate Kiss.

reviewText:
Brutal, Technical, Atmospheric, Complex, Heavy, Melodic, Beautiful. Any one of these adjectives can describe this amazing album. Even after hearing their other works, I can say for certain that it's their best by far. Every single song is well crafted and has at least one interesting hook that you'll pick up on, despite the often chaotic nature of the band. The diversity of songs is also nice. You've got you're all out brutal death metal songs like "The Blessed Dead", "Execration Test", "Churning the Maelstrom", "Kheftiu Asar Butchiu", the latter having an excellent closing moment when the whole band chants the title of the song together in their best death growls. But also some slow and doomy type songs like "Sarcophagus" and "I Whisper in the Ear of the Dead".
The band's technical execution dismisses anyone to doubt their high level of muscianship. The drumming is obviously amazing, from the speed of his blast beats and double bass, to his insanely fast fills and rolls, he adds just the right touch to each song.

The guitar tone complements the album perfectly, being both extremely heavy and melodic whenever called for. The solos are well played, and rather than detract from the song, they make it even better, be it a all out shred-fest or emotional solo.

The true highlights for me, even though every song on here is not to be missed, come from three particular songs. "The Blessed Dead", which must be counted as one of the best opening songs to an album ever, contains one of the best solos on the album among other thrilling moments. Also, probably the best and most well written song on the album, "Unas Slayer of the Gods" is also one of the best death metal songs ever written by any band. Not one dull moment plagues this masterful opus. Not to mention the godly solo that lasts for nearly 2 minutes.

Last but not least, the 20 minute title track, which spans four different songs. Starting with what can only be described as a 'call to war', to two of the most brutal songs Nile has ever written, which ends in total chaos on "Destruction of the Temple of the Enemies of Ra". And to close the album, the last song is almost relaxing, to let you recover from everything you've heard in the last hour.

Oh, and I must applaud the band for their lyrics as they are very original and make an interesting read to anyone who's willing to put in the time. It's no wonder they chose Egyptian mythology to go along with their brutal Death Metal style, as some of the subject matter can be pretty morbid.

All in all, if you are looking for an interesting and original take on Brutal Death Metal, look no further because this quite simply one of the best Death Metal albums ever released and also one of the best Metal bands around today. I cannot stress it enough, just go out and buy it already!

The libretto of this opera is a brilliant poetic patchwork with a long excerpt from Genesis, the book of the Old Testament of course, and several poems from Gryphius, a poet who describes the 30 Years War in Germany. The rest of the libretto uses various sources and alternates Latin and German, and Latin is not gratuitous since it was connected to the Catholic Church at the time and the Lutherans rejected the use of this language. The opening piece and the closing piece are the same epitaph Kepler officially wrote himself for his own death. It is in Latin.

We have to understand this physicist lived in a pivotal period in Europe. He was born in 1571 and died in 1630, very exactly twelve years after the beginning of the 30 Years War in 1618 that was to end in 1648. On the other hand Gryphius was born in 1616 and died in 1664 and he lived his whole childhood and youth in the middle of this war. This pivotal period was centered in Germany around this long war between the Catholics and the Protestants. We have to understand that such religious wars were long and brutal in France, just the same in Germany and at the same time they were the main stake of the English Civil War and Puritan revolution, after having been the main stake under Henry VIII, his son Edward II, his daughter Mary I and his second daughter Elizabeth I. For at least three quarters of a century or even one full century the conflict between the Catholics and the Protestants went on without any visible reconciliation possible.

It is though in this very period that science really started sprouting genuine buds and set its first concepts on the table. We all know Galileo Galilei and his battle with the Catholic Church that forced him to renounce and reject his own scientific results about the sun seen as the center of our universe, earth turning around it and turning on itself and the earth not being flat, but that last idea was already proved. Copernicus went just a little bit further and Kepler was following the same routes and theories. Kepler though was slightly influenced by astrology and he definitely did not leave behind the same heritage as the other two. He is simply part of this vast movement that prepares the next stage with Descartes, Newton and a few others.

Glass is obviously interested by scientists, science in general and cosmic science in particular. What does this opera make of Kepler and his scientific struggle?

All along Kepler says and repeats that the whole world is scientific, is governed by three principles: number, quantity and circular motion. He studies the various planets of our constellation and calculates their orbits. To do so he uses geometry, meaning Greek geometry. We have to keep in mind zero has not reached Europe yet and Descartes has not yet invented algebra and the decimal system. The six planets are Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Venus and Mercury. Earth is the measure for all other orbits that are connected to earths orbit via five geometric figures in fact polyhedrons all derived or connected to the earthly circle: a dodecahedron with twelve pentagonal faces, a tetrahedron with four triangular faces, a cube with six square faces, an icosahedron with twenty triangular faces and an octahedron with eight triangular faces. This gives a rather austere text that has to be vastly compensated by the music.

The long reference to Genesis leads strangely enough to Kepler opposing theology and reason and this theology in the Bible is from people we do not know, who speak some human language but explain nothing. Thats where the evocation of the night is essential, the night of darkness in which humans are kept very systematically. This evocation comes from Gryphius and is the somber reality of humanity, of Gods creation divided in fighting factions in the name of God. And yet Kepler defends the idea that physics is celestial. He uses the famous hypothetico-deductive method: hypotheses, image, construct, calculus, mode of calculation, demonstration, verification and that is concluded with the true rules of our calculation.

The idea is that the mind of man was created for the perception of number and greatness, meaning mathematical and physical science as well as the vastness or greatness of the cosmos. Thus mans mind can only discover the numbers, formulas, rules, figures or patterns that are the architecture of the cosmos. This cosmos is absolutely logical, stable, a true miracle of rationality. And Kepler naturally concludes that this miraculous rationality is Gods creation in gods image, hence is God himself. Kepler is able to reach God in the cosmos, to decipher him, to reveal his real nature and his rational existence and essence.

Thats when Gryphius comes in a second time with a phenomenal Vanitas Vanitatum and there the music, maybe for the very first time, reaches a dramatic power that it did not have before. This is due to the long and heavy repetition of these two Latin words. We always expect the third part of this quotation from the Bible but it never comes and the short German stanza is an evocation of war, destruction, fire, burning, ashes, etc. And the Latin burden that was powerful at the beginning of this track becomes a long dirge chanting the inevitable total destruction that will come without any possibility to escape. Science is beautiful, in the image of God who is then beautiful but humanity is ugly because in the name of God it is fighting to the death divided between various clans and tribes and churches and chapels and orders and factions. There is no hope in spite of the miracle science could bring directly from God.

Yet Kepler reacts and brings questions and questions require answers and that leads us to Keplers conclusion that Without true knowledge life is dead. In the 17th century true could only mean Gods truth. By the way the English translation is questionable many times, with many German structures transferred to English without any difference, distance or reflection and at times with some mistakes. When I quote the English translation I correct such mistakes. The end of the first act gives the last word to Gryphius again and this time we are ripped apart by the dilemma it contains. What eyes see is nothing. When we close our eyes then we will see a lot more. In fact we will see and know everything. How can we see and know everything when we close our eyes? Thats the dilemma. By looking inside our own mind which was created by God in his image we can discover the whole rational calculus God is just as we could discover it by observing the cosmos. This introspection leads us to God and thus justifies, verifies and proves that God is all and we are nothing but a pale image of him. He gave us our mind not to create rational truth but to discover Gods truth in our own mind itself.

At this moment Kepler and this opera reaches up to Blaise Pascal or up to Ren Descartes who both advocated that their scientific work was the only way to prove the existence of God by demonstrating his creation is rational. If it is rational its because there is a rational being behind, and that is God, and since we are made in his image then we can decipher that rationality, though we will never get to the end of it.

The second act though is completely different. Kepler starts with astrology, that fake science, even in the 17th century. What a rational victory to calculate the date and time of ones own conception by looking at the stars and the constellations! And at once he is compared to a dog, an aggressive dog because this astrology is a refuge against the world, and Kepler himself enumerates his enemies, those who want him dead, etc. At this moment he appears as a paranoid person who tries to find some solace in astrology. He is victimized because Mercury is in the quadrate of Mars, the Sun in the sextile of Saturn, and Mercury and the Sun are in the seventh house. And that is dramatic indeed. Mercury in the 7th House with the Sun confers objectivity. . . This combination, however, heightens a persons sensitivity to the expectations of others and creates a correspondingly greater difficulty in defining and supporting his own stance. (http://www.dkfoundation.co.uk/dkfoundation/BookKarmaHouse7.htm) But Kepler seems to be losing his rationality at this science when he says True astrology is a testimonial of Gods work. Of course if it is true it is the direct reflection of Gods intention and will. But this is pure superstition as for astrology and it is pure speculation as for God. Astrology is typically an invention of man that is not rationally based in the 17th century any more and then if it reflected the creative work of God, God himself who was declared before a rational being, would become a superstitious irrational being.

And thats when Kepler really escapes from Gods hand and comes to a conclusion supported by astrology: Mans will, the souls first faculty, is and remains free. I have corrected the translation. There is no future expressed here as the translation says and will always be free. The German text says und bleibt frei. Kepler is just a defensive paranoid person who tries to appear as a true Christian with his reference to the soul, and in the libretto that reference is in Latin (princeps animae facultas) which makes him a good Catholic actually since Latin is rejected by the Protestants. And thats when Gryphius intervenes again with a vision of war in the obvious name of God, a war in which some human blinds some others in the name of God on both sides and we have to understand blinding as concerning the blinding of mans reason with Gods truth as much as the actual blinding of the mortals of one religion by the mortals of the other religion, always in the name of God. That leads Gryphius to an extremely dejected and sad conclusion that God has burned his heart and mind and yet he is expecting to be free of sorrows tomorrow in God himself.

We come then to another scientific moment that is rather light in meaning. At first the physicist thought the planets were running on circular orbits, which was proved false, so the physicist moved to an oval orbit which was also proved false and then the physicist moved to an ellipse. And the choir then comes up with one of these superb moments when this scientific deductive procedure of establishing a model and then verifying it or disproving it and then changing the model accordingly, etc., is seen as the very rational nature of God and this slow moving towards a model that is close enough to reality to be considered as true, for the time being at least, is the proof of the existence of God the creator of all things. The conclusion is dramatically absurd, but note it is in Latin in the original libretto, once more a sign of allegiance to the Catholic Church: From Him, through Him, and in Him is everything, Amen.  And this allegiance is even stronger when we consider your Creator just before was in Latin Dominum Creatorem tuum, thus God was your Lord Creator at least.

Luckily Gryphius comes up again with a long poem on the ugliness of war. War could be compared to a plague, fire or famine but it is a lot more than that. And Gryphius wants to remain silent about whats worse than death, about whats worse than plague, fire, and famine . . . many lost their souls salvation. These wars in the name of God are the worst thing to do because your godlike side and your divine future in salvation are both negated and you are reduced to what was called before nothing but a common dog.

So Kepler can conclude this opera and his life with the fact that his freedom gives him the power to choose but his choice is between present devastation or future devastation, devastation right now or devastation tomorrow morning. And he comes to this realistic and phenomenal conclusion that he is in total loneliness, that he is both a guest and a stranger, that he has lost all identity and is anonymous, that he is a barbarian for the people around him whose language he does not understand nor speak and thus he has only one exit, one hope: to find in death an eternal ground where he could cast his anchor and find some stability.

But the opera is a loop that starts with Keplers own epitaph and ends with Keplers own epitaph, four lines in Latin. Strangely enough the opening epitaph is like a somber Tenebrae by Marc-Antoine Charpentier and the closing epitaph is like a peaceful and pacified Ruht Wohl from Johann Sebastian Bachs Saint Johns Passion. From the descent into a hell of perdition to the ascent into an eternity of dreamlike sleep.

There is something else to say about the music. Of course the minimalist constant and steady at times heavy often humdrum always tantric repetition of two or three or four notes imposing regular and unvarying rhythms, tempos and beats is also regularly superimposed with melodious longer musical sentences that enable the singing to find a tone, a depth and even some more complex emotion like hatred, fright, condescendence, anger, vision, illusion, disillusion, desire to escape and even once or twice some lustful moments. And yet the music is always the accompaniment of the text. If you do not penetrate the words you will get nothing at all. The Word and the Word alone is the creator of this world or existence, and if you believe that Word has created the universe how could you not believe the Word of this opera is the basic creating element, the body of that creator when the music is the soul of it and we only have our mind to capture both and reunite them. But a soul without a body or a body without a soul, that does not sound very sexy.

And for those who will dare get to the DVD I must add the production of this opera in Linz was probably admirable and definitely revealed the real dimension of Glass music? The tempos, rhythms and beats become some accompaniment of what you see on the stage and what you hear from the stage. In fact that accompaniment becomes like a baroque continuo, or the music in a film. Without it the opera would sound empty, and yet we do not hear it anymore because of what is happening on the stage, of what is being sung on the stage.

The production was very pure with a lot of darkness, red light and only one scene really that was ochre and golden. The entrance of Kepler on his gurney horizontal at first and then straightening slowly to end at an angle like the very special gurney on which Hannibal Lecter, alias or aka Anthony Hopkins, was transported from his cell to any place he had to go to. Strikingly impressive for the opening Tenebrae of the first epitaph as if it w<ere a resurrection from the tomb and at the end when he is replaced on it and moved away along with the second performance of his epitaph it becomes pacifying like the vision of a child that is put to bed and slowly rocked to sleep after a long temper tantrum. There is in this vision of death opening and closing the evocation some kind of softening and smoothening of the tough and rough confrontation of science to religion and of man to war, two impossible face-on one-on-ones that no one on earth wants to experience at any time in our short passage on this planet.

Some might think the use of many mechanical elements on the stage to represent the machine of science is sort of cumbersome, but I find it rather pacifying because of the extreme stability these mechanical props have in a story that is and remains very somber and squalid in many ways. That was a time when after 300,000 years Homo Sapiens was finally able to put down on the table of his mind, which was no tabula rasa, the very first methodical principles and concepts he will need to build modern science and the modern world. All that was probably not durable since it had to be reexamined all the time, but it was sustainable in the fact that every moment produced the next one without any stop. The whole history of man is the constant adjustment of a circular orbit to an oval orbit and then to an elliptical orbit, which is like the Mandorla of a Jesus Christ in his Glory, or like the scientist in his never completed quest. Yet too often we are the barking common dogs of the battle fields of all fundamentalists. Isnt there a Jihad behind every scientific concept of human thinking?

A story of some possible melodious salvation on a background of techno rhythmic heart beats stuck forever in what sounds like one groove looping onto itself. That sounds like Frederic Chopins Little Dog Waltz in D flat major and we can end divinely flat on our stomach in front of such major revelation.

Dr Jacques COULARDEAU

reviewText:
Despite the merest hint of remastering echo and an attempt to give channel separation to bass and high frequencies, sound quality of the vintage 78 sides on COLUMBIA Record Club's early '70s double LP set, BIG BANDS' GREATEST HITS (CG 30009) is right up there with the best available on vinyl. (Inside its gatefold cover there's a playlist and notes for most songs.)

RANDOM NOTES
Basie's "One O'Clock Jump" theme has never sounded better (the secret is ANALOG audio, CD fans!). Gene Krupa's skins are on fire on "Drumboogie." Charlie Barnet's "Skyliner" is a live performance. "Take the 'A' Train" is another non-studio cut (thus no chart listing below). It's performed by Duke's guys for a none-too-attentive dinner crowd. "I Got Rhythm" is by Glenn Miller's pre-RCA Bluebird orchestra, one that flopped and was disbanded after a year or so. "Caldonia" is by Herman's original Herd. Woody sings on this hot classic. When Sinatra recorded "All or Nothing At All" with Harry James, he hadn't learned Tommy Dorsey's breath and phrasing techniques, yet this early platter shows us the singing superstar that "The Voice" would soon become.

This transfer of Orrin Tucker's "Oh Johnny" is one of the cleanest COLUMBIA ever issued on vinyl. Added reverb gives depth to Bonnie Baker's vocal. On the other hand, this dub of Orrin's "Billy" has all the surface hiss of every LP copy I've ever heard. (NOTE: Wee Bonnie's real name was Evelyn Nelson.) The Modernaires' remake of "Jukebox Saturday Night" lacks the magic of their performance on Glenn Miller's original version. When Benny Goodman combined Louis Prima's "Sing, Sing, Sing" with Chu Berry's "Christopher Columbus," he provided a platform for Gene Krupa's remarkable drum solo. Presented here is a later "live" performance with the Goodman boys in top form. A klezmer break during Benny's extended solo generates some audience chuckles. Later, he hits a few intentional off-the-scale squeals (achieved by biting hard on the clarinet's mouthpiece).

A hissing transfer of Bunny Berigan's "I Can't Get Started" is by a smaller group. Recorded in April of 1937, it's not as polished as his later RCA hit single, but definitely has much appeal. Clyde McCoy's "Sugar Blues" theme was recorded by him many times over the decades. This earliest COLUMBIA one's darn good, but I'm partial to the '35 DECCA platter. It has more pep. "Snowfall" and "Sunrise Serenade" were both COLUMBIA 78s this reviewer's mom had in her record drawer and they remain personal favorites. "Snowfall" has amazingly deep bass tones I'd never noticed before this listening. "Sunrise Serenade," a Frankie Carle original, topped the charts for Glenn Miller (backed with his theme, "Moonlight Serenade"). Uncredited song on Eddy Duchin's "Chopin Nocturne In E-Flat" is "Time On My Hands."

reviewText: I really like this new album from Ronnie Spector. The choice of songs is great. It fits the time period of the 60's that Ronnie is paying respect to, and certainly lived. The arrangements and performances are different from the original well known hit versions, which I'm very happy to hear. Ronnie does it her way. An added surprise is the rather obscure Rolling Stones song I'D MUCH RATHER BE WITH THE GIRLS. Ronnie knows her music, and chose wisely with the songs here. I really like this new album. I didn't want or expect a Phil Spector type bombastic production. I'm glad this isn't. It's wonderful to get a new album from Ronnie Spector, and this is a feel good album with a beloved artist.

reviewText:
First of all, Afterman: Ascension and Decention are concept albums that tells a complete story between them.  Personally, I love the story and how the songs reflect that.  It makes for a better musical experience.  However, for this review, I'm just going to lay down my thoughts on each song, track by track.

1. Pretelethal
9/10
I was expecting it to be a another "intro" tune that Coheed usually does.  I like those, but only when listening as an album...when they pop up randomly on my ipod, they get skipped.  Happily, this is more of an actual song you can sing along with.  Good song, but nothing mind blowing

2. Key Entity Extraction V: Sentry the Defiant
10/10
Plain and simple, this song just rocks.  Definitely a great "pump up" song.

3. The Hard Sell
10/10
I love the groove to this song.  It's so fun to sing along to as well. Very catchy stuff.

4. Number City
10/10
The first time I heard this one, I was scratching my head.  It was just weird, and reminded me of something Phil Collins would have done in the 80s (like Sussudio).  I wrote it off as the weakest track on the album.  Then it got stuck in my head...and after a few listens, I ended up loving this strange little song.

5. Gravity's Union
11/10
This is probably my favorite song they've done since No World For Tomorrow.  This is just epic Coheed right here.  Perfection.  I gave most of the other songs a 10, so either I'd have to bump them down to 9s....or cheat and give this an 11.

6. Away We Go
10/10
Another great song, and very pretty too.

7. Iron Fist
10/10
Another song that is impossible to get out of my head.  I kind of prefer the live version they did a few years back during the NeverEnder, but it's not fair to compare it to that really.  The album version stands on its own.

8. Dark Side of Me
10/10
What a shock, another 10 from me...  I really do love this album.  This is probably the most radio friendly of the songs on this album.  Just a great straight up rock song.

9. 2's My Favorite 1
10/10
Listening to the album start to finish, I couldn't help but to have an actual emotional reaction to this song.  It's just so uplifting and beautiful.  Taken as a song only, I gave it a 10....when I factor in the story of Sirius and his wife, I'd go with an 11.

Overall, I LOVE this album. On it's own, despite its short length, I'd still rank it up there with Good Apollo and No World (my favorites)...taken with the other Afterman, it's no contest. This is a real accomplishment.

The special editions have 2 other songs, but this review is for the version Amazon sells.

reviewText:
So now we have a choice in our ZZ Top music.  This set, which returns the original mixes to us, or Six Pack, with its remixes.

I bought "Six Pack" a few months back in a used record store for $10.00, and I wasn't mortified by the remixes of the songs.  My thought was "Hey if ZZ Top wants to spice up their back catalogue, It's their music and their prerogative".  But I don't want to do a side by side comparison of the two sets.

I like this 10 disc offering.  Playing the first 4 CDs from start to stop and enjoying the bluesy/rootsy sound of them,  ZZ Top are bluesmen at heart and their deep love of the style shows.  With Eliminator they started a blues rock sound that continued pretty much to the present day.  Blues has depth and feeling to it, ZZ Top expresses both no matter what instruments they use.  In all truth they weren't the first to a synthesizer to fill out the rhythm of a blues song.  If it complements their song and expands their creativity, why not.

I also like the way the emphasis is on the music.  Do we always need a booklet with essays and photos?  Do you always look at it each time you play the album?  Why bloat the packaging, when the music presented here starts out with basic and pure blues and develops in style and instrumentation as we move deeper in to it.  So keeping to the front and back album covers with a few fold outs is not a bad idea.  It keeps you focused on what you are hearing and not on what you are seeing.

And what you will hear on these 10 CDs is good music, well presented and well mastered.  Warners is not adding to the loudness wars CDs here.  The sound on all of these albums is very acceptable.  The sound is well equalized and very clear through the set.  Again, Warners did not over do it.  I hope what we have here is a signal that the loudness war is over.

reviewText: Harlem River Blues is the kind of album that makes me wish that more people I knew listened to Country music. I run in several different musical circles. Many of the jazz lovers I know laugh at me for my love of Indie Rock. And for many of the Indie and Alternative Rock fans I know, the Alternative-Country thing doesn't exist. To them there is only Country, and they don't like Country music much. But an album like this can remind us that good music is just good music, no matter what category you want to put it in. I'll even go so far as to call this "great music" because it resonated with me personally in a way that I think is great. Your individual tastes may vary so please forgive me if this is not your cup of tea. Some people might think a country album inspired by New York City to be a contradiction. I think the juxtaposition works to great effect. The city was once a rural settlement, and away from the business centers and high rises there are still areas that remind you of a different time or place. Not to mention, the city has always attracted people from the country looking for a living. This album is like a chronicle of the songs that just one such lonely soul might have written after moving to NY from Tennessee. Some of the songs are more upbeat romping tunes, like the title track "Harlem River Blues" and the very fun "Move Over Mama." And perhaps the best of the bunch, "Ain't Waitin'," has an infectious melody that just fits so perfectly with the lyrics. But by and large, this is a laid back relaxing album, the kind you might play on a Saturday afternoon. My favorite song on this album is tough to pick. I really love "Christchurch Woman." And "One More Night In Brooklyn" has an easy feel to it and playful lyrics. The simple intro of guitar strumming kind of hangs in my mind. Like all good music, this album reminds one of other great artists. "Slippin and Slidin" evokes the memory of classic Van Morrison albums like Tupelo Honey. "Move Over Mama" sounds like it could have been written by Jerry Lee Lewis for all I know! But "Rogers Park" is probably the song that had the most immediate impact on me. It's a smooth mid-tempo ballad, more in the vein of Lyle Lovett's Pontiac, and I can listen to it over and over again. "Workin For the MTA" also has the sound of a Lyle Lovett tune. Perhaps more artists will start covering some of Justin's great songs. The sound engineering of this album seems designed to evoke a barn burner. In many cases individual instruments sound like they aren't even miked. A song like "Wanderin'" is a great example, with slightly reverberating vocals and a distant harmonica in the background with a fiddle and bluegrass guitar more in the foreground. This record makes the listener feel like they recorded these songs live with one microphone and an analog reel. This minimalist sound often takes a lot of engineering work to sound authentic. I would love to learn more about how this album was recorded for them to get this sound. My only regret is that another Amazon exclusive deal has cost me again. I am an unrepentant collector of actual music media, from compact disks to vinyl records. So the fact that this download is available a day before the actual album means I will probably be buying this record twice. This is an experience that I can live with. This music warrants the investment. Listen to this music. Buy this album, either in the form of the download or in a CD or a vinyl record. This album evokes a feeling of nostalgia that only the best music can. I am really enjoying listening to it. I hope that you will too. Enjoy.

reviewText: So much has been born and bred in the Crescent City besides the talented Harry Connick Jr. Jazz,the blues,rhythm & blues and funk all have a connective origin source somewhere in it's streets. All most people today can remember about the city is that Hurricane Katrina devastated and nearly destroyed the city almost nine years ago. Yet everyone from Satchmo himself,to Gino Vannelli with his Pauper in Paradise and even Harry himself with his Star Turtle have paid tribute to the atmosphere and the groove of the Mardi Gras,which one could call the power source for all the creative energy New Orleans has to offer. Well Harry is back under the influence of Fat Tuesday yet again with this album all the way. The album opens with the title song,a vibrantly spirited R&B shuffle with a beautiful falsetto vocal harmony. "Hurricane" and "Cuddina Done It",with their hot horn charts and "Wish I Were Him" with it's almost stride style piano chords represent some of the finest examples of modern day,slow grooving,foot stomping Crescent City funk that one could imagine. 'S'pposed To Be" brings in the "big four" beat as they call it for a flat out ragtime/dixieland style groove that points to the threat connecting the earliest jazz to the earliest funk in terms of the rhythmic accents. "The Preacher" on the other hand comes straight out of the JB school whereas "Dang You Pretty" and "Angola (At The Farm)",with it's hard grooving guitar go right back to the heavy foot stomping funk. "Mind Over Matter" brings in the Caribbean percussive influence of Congo Square for an enormously poly rhythmic groove whereas "Nola Girl" and the closer "City Beneath The Sea" are richly crafted melodic soulful funk of the highest order. It hardly matters that the final two tracks on the album are take off of the Star Turtle album. In fact it very much goes with the funk tradition of funk artists either remaking,or flat out revisiting,their best songs on later releases. Also it provides yet another connective element to Harry's sojourn into the music of the Mardi Gras that clearly inspires enormous bursts of creative energy within him. Overall this is one of the hardest grooving and funkiest recordings Harry Connick has made for some time,and a very welcomed addition to his vast and often diverse musical catalog.

reviewText:
This two cd set is a considerable upgrade over the previous disc from 2003, "The Very Best Of The Grateful Dead." With two cds and remastered sound, it is now the definitive entry point for any beginning Deadhead.

For the most part, the song selection is great; you get all the classics ("Touch of Grey," "Ripple," "Friend of the Devil," "Casey Jones," "Truckin',"), as well as (mostly) well chosen deep cuts (""Dark Star," "Box of Rain," "Unbroken Chain," "Foolish Heart"), plus the added benefit of fantastic sound and great packaging.

There are a few odd selections here; "Easy Wind" could've easily been cut for "Brokedown Palace," and room should've definitely been made for "Franklin's Tower" on either disc. Similarly, while Brent Mydland certainly deserves representation, "Far from Me" isn't good enough to displace "Althea" as one of two tracks from the mostly dire "Go to Heaven." We also didn't need three tracks from "Shakedown Street," (the title song and "Fire on the Mountain" are fine), and "I Need a Miracle" could've easily made way for "Samson and Delilah." Finally, at least one of the "Built to Last" songs could've been excised for at least one live cut, since no matter what your starting point is, 'live' truly is the best way to experience the Dead, and including "One More Saturday Night," "Jack Straw," "Sugaree," or many other great songs that never made it onto a studio albums are among the best songs they ever did, and are all more important and essential to Dead fans then "Blow Away" or "Standing on the Moon."

Overall, though, no collection is perfect, and "The Best Of The Grateful Dead" does its due diligence in being good primer for beginners.

reviewText:
John Cale first solo album, originally released in 1970, came as a pleasant surprise to many fans of Velvet Underground. After his departure from V.U. in 1968 Cale had among other things produced for Nico, and some may have expected a more radical album, but here Cale reveals himself as a brilliant songwriter capable of writing and producing in a very melodic way, and several of these songs may even have had hit-potentials. Especially the catchy "Gideon's Bible" with its Beach Boys harmonies could very well had hit the charts, given the right exposure.

Among other very memorable tracks is the great opener "Hello There", featuring Cale driving piano. The majestic "Big Cloud" is another stand-out; sound almost like a Robbie Robertson song.

There's a slight country feel to another favourite,"Please", and the haunting "Ghost Story" features lyrics that make you think of Keith Reid of Procol Harum.

This could very well be John Cale's artistically most consistent album; which obviously says quite a lot, and at any rate this is without question the first time he really proves himself as a prolific songwriter.

reviewText:
Easily among the best soul singer/songwriters of the late 60's and early 70's, one of the greatest times for soul artists, Bobby Womack is probably the most under-appreciated. Though he was pretty much a constant voice on the R&B charts in those days, he had only three crossover hits and of those, only Lookin' For a Love (1974) made the top Ten at #10. It sold a million records and got an RIAA gold disc as did Harry Hippie (1972), though that song only made #31 on the pop charts, being more of a strictly R&B hit. It was very common in those days for soul artists to have many R&B chart hits and only a couple pop hits, but Bobby's lacked the #1 level impact of songs like Me and Mrs Jones, Superfly, or (If Loving You Is Wrong) I Don't Want To Be Right. The fortunate use of Across 110th Street in Jackie Brown has made it bigger now than it ever was in its own day and is probably his most frequently played song on oldies radio.

Born in Cleveland, Bobby joined a Gospel group with his four brothers. After being discovered by Sam Cooke, the quintet relocated to L.A. and with Sam's encouragement changed their name to The Valentinos and moved into R&B. They had a hit in 1962 with Lookin' For a Love (the same song that would be Bobby's biggest solo hit later). It has a kind of Staples Singers feel to it and in fact was adapted from the gospel song, Couldn't Hear Nobody Pray. As the Womack Brothers they had toured with the Staple Singers. Also in the early 60's Bobby wrote It's All Over Now. The Rolling stones wanted to record it after Murray the K played it for them, but Bobby didn't want them to sing his song until Sam Cook persuaded him. after receiving his first royalty check he said they could sing any of his songs.

The murder of Sam Cooke ended this period with the group breaking up and Bobby scandalizing everyone in the soul music business when he married Cooke's widow a mere three months after his death. Bobby's life would be troubled by problems, scandals, drug use and personal tragedies that would eventually affect his writing and performing. Virtually blacklisted, he went to Memphis as a session player (guitar, of course) and struck up a good relationship with Wilson Pickett, who recorded quite a few of Bobby's songs including I'm a Midnight Mover and I'm In Love (both on this collection in Bobby's versions, which are sung in the Pickett style). He finally got a solo deal with Minit Records, an old New Orleans label that by that time (1968) had been bought by Imperial Records which had been bought by Liberty Records (owned the Avenet Corp by then). Liberty had a Middle-of-the-Road Radio orientation(they had even had Jan & Dean do a version of I Left My Heart In San Francisco), so it's no surprise that his first album was full of standards. But what he did with them was exceptional. He completely reimagined them; his "San Francisco" is fast and mean,Fly Me To the Moon is fresh and fun in a jazzy arrangement and California Dreamin' is given a minimal backup with Bobby's guitar and voice giving the song great feeling.

The collection spans his glory days of the early to mid 70's along with the early material. Woman's Gotta Have It has one of his famed spoken intros, as does the fabulous Fact of Life/He'll Be There when the Sun Goes Down which has his long riff to a female fan on the virtues of a man at home compared to one on the road. He was nicknamed "The Preacher" and in that cut, paired with More Than I can Stand you get a virtual church service paired with More Than I Can Stand, a cautionary tale about a woman who tells her man to get a job (so she can have other men over when he's working). Harry hippie was written for Bobby by his frien and sometimes co-songwriter Jim Ford, as a funny take on bass-player brother Harry Womack (though he did have a job unlike the Harry in the song). bobby continued to sing it as a bitter-sweet tribute after his brother's murder by a jealous girlfriend. His later take on It's all Over Now is here as are his other hits: Nobody Wants You When You're Down and Out and Lookin For a Love. It ends with a soulful take on James Taylor's song, Fire and Rain, really a look back on his life.

Every song on this collection has a lot to recommend it and with 22 songs it's about the most complete collection out there.

reviewText:
Just like many of metal's most important act's, Fear Factory have alway's been fuelled by the expectations of one album, 1995's 'Demanufacture' was a huge startling energy storm of thunderous riffs, compelling melodies, insane drum assaults, and soaring choruses. However, it was also the album they've never really been able to recover from.

But now, that's all changed, because 'Archetype' is without a doubt the most intense, heaviest Fear Factory album recorded in years.

Burton C. Bell is back at his best, never have his vocals sounded more vicious, or harmonic for that matter! Just listen to the captivating ballad-esque stylings of 'Drones', 'Bite the hand that bleeds', & 'Human Sheilds'. Or for some of his most monster-like roaring's, try 'Slave Labor', 'Cyberwaste', 'Act of God', & 'Bonescraper'.

Christian Olde Wolbers has now moved on to lead guitar, to take a stab at Dino Cazares riff-writing duties and surprisingly pulls it off brilliantly. Byron Stroud ain't half bad at all, and fits in with the band perfectly.

And as for the talented Raymond Herrera, his skillful drumming totally sounds more brutaly powerful than ever!

Overall, fantastic comeback album. To anyone who thought the mighty FF were dead...shame on you! But, to be fair I guess no one knew what to expect, but frankly for a band like this they deserved better credit.

So go on! Buy it, you will not regret it!

reviewText: Fans of Primus definitely need to pick this up. While the stripped down sound of the Duo De Twang is not as raucous and weird as Primus, the music still sounds full of that swampy energy Claypool is known for. I prefer it to the Brown Album and much of Claypool's other records. I've always suspected that Primus, for all its slappy bass, wonky guitars and elaborate drums was really just a folk band at it's heart, given Claypool's penchant for storytelling. This album solidifies that idea. The song selection is eclectic, with highlights being covers of the BeeGee's "Stayin' Alive" and "The Battle of New Orleans" (popularized by Johnny Horton), along with the version of "Buzzards of Green Hill" and "Rumble of the Diesel" from Claypool's solo albums. Frankly, the Primus songs that are on here seem a bit less inspired and more obligatory. It would be nice to hear Claypool write some new material for the duo and maybe expand it to include some more acoustic instruments on a future release. It sounds like he's having fun. I'm surprised he never pulls out an upright bass though.

Even the odd inclusion of David Crosby and Grahm Nash worked in its strange way. All in all, one of the best concert DVDs I have ever witnessed.

reviewText: I have been looking forward to this album, waiting in agonizing anticipation since it was announced and it did not disappoint at all! This album was absolutely brilliant and it is a shame some people can't hear that. Newsflash: Powerslave was released on 1984. Iron Maiden isn't going to do Powerslave part II. If you're one of those fans that listens to new Maiden just to see if it sounds like old Maiden, bug off or actually stop and listen to the music they're making NOW IN 2015! I love their 80's materiel to death, but Iron Maiden has never been a band that lives off of what they did, they constantly push forward to be about what they're currently doing and they put some hard work into this record! The first half of the album had me completely captivated. The songs were amazing and passed by with such a fluidity that they never felt as long as they were (Except The Red and the Black, but more on that later). The second half was just as captivating, if not just a degree less than the first. None of the music over stayed its welcome (except for The Empire of the Clouds, but more on that later). The melodies, guitars, vocals, drums, bass everything just shines, particularly on The Book of Souls, If Eternity Should Fail and Shadows of the Valley. Iron Maiden is obviously known for lengthier materiel, but even the most die hard of Maiden fans became curious as to which way a song can go when its 13:33 or 18:01 in length. This album bore very little negatives to me and the positive definitely outshines all, but I really do feel that The Red and the Black was a bit over in length. The song was great, but about 3 minutes could have been shaved off to save the song from becoming just a tad bit bland. And finally, overwhelming The Empire of the Clouds. Now, this isn't the greatest song Maiden has ever done, but it is close. Unlike The Red and The Black, The Empire of the Clouds, despite being nearly five minutes longer, does not overstay its welcome. The song is muti-layered and beautiful incorporating violin and piano into an already fine tuned array of instruments. The only problem I had with Empire of the Clouds is that the story it told wasn't as captivating or well paced as say, When the Wild Wind Blows from the last album. The lyrics weren't as intense and didn't draw me in as much, but overall the song is a fantastic piece of art and flows beautifully. This was well worth the five year wait and the band still sounds amazing. Up the Irons!

When Martin Scorsese decided to remake "Cape Fear", he paid tribute to the original by featuring original stars Gregory Peck, Robert Mitchum, and Martin Balsam in cameos. Scorsese also recognized the contribution of the first film's composer Bernard Herrmann.
Thus, Elmer Bernstein, himself a legendary musician (and recent Oscar nominee for "Far from Heaven"), adapted, arranged, and conducted Herrmann's original score for the newer film. This is a marriage of two giants in the business.
A score that is as haunting and chilling as the more recognizable works "Psycho" and "Marnie", "Cape Fear" is true Herrmann with its ominous cues and screeching strings.
Fans of Herrmann, Bernstein, or Scorsese must have this one!

reviewText:
My first introduction to Cheap Trick was a 45 rpm single of "Dream Police," in 1979, which my cheap Soundesign turntable with Radio Shack needle ate to dust within a year.  Anyways, I went to an audiophile store and plunked down beaucoup bucks for a Thorens with an Ortofon cartridge in 1981, and then began my Cheap Trick album buying spree.  First I bought their best album, "Live at Budokan," which is without a doubt the greatest live album recorded by any band, period.  Then I got "Dream Police," which features the title track and my favourite all-time song, "I Need Your Love."  But my favourite studio album is this one, "In Color."
What can I say, all the songs on this one fit together like a watch, just like "Live at Budokan" does, and opens with the same opening band (what we used to call tracks in the days of 33-1/3 rpm records), "Hello There."  "In Color" contains no less than 5 out of its 10 tunes which ended up on "Budokan," and the best thing I can say about this album is that the studio versions are (with the exception of "I Want You to Want Me," which has a little too bubble-gum a flavour on this record) just as good as the live versions (yes, like Kiss, Cheap Trick was a band that sounded *better* on stage).
But, the best tunes are "Downed," "Oh, Caroline" and "Southern Girls," and for years I went around saying how these examples of 1960s and Beatles-influenced songs ought to have been on "Budokan."  Of course, my wish came true in 1993 when Epic released the follow-up "Budokan II," and whatya know?  Their live versions are just as solid (on "Southern Girls," even more so) than this studio album.
But don't think this album can be replaced by "Budokan" I & II:  Like the first "Budokan," this album *gels*, each song leading naturally into the next, not a wasted track on the record. Everything you want in a Cheap Trick album is here:  Robin Zander's and Tom Petersson's harmonized vocals, Bun E. Carlos' stellar drumming, and Rick Nielsen's killer guitar riffs.  I'd put Nielsen against Ted Nugent or Eddie Van Halen anyday as a soloist.
In fact, this album is mixed so perfectly, I've never even heard the Compact Disc version -- I still listen to my old 33 vinyl, and the boys from Rockford, Illinois always takes me back.

reviewText: Ben Webster's mature 50's sax sound was magic with strings. The orchestrations and arrangements are tasteful (Strayhorn, Burns..pretty good company) While Brownie blew right through his arrangements, and Bird blew above and beyond his, Ben seems to blow right inside the arrangements written for him. He claimed that strings brought the best out of his playing, and who am I to argue. The first time I heard Webster play with unabashed romantic feel was on the Verve recording of an older Billie Holiday singing "Do Nothing 'Till You Hear From Me". His solo on that blew me away, as does his work here on "Chelsea Bridge".  Almost every ballad he touches turns to pure melting gold on this great, new, expanded collection. As stated in the original liner notes by Bob Blumenthal - "Listen, but be forewarned - grown men and women have been known to cry".

This video captures Stevie Ray Vaughn and Double Trouble as well as anyone could ever hope to.  Bands generally divide into two categories.  The vast majority do their best work in the studio and try with varied success to capture some of what they did in the studio in their live performances.  Then there are those rare bands whose natural element is live performance.  These bands try in the studio to capture some of what they do live.  Double Trouble was definitely the second type.  The performances on this video are every bit as technically proficient as anything Double Trouble ever did in the studio, but they are fluid and alive in a way that is rarely if ever captured in the studio.  Incredibly, Stevie Ray Vaughn and Double Trouble were actually better live than they were in the studio, a rarity.  I had the good fortune to see them live a few months before Stevie Ray Vaughn died.
I only wish there were some more SRV videos of this quality available, particularly some later ones with Reese Wynans, who I personally think made an incredibly good band even better.
If you buy only one SRV video, this is the one.  Buy this one first in any case.

Future Shock was a new sensation when released in early 1983, as Herbie Hancock (and his Rockit band) & Bill Laswell teamed up to deliver electronics with funk, fusion and a sprinkling of avant-garde.

Rockit garnered a Grammy award for best R&B instrumental performance, while the video captured five awards - including Video of the Year - in the first MTV Video Music Awards show.

The CD has five cuts sandwiched between Rockit and Rockit (Mega Mix), the latter not on the original release. A true gem is Future Shock, a Curtis Mayfield composition. Earth Beat and Rough pump the funk through the speakers, while Hancock lets the jazz notes do the talking in T.F.S. and Autodrive.

That the collaboration of Hancock and Laswell was unable to reproduce the magic in subsequent releases speaks greatly about the quality found in Future Shock.

reviewText:
Relient K has grown up. They're less goofy and more serious on "Mmhmm"; their fourth overall and first mainstream record. I've got nothing more to say overall except that this is RK's second-best album so far. Now on to the song reviews...

"The One I'm Waiting For" - I don't know for sure what this song is about. They mention a girl, so I guess this girl must be the subject. It's a good leadoff track. 4/5.

"Be My Escape" - This is a song about giving up on God, and then asking Him for forgiveness. It's also the first single from the album. 5/5.

"High of 75" - This is a nice short song, which relates the weather to God's love. Only problem: it's too short. 4/5.

"I So Hate Consequences" - This is probably my personal favorite. It's a song about doing wrong and facing consequences which none of us like. Just remember, God loves us all no matter what we do. 5/5.

"The Only Thing Worse Than Beating a Dead Horse Is Betting On One" - This is nothing but pure filler. I skip it everytime. 0/5.

"My Girl's Ex-Boyfriend" - Here, Matt Thiessen thanks his girlfriend's ex-boyfriend for dumping her. It's not actually meant to be serious, but it's a nice song anyway. 4/5.

"More Than Useless" - This is another favorite of mine. It's about one thinking they're "not any good at all", but in the end, they are assured that they're more than useless. 5/5.

"Which to Bury, Us Or the Hatchet" - This is a nice song which I'm sure many people can relate to. Sometimes we don't like the people we love the most, for things they may do. It slows down near the end, and fades nicely into the next track. 5/5.

"Let It All Out" - This really isn't one of my favorites. The message is good (sometimes you have to go to the extreme to save yourself), but it's a slow and dragged out piano ballad. 2/5.

"Who I Am Hates Who I've Been" - Good song right here. It's about one apologizing for the things they've done in the past. 5/5.

"Maintain Consciousness" - This wasn't written to be serious (it mentions Attention Deficit Disorder) but it's all too true. 5/5.

"This Week The Trend" - I can't think of a good review for this song, other than the fact that I like it. 4/5.

"Life After Death and Taxes" - This song challenges one to think about what happens after death. It gets slow near the end, but that doesn't do much to hurt it. 4/5.

"When I Go Down" - This is a piano-driven acoustic song which drags out (it's almost 7 minutes long!) However, Matt T. is worshiping God throughout, which is something I like to hear. 4/5.

There you have it. I highly recommend the album whether you're a Relient K fan or not. Casual fans may not like it, however, due to the lack of the silly songs of the past.

reviewText: 5 Stars but flawed? Yes and the song is Madrigal, an obvious attempt at filler but it has no place on a record with such high standards. Similar to Tears on 2112, Madrigal is slow, quiet, acoustic, and depressing. Nevertheless, ALL of the other tracks on A Farewell to Kings are amazing. The title track is probably Rush's most overlooked song and is followed by one of the greatest Rush songs ever written, Xanadu. Lee's bass playing literally takes over on this track and anchors Farewell. This is the era in which Neil had the handlebar mustache and was wearing robes. But the coolest part about this era was Neil's ability to incorporate almost every facet of percussion known to man including gongs, chimes, wood blocks and any other contraption known to man. His drumset at this point was any drummers wet dream. Closer to the Heart is a concert standard and a great acoustic track. Cinderella Man is another hidden Rush song that only the most ardent fan comes to treasure. And finally, Cygnus X-1, the best song Rush EVER recorded which makes this album a must have for any fan. 1977's A Farewell to Kings finds Rush on the upswing toward prog-rock immortality, one step closer to Hemispheres (the culminating masterpiece of the Rush catalog). Highest Recommendation.

reviewText:
Once upon a time there were two savvy guitar players, a bassist, and two drummers.  After an insignificant first outing, they savvied up even more and their sophomore product was a smash success dripping with talent, beauty, art, and soul.  Then they polished it up and served a couple good quality meals that gained them even more adoration, and in the meanwhile they added a third guitar to the recipe!  Their fourth serving was a meal fully as satisfying and delicious as their second one had been, loaded with tons of extra flavor and it even included desert.  It was hopeless to expect a three-peat from these now six total brothers, that would be expecting a miracle!  Well, as many of you readers know, miracles do sometimes happen and we are all blessed that it happened right here.  A fifth serving of extraordinarily delicious victuals, and a third time it being so ultimately delectable that one could not believe it possible to receive so many scrumptious meals without a tasteless interruption of service.  The most impressive fact in all of this, is that this time, another fine cook was added to the kitchen bringing the number of chefs to a total of seven!

Tom Johnston was ill with stomach ulcers to the point where tour shows had to be cancelled.  He felt he needed to decrease his involvement in the band without quitting it altogether so he penned and performed one song, and provided duet and backing vocals to another.  Bill Payne of Little Feat was no longer available for session keys so The Doobie Brothers were in serious need of a vocal replacement for Tom and a keyboard player.  Jeff "Skunk" Baxter was already their third guitarist so throwing back to early Doobie days they could accomplish a lot still with only two.  Skunk suggested another out of work Steely Dan player to fill both roles.  Michael McDonald was hesitant to fill Tom's shoes, he felt he was only a "songwriter - piano hacker" but after they met and rehearsed, the band was overjoyed to have him.  Producer Ted Templeman called Michael a "diamond in the rough" and told the band that he could take them to totally new directions (that being a somewhat good idea at the time).  The "new" Doobie Brothers sound was not so much new as it was a steady progression from where they had been to where they were already going.  Michael added a new vocal dimension for sure but the larger change in Doobie sound would not come for another two albums when they smashed their own records with MINUTE BY MINUTE.  The real "change" on this album, in Doobie sound actually came from a more concerted effort between Pat Simmons and Skunk to jazz up the overall Doobie Brothers technique and the result is another astounding step in Doobie history.  TAKIN' IT TO THE STREETS is a third definitive moment in Doobie albums (the other two being TOULOUSE STREET and STAMPEDE) which once again breaks ground solidifying the group as one of the most talented pioneers in 70's classic rock.  The more critically acclaimed CAPTAIN AND ME, for me, is just a fond stepping stone from TOULOUSE STREET to these STREETS.  Pat and Skunk really worked well together on compositions and Tiran Porter finally recorded a wonderful song with his own vocals which augmented all the R&B/Jazz on this work of art.

"Wheels Of Fortune" begins the album with familiar strains of Doobie guitars but they are quickly all jazzed up and the three part harmony vocals and interchanging leads of Pat and Tom, typifying Doobie art, are about to get a new kick in the pants.  First of all this is a joint composite venture between Pat and Skunk on guitar and John Hartman's fabulous drumming which takes center stage like never before.  Accent this all with Michael tripping on the electric piano and you have one of the jazziest ever Doobie Brothers songs and one of the funkiest beat songs ever!  This song can actually quickly climb to the top of your list of favorites if you have never heard it before.  It is a cabbage patch of exchanged instrumental leads, amazing guitar technical dog-and-pony show, and mad rhythm!

The title track "Takin' It To the Streets" is Michaels first foray out into the wilds of Doobie Land and the song is actually one of his finest ever.  An R&B ballad that seems to draw heavy influence from Marvin Gaye's classic album WHAT'S GOING ON?, per street level social protests, Michaels vocals are plaintively Motown, and his keyboards winding their way through the double drums and bass line are a classic song in the making.  Pat and Skunk augment without intrusion.  A first rate "Doobie Brothers" song!

Pat's "8th Avenue Shuffle" is the evolutionary result of all the songs he ever composed.  Drawing a bit from 50's rock and roll, with hints of bop-jazz guitar, the "shuffle" works its way into a guitar lovers paradise and Pat's technical prowess (easily illustrated on "Neal's Fandango" on the previous album STAMPEDE) just goes to town.  Another of the finest Doobie Brothers compositions out there that many people have never heard.

Michael lays down a sad jazzy R&B ballad called "The Losin' End" to close side one of the vinyl album.  It was a work in progress with him as he had previously recorded a demo by himself and then recorded this version with the Doobies.  A 3rd version at another speed entirely would end up on his solo debut album a few years later.  "Losin' End" has the St Louis blues feel that Michael grew up with, but that would actually hit the mark even better with the last song on the album, a joint composition with Pat and Skunk.

"Rio" is just an all around world fun Brazilian jazz (no kidding?  Brasil eh?) fest.  Get dressed for Carnavale time as Pat and Skunk composed a killer track with all the Parrot chords they could find.  Look for the vocal cameo from Maria Muldaur too!  The real Memphis Horns throw down on this track as well.

"For Someone Special" by Tiran Porter is another landmark track for the Doobies.  Taking lead vocal for the first time (and he has one velvet smooth R&B voice), Tiran wrote this song as an affectionate tribute for and about bandleader Tom.  It is a beautiful composition and perfectly executed including a fantastic progression change with jazz guitar flourishes, electric keys, and power-down beats that swirl into a kaleidoscope of textures and colors.

The hit single "It Keeps You Runnin'" is probably the weakest track on the album.  Rather a pop R&B song of the hum drum variety it was obviously tailor made for single submission and since we all know Michael McDonald was fully capable of way more enriching compositions, I file this one away as the song that should have been on MINUTE BY MINUTE, an album ideally designed as a hit factory product.  Don't kill me too badly, "Runnin'" is a nice song, but that's about it, nice.  I like it, but I like it last on this album, LOL.

"Turn It Loose" is Tom Johnston in full guitar rock regalia with all his usual bells and whistles.  Many seem to think this was a toss off by Tom but far from it.  If you really listen to the guitar work and have a full grasp of Tom's composition styles, "Turn It Loose" is a hot rocker, with well crafted guitar licks and riffs, and the rhythm section pulls out all the stops to back him full force.  This was a sort of swan song for Tom at that time as he would disappear from albums for quite a while.  Yes his picture is on FAULT LINE which came out next but there were zero contributions from him on it other than "spiritual" leadership.

TAKIN' IT TO THE STREETS ends with the same bang it began with, a three way composition, this one by Pat, Skunk, and Michael, in a true ode to the St Louis blue-note music that forms a core base of The Doobie Brothers music genre.  "Carry Me Away" is a fine finale for a fantastic album and leaves the listener just that...carried away.  You might even hit play to start it all over again!

If you are staring at the catalogue of Doobie Brothers music and trying to decide what albums to get, if you like diversity, pure talent with little corporate intrusion, songs composed naturally rather than cookie cut in a hurry, buy yourself TOULOUSE STREET, STAMPEDE, and TAKIN' IT TO THE STREETS.  You will ultimately travel across a huge landscape of American music drawing its deep breaths from the fusion of musical genres originally explored by the pioneers of the Bay Area music scene in the 60's.  The Doobie Brothers took that fusion to the next level and advanced the cause to this point on this album, with an energy not rivaled by many other artists.  If you buy this album here, you are in for an ear-candy extravaganza!  Taste!  Enjoy!  Bon Apptit!

First up, this album isn't really a "greatest hits" album. Instead of including of being handpicked by money - hungry Capitol exceutives, they asked the man who made the music to pick his 19 favorite Beach Boys tracks and put them on a single disc. This is Brian Wilson's personal collection.
This album doesn't feature as much as hits as you'd expect. Brian heavily relies on the reflective ballads like the sublime "In My Room", the morbid "Til I Die", and the eloquent "God Only Knows". Granted, Brian does show his respect for the big hits, as he includes "Good Vibrations", "California Girls" and "I Get Around". I'm sure some selections will surprise you - "Time To Get Alone", "Don't Worry Baby" (these are my two favorites) and "Wonderful" make this an obscure collection that will no doubt appeal to hard - core fans.
As an added bonus, Brian also includes a brand - new recording. "California Feelin'" was written by Brian for The Beach Boys in the early 1970s', but was never officially released. (It has been floating on various bootlegs over the years). it is a very good song and features harmonies very reminiscent of The Beach Boys themselves.
Overall, this really an excellent album. It really shows what fondness Brian jas for his material, and his notes on the songs in the booklet are really well thought out. Brian, welcome back.
