reviewText:
The way I see it, this is the kind of music that Mudvayne does best. It is made up of heavy riffs, heart-wreching well thought lyrics, solid and creative drumming, beautiful-yet-sober bass work, and, above all CONCEPT.

What I mean is that we all know that these artists are great technically, but with "Lost and Found" they have come across something much more valuable in terms of music: a direction. This is no longer about pretending to be aliens, or wearing some kind of disguise. The album represents what they truly are, and that is precisely what bands should be aiming for.

It seems to me that most bands out there are trying to copy their own favorite albums. I don't want to start any kind of controversy, but it seems to me that "L.D.50"'s direction was pretty influenced by the Tool dominated musical influence of the time. This became more obvious to me when they chose David Botril as the producer of their second album "The End of All Things to Come". Now, David Botril knows better than to produce anything in a formulaic way, so he did not try to imprint the Aenima sound on Mudvayne, and instead came up with a different concept for the album, something that was not intended to sound so much as a band anymore; some fans, myself included, might describe Mudvayne's second album as overproduced.

This doesn't mean that the two previous ones were not good albums. THEY WERE AMAZING ALBUMS, five star albums according to my perception, but I would feel confident to say that "Lost and Found" is a better one. GLORIOUSLY TWISTED in its concept, Mudvayne's third album is filled with just amazing songs. Some tracks you might not understand at first look, but in time you will see the concept behind them.

The most outstanding points of the album for me do not include any of the singles, although these are beautiful songs as well. "All That You Are" is my favorite song in here. Besides the twisted mellodies which are true of the whole album, this particular song gives me the chills. It brings out everything that any person feels when they have lost love... all the things that one really feels like saying and making the other person feel. "Pulling the String" is the track that appeals the most to me, musically. The rhythm is marvelous in every aspect and element of the band, and progresses with a twisted tendency throughout the song. Another track that really grabbed my attention is "Pushing Through" which seems to deal with the exasperated feelings of a human being at the moment of birth.

That's it for this one. Probably the year's best in heavy music.

reviewText:
Few soundtracks have impressed me these days, but 2046 has been a superb enjoyment. I haven't even seen the movie before I bought the soundtrack, but after visiting official websites, and heard bits of it playing in the background, I knew this was going to be no ordinary soundtrack for a chinese movie.

It's an entrancing soundtrack from start to finish with dark, dramatic orchestrals, a few catchy upbeat songs, and moody jazz.

There really isn't a track I don't like, but my personal favs are:

1. 2046 Main Theme (With Percussion)/(Rumba version) - One of the most entrancing opening track, simply amazing. The rumba version is also a really nice dance worthy track, pretty romantic with the violin.

2. Siboney and Siboney Instrumental - At first I got a bit annoyed with how loud Connie Francis sounded as she sang, but after a couple of listens, it definitely grows on you. The instrumental version is more upbeat and party like.

3. Sway - I never realized this song had many covers, but Dean Martin makes a fine rendition, pretty classic.

4. Julien et Barbara - Sad and melancholic, yet still retains a certain air of beauty.

5. Polonaise - Probably my favorite instrumental track on the album. Pretty waltzy without being annoying, there's just something about it that makes it seem magical.

6. Lost - Even more dramatic and sad than "Julien et Barbara", the clarinet really hits the emotional spot.

7. Dark Chariot - A simple waltzy piano tune, very pretty.

8. Sisyphos At Work - A jazz club-like song with great sax with a mix of strings, the song runs a bit long though.

9. Decision - For a while I thought I heard this song had a familiar melody, and it does retake the melody from "Lost" but was redone by a different composer. There's a definite difference here, shorter but just as compelling.

10. Adagio - This is probably the "love theme" I would consider for the entire movie. If there's any song on this album that would express "love" it's this song. Utterly beautiful violin work.

In essence, this an album you won't be disappointed with. It's hard to believe this is a soundtrack made in 2004, it sounds like a time-worn piece of work that was uncovered, dusted, cleaned and remastered for the modern listener. The movie is equally as poetic as its soundtrack, people should also give the movie a shot.

reviewText:
It's amazing how much consumer opinion can change some 27 years after the Beatles finally debuted on compact disc.  The first four Bristish albums debuted in mono, and EMI, The Beatles and George Martin were given a drubbing for committing musical heresy for putting them out that way.  Never mind that the sonic quality was terrible to begin with, but, why not stereo - that's how they'd remained available on vinyl for years, with mono having fallen out of favor.  However, for hardcore collectors, there had always been a want for lost mono, even from the first UK red box mono LP set, which included a "fold-down" fake mono "Yellow Submarine".

Audiophiles now have the Beatles mono catalogue in ways they could never have dreamed - vastly superior vinyl, played on high end turntables and rich, warm tube-driven amplifiers are a night and day experience from sample-rate compromised compact discs played through big-box dealer solid state amplifiers, let alone compressed digital files (.mp3 and AAC .mp4) for the portable generation. Vinyl Beatles still sounded better back when MFSL was given the rare opportunity to make limited pressings of their UK stereo albums from the original master tapes (except for 'Magical Mystery Tour' which was made from the Capitol second generation masters).

By following the original mastering notes, and going direct to the cutting lathe, bypassing any sort of digital conversion, people who buy the set or its individually available albums get a sound as close the the original master tapes as they are ever going to get. It goes a long way to help explain why a band with recordings from up to over fifty years ago can still find relevance, and sell their complete catalogue and rarely rely on compilations (which now be meant as introductions to influence new generations).

Congratulations to Apple for for hitting this one out of the ballpark, and not screwing it up like they did with the stereo vinyl box set...

The fact is that he has taken fine talent and crafted it from prog rock to a celestial art form.  "And...Somewhere I've Never Travelled," is an absolutely fabulous piece of music with lush production that sparkles and has decidedly cool melodic passages both vocally and instrumentally.  "Cowboy Star" makes you feel sorry for our guy who's "passed the buckaroo."  At first you empathize until he actually becomes a cowboy...and dies like one.  Epic orchestration makes you travel back with our character quite effectively, and the shotgun blast at the end is a pure stroke of emotive genius.

Okay, purists, so David Pack's "Runnin' Away" obviously sounds like it could fit in on Life Beyond LA, but that's what makes the sophomore effort so appealing in the first place.  It's a great love song without the overly blatant commerciality to come.

"Harvey" is a short but sweet statement on the disappointments of life, and it is totally relatable.  The fact that "I Wanna Know" and the questioning of the futility of living follows it seems very appropriate.  "Still in my heart I feel such purpose, a reason for being alive."  You have to believe there's more.

"The Brunt" is an interesting band collaboration with a strong jazz fusion feel and David Pack's aggressive vocal portraying the animal in us all.  LOL, I'm one of those to whom "it matters nothing."

"Can't Let a Woman" also sounds like it could fit on LBLA, except it's got more drive than anything on that album, and "We Need You Too" is a lovely closing ballad that features Joe Puerta's sensitive vocals and Christopher North's gorgeous piano accompaniment.

Saving the best for last, we have the finest track recorded by Ambrosia, "Danse With Me George."  A charming and comical piece that's virtually 8 minutes long and worth every bit of it, this is one of the most enjoyable alliances of art rock, jazz, and classical that I've had the pleasure to hear.  Too bad the people who brought us the romantic comedy Improptu about Frederik Chopin and George Sand didn't think to include this song in their soundtrack! It is both a loving tribute and a farce at once, and the vocal harmonies these guys could lay down are second to none.  So many different movements in such a short timespan!  This song has my vote as one of the best prog/art rock songs of all time and it is worth purchasing this album alone.  Check out Christopher North's virtuoso on piano!

ASINT is a marriage between Ambrosia's debut and Life Beyond LA, which makes it very nearly perfect.  Not as heavy as Argent can sometimes be, yet not as boring as Yes can, this album is your best evening of the scale in that respective genre.

reviewText:
Van Halen (1978) rocks! It's a hard rock classic, and the best album the band has ever released. It sold over 10 million copies, and introduced the world to Eddie Van Halen's wild guitar pyrotechnics including an unusual guitar playing technique, (fretboard) tapping. Eddie's brother Alex plays the drums and Michael Anthony plays the bass on this album. Last but not least, the charismatic frontman David Lee Roth provides the over-the-top vocals and wild screams.

Runnin' With The Devil sets the tone for Van Halen with a killer guitar riff and a demonic scream-sing. The first lines of the first song on Van Halen's first album tell the tale.

I live my life like there's no tomorrow
And all I got I had to steal
Least I don't need to beg or borrow
Yes, I'm livin' at a pace that kills
Runnin' with the devil

The electric and blistering guitar solo Eruption follows and pretty much just blew everybody's mind in 1978. And if that wasn't enough of an entrance, they perfectly nail The Kinks' You Really Got Me with a heavy rocking version that makes the song their own. Classic! Ain't Talkin' Bout Love is another smoking guitar classic that rocks hard and adds more desperation and menace to the works. Right out of the gates with four hard rock classics! Yeah! Jamie's Cryin', Feel Your Love Tonight and Little Dreamer are all rock classics, too, and keep pace with the others here. Atomic Punk and On Fire are solid rockers, and the blues parody Ice Cream Man starts out acoustic before morphing into a wild electric blues free-for-all.

If you get any of Van Halen's albums, get this one. A must-have for party rockers, rock guitar fans or anybody who likes to listen to hard rock music while they're runnin' with the devil.

reviewText:
In many ways, this is a very simple CD, featuring Cecilia Bartoli as her voice was back in 1992 (Decca re-issued this in 2005) Arie antiche are a collection of pieces, put together at the end of the nineteenth century, which were designed to train classical singers in vocal smoothness, control, pitching, ornamentation and expressiveness, particularly in the Baroque tradition - or at least the baroque tradition filtered through late nineteenth century vision. So we have pieces by Scarlatti, Vivaldi, Giordani, Paisello - all Italian baroque

Simply arranged with only an accompanying piano, there is no where for the singer to hide

The CD comes with an accompanying booklet with the words of each aria in Italian and translated into English

In Bartoli's hands (or most properly larynx pharynx et al) these are far far more than the vocal equivalent of practicing scales, they are intensely musical pieces in their own right which will reveal both the strength and the weakness of the singer.

Listen, for example to the utterly haunting Caro mio ben, by Giordani, where Bartolo's rich but never florid mezzo caresses this love song. What lover could fail to melt, and 'put an end to this coldness' as the singer implores! Lotti's Pur dicesti o bocca bella, a little song in praise of the lover's kissable mouth is splendidly flirtatious and seductive. I could go on, pulling out track after track to enthuse over, - of the 21 tracks, about half are, in my opinion, as pieces of music, quite stunning. And all are breathed into life by Bartoli's deliciously un-strained, flexible vocals. She strokes, not stabs, the listener's ears

reviewText:
Before anybody blindly buys this record based on media hype or this album's place on BEST OF '03 music lists, it is extremely important to know that this has fallen under that all too frequent "love/hate" category where some people love the record and others just can't figure out what the hell all the fuss is about.  I personally thought this exceeded the hype and was truly the record of 2003, though the 40 Ft. Ringo debut and Harem Scarem's "Higher" were better song by song, I felt no other band exuded the personality, sense of humor, and great blend of influences as the Darkness.
This album simply rocks from start to finish, with only two tracks that don't stand up to the rest of the album.  Eight of ten is already a great percentage, but those eight are simply amazing.  Their AC/DC meets Queen (a comparison you'll hear often) rock tunes are peppered with bits and pieces of undeniable humor and fun, I mean I haven't heard had a band that made me smile like this since Van Halen in their Women And Children First days (or, at least, the Wildhearts).  The fact that the first two songs end with a drawn out vocal screaming the F-word show that this band isn't 100% serious, but is still enough to scare away some parents.  Of course, what will scare away some listeners from these otherwise straightforward rockers is lead wailer Justin Hawkins' voice, the topic of much debate among fans and critics alike.  He overdoes it on some tunes, but the more you listen the more it fits, and is certainly the main element in getting this band some deserved attention.
Best Tracks:
"Black Shuck" - Pounding AC/DC homage with Dio-like verses, this track is pure rock like you just don't hear anymore.  Heavy and totally classic metal.
"Growing On Me" - The totally anthemic track with great guitars and a catchy chorus, this song has less of the vocal histrionics, and may be a great way to introduce new fans to this great band.
"I Believe In A Thing Called Love" - The single, and desevedly so... You don't realize what a great riff it is until your fist starts pumping to the instrumental outro, and you can't ignore the best scream on the whole album (the final pre-chorus).
"Givin' Up" - Pure and simple rock n' roll.  The drug lyrics may turn some off, but it's all pretty tongue-in-cheek.
"Friday Night" - This is some unholy combination that takes a Bay City Rollers-style glam tune into a great chorus lifted from the Cure, into totally goofy vocal histrionics (including a cat purr!) in the span of a minute and a half.  But it's not over yet, it kicks into absolutely epic "Bohemian Rhapsody" guitars, a final chorus, and a brief outro with more great guitar.  I think I may be the only one who thinks this is the best track on the CD, but I can't hear this song enough.  It's got everything rock n' roll should have and there just aren't enough songs that mix humor, chops, hooks, and unabashed cheesiness like this since the heyday of bands like Van Halen, Sweet, and Poison.

reviewText:
From someone who buys a lot of music, this is one of the richest purchases you can make. Bill Withers is that rare breed of performer who gets to you on an even greater level personally than he does musically. This set neatly compiles all of his albums, and leaves us to treasure hunt for some very worthwhile material. However, given the low price, and the company's admission of most of these omissions in the original press release, it's hard to get too sour. Here are the main (i.e., songs with Bill on lead vocals) omissions I've identified:

1.) Better Days - theme from the 1971 film "Man and Boy".  It can be found as a bonus track on the 2003 Raven twofer CD of "Just as I Am" and "Still Bill".
2.) The Gift of Giving - 1972 holiday single.  It can be found on the "Smooth Grooves: Sensual Christmas" (!) compilation.
3.) Let Us Love - the studio b-side to the above track, included in a live version on the Carnegie Hall album. It appears the original version has not been released on CD or for download.
4.) It's All Over Now - 1975 duet with Bobby Womack.  It can be found on the same CD as #1, as well as "The Essential Bobby Womack".
5.) Rosie - a beautiful demo recording of an otherwise-unreleased song off the 2008 reissue of "Menagerie," which also contains a single edit and instrumental track of two songs originally on that album.
6.) Just the Two of Us - The hit 1980 duet with Grover Washington, Jr. off the latter's "Winelight" album, and any Bill Withers compilation.
7.) Soul Shadows - 1980 collaboration with The Crusaders, off their "Rhapsody and Blues" album. It can also be found on Bill's 1989 "Greatest Hits" compilation.
8.) USA - 1981 solo single. Unreleased on CD or for download.
9.) In the Name of Love - 1984 duet with Ralph MacDonald.  I believe this is a vocal version of an instrumental track that originally appeared on Grover Washington Jr.'s "Winelight" album. It can be found on the "Love & Happiness Mix - Classic Soul,R&B,Slow Jams - 8" compilation.

*UPDATE: Tracks 1, 6, 7, and 9 can now also be found on the recently released "The Essential Bill Withers".*

The majority of these tracks are terrific, and would make for a helluva compilation to complement this great and well-priced box set (shop around and you will find some ridiculously cheap prices, but the difference in retail between the US and UK puzzles me).

Other, more recent guest appearances:

10.) Playin' the Loser Again - 2004 duet with Jimmy Buffett off the latter's "License to Chill" album.
11.) Lovely Day - Maroon 5's cover from the 2006 "Hoot" soundtrack, featuring Bill and Kori Withers on backing vocals.

Bill also wrote and played on two otherwise-unreleased songs (Better You Go Your Way, Tenderness is His Way) from Gladys Knight & The Pips' 1974 "I Feel a Song" album.

So nice to see the humble master get his due, and hopefully sales and renewed interest in his overall work will spur further releases of archival or new material (the documentary "Still Bill" indicates he has hardly been twiddling his thumbs these last three decades).

There's some very impressive renditions here, some of them better than the originals and that's saying something.  I agree with one reviewer that the first three songs really bite the dust and cut the wind but all of the rest are winners.

Brad Mehldau performs a very intricate pleasing piano rendition of "Don't Interrupt the Sorrow." He uses some Keith Jarrett motifs.  The only problem is he doesn't integrate the more complex interpretation into the original all that convincingly.

Cassandra Wilson starts "For the Roses" with a ponderous sweet acoustic guitar intro with harmonica accents.  Her voice is a little off and flat at first  but finds the groove and the acoustic double bass is as scrumptious as it gets. Like many of the renditions, the songs are performed slower with more colorful accents than the originals.  The lyrics are easier to hear to.  But this is 2007 when recorded by a number of very talented musicians so it's  not a criticism of music performed by one person, most of it between 1967 and 1975.

Prince's rendition of "A Case of You" is smooth and soulful.  Joni's sojourn into jazz generally is very weak but her compositions before that offer so much in terms of wonderful jazz interpretations.  As a sax player I just wonder why none of these artists included one.

Sarah McLachlan's "Blue" is sublime and she actually sings a little better than Joni.  The overdubbed harmonies are more parallel than Joni's which takes the original idea and reinterprets it nicely.  The rendition is stunningly good - actually improves some aspects of a song that I didn't think could be improved.

Annie Lennox brings in a synthesizer right out of strawberry Fields and gives straight version of Joni's otherwise meandering vocals.  "Ladies of the Canyon" can be folksy or tight and expansive as its done here. The chord structure is so sad and elegant.  Joni is the saddest person I've ever encountered other than me.

All of the artists on the songs I like are great singers with compelling interpretations and phrasing.

"The Magdalene Laundries" is a real country heartbreaker.  That dignified, straightforward way country balladeers confess their sadness and regrets can't be topped by this song and Emmylou Harris does it justice. The subject is not country typical tho.  Unwed pregnant girls being turned over to nuns where they'll be forgiven, and then buried. Only a woman could get it this right. The shamed fruit gets reburied.

Then there's Elvis Cosrello's version of "Edith and the Kingpin" flirts with lounge lizard schmaltz  and classical orchestral formalities at the same time.  It's sounds like one of his songs. Only better. The bass clarinet reminds you of he sang real good for free.  But the biggest hat tip here is to miles Davis especially his formal highly dramatic period like Sketches of Spain.  It's here.

K.D. Lang covers "Help Me" with her heavenly voice alittle slower though .  Her voice is very close to Joni's.  The slower pace captures the topic of "falling" in love and the high it produces.  It's an incredibly good song and the rendition is picture perfect.

Though James Taylor usually gets on my nerves, his rendition of "River" is excellent and his vocals are better than I expected.

All in all, this tribute captures both the melancholy and grace of an artist who really has no equal overall except maybe Bowie.

One reviewer complains cindi Laupers Carey isn't included.  It's starts off interesting.  Lauper can sing but it's an LA train wreck because you can't slow this song down that much.  It's doa by the second stanza.  You have to know how far you can deviate.

But for the most part,

  Grace begets grace.

As I mentioned earlier, I thought the last few tracks were really the band's strongest material, especially "Shimmer" and "Complicated" (and no, it isn't a cover of that atrocious Avril Lavigne song). reviewText: Searching For Sugar Man is a film about Sixto Rodriguez -- he was a folk musician from the early 1970's, and after two albums and a compilation disc, he seemed to disappear off the face of the Earth. While gaining some popularity in South Africa (likely due to the thematic content of his lyrics), he's been relatively obscure in America. The documentary chronicles two longtime fans who attempt to find Rodriguez and discover his fate. Searching for Sugar Man uses many of the songwriter's best songs from his only two albums (COLD FACT and COMING FROM REALITY) and effectively functions as a lovingly made greatest hits collection. Many of the lyrics and themes that Rodriguez penned pegged him as a "protest artist," similar to Bob Dylan. Many of these songs are pessimistic; ideas of oppression, loss of control, and civil unrest fill many of his songs. Even though these songs come from different albums, the lyrical themes and style that Rodriguez uses makes this soundtrack feel like a cohesive and cogent record. For fans of Bob Dylan, I would highly recommend this soundtrack -- it's a great sampling of a long lost artist's work. For those interested, I would highly recommend the opening track, "Sugar Man." It's Rodriguez's biggest hit, and it sums up his work nicely. For a singer/songwriter whose music has been lost for quite some time, this compilation is quite a gem.

reviewText:
What can I add to all the previous glowing reviews? Like many, I bought this album on vinyl when it first came out; now it's a delight to have it available on CD. And the intervening decades have only made it better, like a rare wine mellowing & ripening with time. Yes, all the comparisons to other bands are apt enough -- "Snake Bite" is kin to such King Crimson songs as "Pictures of a City" in its snarled lyrics & ferocious guitar; the Jethro Tull sound of the flute is there; the early 1970s blues-boogie sound comes through on tracks like "The Demon Trucker", the English acid-folk otherworldliness shows itself in songs like "Morning Hymn" & "Lady of the Lake", and the distinctive instrumental soundscapes that later defined the band are present in tracks like "Dark River" & "Borne on the Solar Wind" -- but in the end, these comparisons are unfair to the band & do it a disservice.

Because Jade Warrior was very much its own band right from the beginning. In the hands of lesser bands, these songs wouldn't fit together comfortably on one disc -- they would sound like a desperate attempt to imitate Band A, then Band B, then Band C, etc. But no matter what the style, every song here fits in seamlessly with the others; the sound & the distinct musical vision is cohesive, clear & strong. Jade Warrior was serious about their Japanese-Chinese & Afro-Jazz influences, using them with subtlety & complexity, rather than just as exotic seasoning on ordinary songs. This even extends to the lyrics, which have genuine poetry to them & are actually understated, rather than plunging headlong into overwrought bombast, as too many prog bands eventually did -- and they never lost their sense of humor, either, as evidenced by "Joanne". Jade Warrior was & still is a finely cut & polished jewel of multiple facets, wreathed in incense & electricity, unlike any other band of its time. While the later all-instrumental albums are superb, I dearly wish we had more from this original lineup. It's a gorgeous, atmospheric window into another era of beauty & wonder -- most highly recommended!

reviewText:
And I thought Dark Adrenaline was a return-to-form effort.  Broken Crown Halo in my opinion is actually Lacuna Coil's best work since Karmacode.  It is also the first album I can listen to without skipping a track since that album.  This brings back even more of the Gothic tones alongside with the newer Alternative Metal influences we have come to enjoy from them.  There are moments in some of the songs crafted for this album that will remind you of who Lacuna Coil is from previous efforts but includes some new elements that will make them sound fresh.

The opening track, "Nothing Stands in Our Way", begins with keyboards that sound like they are from a horror movie from the 70s or 80s as they stated in interviews of what inspired and influenced them on this release.  And what's this?  A growl from co-vocalist Andrea Ferro which is something we haven't heard since "Fragments of Faith" from Karmacode right when the heavy chugging guitars kick in.  I think the verses soften the song a bit as far as such a heavy opening but Cristina's vocals shine nonetheless.  The heaviness doesn't stop with "Zombies" in which we hear more growling from Andrea.  He takes lead in the verses in which I ironically think sound like they would have come from a Rob Zombie tune due to its tempo and rhythm.  The chorus from Cristina starts off kind of eerily at first with "Our lost souls..." but then flows into something more poweful when "We are alone..." comes in.  For those of you more interested in Cristina taking the lead, next comes the first of three Cristina-only songs with the ballad "Hostage to the Light".  The verses are very melodic and steps into a strong and powerful chorus to maintain the mood of the song.  Next is one of my favorites, "Victims".  This sounds like it wouldn't sound out of place on the group's first full-length album, In A Reverie.  The guitar work is very similar to songs you would hear from that album as well as the overall tone of the song.  You can hear aggression through the chorus.  It seems that not a lot of people care much for the middle of the song with the "rapping" from Cristina but I think it stands out and puts emphasis on some aggression in the song.  The next song takes you through a time warp with some evident Karmacode influence on "Die & Rise" with its guitar tuning and chugging korn-like bass that was heard on songs like "Our Truth" and "What I See".  This is the first radio single and it is a wise choice as it is one of the most radio-friendly tunes on the album with its simple, catchy chorus.  Not much is heard from Cristina in this one with the exception of a line in the chorus and the Italian bridge.  At first, I was turned off by the "riiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiise" part of the chorus but it grows on you.  I've always enjoyed when they incorporated choral effects in their songs like during the verses of this song as well as the next song up which is "I Forgive (But I Won't Forget Your Name)".  An eerie guitar begins the song with haunting choral elements throughout.  This could be another contender as the next radio single.  Next comes the second Cristina-only song, "Cybersleep".  A true standout that to me oozes some of Comalies and Unleashed Memories with its guitar work and melodies.  The autotuning on Cristina's intro and outro actually works very well for the song.  The heavy hitter "Infection" slides in next with some Middle-Eastern chanting from Cristina in the bridge that what have come to know.  "I Burn in You" brings their Middle-Eastern influence to a whole new level.  This may come off as a ballad but once the heavy bridge comes in it adds even more power to the song.  The tenth track, "In the End I Feel Alive", starts off with some melancholic keyboards and breaks out into a Nu-Metal influenced track.  The chorus is one of my favorites from the album.  I kind of think the "Burn baby! Burn baby!" from Andrea is a little out of place, but it's not enough to ruin the song.  Finally is the next Cristina-only ballad "One Cold Day".  To think that I thought "My Spirit" was their best closer.  This definitely takes the top spot as the best and ends the album on a strong note.

Overall, I believe this album stacks along the side with Karmacode and Comalies as one of Lacuna Coil's best.  I was impressed with the comeback of Dark Adrenaline after the disappointing Shallow Life.  However, when I go back to listening to Dark Adrenaline after this I can't help but feel that I wanted more out of some the songs from that album.  Along with others, I believe Don Gilmore simplifies a band's sound to making more no longer than three minute radio-friendly tunes that suck some of the creativity out of them.  Not to mention, the vocals on this album are a great improvement as they don't sound as processed as Dark Adrenaline or Shallow Life.  Well, Scabbia and Ferro didn't hold back on this one as this is the best vocal delivery both of them have ever delivered.  Jay Baumgardner did an excellent job at producing which puts it up their with Waldemar Sorychta's.  All in all, if you fell out of love from Lacuna Coil's past two efforts for bringing a more commercialized appeal then give this one a shot.  It will make you become a fan again.

Top favorite tracks (then again they are all good): "Zombies", "Victims", "Cybersleep", "Infection", "One Cold Day"

I bought it with much haste and am so glad that I did because it fuses everything I look for in world music.
My favorites (though I love them all) would have to be the catchy single "When You're Falling" and "Persistence Of Life," which both feature the incredible male vocals of Peter Gabriel, the electronic-based "Shadowman," the African-dance tune "Further In Time," the rock/egyptian-tinged "Life Begin Again--" which is sung by Robert Plant--, "Go On Through" with its Celtic opening and its breakthrough to airy, alternative female singing by Pina, and the final track, "Onwards," which will enrapture you in its timeless beauty. In other words this CD is dazzling, notable, mesmerizing, and, simply put, world without boundaries. I'd suggest this record to anyone who likes plane good music. It's a good accomodation to anyone's home...

reviewText:
Man, what can i say.  The Bros. Ween have done it up in the most  exsquisite way this time.  Easily the most solid album i've heard in a LONG  TIME!!!!  Actually, it's honestly one of the most satisfying albums i've  ever heard.  As a fan of every single one of their records, b-sides,  outtakes, throw-aways, and above all live shows, i can say that this is  undoubtedly the cream of the crop...for me at least.  I know many hardcore  fux out there could possibly disagree, but you're also probably the same  dudes that were booing the country record, not realizing that all that Ween  touches turns to gold...er...um...brown.  But we all know (or should) that  Gener's one of the best singers around, and that Deaner is THE MOST  underrated guitarist ever (even more than Alex Lifeson!)but what really  stands out here are the SONGS!  WHOA MAN!
The opening of the album is  perfect with the sonic blast that errupts after the first verse of  "Exactly Where I'm At", with obligitory cool Dean freakout for  the last minute or two. And it doesn't slow down from there.  "Flutes  of Chi" is a Floyd-cum-Tull-cum-McCartney gem.  "Even If You  Don't" is the perfect pop masterpiece that should have been a  worldwide hit (tho i'm glad wasn't so we can keep those fux not in the know  drifting in the dark a little longer).  "Bananas and Blow" takes  the piss out of Jimmy Buffet and surpasses everything in his catalog.  But  i would have loved to have heard the results from the earlier proposed EP  that would have resulted from Gene and Dean living, writing and recording  tunes in a bungalow with nothing but coke and bananas for sustinence.  But  this will do.  (And White Pepper's probably a better record than that would  be anyway).  "Stroker Ace" ROCKS, MANG.  Say no more.  "Back  To Basom" is one of the best songs i've ever heard, and is great for  roasting.  "The Grobe" will delight any Sabbath fan as it gurgles  out of your speakers.  Also great for roasting.  And altho "Pandy  Fackler" has been called a Steely-Danism, i see it more as a  Zappa-esqe tune.  Fun and funny and grows on you big-time.  "Stay  Forever" is a damned love song that ain't funny!  And it works!  I  love it!  Catchy as all hell.  "Falling Out" almost sounds like  it has a Western feel (Think Steely Dan's "With A Gun", but  better).  And too soon, the album is closing with "She's Your  Baby" which sounds like Lennon-McCartney offspring.  The whole albums  has a definite Beatles/Floyd vibe, and is sonicly as adventurous as some of  rocks best.
This thing will grow on you no matter who you are.  And even  if you love it on first listen, it still will grow on you!
The only  negative things i can say about it is that it's over too fast (leaves you  wanting more) and the b-side to the Stay Forever single, "Who  Dat?" is on the Japanese pressing, but not ours.  Oh well, i got the  single too, and the song is great.  What else do you expect from WEEN????
BUT here's the main thing:  Don't get caught up in comparing these songs  to other artists.  WEEN definitely does their own thing, and while the  mannerisms of other bands may pop into your head on first listen, you soon  hear nothing but the sound of Ween as they infiltrate your brain.  Good  luck getting these tunes outta your head, folks.  Well, i'm getting sick of  writing like a fool rock critic.  The point is GET THIS ALBUM!!!  I'm sure  you'll want all their records after hearing this one tho.  Right Phil?  Anyhoo, i'll leave you with a quote that thwarts all the nimrods out there  that think Ween is a joke band:  "We're not trying to imitate great  music.  We're trying to CREATE GREAT MUSIC"...and lord do they ever.  I LOVE WEEN.

reviewText:
For once the All Music Guide is right.  Somehow the critics at the AMG found their way out of the church of `60's rock and found a part of the modern world. Along with Metallica's "Master of Puppets" and "Kill `Em All," Slayer's "Reign in Blood" also got a five star rating from the AMG.
Like Metallica and Sepultura, Slayer really can't be considered pure metal.  They were one of the first to walk the fine line between hardcore punk and heavy metal without falling into either classification easily.
"Reign in Blood" sounds like a heavy metal band who decided to do a punk album.  When they released this album in 1986, there weren't many bands who were willing to take the risk of mixing those two genres so blatantly.
Lyrically, this album marked the point where Slayer would move away from the typical Satan and black magic themes of heavy metal and start singing of real life horrors, such as the Nazi doctor Josef Mengele ("Angel of Death"), serial killers ("Criminally Insane"), and confronting the fear of death in general ("Necrophobic").  Just like a punk band, they wanted to confront reality that nobody else wanted to see.
Of course they still had a few songs about Satan ("Altar of Sacrifice," "Raining Blood") and black magic ("Reborn").  In the 1980's, when the "moral majority" ruled and there were countless exposes (by such prestigious men like Geraldo Rivera) in the media feeding the hysteria around Satanism, and it was Slayer's duty to give the "moral majority" and the media the middle finger with the tributes to Satan.  It could be said, at that point in time, singing about Satan was very punk.
However, they are at their best when they directly attack the conformity and false promises of Christianity on "Jesus Saves."  That song makes it clear that they're coming from an atheist point of view.
The cover of "Reign in Blood" was also a little different from the average metal band.  While most metal bands' Satanic cover art looked like a cartooish doodling of some teenage stoner in his high school notebook, Slayer's art work looked more like a Mediaeval painting by Leonardo Da Vinci depicting hell.
The metal element of this mix comes through in the music.  All the musicians are skilled, but they don't get caught up in self-indulgent musical showmanship like most all other metal bands.  Being overly technical will drain the excitement right out of the music quicker than anything else.  Slayer avoids that pitfall but doesn't over simplify their music like hardcore bands.
The high speed of the record is absolutely exhilarating.  The way they race through songs is like being chased by the threatening characters they sing about.  It's a perfect match.
The solos sound as if they've lost control of their guitars.  They scream in a chaotic, uncontrolled way that sounded like nothing else in metal at the time.
Slayer reserves the heaviness for the parts where it can really stand out.  In "Angel of Death" speed along, hit a brick wall, and then let you feel it with an ultra heavy riff.  The same happens in "Raining Blood" they begin with an ultra heavy riff and then fly off into absolute chaos, then comeback to where they started.  Once again, Slayer steers clear of overkill.
Vocalist Tom Araya's vocals are purely hardcore punk shouts, which is a much better match for the music than some wannabe opera singer like most other metal bands had.  The only hint of traditional metal is the opening scream on the album.  Otherwise, he attacks in a no bullsh*t  manner, concentrating on content rather than delivery.
 "Reign in Blood" will make most people uncomfortable because it doesn't fit into any neat category.  They were too technical to be punk, too reckless to be metal.  It's true art when musicians set out to please themselves and not a group of people with preconceived notions of what the band should do.  That seems what Slayer was doing here.

Amazon's Recommendations Explorer has scored a DIRECT HIT.  I had never heard of almost any of these people but Amazon has tracked me through Heifetz, Segovia, Mendelssohn String Symphonies, the Beethoven Violin Sonatas, Walter Piston Violin Concertos, a Latin American Guitar Festival, Magic of the Greek Bouzouki, Dvorak, Prokofiev -- I was getting tired of all of them!!!
"Heartland" is NOT "Appalachian" except in minor aspects.  It is also not much of an "Anthology" either.  (Whose Heartland is it?)  What it is is a combination and ensemble get-together of the finest "string" performers across the country.  There is the usual violin, cello and bass, but there is also the mandolin, the mandola (what's a mandola?), the banjo, the "fiddle" (a violin in the right hands).  They strum, they pick, they pizzicato -- there are fugues and there are ballads.  A couple of the numbers have vocalists but not many.
All of the collective performers on this album have a profound sense of the acoustics of a "string" and they blend them beautifully.  GO FOR IT!!!

reviewText:
Serafin knew exactly how to handle Renata Tebaldi and the miracle of their partnership is evident in this live 1954 Traviata from Arena Flegrea. I've heard most Traviatas and no other performance (Tebaldi's or else's) broke my heart like this one. I actually didn't like this opera that much until this recording. It used to be the Sempre Libera opera and I'm afraid because of its importance for modern audiences, it will remain so. Now I understand why Caballe (who used to queue as a student to get Tebaldi's autographs) said that we'll probably never get to hear a riveting Violetta like Tebaldi again. Oh well, she can't prevent me from hoping, can she?

I've come to believe that Verdi didn't write the famous E flat simply because the Violetta he had in mind didn't have an E flat in her throat. After all, almost every soprano who does sing it has disappointed me in the other acts. Once past Sempre libera, which is much better than I expected but of course nowhere near the spectacular florid singing of the young Callas (Mexico '52), Moffo or Sutherland, Renata Tebaldi shows how perfectly her strong, plush instrument suits Verdi's music. It must be said that Tebaldi was in extraordinary good voice that night. Acts two and three will never sound the same to me. The A flat in addio del passato is a miracle by itself (no cracks thank you). Prendi, quest'e l'immagine breaks my heart every time I hear it.

The male cast could be better but I'm pleased that at least Poggi didn't crop up like on the decca studio recording. Prandelli is an attractive Alfredo but I can't stop thinking how Bergonzi would have sounded next to Tebaldi. Tagliabue is a great Verdian, heard here near the end of his distinguished career. No longer a spring chicken but then neither was Germont! Now the sound quality varies. Most of the time it's unbelievably crystal clear, well done Archipel (think of a good MET broadcast); others, most notably in the end of the opera, it's dissapointing. Anyway this recording never stays far from my cd player.

There's so much more to Traviata than Sempre Libera and Tebaldi's Violetta certainly knows it!

reviewText: Little Feat's classic Waiting for Columbus (1978) is one of rock music's most distinguished live albums, and deservedly so. The performances are enthusiastic and professional, and the song selection is everything that you would expect from this Lowell George fronted version of Little Feat. The musicianship is outstanding! These performances were recorded in August of 1977 at The Rainbow Theatre in London and George Washington University in Washington, D.C. Although enough material was recorded for a 3-record set, Waiting for Columbus was originally released as a double album. With this reissued 2-disc edition, we get all of the original songs plus the unreleased archived recordings. It all sounds great, too. The music of Little Feat is a mix of laid back and funky New Orleans piano blues and slide guitar dominated electric rock n' roll. They also incorporate a lot of jazz and a little of country into their sound, and vocalist/slide-guitar legend Lowell George's wry and demented lyrics suggest a Frank Zappa influence leftover from his days as a guitarist with Zappa's Mothers Of Invention. The Little Feat staples from this era are covered nicely here; Fat Man In The Bathtub, All That You Dream, Time Loves A Hero, Spanish Moon and an incredible 9:00 minute version of Dixie Chicken. They go hippie country & western with semi-unplugged versions of Willin' and the high-larious Don't Bogart That Joint. Most of the songs feature excellent solos from Lowell on slide guitar, Paul Barrere on electric guitar and Bill Payne on piano and synthesizer especially, but the Tower Of Power horn section is smoking hot as well, and they add tremendously to the sound of the entire album. Guest performances include ex-Rolling Stones guitarist Mick Taylor on Apolitical Blues, and the Doobie Brothers' Michael McDonald and Patrick Simmons provide the backing vocals on Red Streamliner. Unfortunately, Lowell George would die of a heart attack at 34 less than two years after these shows were recorded. While Little Feat has continued to record and tour with several different lineups since then, this album captures the classic band in peak form. Waiting for Columbus features the talents of many, but for much of the album, it's Lowell George who takes center stage, and his singing, songwriting and slide guitar playing are clearly the primary focus. He doesn't disappoint anybody, either. Waiting for Columbus is an essential live rock n' roll album that's in a class with the best of it's time.

The music at times is reminiscent of 'The Traveling Wilbury's' with lots of acoustic guitar and sparse instrumentation. George knew how gravely ill he was at the time these songs were written and they're full of introspective reflections on life. It's the most substantial piece of work he's done since 'All Things Must Pass' and it's head and tails above anything McCartney has done in decades. reviewText:
Released in 1992, WORTH THE WEIGHT was Anvils sixth of sixteen albums (as of this writing). It marked a dozen years of recording albums; and almost four years since their previous release. The group obviously wanted to make a statement with this album and they did in spades. The riffs seem more technical, more innovative; mixed with tempo changes and start/stops, which all make for more compelling songs than anything from POUND FOR POUND (1988) or THIS IS THIRTEEN (2007) or JUGGERNAUT OF JUSTICE (2011).

My three favorite tracks are in the middle of the disk: Embalmer, Pow Wow and Sins of the flesh. Embalmer is quirky, speedy and catchy. Pow Wow features a nigh stunning epic beginning and, later, a part obviously taken from Thin Lizzys Bad Reputation, but made more metalized, of course. Sins of the Flesh is catchy with Lips weird falsetto singing Sins for the chorus, plus surprisingly insightful lyrics. Lips is goofy, for sure, but hes also a musical genius in his chosen genre. Anvil in their own unique way place easily with the so-called Big Four, or any other Four, when they're at the top of their game, as they are here.

A good example of the innovative riffing noted above can be observed in the stanzas of the curiously titled AZ 85. The following Sadness is a moving acoustic ballad, which well shows off Anvils dimension as musicians & songwriters, but its unfortunately too short. It seems like a prologue to the closing Love Me When Im Dead, which has elements of Alice Cooper and Ozzy-era Sabbath, but less doomy than the latter and generally more dynamic. The offbeat and punchy Bush Pig is also likable featuring more inventive riffing in the mid-section.

GRADE: A

reviewText: This is not only the most underrated and underappreciated reggae album, it is the most underappreciated album period.  This is one of the ten best albums released by any group, not just Steel Pulse.  It is one of my favorites and I listen to nearly every genre in music, including jazz.  Every song is intense, flawless at the rhythmic level, and inspiring.  This is a militant album, which is perhaps why it is so overlooked, but this is its strength.  The material here inspires the band to reach heights they would never reach again, and came close to in Handsworth Revolution.  Every song belongs amongst reggeas best, the lyrics on some are as good as Bob Marley's militant lyrics on Natty Dread and Burning.  Proverbs and quotes by prominent figures throughout black history are littered throughout, all to great affect.  It is rare to get absolute chills during a song, but at least three songs on this album accomplish the feat.  Their is a moment at the end of Unseen Guest ("trod to victory"), where I nearly have an out of body experience without fail.  The material is sad, and uplifting at the same time, it reminds the listener not just of horrors from the past, but also of hope and redemption.  This album should inspire every type of person, there is no one who would not be touched.  Never mind that this album jams.  One of the essential albums in any genre.  A must own for reggae fans, or any fan of music

reviewText: While not a big chart hit, Kenny was wise in doing a sequel to RETURN TO POOH CORNER. Now with a fifth child Hana Aluna he does a good job in singing his favorite Disney and movie songs are well as some original compisitions. 1. Your Heart Will Lead You Home- the only Pooh-related song on the album from Disney's Tigger Movie written appropiately enough with Richard and Robert Sherman aka the Sherman Brothers who had written the songs for the original Pooh cartoons around the same time Kenny was in high school writing "House at Pooh Corner" (the song starts with a brief quote from the original song) The song wasn't a big hit but has become popular with graduation ceremonies and other events. 2. You'll Be In My Heart- Perhaps the Tigger Movie song wasn't big because it was written around the same time as Phil Collins' theme from "Tarzan" (He mentions Glenn Close and Phil Collins singing it in the movies although Close's character sang only one line)... 3. Always In All Ways- "You'll Be In My Heart" leads into this Loggins original written with Mark Mancina who arranged many Disney musicals and films (including Tarzan and The Lion King) It was written when his eldest child was leaving home for the very first time and how emotional he felt. There is a very touching music video of this song featuring all of Kenny's kids 3. Flying Dreams- A little known Paul Williams-Jerry Goldsmith tune from "The Secret of NIMH" features Kenny paired with Olivia Newton-John (they had previously done a Christmas special together) 4. That'll Do- As the title suggests this is from the second "Babe" movie written by Randy Newman but sung by Peter Gabriel in the film. Of course the famous phrase from the first movie "That'll do, pig" is changed to "That'll do, Babe" to suggest it could relate to a person. 5. Turn Around- Kenny first heard this Harry Belafonte- Malvina Reynolds classic when he was 10 or 11 and said it has haunted him for the rest of his life. 6. Beauty and the Beast- How many parents would sing this Oscar winner to their children? On an interview for Barnes and Noble.com he says he sang this to Isabella (Bella) Not as good as the other versions, but has a good string arrangement and is co-produced by David Pack who produced the songs on the first Pooh Corner album 7. Baby Mine- Known as the song from the Dumbo scene that makes everybody weep this is a rather lame version of an overdone song.. 8. The Inch Worm- "Two and two are four, four and four are eight" aka Inchworm this features Bella Loggins on harmony vocals. As Kenny says in the liner notes Bella was in the studio listening to her dad sing the "measuring part" for a future session but she said he wasn't good. So he requested she sing with him.... something she would do again along with more of Kenny's kids on the not yet official ALL JOIN IN album. 9. Hana Aluna Lullaby(e)- The third original is a collaboration with members of the Hawaiian group Hapa with English lyrics by Kenny and his second wife Julia who fell in love on the island of Hana in Maui and that's how his fifth child got her name! 10. Goodnight- Kenny is an avid Beatles fan and he does the classic Ringo Starr-led lullaby from The White Album (Remastered) with Alison Krauss on harmony vocals. Legendary harmonica player Norton Buffalo joins for the best way to send Kenny's fans into dreamland.

reviewText:
It is heartening to read of the affection this record inspires. I have a huge collection and hadn't listened to "The Soul Cages" in two or three years, so I had forgotten why I had loved it so when I first discovered it. His lyrical composition is at its finest, as other reviewers have noted.  He seems less self-conscious here. The orchestration is rich and varied. I take exception with those who say this is a somber, dark work. I have been enjoying this on a well-placed pair of Klipsch kg4 speakers and a hefty Onkyo amp. The clarity isn't depressing.  It's uplifting. Jeremiah Blues (Part 1) is a rocker!
The artistic zenith of this album is reached at "The Wild Wild Sea." I will admit a bias here: I am an amateur sailor, and in this song the entire thrust of Sting's grappling with the mysteries and pain of life are brought into focus: "And my anxious eyes searched the horizon, With the gathering sea at my back." Such a metaphor as we look ahead in our lives and consider that which has gone before. And folks, here is the clincher. The apparently shimmering music that accompanies this trip is, get this, boogie!  Yes, this is boogie!  The damndest thing I ever heard. Incredible!
One parting shot to the naysayers, what few there are.
After rocking with "The Soul Cages," Sting signs off with "When the Angels Fall." As I was reading the reviews, I noted a few singled this out as their least favorite. I simply couldn't remember it and I listened to the entire CD. It is perfect, and this coda (it is terribly sad, I will confess), brought me back into touch with emotions I had sublimated for years. This entire CD is a gift, an expression of sentiment and love, a communication of struggle and growth, understated, beautiful.

reviewText: Music legends sometimes are born with their debut album and such was the case with Canada's Blue Rodeo. Blue Rodeo had been creating quite a buzz from their energetic live performances in Toronto since 1985, but with the release of Outskirts in 1987, the band's distinctive musical vision came together on ten of the best songs recorded in the 1980's. As soon as I heard the first chords of "Heart Like Mine" from a cassette my brother gave me, I knew I was hearing a great band. Tremendously melodic, each song pulls one in and once there, the lyrics fascinate and hypnotize with tales of hard luck, reckless abandon, the need to connect romantically, seemingly unexplainable self destructive behavior, low men in high places, distorted views of reality, lost possibilities, and the unending struggle to clarify feelings and relationships. The song writing credited to Jim Cuddy and Greg Keelor was razor sharp in its' attention to details that make memorable often times ordinary events, "These late night conversations leave a strange taste like French cigarettes." Keyboardist, Bob Wiseman contributed inventively weird piano and organ fills that give these songs an added depth of mystery ("Floating", Piranha Pool"). Reviewers at the time compared Blue Rodeo to The Band, The Byrds, and Elvis Costello and the Attractions and one can hear these influences on Outskirts. But what made this record so smart was that young ambitious musicians had synthesized the best of what they heard and liked and forged a unique and distinctively exciting post new-wave rock sound that emerged from the then happening scene in Toronto, Canada. Blue Rodeo's sound and style would, evolve into a more alternative country rock sound in later years, but Outskirts still stands as the testament of a very talented young band who were fairly bursting at the seams with musical energy. A promising start for a unique band. "And when they ask you why, you say the joker is wild!" Outskirts captures this energy and then some and it still sounds as fresh now as it did twenty years ago.

reviewText:
To say that Sly & The Family stone were influential is probably an understatement. Prince has admitted many times that he grew up listening to (and loving) Sly & Company's music, and if you listen to Prince's music, you can hear where he got some of his ideas and techniques. George Clinton and Parliament/Funkadelic were influenced as well. Sly was probably the singlemost interesting (not to mention, the baddest) funkmeister this side of James Brown (and for what it's worth, I grew up listening to, and loving the music of other funksters like The Ohio Players, Rufus/Chaka Khan, Earth, Wind & Fire, George Clinton and others.)
1969's _Stand_ is a non-stop joy-fest: it's almost impossible not to feel uplifted after listening to this. Similarly, it'll also be difficult to stay still, as the grooves on here are just sexy, funky, infectious and downright delicious. Sly mixed up genders and races in his band, and when listening to the music, you can feel the celebration of harmony, and desire for transcendence over the many ills that have plagued society for the longest time. It was all about injecting positivity and exuberance into this mix of psychedelic funk, soul and rock, and the sunny vibe that runs throughout this album is one of the many things that make this effort highly intoxicating - so intoxicating, that even after three decades since it's release, listeners are, more than possibly, still feeling drunk from it's juices.
Just take a look at some of the song titles: "Stand!," "I Want To Take You Higher," "You Can Make It If You Try" -- the vibes are positive and spiritually uplifting throughout. And leave it to clever Sly to turn something as controversial and touchy as racism ("Don't Call Me...") into something so sexy, intoxicating, scrumptious and downright orgasmic. It's one of the most powerful forms of irony, I think. A reviewer below says there's not enough substance in the lyrics to support the topic. Well, all I have to say about that, is sometimes it's best to let the music do most -- if not all -- of the talking.. and this music doesn't just talk, it hollers! Just listen to the motif in particular (it opens up the song) where Sly is featured on what sounds like a guitar talk box (not sure if it's that, or a production technique), and how it blends with the trumpet calls, the wah-wah (or what I call the 'wow-wow') pedals, the underlying funky two-note bassline punch, and other subtle things. This particular motif is repeated many times throughout the song. However, when this particular motif is heard the final time, it reaches such an intense climax, as these instruments increase in volume and dynamics, not to mention sprinkles of soulful voices coiling around the whole thing, it becomes a devouring, orgasmic ocean of sound and emotion.
The aforementioned gargantuan of sound heard in the previous track said alot more to me than most things ever have (or could) through words. What is it that this music is hollering about? What is it trying to say? What is it pleading for? Transcendence - it's begging and screaming for transcendence over most of the unfortunate happenings (and stupidity) that plague society - racism being a part of this stupidity.
Elsewhere, tracks like "Sing A Simple Song" will get you to do just that -- sing (and dance) right along, and many people (especially of this generation) must be familiar with "Everyday People," as it's been used in certain commercials (as well as being covered by hip-hop band Arrested Development), and the 13-minute "Sex Machine" gives a bluesy I-IV-V a sexy, intoxicating, psychedelic twist, topped off by a drum solo, and some joyful laughter from Sly and gang at the end of the track.
Not much more can be said from me, as words fail to do this band and album justice. The positivity sadly turned sour on their next effort, 1971's _There's A Riot Goin' On_ (another intoxicating effort), as Sly would fall (deeper) into drug abuse and depression. Sly & The Family Stone's music has influenced countless musicians, and they are revered for good reason. This album is one example of their talent and influence.

reviewText:
I was in college when I heard and saw the William Katt version.

You know how whatever you saw FIRST is the best?

Well, no, not for me, not in this case.

I initially found the concept of Pippin to be very good, the music pretty good, and the story, oh god, my brain hurts. Make up your mind whether you are breaking the 4th wall or not. Make up your mind whether the characters are archetypes or not. Catherine was annoying in every note, every second she was on stage. The ending, where Pippin says, he feels "trapped," struck me as very much out of tune with the rest of the character and the story.

Ben Vereen's choreography and his own dancing were what made it worth it.

I've since read that Vereen, the incomparable dancer, insisted on the cynical ending and on interpreting lines written to be light-hearted in a a cynical way.

And THAT, my friend, is why I much prefer the new Pippin with the now famous "Theo Ending."  This Pippin sees the pain and aches of the world while realizing that young idealism transfers to the next young idealist.

Catherine--well, there's nothing to be done with her. The character is awful. In one scene she is the perfect woman, in the next she's a flesh and blood creature that complains about Pippin's moods--but what the hell is she even talking about? Pippin is for the most part a joyful person--and putting the actor playing Catherine in the company made her character better some, but not much. Her music is so awful I skip ahead within the first few notes.

Berthe being played by a younger actor was a problem for me. The whole point of Berthe was that it is OK to be old, and to enjoy your whole life. However, the improvement in the sing along, now so exuberant, made up for that casting problem.

The Leading Player works much better in a woman's voice. I don't care much for her voice, but that is a taste thing. Her voice is on pitch, her diction is good--that I personally wouldn't buy an album of her solo covers doesn't take away from the excellence of her portrayal.

Matthew James Thomas as Pippin not only has a lovely voice, he works magic with it.

An excellent interpretation that makes me love Pippin all over again.

reviewText:
I will admit to being about 10 years behind the rest of "hip" America when it comes to music.  The year that the Jon Spencer Blues Explosion released arguably it's finest album, Orange, I was knee deep into bands with happy names like Slayer and Napalm Death.  Then, I entered the realm of the liberal university life.  There, I met friends who owned CDs from bands like Jon Spencer Blues Explosion, Guided by Voices, 30-Ought Six, and so on; bands that intrigued, but scared me.  Yes, even more than bands with names reminiscent of love and flowers like Slayer and Napalm Death.

So when it came to reinventing myself as a late 20-something (not by choice, mind you), I decided to rediscover some of the music I missed out on in the mid 1990's.  Orange fit that bill.  The reality is, I have enjoyed this album for the better part of the past 10 years, but it wasn't until recently that I dusted off my copy and put it back into the rotation.  I won't say what I think Orange or JSBX is a mixture of, because I don't have the slightest idea.  What I do know is that it is an ecclectic mix of something, that when combined, is infectious and numbing all at the same time.  Someone mentioned "memorizing" Orange...I suppose that it would be possible, if you were an idiot savant.  Orange sounds more like an amalgamation of guitar and drums played by drunk 13 year olds than something you would hum on your walk to class.  But despite the lack of any cohesive sound (in my opinion), there is something appealing about JSBX, and Orange in particular, that I can't put my finger on.  So I'm not even going to try.

What I will say is that as bluesy rock music goes, I imagine JSBX is at the top of the list.  I don't have any clue who else is on that list...and don't really care.  Orange is a unique album that stands alone in terms of any genre or label you place it in.  It is truly a fun album for fans of rock, blues, hip hop...whatever.

reviewText:
The second soundtrack in the OC series picks up right where the last one left off - about halfway through the first season.  Don't get too excited about the fact this album has more tracks than the 1st one, each of the four soundtracks averages 12 songs per album (since the Chrismakkah album served up a paltry 9 songs).

This album is overall strong - with not a ton of standout tracks - but lots of great stuff to listen to.

The two covers, Nada Surf's "If You Leave" (from the episode where Anna leaves I believe) and Jem's "Maybe I'm Amazed" by Paul McCartney (from the season 1 finale) are excellent and worth listening to again and again - both do their own things with the songs, particularly Jem who does a rousing folk take on the original (albeit a little bit drawn out).

Quite a few of these songs actually reminded of one another, Keane's "Walnut Tree" and Dios Malos "You Got Me All Wrong", and Beulah's "Popular Mechanics for Lovers" channeled the vibe of a couple of other tracks.

There are a few slightly bigger name (yet still indie) acts on this disc - moreso then any of the other ones.  Among them, the Walkmen do an almost U2-esque track called "Little House of Savages", and Super Furry Animals "Hello Sunshine" is a friendly reminder of Seth and Summer's 'first time' together.  90's alt-rock gods Eels offer the opening fun track "Saturday Morning", and current chart darlings The Killers serve up an awesome  80's-infused track (hopefully a future single) in "Smile Like You Mean It".  Slightly less known (but loved by Seth Cohen & Adam Brody) band Death Cab For Cutie sings a sweet, mellow, track (like most of their music) entitled "A Lack of Colour" which I also believe is from the episode Anna leaves.

All together this is a great album - while I said some of the songs remind me of one another, and none of them truly just pop out (like on the 4th soundtrack), this is a cohesive blend of Indie tunes that each bring something unique to the table - whether it be their use of synthesizers, keyboards, acoustic guitars, or fun vocals & arrangements, this is one album not to be missed.

How sweet it is to know that the outstanding quality of his previous album, "Higher Ground", was not just a fluke! Our favorite singer really has come back! This album rates as his best work since "I Want To Live". There's a comfortable flow here, from one great song to another.

The title track nas a mellowness reminiscent of "My Sweet Lady" and "This Old Guitar." There are two charming ballads of gratitude and romance, called "Thanks To You" and "The Gift You Are." Political commentary is also represented in fine form, with "Raven's Child" and "Stonehaven Sunset." "High, Wide & Handsome" is a playful little western number with some great dobro licks. But my favorite is a brilliantly soaring wildlife piece called "Eagles & Horses". As you listen, you get a panoramic vision of wide-open wilderness, where eagles race with horses in blissful abandon, filled with the exuberance of freedom.

John's peerless gift for celebrating the splendor of nature is as strong as ever! Add to that the touching romance, the social admonition, the stylish production work, and the splendid musicianship, and you have a truly beautiful album. Perfect for anytime, anywhere.

reviewText:
Pat Travers has been in a rich musical vein of form of late.

The excellent but criminally under-heard Fidelis (2010) was followed by the equally worthwhile Blues On Fire (2012), the collection of 1920's blues standards given a rock-edged twist.

And now Can Do, which carries the sound and vibe of the high-energy Heat in the Street album, enthused with plenty of melody, harmonies and the subtleties of the spacier Radio Active.

All of which tells you Can Do unashamedly and intentionally hearkens back to that late 70's and early 80's Pat Travers Band albums, right down to the iconic Pat Travers Band logo (not seen on a cover since the band's classic 1980 release Crash and Burn).

But in amongst the gritty yet melodically built rock guitar tracks are reflective moments, an interesting cover, an instrumental (a Pat Travers trait back in the day) and a bluesy groove or two.

Pat Travers is in fine form throughout Can Do, both vocally and musically, and the current Pat Travers Band is as strong a line-up as you'll find this side of the acclaimed Travers - Pat Thrall - Peter "Mars" Cowling - Tommy Aldridge quartet.

Texan guitar slinger Kirk McKim is the perfect six-string partner for Pat Travers and a fine lead guitarist in his own right.
Rodney O'Quinn can anchor or drive the sound with equal measure and is the first bassist to have played with Pat Travers that can rightfully be compared to the inspirational "Mars" Cowling.
The big beats and percussive panache of Sandy Gennaro returned to the fold in November 2010, Gennaro having served his first tour of duty with the Pat Travers Band in the early 80's.

Sean Shannon, the powerful drummer and studio producer who played on Fidelis and Blues On Fire, also contributes to Can Do, both behind the kit and with an excellent job at the production and mixing desk.

Opening with the feisty and vibrant title track, the big guitar sound of Heat in the Street is back and just as ballsy, backed by twin-harmony leads, melodic interjections, gutsy lead vocal and a punchy chorus.
`Can Do' is guaranteed to become a PT classic and a staple of the live set for years to come.

The raunchy and funky `Stand Up' also recalls the hard melodic rock past (with lead guitar lines reminiscent of the guitar tone and style employed on Radio Active) before the volume drops a notch for the American coastal sound of `Diamond Girl,' all bright guitars and harmonics.

The hard rock and harmony guitars return for the mid-tempo `I'm With You,' a song that contains an incredibly simple yet ridiculously infectious chorus hook.
`Long Time Gone' then picks up the pace and thunders out the speakers like a freight train at full speed, delivering its big chorus cargo and message of early musical roads, teenage years and how "those were the days."

The past is also revisited on `Wanted (That Was Then, This is Now)' an atmospheric, rhythmic and slow-tempo number that lyrically recalls a very different time.
The Pat Travers Band have never been the darlings of the melodic rock charts (nor geared to be), but if Bon Jovi recorded `Wanted' they would have a song that was never off the radio.

The rhythm `n' slide blues of `Armed & Dangerous,' with its roots in southern Floridian rock, precedes the surprise of the album...

The Eurythmics 1984 electro-pop hit `Here Comes the Rain Again' is given a rock-reggae treatment, floating guitar leads, a pumping bass line and a big-beat chorus featuring Pat Travers' wife Monica on backing and harmony vocals.
It's the grower of the album and clearly the hope is lightning can strike twice, based on the airplay received for the cover of Bob Marley's `Is This Love?' the surprise highlight of Crash and Burn.

The groove of `Here Comes the Rain Again' is continued with the spacey instrumental `Keep Calm & Carry On' before the rockin' blues of `Dust & Bone' heralds some foot stompin' fun.

The melodic `Waitin' On the End of Time' gets a deserved outing on a full-length Pat Travers album, having first featured on the 2012 Dogs & Guitars EP.
The song has a musical vibe and sound reminiscent of the Radio Active era, while lyrically reflecting on teenage days, five bucks for the weekend and the highway of life ahead of you.

The rock `n' honky tonk roll of `Red Neck Boogie' closes out yet another incredibly strong release from Pat Travers, who is currently producing some of the best music of his career.

Fidelis is a more instantly accessible album. Blues on Fire is a great set of old blues covers.
But this album, which takes multiple plays to get the very best out of it, is, sonically and song-wise, the perfect calling card for the Pat Travers Band to re-establish themselves at the top table of classic rock.

It's also further proof that those that CAN, DO.

reviewText:
Images & Words(1992). Dream Theater's Second Album, And the First To Feature Vocalist James Labrie.

In 1992, when Grunge and Alternative Rock dominated the Charts and the airwaves, Progressive Metal, helped along by the releases 'Metallica' and Queensryche's 'Empire', was finally breaking through to a larger audience. Dream Theater is typically classified as Progressive Metal, yet they are so much more. They incorporate Jazz("Another Day"), Reggae/African Influences("Surrounded"), and at times, seem the furthest thing from Heavy Metal. To define Dream Theater, I would take Rush(of 'Moving Pictures' fame), except add in Zakk Wylde on guitar(of Ozzy Osbourne fame). John Pettruci, Dream Theater's Lead Guitarist, is not only capable of Heavy Metal riffs but also pulls of melodic chords with ease. Upon its release, 'Images & Words' entered the Top 40, eased along by the success of "Pull Me Under", which became an MTV Video hit, and over time, 'Images & Words' has received the most critical and commercial fame of any Dream Theater release. Each musician in Dream Theater, with the exception of vocalist Labrie, is a virtuoso musician, with Petrucci taking technical mastery of the guitar to new levels, Mike Portnoy rythmically defining every song, Kevin Moore blending an intrepid mixture of Keyboards and Piano, and James Myung shelling out some excellent bass work. So, is Dream Theater just a bunch of technical wizards with no substance, or a phenomenal band that's just below the public's eye? Read on to find out!

Track Ratings-

Pull Me Under- Arguably 'Images & Words' standout track, "Pull Me Under" is the album's darkest and heaviest track, from Petrucci's gloomy opening chords to Labrie's haunting vocals, "Pull Me Under" remains consistent throughout. Petrucci and Moore out-do themselves here, interweaving their instruments beautifully. A dark and thought-provoking Heavy Metal masterpiece!

Another Day- Jazz you say? Why yes! "Another Day" is an optomistic, heart-warming ballad, featuring Moore playing a soulful keyboard melody and Labrie taking his melodic vocals to the next level. Listen for the Saxophone and guitar solos, as they are both equally brilliant and engaging!

Take The Time- See the Rush influences yet? "Take The Time" starts as a typical Heavy Metal song, yet, much like Rush's "Roll The Bones", Dream Theater molds the song into a sarcastic look at today's culture. Portnoy's "bullet" drumming and Petrucci's ever-changing guitar(He can go from Dark and Heavy one moment to Light and Up-beat the next), not to mention Labrie's operatic vocals never cease to amaze me. Take the time to listen to "Take The Time"!

Surrounded- Beginning as a ballad between Moore and Labrie, "Surrounded" veers suddenly into an upbeat and fun song that seems to adapt Reggae and African influences. Labrie's vocals clearly seem to sound like Geddy Lee's, and Petrucci much like Alex Lifeson(of Rush), uses a melodic, "synthesized" guitar melody. Moore is "Surrounded"'s backbone, carrying the symphonic keyboards and piano to define the song. Brilliant.

Metropolis: The Miracle And The Sleeper(Part 1)- A prequel to Dream Theater's lengthy concept album 'Metropolis: Scenes From A Memory', the prequel is no less engaging. Petrucci's hypnotic and ambient guitar chords, which can be metallic one second and dizzyingly melodic the next fit in perfectly with Labrie, who can go from moody to upbeat in a split second. Simply beautiful and enthralling!

Under A Glass Moon- Considerably gloomier than the past few songs, "Under A Glass Moon" finds Dream Theater playing in a melodic Progressive Metal epic, and from Labrie's pained vocals to Petrucci's wailing(not to mention shredding) guitar harmonies, you can't help but not listen. Portnoy's fever-pitch drumming also stands out of the crowd! Don't like this song? If so go get some taste!

Wait For Sleep- 'Images & Words' shortest track, "Wait For Sleep" is in no way a filler track. Picture a melodic Tool song("Parabola"?), but replace all the instruments with a keyboard and put Labrie instead of Maynard and you've got yourself a helluva song.

Learning To Live- Epic and Mind-Numbingly masterful, "Learning To Live" is a mystifying track that rotates from a melodic, keyboard driven rocker to an instrumental piece la resistance, combining instrumentation that verges on the apex of technical mastery. A Progressive Metal epic that ends 'Images & Words' appropriately, as it leaves you speechless.

Overall, 'Images & Words' is quite a listen, from the gloom and doom of "Pull Me Under" to the melodic Progressive epic of "Learning To Live", Dream Theater pushes the limitations of technical and musical boundaries. Dream Theater still allows a certain emotional and optomistic tone to the album, and unlike another reviewer said, they're not all flash with no substance....these guys have heart! Although I'm not sure if this is one of my absolute favorite records, 'Images & Words' is a Progressive Metal masterpiece, and along with Queensryche's 'Operation: Mindcrime' deserves to be in EVERYBODY'S collection. Peace fellow metalheads!

HIGHLY RECOMMENDED! FANS OF HEAVY METAL, PROGRESSIVE ROCK, AND DREAM THEATER WOULD ENJOY 'IMAGES & WORDS' IMMENSELY! DON'T BELIEVE THE CRITICS, DREAM THEATER HAS SUBSTANCE AND TALENT!

Killer Kuts- "Pull Me Under", "Take The Time", "Metroplis: The Miracle And The Sleeper", and "Learning To Live".

Also Recommended-

Awake- Dream Theater

Operation: Mindcrime- Queensryche

Liquid Tension Experiment- Liquid Tension Expirement

Thanks For Reading!
