reviewText: First off, let me say to the uninitiated, the Firesign Theatre are very funny.  Definitely one of the most unsung comedy teams ever.  Why?  Well,  first, their primary medium was the comedy album, a dying artform, and they  revolutionized it.  Second, the laughs require some degree of patience and  intelligence: literary references, outrageous word-play, and surrealist  humor pepper the landscape of their albums (though they're also adept at  funny voices and TV riffs).  Plus, they're constructed as  movies-for-your-mind, massive radio drama/comedy.  The Firesign can and  will transport their listeners everywhere, from the eye of a tornado to the  Academy Awards.  And they'll have you laughing in wonderment all the way.  Luckily for newcomers, this album is quite accessible - set against  the  back-drop of a fictional radio station, "Radio Now," it's a  device anyone can identify with.  The four take stabs at the paparazzi, Joe  Camel, Princess Di, overblown epics like "Titanic," self-help  gurus, and much, much more.  And, the CD deals with the paranoia gripping  the nation as the new milennium draws nearer (it's set on the final day of  1999).  So funny, it holds up to repeated listenings... one finds something  new everytime.  How many other comedy albums can you say that about?  Answer: barely any.  This is the genius of the Firesign Theatre, shown here  and on all their other mostly out-of-print-but-hopefully-not-for-long  titles from the '60s and '70s.  Viva el Firesign!

reviewText:
It's been 13 years since "Jagged Little Pill" owned the Billboard charts, but this CD explains why Alanis still has a large, dedicated fan base.  She still remains one of the most important singer/songwriters in the music business.

The first single off of "Flavors" is "Underneath," an upbeat song that compares personal relationships to large-scale wars.  Though it may not be the best song on the album, it highlights Guy Sigsworth's production.  The verses also sell the song.

Other highlights are "Not As We," a heartbreaking piano-based ballad. "For now I'm faking it, til I'm pseduo making it, From scratch begin again, but this time I as I, and not as we."  This song is lyrically one of the strongest songs on the album, and the simple piano arrangment suits it well.

"Incomplete" is one of the strongest songs on the album.  The upbeat, techno-influenced track is about her hopes that she will someday be happy and fulfilled.

As far as the bonus tracks, "Madness" is the best.  It's another sad, piano song, though it's not as big of a standout as "Not as We," which explains why it is a Bside.  The other bonus tracks are hit-and-miss, but this track is a must listen.

This album was worth the four year wait.  Alanis may not put albums out often, but when she does, it is certainly a big event.

reviewText:
Nikolaus Harnoncourt has specialized in rethinking classical music, sometimes to my horror (as in his aggressive, punchy Mozart and Beethoven) but other times to my delight. His Dvorak is full of surprises: lots of tempo changes, unusual balances, sudden accents and mesmerizing hush. But innately Harnoncourt takes a warm, relaxed view of the "New World," rushing nothing, letting the lyrical side speak patiently--you will think you've never heard the Largo before, so original is Harnoncourt's way with it. The only possible drawback is Harnoncourt's lack of excitement and drive in the finale.

I had already rated his Dvorak Seventh and Eighth as among the best I've ever heard; so is this Ninth, aided by lovely sonics and the gorgeous Concertgebouw, here caught live. The audience must have held its breath every bar; I owuld have. The filler is a late tone poem, The Water Goblin, done as superbly as the symphony.

reviewText:
This is my first Ultravox album.  For some reason I'm expecting a weird synth album with dreamy atmosphere.  Probably because I heard some song of theirs a long time ago and dreamy synth rock fit this description.  Let's see if I get that or something else!

"Saturday Night In the City of the Dead" opens this energetic punk-influenced Ultravox album with some speed-talking vocals, a catchy guitar riff, bouncy rhythm and a memorable chorus.  Reminds me of REM's "The End of the World" but not quite as legendary.  The harmonica is a nice addition.  "Life At Rainbow's End (For All the Tax Exiles on Main Street)" continues the youthful punk exuberance.  Not one of the better songs on the album due to a rushed and unfocused chorus, but decent enough.  I enjoy the glam-rock verse melody at least.  Immediately I can tell Ultravox has all the signs of being a phenomenal band.  The seeds were planted early right here on this debut.

"Slip Away" has some memorable new wave characteristics.  I really enjoy the line "Was I dreaming or did you say, the frontiers are falling, it's time to be slipping away".  This reminds me a Sparks song called "Saccharin and the War" from their debut.  That means this is instantly awesome.  Some of the synth work takes me back to the early 80's and reminds me of NES gaming generation, haha.  Despite that, I (perhaps wrongly!) detect sadness in the vocal melody.  Fascinating tune!  This song manages to combine dreamy guitar work with awesome piano playing near the end.  Very experimental I can see.

"I Want to Be a Machine" totally reminds me of Space Oddity-era David Bowie with the guitar playing and vocals.  The lead singer has a really beautiful voice, perhaps even better than Bowie's voice.  So far the song is similar to "Space Oddity" in terms of atmosphere and vocals.  "In flesh of ash and silent movies I walked that boulevard again, a nebula of unfinished creatures, from the lifetime of my friends, I howled your innocence has deprave me" is a scary line.  I love the way the lead singer sings "I want to be a machine" and carries out certain lines at the end, but when he does this same technique again the second and third time the rhythm gets funky, the bass gets heavy and this unusual orchestration comes in.  VERY cool!  This song even utilizes some country violin funk later on with forceful cymbal smashes and drumming which is quite the moment of creativity.  I LOVE creativity!  I want all bands to experiment just like this song does!  Recommend me more artists who write songs like this readers!

"Wide Boys" is based around a heavy guitar riff with deliberately blurry/frantic vocals.  The vocals remind me of Roxy Music's "Virginia Plains" a little bit.  "We're the wide boys up on the streets, wide boys ah come on and meet me!" and my favorite line "Delightfully unpleasant with our foxy adolescent sneers!"  "Dangerous Rhythm" has a mysterious and danceable "(I Don't Want to Go To) Chelsea" vibe  (the Elvis Costello song) going on which is really memorable and catchy to me.  The line "Dangerous rhythm in the air!" perfectly describes the atmosphere.  I really dig the funky bass work.  "The Lonely Hunter" is the weakest song here probably.  I just don't care for the way the lead singer carelessly blurts out "lonely hunter!"  Okay maybe "carelessly" is a bit of a stretch- I've heard worse, but meh, this band's too awesome for that kind of lazy songwriting.  At least the Clash-resembling verse melody is respectable.  The guitar work is awesome too.

Ultravox blows me away with the use of violins in the beginning of "The Wild, the Beautiful & the Damned".  I mean what other new wave band played violins like this?  Granted they only appear once in a while, but when they *do* appear they make a really unforgettable impression on me.  This song is really good for the way the lead singer sails his vocal range to a much higher register for the chorus ("The w-i-i-i-ld, the beautiful, and the damned!") and the guitar solo after is really unique too... and perhaps sad.  Wow what's with this sadness I feel?  Am I supposed to feel SAD while listening to this stuff?  No I don't think so, haha.  "My Sex" starts off with hazy piano playing and a strong feeling of depression.  But of course, it's not.  "My sex waits for me like a mongrel waits downwind on a tight rope leash" is a funny line.  The lead singer basically talk-sings about his sex!  The weird dreamy synths make this really bizarre- REALLY bizarre.  Move over Kraftwerk!  The odd way the piano plays makes me think I'm living inside a robots body.

Overall well I'm certainly VERY impressed with Ultravox's debut.  I get the feeling this band could've been humongous around England and the United States right from their debut if they could've caught on with crowds.  Maybe they were just too weird for most people but I find that hard to believe with the Talking Heads, Elvis Costello and others dominating the new wave scene at the time.  Must have just been misfortune.  I mean only a handful of reviews here on amazon indicates to me that this band just never found the success in the late 70's that could have escalated them to worldwide fame.  No exaggeration either- the songwriting certainly sounds quite competent and staggeringly unique to me.  Buy this one folks.

reviewText:
This is what real heavy metal should sound like.  The music is far more complex than what it is today, which lends to replay value.  The song Stairway to Heaven is popular for a good reason, and alone is worth the price of the album.  The song Black Dog seems to be nearly impossible to remake, which is a testimony to the real talent of the band.  Bear in mind that this was before the days when technology could sanitize a take to make it totally error free (and sterile).

People who were around in the 1960s and 1070s are probably familiar with this music.  Unlike many popular artists that seem bent on releasing strings of hit singles, Led Zeppelin only had six hits on the top 40 charts.  And only one got into the Top Ten.  However, they are still the most successful rock band of all time, possibly barring The Eagles.  And this album is their finest--this album deserves to be ranked highly.  By sales, only the Eagles' Greatest volume 1 and Michael Jackson's Thriller, both great albums of their own rights, did better.  And they all had many big radio hits.  Led Zeppelin made this album a blockbuster without releasing too many singles--only Black Dog was formally released and hit the Billboard Top 40.

Even younger listeners should give this a try.  People that are teens, or even pre-teens, can sample the album.  Listen to Stairway to Heaven and see if it is not worth the price.  And see what you are missing out on with that sanitized mush they call music today.  Led Zeppelin is definitely not sanitized, and definitely not mush.  About the only word of caution is that very devout Christians may find this album offensive or that their church might not condone it.  Even there, Led Zeppelin manages to make a solid album without the use of cursing, blatant references to drugs, or senseless violence--so even you might find it worth listening to.  For sure, this is one album your parents will NOT likely object to.

Also, Led Zeppelin's other albums are worth checking out.

Ever since Haden joined Ornette Coleman to take Jazz into yet a new direction almost forty years ago, his playing and composing has shown the kind of artistic integrity which is far from common these days.

So here he chooses to revive the Liberation Orchestra, along with the great Carla Bley, and delivers another astounding set of tunes that confirms his musical stature.

As far as the new Orchestra is concerned, the playing is tremendous, at once conscious of being an ensemble and blazing through their solos, whether it is Steve Cardenas on guitar, the horn section or Haden himself -precise and poetic, giving the music its hearbeat- every musician contributes to the beauty of these tunes.

As far as the songs, "Not In Our Name," "Throughout," "Amazing Grace" or "Blue Anthem" particularly stand out, yet the whole set is wonderful. Moving music for troubled and sad times from a man who has always understood that an artist is not above his peers nor his moment in history.

reviewText:
Underneath the profanity and vulgarity, Trey Parker and Matt Stone have, unsurprisingly, delivered a musical triumph that provides a stage to display absolutely beautiful singing combined with biting satire.  Some songs may be direct parodies - You and Me (But Mostly Me) is definitely a parody of The Wizard and I from Wicked - of other contemporary targets, the undeniable theme of poking the Mormon religion, and the super-secret gold plates dug up in Joseph Smith's backyard, with a stick is the true aim.

Three or four references to baby rape and clitoris mutilation in AIDS-stricken Africa automatically precludes the easily offended.  Their loss.  The whole album is not only a collection of amazing vocal ability, but it's also instructional.  Before listening I had no clue Jesus was an American who enlisted the help of Boba Fett and "the Bible is actually a trilogy, and the Book of Mormon is Return of the Jedi."  Yoda voice: [Making things up again, you are.]

A mix of the religious, epic, Disney, African tribals, and show-tunes await the lucky listener who opens their mind and actually listens to the content.  Like them or not, Parker's and Stone's collective brilliance is the ability to blend vulgarity, intelligent musical composition, and real-life commentary.  The ironic thing is, the overall content is a true parody of the Mormon religion, but throughout numerous songs there are unequivocal Mormon affirmations ("I Believe" is actually an incredibly uplifting song that supports Mormonism more than mocks it.)

I'd be remiss if I didn't mention the fact that Nikki M. James is amazing, and Hasa Diga Eebowai was the original reason I listened to this album.  Quite surprised by the quality of the rest, HDE still slayed me.  The fact that it has the happy sound of an African-infused Disney song only amplifies the message and content.  "Here's my daughter she has aaaaaaaaa"...seriously, this song gutted me and fed on my entrails.

Each song of the musical deserves its own review.  Simply hilarious.  I'll go see the show when they tour in years to come.

reviewText:
This album was released in the spring of 1968. By that point they had achieved full artistic autonomy from the record studio and their weekly show on NBC was going off the air, severing their last real commitments to the mainstream. Later that year would come "Head," the movie and soundtrack, both of which mainly functioned as a bonfire of the vanities, the Monkees setting fire to their Top 40 bubble gum lovable sitcom rascals image. Over the next several years Peter Tork would buy his way out of the group. While the remaining members would still release recordings, including "The Monkees Present," For most intents and purposes, "The Birds The Bees & The Monkees" is the last real album put out by the group that most fans fell in love with.

I'm fully aware that Monkees fans tend to be very divided over "Birds & Bees," but I come down solidly on the side of those believing it is the best album the group released, not because it represents the Monkees "sound" but simply because it still stands up today as a highly  enjoyable product of mid to late 1960s pop craftsmanship and artistic vision.

The opening song,  "Dream World" gets the album off to a strong start, featuring strong Davy Jones vocals and a horn-driven pop sound that was stylish in the 1960s and still does not sound dated today. "Auntie's Municipal Court" is one of Michael Nesmith's four contributions to the album, a successful experiment in merging country, pop, jazz, and trippy sound effects. The Carole Bayer co-written "We Were made for Each Other" is a fine work of 1960s orchestral pop. After "Tapioca Tundra," another Michael Nesmith success, comes the iconic "Daydream Believer," a Top 40 song produced by Chip Douglas before the group handed him his walking papers. The song still stands up today as one of the finest pop singles that came out during. The song features Davy Jones' finest hour as a vocalist and one of the most irresistible hooks in pop music.  Even after hundreds of listenings it's still  guaranteed to blow away  the mean reds away every time you hear it.

"I'll Be Back Up On My Feet" is one of the album's songs that comes closest to being typical of the group's earlier efforts. "Writing Wrongs" features Michael Nesmith in full Joycean mode, while the Beatlesque "The Poster," co-written by Davy Jones, evokes a circus. "P.O. Box 9847" is a witty, drum-driven story of a man's experience in answering a classified ad for a date;  classified ads were like the social media of the day. "Magnolia Simms," another Michael Nesmith song, predates the Beatles' "Honey Pie" in its use of modern studio technology to evoke a 1920s sound, while "Valleri" is another fine example of horn-driven 60s pop. The album concludes with "Zor and Zam," a slowly-building anti-war anthem that is as timely today as it was nearly 50 years ago and features one of Mickey Dolenz' best vocal efforts.

This release has the original thread-bare record company package. There are no line notes, no performer credits, just a reproduction of the album's original covers -- front -- which fittingly evokes an Americana image for this most American of bands -- and back -- featuring individual facial shots of the Monkees along with individual quotes designed to pithily sum up their philosophies of life.

So, where does "Birds & Bees" rank in the Monkees canon? For best collection of sheer 1960s Top 40 pop sound, "More of the Monkees" takes the prize, while "Pisces, Aquarius ..." best captures the Monkees as a fully coherent group. But as an album, one that holds together and holds your attention while listening to it,. and leaves you with sounds and images in your mind after it is over, for the Monkees it doesn't get any better than "The Birds, The Bees, & The Monkees."

reviewText: This album marks a first for many reasons: first Coltrane recorded for Atlantic, first where all of the tracks are his compositions, and the first where his "sheets of sound" phrasing was prominent (it was not new, but came to the forefront with this album.) In a way, Coltrane is finally 'discovered' on this album because he is neither in the shadows of Miles, nor is he displaying his abilities on standards and compositions of others. Everyone - every jazz aficionado and all musicians regardless of genre - should own this album. It broke new ground when it was released in January of 1960, and continues to this day to exert a major influence on musicians as well as listeners. I could blather on about changes and progressions, but that does not describe the music to the non-musician listener who has every right to enjoy this album on its own merits without some snob implying that its too sophisticated. The samples on this page give a hint, but that should be all you need to make a purchase decision. For musicians I highly recommend augmenting with album with Giant Steps: A Player's Guide To Coltrane's Harmony for ALL Instrumentalists. For Everyone else, I recommend purchasing it without further thought.

I love "Dollar Dan"... look for his review.  It pretty much sums up the "opposition" to the Guided by Voices hodgepodge ethos.

I was unprepared when I heard this being played in a little record store near where I lived at the time it was out... it was one of those "WHAT THE F***?" moments:  "Did that lead guitar just cut out briefly like someone just taped over it?  Did that amazing song just end after only one verse/chorus?" and so on.

I've written a lot of songs in my day and loving this album started to reveal and challenge the rigidly constructed walls in the fortress i'd constructed in my mind of What Is A Song.

It must be what many classical music fans thought when their first heard Webern's odd miniatures.  IT'S TOO SHORT!  IT DOESN'T COUNT!

So I will say this:  If you feel that a rock song must be at least two minutes long and repeat choruses, or if you are hard-core (songs must have this: intro-verse-chorus-verse-chorus-bridge-solo-chorus-chorus-fade), or whatever rigid song format fortress you've built, you may very well be disappointed in this album, and down with Dollar Dan.  You can still be hip to GBV and get Mag Earwhig or one of the other more fleshed-out normalish GBV records, or pull back further for safety's sake and get the Best Of they put out a coupla years ago.

But, maybe you should try this, seriously, it might change how you feel about rock music, which isn't something you can say about many albums.  For me it's one of my favorites of the '90s for sure.  One of the best things about it:  there's nothing else like it, from the weird production, the super-hooky melodies and kaliedescopic lyrics.

My fortress walls don't go so high anymore and the gate is always open.  Hooray for GBV!

Same goes with the third movment. The fast, nailbiting tempo is much more demanding. More "jokeful"; after all, scherzo literally means "joke".

  As for the more profound Unfinished Symphony by Schubert, I don't have much to say, but it is overall a nice, performance. Not too clumsy.

reviewText:
I have been going through all of the four major completions of Mahler's tragically unfinished 10th symphony.  I came across them in this order - Wheeler, Cooke, Mazzetti, and I'm awaiting the arrival of my Carpenter version.  I fell in love right away with the Wheeler recording (my first hearing of the symphony) - it wasn't till several months later that I stumbled upon a Cooke version (Inbal's) and gave it a whirl.  Right away I noticed the fuller sound in many portions where Wheeler had purposefully left things bare.  However, I was not too impressed with the poor recording quality of the Inbal performance (too much room noise for my taste, especially as this was supposedly a studio recording).

Well, since I am a completist, I ordered this disc of the Mazzetti for my collection.  When I first listened through it, I almost took it out and chucked it without finishing!  It was drastically different enough to shock me (particularly the 4th movement and parts of the 5th).  However, I then listened to Slatkin's explanatory disc (about a 15 - 20 minute discussion of each completion including samples of the same passages from all four composers and descriptions of the differences) - for whatever reason, after listening to that and then giving the Mazzetti completion another whirl, it almost instantly became my favorite!  Now, I understand Carpenter took the most liberties with the score and added much of his own style which was distinctly un-Mahler - so, I've yet to hear his version, but the clips played by Slatkin sounded a little too over the top to be taken as anything more than an "interesting alternative" to what Mahler intended.

Mazzetti likely took his own liberties (the consensus seems to indicate that Wheeler left it the barest and closest not only to the original notes, but also to the style Mahler had adapted in his final symphonies).  Even so, I like Mazzetti's ideas - whether or not it is Mahlerian, I cannot say, but it sure makes the piece sound more complete and fleshed out - it was beautiful to begin with, but now it brings tears to the eyes!  Not only is it a great interpretation, but the recording is near flawless - particularly impressive if it was indeed recorded in live sessions as Slatkin indicates.

This is a great package, along with the bonus disc.  A steal at any price, to be sure!

reviewText:
I bought a new car recently and it came with satellite radio.  I hadn't heard much satellite radio up to now because my average drive time doesn't merit the cost.  However, three months come free with this car, and I have enjoyed farting around checking out various formats, although none of them particularly stand out.  To get to my point, I settled on Liquid Metal, the heavy station from Sirius, and a few things come to mind:  far too many metal bands have lapsed into the same trap everybody else does, and that is mediocrity.  I listened sometimes for several songs at a stretch and I won't name names, but the tunes, while they were heavy enough, were so by-the-numbers that it was difficult to tell the bands apart, if not impossible.  Only Opeth stood out at first, and that's because I already have several of their CD's.  Out of dozens of bands that all sound exactly alike, especially with those stupid grunting vocals, only one stood out over the last three days as having a shred of originality, a real beat, and some great melodic moments that most metal reviewers seem to really hate nowadays.  That band is Daath, the Atlanta metal outfit that is probably the most technically proficient metal outfit out there right now.
  "Concealers" isn't prog rock, either.  Daath are extremely heavy, but they share a musical adventurousness with Opeth that makes them stand apart and above their contemporaries.  This band doesn't sound like Opeth, but they aren't afraid to mix in moments of melody, some of the best guitar slinging out there today and even a simple beat instead of the blast beats that are contaminating everything in metal anymore.  Some intolerant reviewers knock Daath for these qualities, but to me it makes them recognizable and offers an actual individual sound, something most bands can't do anymore.
  Now, I double dog dare this fine outfit to employ some clean vocals.  Fear Factory does it to no harm, Killswitch Engage does it, and these bands have much more of an identity for it.  Voices are unique - vocalists who sound like they have extreme irritable bowel syndrome do not sound "evil" or tough.  They just sound stupid, and I'm sick of it.  I'd never go near death metal, black or metalcore based on vocals - if the music isn't good and original enough to override the belching, I'm not listening.  Daath have the chops and real vocal melody would add a great dimension to an already impressive style.  Why sound just like everybody else?  Being a clone band ain't rock and roll at all.

reviewText:
What do you need to know?

Should I bolster Dylan's incredible reputation as an incredible songwriter? Should I tell you that he wrote a Christian rock album based on his own genuine faith at the time? Will you buy the album if I tell you it is among my favorite Christian albums, along with Phil Keaggy's (great guitarist with a Paul McCartney voice) and Larry Norman's (singer-songwriter with a folk-blues flavor) groundbreaking work?

Listen to the clips. Dig the blues and black gospel influences. Groove with it. You like Dylan. Of course you do. Even critics of Christianity claim this to be among his best works. When you get into it and feel the verve of his sincerity and depth, you're bound to agree that as a Dylan fan, you have not been disappointed. You'll find he was hardly fundamentalist in his theology, but rich with a complex faith that charged that he should be living out what he was singing about. Nothing namby-pamby is  going on here.

The same Dylan who wrote, "The Times They Are A-Changin" wrote every word of "Saved."

If matters of faith cause you to tremble, join the ranks of pop music fans. If spiritual questing, search for meaning and the desire to believe in something that matters in your real life is part of what makes a classic song, buy this CD.

For the less timid, dust off your family Bible and find out he's pulling much of his lyrics straight from Scripture. Check out "Slow Train Coming" or "Shot of Love" to hear more of his work in this genre. If you find out Christian rock is more than Stryper, Amy Grant and jazzed-up versions of "Amazing Grace," boldly go where Christian rock has gone before, and search the net for "In Another Land" or "Only Visiting This Planet" by Norman, or any of Keaggy's stuff.

I fully recommend this album.

Anthony Trendl
editor, HungarianBookstore.com

reviewText:
I wasn't expecting as magnificent a combination of advanced "new age" and smooth jazz as I did here.  Lanz' piano work shines through on each arrangement here, often with a singing quality to its sound.
This album also awakened a new admiration for Dave Koz, a musician who previously, in my estimation, seemed to be trying to become a second Kenny G, a rather questionable goal maybe.  But, here he shines on several fronts.  He produced four of the cuts starting with the opener, "That Smile".  He performs on "Walk On Water" (which was composed by Snuffy Walden along with Dave Lanz), "Romantica" (a smooth, exotic number composed by Lanz along with Dave Koz), and "Luna".  Each performance shows a new individuality, a breaking away from the commercially smooth Kenny G mode and a finding of himself musically.
The cover of Neil Diamond's "America" is an expression of a great love, of reaching for unity and healing, and encompassing the globe, not just this country.  This highlight performance would've made this CD noteworthy even if the surrounding pieces didn't match it...but they do.
The hheart-searching "Tears For Alice" and the last cut, "Love Lost...Love Found", each features a rich string & harp accompaniment.
This whole performance has Lanz branching out, developing, expanding and should be heartily welcomed by his followers and by those discovering him for the first time.

reviewText:
I guess "Mr. Vain" is the best-known song on this 1993 album "Serenity", but by no means is it the only thing of interest. In fact, the entire album is quite an awesome show. The opening track, the "Prolog", starts with dramatic, futuristic techno, followed by a voice announcing "You are now entering a dimension on the boundaries of conscious perception ...the hypnotic sound of Culture Beat". Then the hot dance beat kicks in, and you get to hear the extremely catchy "Mr. Vain". Vocalist Tania Evans describes him: "Call him Mr. Raider/Call him Mr. Wrong/Call him Mr. Vain... Call him insane", and rapper Jay Supreme's swag response is, "Call me what ya like/As long as you call me time and again". (The talents of both Jay and Tania are featured on most tracks.) The following track "Got To Get It" continues the same general pace, beat and song structure. Next, the pace is noticeably toned down as Tania repeatedly tells some very lucky person, someone who gets everything he needs, "Just think the world is in your hands", and that last word "hands" reveals a very pronounced British accent, just one of the delights to be found on the album.

The pace is hard and fast again as Jay switches to Spanish in "Adelante!" ("Come in!"), telling us that his "hermosa" ("lovely lady") has assured him over and over "La puerta está abierta" ("The door is open"). The pace gets even more frenetic when Tania sings "Rocket To The Moon" and "Anything", the latter referring to what she will do to continue the relationship she has. Things calm down again as Tania gives a very good vocal performance on "Key To Your Heart". It sounds almost like a mainstream ballad but is saved from that by the atmospheric techno effects. The next 2 tracks, "The Other Side Of Me" and "The Hurt", pick up the fast, hard beat again, with some nice rhythmic piano included. "Mother Earth" opens with serious, somber synths before the beat resumes, in this song which warns us about pollution. Tania cries out passionately  "Mother Earth, tell me how much longer will you let your children treat you this way?" And all of this takes us finally to the last track, the "Epilog". This primarily instrumental track opens dramatically like the "Prolog" does, and from there switches back and forth between sections of soft, pretty synth lines and sections of hard, fast techno decorated with tinkling piano. It all melds, and it all ends with a crash. All things considered, I think maybe I would have called the album "Intensity".

reviewText:
With success comes pressure to keep the good stuff coming, and if you're Keith Urban, you know about pressure. It's bound to come from somewhere when you've sold eight million records in seven years, had 14 top ten and six #1 singles and won a Grammy. Fortunately, it seems that Urban works well under pressure, and falling in love with and marrying Nicole Kidman inspires some wonderful new songs.

This album finds Urban in a whole new place. There are songs about pain, but instead of being dark and regretful, they seem to say "I was in pain, but now I'm not. I'm moving on with my life." "Used To The Pain" says it best.

"Every step I take I get a little less afraid

Of givin' in to love

Believe me when I say it gets better every day

Once you get used to the pain."

This is perhaps his most upbeat record. Nicole has definitely changed his way of thinking and is giving him new reasons to write. Love is always a dominating theme on his records, but longtime listeners will be able to sense the difference she has made. The boy is in love!

We are treated to more glorious guitar work on this one, but this album is so diverse and textured that the production alone sucks you in, and Urban's vocals keep you in. There's a reason this guy has won CMA Male Vocalist of the Year three years in a row: He puts all of his emotions in his vocals and doesn't hold back.

Every song is single worthy, but highlights include "Shine", "I Told You So", "Faster Car", "Raise The Barn", and "Tu Compania". "I Told You So" features a pounding rhythm and many layers of percussion including a tin whistle and uillean pipes that give it a celtic flair. It will knock your socks off. "Faster Car" was surely written while he and Nicole were first dating. It is insanely infectious and to poised to be a big hit. It is the furthest thing from country I've ever heard him do, but it's one of the best. It has a killer base line, which Urban plays, and sounds like something U2 would do.

"I need a faster car now

I'm a rocket man in love with you."

"You got me talkin' to an empty pillow in the middle of the night

I ain't slept in quite a while."

I am so sorry that all the people buying it outside the United States don't get to hear "Raise The Barn", because it is one of his best songs. It was inspired by Hurricane Katrina, but it is so upbeat and praises the spirits of all our brothers and sisters in the Gulf Coast who are rebuilding their lives, and having Ronnie Dunn as a duet partner is always a good thing. Dunn's and Urban's voices are a good pair, the two best tenors in Nashville, and Dunn delivers another fantastic vocal. Even though it references Hurricane Katrina, it's a great party song and everybody should hear it.

"We'll be square dancin', toe tappin'

We'll be kickin' up our heels to the Cotton Eyed Joe

Music and laughter, gonna raise the rafters

A little boot slidin' across the floor

Do a little hand holdin', hay rollin'

Strollin' with your honey by your side

Dixie cups and paper plates

Fiddle tunes and Amazing Grace

Hallelujah gonna raise the barn tonight."

This was definitely worth the wait to see what he had up his sleeve, and I can't wait to see him perform some of this new stuff live. This new music is so fresh and invigorating, like sunshine after a long cold winter. Urban is awfully good at bringing the sun with him wherever he goes, and this is no exception.

reviewText:
UK dancepop duo Moloko are in fine form in "Things to Make And Do," their third blend of acid jazz and trippy electronica. The talented Roisin Murphy and Mark Brydon create a charmingly erratic dance album that sounds like nothing else, yet never fails to draw you in.

It opens with a peculiar piano solo, before kicking into the sexy sax-keyboard of "Pure Pleasure Seeker," and the ominously trippy "Absent Minded Friends." A darker note enters with songs like "Being Is Bewildering," which is technically a more "normal" song, a slow and rather melancholy song based on acoustic guitar and organ. Same with the lower-key pop song "The Time is Now."

There are also some more experimental songs, such as the nonsensical funk of "Indigo" or the creepy psycho-vocals of "If You Have A Cross To Bear You May As Well Use It As A Crutch." "Remain the Same" is perhaps the most experimental, with the vocal sampling and sound of the organ being overwhelmed and sunk by the electronic bleeps.

In this release, Moloko downplays the outright weirdness in favor of a more subtle sound. Call it experimental ultraquirk acid-jazz-funk-house-trip-hop. That more or less describes it. It's not just a fun album, but a richly engaging one with some deceptively simple-sounding songwriting.

Roisin (no, it doesn't rhyme with "raisin") Murphy has an excellent voice for this type of music -- it sounds clear and flexible, while being strong enough to rise over powerful music that could have overwhelmed her. And she brings depth to certain songs like "Mother," where she lashes out at her mother in a restrained manner: "I know somehow somewhere I'll be bumping into you/you see I'm blameless/I had a mother who was shameless/no wonder my life collapsed!" Elsewhere the songwriting is just deliciously bizarre.

Mark Brydon takes charge of the musical backdrop for Roisin's voice. And a fine job he does too, blending organic instrumentation like piano, acoustic guitar and rippling strings with some vocal sampling and deliciously wacked-out beats, sounding like anything from a DJ on acid to the funkier twin of Portishead.

Erratic it may be, but "Things to Make And Do" is also fun, wild and extremely eclectic, switching styles the way most musicians do instruments. It may not be their best album, but it is a wonderfully engaging, trippy one.

reviewText:
Ah, I have a feeling Good Feelin' to Know, despite lacking commercial success at the time, is the style Poco had been searching for because it just sounds so *right*.  You can just tell Poco enjoyed making this album and that the music touched them on a personal/emotional level.  Yes it's a good feeling to know this album.

"Ride the Country" reminds me of Neil Young in the vocals, especially the way Paul Cottons sings the line "And I wonder, now I wonder".  It's dreamy and soulful in a Neil Young kind of way especially with lines such as "We've been living all of our lives on the other side of the hill".  You can tell Poco's approaching the commercial success they've been searching for with this release.  "And we ride the countryside, take it high and wide" is when the mood shifts.  A different singer sings this part, and it drastically changes the mood with still maintaining the beautiful country/rock vibes.  For a 6-minute song, it's surprising how much of it emphasis the vocals.  They simply overshadow everything else, though I can't help but think the brief guitar solo at the end reminds me of Crazy Horse.  I love this song quite a bit.

For some reason the intro to "Sweet Lovin" sounds spiritual to me in the same way as Steve Winwood's "If You See a Chance" but this is more spiritual and lasts a minute longer.  Soon a gospel choir enters as the lead singer sings gently and somberly the words "Wordless are the thoughts she's trying to say, oh my maybe she's seein' the light of a brighter day".  This vocal melody is slow overall but really memorable.  Maybe the gospel singers are out of place somewhat, but not distractingly so.  Beautifully written song.  "Restrain" shows more of that Crazy Horse-influenced guitar styling.  The vocal melody is soft like an Eagles song, but if you listen to it carefully you can tell it's inventive like a Band tune.  I wish they didn't say the lyrics "Victim of circumstance you'll say 'till the end" because it reminds me SO MUCH of the Eagles "Victim of Love".  Obviously that song came out a few years after this one, but like most people can say "Victim of Love" is the song I'm familiar with.  It's hard to believe a song that chugs at such a safe pace, and sung identically to an Eagles song, I'd actually love so much but I do!  Great song!

"Keeper of the Fire" contains a GREAT forceful beat.  It's bouncy and memorable.  I know I've heard a similar guitar line that carries this song somewhere else from another artist.  Why am I thinking Jefferson Airplane?  Who knows, it's probably not them.  And you know what?  I'm making WAY too many comparisons here.  Good Feelin' to Know is a GREAT album!  I love singing the line "Lookin' out there was a new light burning, I turned about, everyone there kept on turning".  You'll be singing along as well because it's too memorable NOT to!  "Early Times" opens with a plodding heavy guitar riff, and I enjoy all the tempo changes that occur during the "Long time" lyrics.  Actually the melody jumps all over the place, but not in some overbearing kind of way but rather a beautiful, smooth sailing and highly emotional kind of way.

The title song sounds familiar.  Not that I've ever heard it on FM radio.  No, they don't play Poco AT ALL anymore, not even "Crazy Love" which was once a popular favorite not so long as 20 years ago.  Boo to their short playlists now!  Anyway this song has a swift rhythm and a memorable chorus the way the lead singer and background vocals both contribute to give this vocal melody a TON of emotion.  The verse melody is really good too- "Yes I've got that old time feeling burnin' deep inside my soul and I am yours, and baby I'm home".  The opening riff to "And Settlin' Down" had serious potential if the band wanted to continue building on that, however it soon changes into a more chugging laidback tune.  But there's a steady beat assuring it's not *too* laidback, and the sincerity that occurs throughout these many vocal melody shifts is staggeringly good.  "I miss my woman yes, I miss my woman, and settlin' down she's hummin' another sound" is a good line.

'I Can See Everything" (wow I wish I had the ability to do that!  I'd be watching Taiwan, Brazil and New Brunswick all at the same time!) has tender vocals.  I'm... not sure who's singing this song.  I almost think it sounds like a female because all these high notes are going off like fireworks in the night.  This is balladry, but there's *something* extra about it that elevates it above your average ballad.  It sort of reminds me of the Eagles "Witchy Woman" but a LOT better.  I never cared for that Eagles song much.  This reminds me of Jim Messina but well, it can't be.  He left a couple albums ago!  "Go and Say Goodbye" has a heavy Chicago-like guitar riff.  Reminds me of the riff from "25 or 6 to 4" but a lot better.  Nice steady pace too.  The vocals remind me of the legendary Byrds which can only be a BRILLIANT thing.  I'm thinking of the song "Born to Follow" in particular.  It's so sad the way certain lines like "Is it you don't want to see her cry, is that why you don't go and say goodbye" are sung.  Tear-jerking stuff.

Overall, WOW!  I love this album!  A must own.  Apparently the departure of Jim Messina didn't slow these guys down a bit.  Well actually it sort of slowed them down for their From the Inside album, but that was only temporary my good people!
label: positive

reviewText:
This is by far the best CD System Of A Down has released since Toxicity.  They have kept the intensity/humour contrast that is so characteristic of them : among the emtionnally intense songs of this album, you will find Soldier Side, Hypnotize, Dreaming, Holy Mountain, Lonely Day and most definitely Tentative, which is undoubtedly my favourite song off the album, and the closest song to Chop Suey! which is my personaly all-time favourite SOAD song ever.  And then there are the funny songs : U-Fig, She's Like Heroin and I would even add Kill Rock 'n Roll.

All in all, great album, I was mezmerized by System's capacity to surpass themselves because I honestly wasn't expecting something THIS great, since Steal This Album! was decent but not excellent, and although Mezmerize was much better than Steal This Album!, it wasn't really anywhere close to Toxicity.  But Hypnotize makes you forget those little "downfalls" and gives hope of an SOAD forceful return.

Their lyrics remain very political in many songs, and when they are not, they are plain ridiculous.  I love listening to a new SOAD song for the first time cause I never know if it's gonna give me chills or make me laugh.  And I definitely chuckled when I heard U-Fig on this one, just as I had laughed my head off when I had first heard Pictures off of Steal This Album!, which Serj going "Pa-pa-pa-PA!" in a really high-pitched tone.

This band has such incredible potential it amazes me.  I'm looking forward to new material already, but for the moment, I'm probably gonna keep listening to Hypnotize daily like I have been doing since I bought it on Nov. 22nd.  If you are a System Of A Down fan, or if you're only into them a little (which probably means that you liked Toxicity a lot but the other CD's a little less) and are hesitating to buy this CD, I hearten you to buy it, you will not be disappointed!

reviewText: What can I say about Jazmine Sullivan? Well, first, she is an amazing vocalist; her soulful and raspy alto is simply beautiful. And her songwriting is just as amazing. When the two are mixed together, you get what is one of the best R&B albums of 2008, along with Erykah Badu's last effort and Estelle's second album. "Bust Your Windows" and "Lions, Tigers & Bears" are both mini-epics of songs with Jazmine emotional vocal delivery gliding over a full orchestra. They sound like perfect candidates to James Bond themes. (And goodness knows either one of them would have served as better choices than that mess Alicia Keys and Jack White just released). The #1 R&B smash, "Need U Bad," still remains an incredibly catchy and enjoyable song, even after months of hearing it. "My Foolish Heart" is a bouncy heartbroken. The dramatic and emotional "Call Me Guilty" is a tale of domestic abuse to the point where the protagonist feels the only choice is to kill him. "One Night Stand," about a reformed female playa, is a playful song with girl group-esque backup vocals. "After the Hurricane" is probably my favorite track off this set. It is an ominous, foreboding, and heartwrenching ballad with beautiful harmonies. "Dream Big" is a creative autobiographical jam that samples Daft Punk, which is apparently becoming a very popular trend in urban music. Jazmine's voice here is full of force and determination, showing what got her to where she is today. "Live A Lie" is a nice slice of laid-back throwback soul full of regret. "Fear" is a very vulnerable track in which Jazmine admits her many fears and it is laced with beautiful harmonies. "In Love With Another Man" finds Jazmine backed by a simple piano and nothing more. Even without all the production, she can convey emotion and tell a story. The bonus track, "Switch" is a whimsical and fun song, and a nice way to close the album. This album, in my humble opinion, is absolutely flawless. The songwriting, the production, and most importantly her voice are all on point, making this one of the best R&B albums of the year and Jazmine one of the most promising new acts on the rise.
label: positive

reviewText: As the other review stated, the two-note theme of this score is repeated throughout, echoing the two main characters (if you will), almost revolving around each other like a binary star.  As with his other great themes, like those of Requiem For a Dream, and The Fountain, the emotional tones stay with you long after the movie ends.  Here, Clint manages to make tangible the feeling of desolation and loneliness that pervades throughout the first act of the film.  It's almost as if you're inside Sam's head, losing your sanity along with him.  I love that this score was done by Mansell almost entirely alone, just him and his piano, as he usually collaborates with the like of Kronos Quartet, or bands like Mogwai.  Here, it's just Clint and his keyboard, which reinforces the feeling of isolation, and illustrates the genius this man is capable of.  I highly recommend seeking out his other soundtracks, as they are almost all worth owning.

Although it didn't sell as well as "Nilsson Schmilsson" "Son of Schmilsson" was every bit the equal of its predecessor albeit wackier. As everyone else has reported the remaster sounds great--it's even better than the Japanese import I paid top dollar for a couple of years ago--with bonus tracks. Curtis Armstrong ("Moonlighting") a committted Harryhead co-produced and wrote the booklet with plenty of comments from surviving participants (and Harry via older interviews). From Ray Cooper to Chris Spedding we get an idea as to how the sessions went. Although Harry and producer Richard Perry didn't get on quite as well here as the previous album (Harry was in the middle of a messy divorce which had an impact on this album. It took a while for him to recover)Perry and Harry still managed to create a great album.

The four bonus tracks (one is unlisted and starts a few seconds after the single version of "Daybreak" ends)includes an alternate take of "Take 54", a Perry produced version of "What's Your Sign?" (which would show up on another Harry album), "Camp De Encino" written by Jimmy Webb (it is presented with just Harry singing and playing piano), the single version of "Daybreak" and the off-the-cuff bonus track where Harry riffs backed by his band.

This is a terrific reissue and well worth paying the extra $$ for as the sound has been improved and the bonus tracks are a marked improvement over the import version.

reviewText: While he helped Crowded House during Neil's crippling case of writer's block during the Woodface era, Tim Finn hasn't experienced his younger brother's level of fame since his solo album Escapade climbed the charts in 1983. As a well-documented sufferer of depression, only Tim knows whether watching his sibling earn the greater share of acclaim has heightened his dark days. Having invited his teenage brother to join his band Split Enz in the 70s, the elder Finn has somewhat existed in the shadows of Neil's songwriting prowess ever since, but perhaps the fresh sounds of Everyone Is Here will act restoratively in gaining a fairer equilibrium in Finnish history. While 1996's debut Finn Brothers album had beautiful moments such as Angel's Heap and Paradise, Everyone Is Here finds a more robust sound and a powerful fulfilment of the Te Awamutu brothers' talents. The first taste of the second Finn project came on Neil's incredible 2002 live album Seven Worlds Collide, where Tim lead a stark and stirring take on the mortality-questioning Edible Flowers. While hard to believe that the splendour of this early airing could be surpassed, the rasp in Tim's voice, the additional strings and the delicious harmonies of the brothers renders Everyone Is Here's version the quintessential take. Other highlights include Disembodied Voices (where the brothers whisper fragile verses about their shared childhood in a sweet rather than cloying way) and the jubilant first single Won't Give In. Legendary producer Tony Visconti (David Bowie, Dandy Warhols) appears to have influenced the Finns on All God's Children (with catchy T-Rex fuzz employed liberally), although it's old pals Mitchell Froom and Bob Clearmountain who steer the greater portion of production here. While some ideas appear to be slight retreads (Anything Can Happen sounds a little too close to the One Nil track Into the Sunset), the glowing harmonies of Tim and Neil on Luckiest Man Alive and Homesick trounce fears of a creative void. Although it's always going to be hard for them to top the clever hooks available on their compilations History Never Repeats and Recurring Dream, the focus of The Finn Brothers' Everyone Is Here is more about the songcraft lurking below the quick-fix surface of regular pop. With that in mind, they've once again succeeded brilliantly.

reviewText: Every song's a winner on this album with the possible exception of "EXP" which is just a bunch of feedback with a silly introduction to let us know what the noise is all about...but the thing I like about this album is that all the tracks, save "If 6 was 9" (which is a great song!), are fairly short and have a lot of continuity. "She's so Fine" (think "Little Miss Strange") isn't all that, but it is still a decent song which features Noel Redding's abilities. But song for song, this is a very strong album and excluding some of Hendrix's most memorable cuts on his other albums, this one contains more quality on one album than the others.( with the possible exception of his first). I bought this vinyl when it was first released and remember marveling at Hendrix and, at that time, even loved "EXP". But after 38 years (and many years of sobriety!) this album still plays very well, even "EXP" conjures some memories. This album is definitely a favorite of mine and gets a lot of playing time. If, like me, you are re-collecting your favorites from the 60's and  70's this is a must. Lots of good stuff and some long forgotten songs that I had to just slap my forehead and wonder how I could have forgotten such classics. Truthfully, I've put off "rebuying" this album choosing to buy other Hendrix stuff ahead of it...but now that I have it, I'm not sure why I waited; maybe my early brain cell losses contained the memories from this album! But seriously, I agree with another person who reviewed this album: it should be the first or 2nd Hendrix album you buy--in the first three minimum.

reviewText: Like most of his stuff, SOTLS is dreamy, melodic, thematic and eclectic.  His style has matured subtly and well.  This isn't Saturday Savior or Undone; angst has been usurped by contemplation, and rather than pushing away he is reaching out on this album.  However, some of the good old naughtiness is still here, sans bitterness, especially on the very sexy second to last track, 23rd Boy.  Rock musicians don't usually age well, but Ken Andrews is at his zenith here, lyrically and musically.  The album may not be necessarily conceptual but is lucidly thematic, telling a story with an impressionist narrative.  Its a far cry from Failure, but a powerful one still, one that reaches back to its roots buried in some more hostile past; less raw, more bare, heavier fans might write it off as sappy pop, but pop is a medium Ken Andrews dabbles in with the skilled hand of a seasoned artist.  As with Fantastic Planet, I've listened to this album over and over for days straight.  Ken Andrews kicks ass.  Get it, you won't regret it.

reviewText: I take my cue from the perceptive review by the late Colin Fortune on Amazon UK, who observes that while this live performance might not be the one you'd suggest to introduce a Bruckner novice to the Fourth, nor is it necessarily the one to live with, its unique appeal and highly personal vision make it compulsory listening for any Bruckner aficionado open-minded enough to welcome an interpretation which radiates conviction and sincerity. Celibidache's legendary slow tempi are in fact not so much in evidence until the last movement which is a tour de force. Otherwise, the listener is simply aware of a massive yet melodic and free-flowing pulsation to the music which never drags. It is simply crass to caricature Celi's tempi as "slow"; the word is inadequate to describe his uncanny ability to find the "still point" in this music and embrace the infinite. Slowness is usually associated with heaviness but not here: there is a kind of balletic grace to the music's unfolding like watching planets or building blocks swing into position. The Scherzo is - well, if not exactly perky, certainly fluid, lithe and nimble without sacrificing grandeur. But of course it is the Finale which separates the wimps from the True Believers and while I can surrender disbelief sufficiently to be caught up in its spell, I can quite understand those for whom it is all too much at 27 minutes. Celibidache secures lovely playing from the Munich Philharmoniker: all the rehearsal time he demanded is manifested in the beautiful control of dynamics, smooth phrasal transitions and singing tone in the strings, especially the cellos and violas in the Andante. A few regrettable percussive coughs apart, the ADD sound from 1988 is excellent. Unrelenting spirituality might be too much for some listeners who would prefer more contrast between the different sections and less restraint at climactic points. A much more conventional recommendation would be Karajan's lovely, dignified recording: Bruckner: Symphony No. 4 "Romantic"

reviewText:
Disc One contains the complete tribute concert, uncut and unedited. Disc Two includes the edited theatrical version, plus some bonus rehearsal footage and interviews.  Every phase of George's career is covered.  Eric Clapton organized the concert and turned in brilliant performances of the songs "If I Needed Someone" and "Beware Of Darkness."  I especially enjoyed Gary Brooker, lead singer of Procol Harum, doing the Beatles' era song "Old Brown Shoe."  His outstanding performance was not in the theatrical version, although the song is heard over the closing credits.  Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers performed the Beatles' songs "Taxman" and "I Need You."  Jeff Lynne joined them to perform the Traveling Wilburys' song "Handle With Care."  It's too bad Bob Dylan wasn't able to be there.  Not only is he the other surviving member of the Traveling Wilburys, Bob also participated in George Harrison's 1971 "Concert For Bangla Desh."

Ringo Starr remained upbeat while mentioning how the meaning changed of the song "Photograph," which he wrote with the late George Harrison.  "But all I've got is a photograph, and I realize you're not coming back anymore."  Ringo then launched into a spirited version of the Carl Perkins' classic "Honey Don't."  Paul McCartney followed with the Beatles' era song "For You Blue."  Paul started the George Harrison song "Something" on the ukulele, before Eric Clapton and the band joined in for an electrifying finish to that song.  Paul and Eric also did a duet on the classic song "While My Guitar Gently Weeps."  That was followed by Billy Preston sweetly singing "My Sweet Lord."  The excitement level really built up in the next to last song, "Wah Wah," performed by almost all of the participating musicians.  Amazingly, that song wasn't even included in the theatrical version of the concert.  Joe Brown, an English singer also managed by Brian Epstein back in the sixties, joined everybody to sing a moving version of the final song, "I'll See You In My Dreams."  It was a fitting farewell to the late, great George Harrison.
label: positive

reviewText:
In Real Time was produced by the band for Release in 1987 so they could have something to peddle to the masses that would be seeing them as the opening act for a certain Jethro Tull during the "Crest Of A Knave"  tour.
  It was recorded live in the studio (at the band's own Woodworm Records) with pre-recorded audience sounds tacked on, pictures from the Cropredy Festival were included to lead all to believe it was recorded there.
  That said even if it is "The Phony Live Album" it is a most excellent one and also one of the best recordings in the band's history.
  It begins with "Reynard The Fox", and the playing is stellar, Ric Sanders is way on top of this one, taking is fiddle where no one has gone before or since. "Widow of Westmorland's Daughter" has about a million words in it and vocalist Simon Nicol sings em' all in just over three minutes, best version of this ditty on record. reviewText: Keith Jarrett's "American Quartet" of Dewey Redman, Charlie Haden and Paul Motian was one of the very greatest jazz bands of the seventies, or really, ever.  these two Impulse sets, recorded less than a year before their breakup, show them still at the top of their game and finding new fertile ground within their unique idiom.  (They are augmented here by percussionist Guilherme Franco, who sounds lost, but usually in a good way.)  Stunning performances include "Everything That Lives Laments," a dirge-turned-modified-bossa that achieves a sort of modern Nawlins funeral euphoria;  the unbelievably swinging "Shades of Jazz" (those  who think Paul Motian can't swing should listen to this);  the quirkily funky "Southern Smiles."  Each of these feature brilliant solos from Jarrett and Redman, but Haden tops even them on the beautiful "Rose Petals."  As always, the group explores a variety of directions while sounding utterly like themselves.  Recommended for humans with ears.

reviewText:
This album was popular all over Europe and remains one of the finest disco albums ever recorded. It included four tracks that, released as singles, became huge UK hits for them - and the other tracks were also of a high quality. The title track (included here) was not released as a UK single but must surely have been considered for such a release.

The first single off the album was Rivers of Babylon, a cover of a reggae song from the sixties that was originally recorded by the Melodians. It spent five weeks at number one in the UK before beginning a slow decline. Just when it looked as if it was near to dropping out of the charts (over three months after its original release), the record was flipped and its B-side, Brown girl in the ring, was heavily promoted. The record climbed the charts again and eventually re-entered the top five. By the time the record finally dropped out of the UK chart, it had been there for forty weeks.

While the above double-sided single was still in the charts, Boney M released Rasputin, which made number two in the UK. Following a Christmas single not taken from the album, they returned to this album for one more single, Painter man, which only just made the top ten. Being released more than a year after the album from which it came, I suspect that a lot of people already had the album by then.

The other tracks include unlikely but brilliant covers of King of the road (Roger Miller) and Heart of gold (Neil Young) as well as three original songs of which my favorite is Never change lovers in the middle of the night.

The hits are, of course, available elsewhere, but this fine album is worth hearing in its entirety - if you can find it.

reviewText:
As I write this, Ghost Reveries has been reviewed and rated 177 times and the average rating is 4.5 stars. So, there's not much I can say that hasn't already been said.

In short, it is extreme music at its most brilliant. I really hate tossing around the word "brilliant" even though I use it frequently. But "brilliant" doesn't even begin to describe Ghost Reveries.

The opening song, "Ghost of Perdition", is so powerful and innovative I would buy this CD if it were the only song on the entire album. It's over 10 minutes long and it is well worth a dollar a minute.

There are few heavy bands that have a unique sound and a unique style. Opeth is one-of-a-kind. There's no band on the planet that even comes to Opeth as far as marrying harsh, roaring death metal elements with beautiful, inspired acoustic melodies so effortlessly and seamlessly.

It is truly ground-breaking music. If you are someone who can listen to a Lamb of God CD and immediately after pop in a Mazzy Star CD, then you owe it to yourself to buy Ghost Reveries and every other Opeth disc.

I thought Opeth hit their creative peak with "Damnation". "Ghost Reveries" shows their creative abilities knows no boundaries. I am truly in awe. Un-be-liev-a-ble.

Pay no attention to those critics behind the cathode ray curtain who lament all evolutionary influence. Sure, at times these Llamas do sound a bit like Brian Wilson or Steely Dan. Everything - including music - is  evolutionary - reguardless of your perticular genius. This music surely  stands on it's own. Things get off to a bright start with  the acoustic  guitar and banjo of "Bach ZE", with just enough strings to warm  and soothe. Not only will you not tire of "Harper's Romo", but  you will likely join in with your own improvised melody. "Hoops"  is probably best appreciated while driving through a very slow carwash  (you'll see). "Cookies" is a tasty, casual Euro-Pop ditty with  generous portions of signature "Ba-ba-Bahh" harmonies, followed  by an agreeable "Triads" containing some nice rythmic and  instrumentational foils. Be patient with "American Scene",  "Montecito", "Janet Jangle" and "Amin".  Although they don't surprise, they will delight.
The 45 seconds of  "Daltons Star" is really enough. With all of it's  Baldamenti-isms, "Cotton to the Bell" could have been a more  memorable theme song for Lynch's Twin Peaks. "Green Coaster" is  just plain perfect pop with great ensemble playing and singing. The pure  beauty and deceivably complex layers of "Cut the Dummy Loose"  make it one of the prettiest and most unforgettable songs the Llamas have  ever done. This is one chance you should take. It sounds damn good in the  morning - and nightime too!

reviewText:
The Beethoven and Brahms violin concertos are the two pinnacles of the violin concerto repertoire, and Nathan Milstein is many a violinist's violinist, so it's hard to ignore this CD.  Throw in that these are the finest of Milstein's several recordings of these two classic works, both exceptional accounts of the artist at his peak in the mid-1950s, skillfully remastered in 2001 by Angel/EMI at Abbey Road Studios using state-of-art "noise-shaping" technology, and you end up with a desert-island CD.
There are other reasons to have this recording.  Milstein and conductor William Steinberg collaborate magnificently with the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra in the acoustically rich setting of Pittsburgh's Syria Mosque to produce a masterpiece.  It is technically superb and artistically inspired.  Milstein's cadenzas on these classics are reason enough to have this recording.  That it is available in the affordable mid-price range is a bonus.  This is about as good as it gets.

reviewText: I think the highest compliment I can pay to Candiria is that they take hardcore, extreme metal, jazz, hip-hop, and progressive rock sounds, throw them all together, and make it sound completely natural.  Candiria have an originality and eclecticism that never comes across as forced or pretentious.  They're just thoroughly committed to exploring the stylistic and technical possibilities of heavy music, and I for one think they're exactly the band to do it.  "300 Percent Density" is the latest, and arguably greatest, example of Candiria's almost unparalleled songwriting and musicianship.  Candiria have a knack for composing songs that have creative and irregular time signatures, but are still highly listenable.  Their riffing and drumming may well be the heaviest this side of death metal, and the precision of the attack is mind-blowing.  This isn't just a band out to steamroll the listener with their heaviness; Candiria manage to create some very complex and interesting song structures that put virtually every band on the radio to shame.  Vocalist Carley Coma, apparently in an effort to push the human voice as far as it will go, spits out his growled vocals with a flow that most rappers would envy (or at least they should).  The band does also do a couple of rap songs on this album, but even for a non-rap fan like me they have some appeal.  Candiria's rap songs bear somewhat of a resemblance to those of A Tribe Called Quest, whose sense of musicality made them one of the few rap acts I could listen to, and they provide a nice break from all the heaviness.  I really have to wonder about the people giving this album negative reviews.  I understand and respect the opinions of others, but I think with a little close listening the greatness and uniqueness of Candiria becomes apparent pretty quickly.  I find "300 Percent Density" to be an album of the highest quality, and I highly recommend it.

reviewText:
"Sinatra at the Sands," recorded in April 1966, was the first Frank Sinatra concert to be released commercially.  Sinatra is singing with Count Basie and his Orchestra, which was conducted by Quincy Jones.  As you would expect, this is classic Sixties Sinatra, putting on a show for the Las Vegas crowd performing the songs you would expect the man to sing, starting big with "Come Fly With Me" and finishing even bigger with "My Kind of Town."  The best of these tracks are "I've Got You Under My Skin" and "Come Fly With Me," where the arrangements for the Basie Orchestra are arguably an actual improvement over the original recordings.  However, when Sinatra goes to his repetoire of saloon songs the results are more mixed; after all, he is singing in a really big room.  One of my all time Sinatra favorites, "It Was a Very Good Year" is a bit disappointing for me, but this is offset by his performance of "Angel Eyes."
Sinatra's between song banter displays the expected level of charm, although the mavens of political correctness will wince several times while listening to some of the jokes in his rather long monologue.  "Sinatra at the Sands" offers up almost an hour of live singing from Ol' Blue Eyes, once you subtract the talking, and shows that there are a few songs (e.g., "Luck Be a Lady Tonight") that you might actually prefer to hear Sinatra sing live.  Final Note on Album Notes: The album notes by Stan Cornyn won the 1966 Grammy for Album Notes, his second year in a row for winning that award for a Sinatra album (See: "September of My Years").  Do they still give out that particular Grammy?  Anyhow, I was vasilating between 4 and 5 stars for this review, but those album notes tip the scale up for sure.

reviewText:
What is it about Il Trovatore that divides opera lovers?  Oh yes, I keep hearing that nonsense about the illogical plot scenario and the fact that you need four phenomenally fine singing actors for the principal roles.  Well, I'm not going to argue about the latter, because you do need four great singers to fulfill Verdi's requirements.  The plot?  Get over it and just luxuriate in the genius of Verdi.  My quibble with this masterwork is that for far too long the role of Leonora has been sung by sopranos ill equipped for the requirements of this most central role in post Bellini and Donizetti bel canto oeuvre, which basically all Verdi was.
I was raised listening to this work with the Price 1972 RCA recording...thought it was beautiful...then I discovered the 1956 Callas take on it and I felt as if I was  listening to this work anew.......never before hearing any of these trills and delicate embellishments.......never heard such a vocally flexible Leonora as this....stunning hues of delicacy, power and good taste..... like I was listening to a Violetta voice in the role.....
Well, that's when it dawned on me that this role SHOULD be sung by a Violetta...and that's been my problem with this most special and spectacular of operas....not the plot and getting the four greatest singers....but that the role of Leonora has been abused and not sung properly for much, if not all of the 20th century.  This is not Aida, let alone verismo.
This is a most marvelous recording of this work, and Callas is supreme in this role and this recording.  Bel canto at its definitive definition is her interpretation of Leonora.....yes, the previous live recordings find her more vocally athletic....throwing out high, unwritten interpolations.....but here, she's completely at one with the role....singing and acting with complete elegance, finesse, and impeccable bel canto soul and technique......
....I don't believe in desert island mentality, but this is my choice Trovatore to take with me!!!

reviewText:
Until roughly a week ago while attending my aunts wedding I knew nothing about Florence + The Machine. It wasn't until the daughter of the groom played some of this album for me did I know. And I must admit I was pretty captivated by the sound of everything right off. But it didn't hit me until actually sitting down and taking the entire album in did I realize how important this album is right now. As far as I could see,we were living in a rather non musical culture at the turn of the new millennium. It's either existed purely for entertainment or as an expression of some variety of angst for the most part. In a sense that's been a positive force: it's allowed the the individual artists to stand out more because there isn't a lot of "competition",frankly. And that's not a word I enjoy using in reference to music. Lead by singer/songwriter Florence Welch this quartet has done something very important perhaps without even realizing it. And that's free pop music from the NEED to be free.  What they do flows very organically.

  What they do now is a little harder to explain. This albums rhythms don't come from a conventional rock n roll standpoint at all. In fact the drums rolls and thuds have a strong world beat fusion quality about them. Melodically this album is just as strong-with a mixture of styles ranging from tribal dance,soul,1980's dance music and baroque pop. Not since Rufus Wainright emerged with his debut in the late 90's have I heard such a big,melodic and diversified whole of music in one album. "Only If For A Night","What The Water Gave Me","Never Let Me Go","No Light,No Light","Seven Devils","All This And Heaven Too" and "Leave My Body" dig right into the bigness their sound provides and doesn't let go. Of course Florence's soulful chant of a vocal instrument almost adds three other musicians alone,metaphorically. These songs are deeply romantic styled poetry-with a lot of spiritual overtones in it's outlook on life,death and speculation on the nature of both.

  "Shake It Out" of course makes the most use of the wildly rhythmic sound of the album. "Never Let Me Go" is one of my favorites with it's orchestral pop sound of Jeff Lynne meets Bruce Springsteen. On "Lover To Lover" it's out and out uptempo,grooving soul. Again with that big production and musical back round. Another favorite of mine is "Spectrum",a well produced and lightly electronic 80's style boogie dance/funk type number. Even for that,this is definitely music made by and for human beings. Humans making music. And humans doing so with a strong and deeply passionate personality.  While I've seen people such as Bjork and others strive most of their careers for a sound like this,it's still easy to get lost in eccentricity. Somehow these Londoners manage to avoid that situation by consistently speaking directly AND poetically to those listening to their music. Already with this two albums into their career,Florence + The Machine have a long and very successful musical life ahead of them.

After the success of the Phil Ramone produced "A Star Is Born" soundtrack, not to mention the Richard Perry productions from the early 1970's, the proof was evident that Ms. Streisand was now a soft rock star.  This album shows it in every way and then some.  From "Evergreen" as the first song on side 1 and "The Way We Were" as the first song on side 2, we know there was a different groove from the Broadway scene.  Yet, if you think these treasures were too soft, wait until you hear the rest of the magic.

"Prisoner" from Jon Peters' The Eyes of Laura Mars is so powerful in structure, that you wish this was the song that had constant radio play.  Without a doubt, this was producer Gary Klein's shining moment.  "My Heart Belongs To Me" and "Songbird" are in the same semi-tone as "Evergreen", but the former is just as good as that song itself.

However, the real "killer" on the record is "Sweet Inspiration/Where You Lead".  This was before "A Star Is Born" and it purely showed Barbra as the new rocker of the times.  Yet, I am not forgetting Gene Page's arrangement of "Stoney End" (produced by Richard Perry). Streisand can always hold her own, which was the proof here.

Each song was picked out perfectly, with the awesome "Superman" appearing here as part of the final.  "Stoney End" is the final, and with "Superman" preceding it, I call the pair of songs "SS".  They make you want to jog 1 mile and 1/2.

As for the artwork, it is her best cover yet, simple but touching, from the flawless photographer Francesco Scavullo, who also photographed "A Star Is Born".  Actually, it appears this was shot during the ASIB sessions when she was going to sing "Evergreen".  Great judgement again by Jon Peters on the artwork.

Thanks for reading my friends, Joseph

reviewText:
Such a wonderful recording!  Mozart's symphonies, each of them its own jewel, must be handled lightly by modern orchestras.  I don't know whether this orchestra is using authentic instruments from the era, or simply playing modern instruments in a more traditional, eighteenth-century manner, but the effect is so light and lyrical that I find myself falling in love with what I have always considered one of the least interesting musical eras.

I've never doubted Mozart's genius for a second, nor have I ever doubted Mackerras's interpretive ability, but the Classical era as a whole has never held my attention for long.  Perhaps the thinner texture of the strings and the punctuation of the brass on this recording were enough to arouse my curiosity.

Here, Mackerras and the Scottish Chamber Orchestra demonstrate a finely-rendered mastery of the last of Mozart's symphonies.  These performances aren't just faithful and technically sound.  The music is revitalized and transcendent.  You can hear the composer working out the whole of the work from start to finish in his head, as he supposedly actually did.  The musicians deserve high praise for what they've accomplished here, and this recording deserves to be in your collection.

reviewText:
I'm not sure how this session, recorded in 1969, was not released until recently.  I can see only two possibilties.  First, other than Hill, there aren't a lot of big name players here--Woody Shaw on trumpet is the most prominent--which may have led to concerns about marketing the album.  Second, the compositions are significantly less avant garde than other Hill recordings, so maybe Blue note felt like it would not appeal to Hill's more sonically adventurous fan base.

As the other reviewers have said, those making the decision at Blue note were clearly wrong.  As is common in his 60s sessions, Hill leads a rather large group of musicians--a nonet, in this case--that includes such uncommon jazz instruments as tuba and French horn.  This large group allows Hill to layer rhythms and harmonies in a variety of interesting and diverse ways.  However, for Hill, this is notably more straight ahead stuff than was typical of his output in the late 60s.  While retaining all of the qualities that are inimitably his, Hill sounds as close to Herbie Hancock's early 60s Blue Note material than he has befor or since(and Hill and Hancock do not usually sound very similar to me).  The track "Passing Ships" sounds a lot like Hancock's "Speak Like a Child" (one of my all time favorite tunes).

The playing here is uniformly excellent.  Hill's rhythms are brilliant as always and the playing of the other musicians is uniformly excellent--emotionally resonant and delivered with the incredible precision required to blend such a wide variety of notes and timbres.  The solos--mostly on trumpet, tenor, and flute--are all elegant (especially Joe Farrell's tenor solos!) and the interplay between the musicians is exciting to hear throughout.  In addition, the sound quality here is phenomenal, as it is possible to clearly differentiate between all of the instruments, even when they play together.  This is highly recommended not just to Hill fans, but also to beginning jazz fans and even those who may have been turned off by some of Hill's more avant garde recordings.
