reviewText: The Maitines para Nuestra Seora de Guadalupe, by Ignacio de Jerusalm, receives on this recording its first performance since two hundred years ago. Music lovers must be very thankful to Chanticleer for their interest in reviving works from the Mexican Baroque. Matins (a religious service that was performed in the Roman Catholic Church in the early hours of the morning)were a vehicle for composers in the New Spain to showcase their skill using texts of different moods. These Matins in particular, for the feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe, bear ressemblance to the early Catholic works by Handel, where a capella chant was alternated with elaborate solo and choral movements with orchestra. Jerusalem, an Italian composer established in Mexico by 1742, borrowed music from other composers for his services: Beatam me dicent omnes is by Giacomo Rust and there are two wonderful works by Manuel de Sumaya. These two pieces, "Albricias mortales" and "Anglicas milicias" are in my opinion, the most interesting works of the CD. With their poetic Spanish texts and baroque polyphony, they illustrate the situation of Latin America during that period: great European influence with a new conscience of being part of another new reality, something similar to the literary work of the great Sor Juana Ins de la Cruz. The choral and orchestral forces of Chanticleer perform with such beauty and expression that it is difficult that even Jerusalem could have imagined that this work could sound so great. I hope Chanticleer continue to revive great works from Latin America.

reviewText: The reviewer below me feels that he hasn't gotten enough and has been ripped off.  Well, if you're looking for the Beach Boys Greatest Hits Volume 1 and 2, um, buy those albums instead.  Anyone that looks over the  tracks before he purchases would have known that this isnt' it.  But in a  way, to the more serious fan of the group (and you're invited, casual fans,  all it takes is one listen to Pet Sounds) it is!  Instead of feeling empty,  you'll be wanting more, more, more.  The influence of the Beach Boys is  shown here, whether it is the 'unfortunate' influence on the throwaway pop  of the day (check out the concert medley, something very few bands pull off  today but countless teenyboppers attempt) or the trancey shadow that  "Til I Die" casts over the 1990's more advanced rockers.  (The  first song on Spritualized's 'Ladies and Gentlemen" album is great,  but it can't hold a candle to this gem).  While so many releases and  reviews are dedicated to endlessly reaffirming Brian's genius (and this  collection once again does its job in this department), Endless Harmony  also dispells the myth that the Beach Boys were compromised of 1 genius and  4/5 also rans.  Al's lead vocal on 'Help Me Rhonda' was about as honest as  pop music could get in 1965, his 30 year Loop production shows that he  learned something in all those years of studio work, and that he isn't such  a slouch after all.  Before it all went wrong, Mike and Bruce's campy songs  (Endless Harmony and Brian's Back) at the very least show that at the start  the descent into parody wasn't such a bad idea, at the best they offer a  knowing wink to historians of the band.  Dennis comes into his own (though  sadly, on only two songs and only one of his own) on this collection, it  should whet the appetite for the Brother re-releases on which he plays a  much larger part.  Carl's vocals and contributions make new  "soul" artists like Eric Benet sound like English skiffle  players.  In summary, a brilliant collection, and very frustrating too-why  not 10 discs instead of only 1?

I've been wanting to delve further into their catologue of music for quite some time now but I always feared nothing would live up to my rather high expectations. This, however, has proven me wrong! "Nemo" is the first single for their upcoming album, 'Once', and while it's a teaser that makes you want to hear more, it's full of promising material. Tarja's voice is as gorgeous as ever and the music here is simply amazing! "Planet Hell" starts out with dramatic choral singing that eventually leads into some heavy progressive rock beats with both male and female vocals. The real highlight for me, though, would have to be the exclusive "White Night Fantasy", which is essential for Nightwish fans who particularly love their passionate ballads. It's a beautiful song with sweet, soaring vocals and it's a non-album track so fans must get this, if only for that! Also, I noticed there to be a lot more orchestration than usual here which adds a really nice touch to the melodies. There's even an orchestral version of "Nemo" that substitutes the pounding guitars and drums for lush strings instead. I especially appreciate how the lyrics for "Nemo" and "Planet Hell" are included for that's a rare thing to find in singles.

If this was meant to entice listeners to check out their new album than it has been a success! I'm dying to hear 'Once' now...

And once again, Maria Callas proves me wrong.  Her interpretation of the fragile Cio-Cio San is admirable, if not amazing.  The vocal shades she uses to create her own Butterfly is simply unmatched by the whole shebang of great Butterflies out there, and this can be heard if you were to compare her Madama Butterfly to that of Freni or Tebaldi or another one of the standard Butterflies.  Her childish tone is brought out in this recording, and one can once again witness Callas' mastery of bel canto when her voice changes colors from the young naive geisha to the mature tragedienne that she transforms into at the end of the opera.  Her "Che tua Madre" is simply the best I've heard in years, and Un Bel di is beautifully sung, always imparts a sense of hope as the fragile Butterfly waits for her beloved Pinkerton.  At the end of the opera, her remorse, anguish, pain, and pride is released and the true Callas emerges as she breaks into Butterfly's death aria, "Tu, tu piccolo iddio...", and it is at this point that Callas becomes the mature woman that Butterfly realizes to be.  This isn't a recording to be missed.  Nicolai Gedda proves to be a most satisfying Pinkerton, and he is Callas' equal when it comes to this part.  Listen to his Addio fiorito assai, and Lucia Danelli, who appeared in Callas' Gioconda, defies the meaning of small role when she sings as Suzuki.  Herbert von Karajan provides one of the most heartfelt conducting of Butterfly, and his manipulating of the orchestra here is miles better than the recording he made with Freni and Pavarotti for Decca.  Do not miss out on this one.

reviewText:
Okay, "Master of Puppets" is a songwriting masterpiece, as are "Ride the Lightning" and "...And Justice for All." These are all incredible albums that bridge the gap between hardcore thrash and progressive musicianship. However, there is only one Metallica album of the big four (the first four albums...I don't consider the "Black" album to be all that great) that I can listen to without skipping tracks, and that is their first..."Kill 'Em All." This is the only Metallica album I listen to front to back, never skipping a song, and never getting tired of it. This is thrash at its purest and the band at their best. Maybe youth had something to do with it, but the first album captures a fire in the hearts of the members that they just spent the rest of their career grimly trying to hold on to. Every song is a thrash classic.
-"Hit the Lights": this song hits hard and fast to start the album off right and pounding away.
-"The Four Horseman": one of few songs on this album that cling to the days when Megadeth's Dave Mustaine was still in the band. "Mechanix" off Megadeth's debut was the original, faster version of this song. Metallica's rewrite however showcases what was to come in terms of their progressive styling coupled with Kirk Hammett's unforgettable solos. My favorite Metallica song PERIOD!!!
-"Motorbreath": thrash in its rawest form. This is the most punk Metallica have ever gotten, and the song echoes the sound of their biggest influence Motorhead, both in the title and in the music. A furious song...but alas, it's the shortest song on the album.
-"Jump in the Fire": another Mustaine song. The riff to this song is infectious, and not without an element of humor. It brings to mind images of a monstrous figure creeping up on you from behind, chasing you.
-"Pulling Teeth (Anesthesia)": the late great Cliff Burton showing off why he was one of the greatest bassists to have ever lived. He plays the bass like a lead guitar on this track, and it is a glorious testament to his ability as a great musician.
-"Whiplash": another thrasher that shows Metallica celebrating their hardcore lifestyle. Great chorus too.
-"The Phantom Lord": this one is a bit creepy, probably because of the eerie intro. Like "Jump in the Fire," it makes one think of evil demons, something of the sort. This works well with the lyrics and the overall title of the song.
-"No Remorse": what can one say? It's another great thrasher with all the hints towards progressive that the band would soon be revelling in.
-"Seek and Destroy": any Metallica fan should know the riff to this song. It's a classic, and from what I hear, it's the song with the solo Kirk Hammett had to nail to win the audition after Dave Mustaine was given the boot.
-"Metal Militia": well...who will argue James Hetfield ain't a redneck at heart? Jokes aside, this closes off the album nicely, as fast and as furious as the rest of the album, and ending with the sound of marching stomps.
Some might say the album gets repetitive. This may be true, but what can you expect from thrash? There's never a slow moment. The music just beckons the listener to bang his head for as long, hard, and fast as they possibly can. Like the lyrics to "Whiplash," "Make it bleed, make it really sore." This whole album is a thrash masterpiece...it's consistent, but never boring. For these reasons (and because I'm also a Megadeth fan and this album has some of Mustaine's songwriting in there), this is my favorite Metallica album!!!

reviewText: Coming off the beloved major debut album of 'Gordon,' BNL fans were expecting yet again, another funny album.  An album that made little sense except the fact that it's funny!  Well, BNL certainly surprised their fans  with 'Maybe You Should Drive.'  This has got to be my personal favorite BNL  album.  The songs have meaningful lyrics, and a tone that BNL has never  used in any of their albums since.  Maybe that is why true BNL fans really  love this album.  The sincerity really shines through on this album.  The  opening track, "Jane," similar to "Enid" on 'Gordon,'  is a song describing Jane, and how she can't open up to guys.  The humorous  note is when the listener hears the lyric that states he discovered Jane  while shoplifting form the store.  "Intermittently" sounds like a  1960s British swingers anthem.  It describes the mental status of how  people can love each other off and on.  "Intermittently" might be  Darryl Strawberry's favorite BNL song, who knows?  Maybe the song off  'Maybe You Should Drive' most like anything off 'Gordon' is "These  Apples."  At first listen, the song seems to be senseless, at best.  Yet each time you listen to it, you can hear that BNL really spent some  time on these lyrics.  The song is a true masterpiece of BNL, and still one  of my most beloved BNL songs.  The next track, "You Will Be  Waiting," is a song that anyone can hear is a song with a lot of  emotional attachment to it.  I believe that BNL wanted to prove to its fans  that it could write serious songs with emotional feelings tied in.  After  the emotional "You Will Be Waiting," the album kicks right into a  cunning "A." It goes through many words beginning with the letter  "a," and talks of a girlfriend being extremely upset with her  boyfriend (the singer).  Even the title, "Everything Old Is New  Again," is an oxymoron.  It could be that the whole song is an  oxymoron, but I beg to differ.  It talks of children in their mothers'  cars, with an expressionless face.  I think it talks of the old wanted to  be young, and the young wanting to be old.  Now I really like the song  "Alternative Girlfriend," although not one of the more popular  singles by BNL, the song is rich and fertile in lyrics.  Usually by track 8  on an album, you would expect to start to run into fillers.  But that is  not the case on 'Maybe You Should Drive.'  "Am I The Only One?"  is a great song!  It talks of being a stranger everywhere you go.  "Life, In A Nutshell" mocks the "The Brady Bunch  Lifestyle."  It talk of always being happy, and never running into any  problems in life.  The last outstanding track on the album has got to be  "The Wrong Man Was Convicted."  It talks of an over used tale of  a man dying for a crime he did not commit.  Although BNL seems to revive  the sharp idea with this song.

reviewText:
BNL's debut album, Gordon, was an amazingly well-crafted pop album with each song striking a brilliant chord. Follow-up albums have been hit-and-miss, where the strong tracks have been fantastic (Stunt's "One Week" and "It's All Been Done" come to mind), but they stand out all the more because they are surrounded by weak filler. Maroon marks a return to form; each single is pure pop that combines the best elements of music we already know and love and produces a result that is something unique.
Just as the Beatles were obviously influenced by Chuck Berry and Buddy Holly and Elvis -- and yet, they produced a new sound that is all their own -- BNL has managed to take influences like the Beatles, XTC, and others to create fun new tunes with crafty lyrics. "Go Home" is a stand-out track with a Beatle's guitar riff (from "I'm Looking Through You") and a Jellyfish-esque chorus ("Baby's Coming Back") that is up-beat and twangy... even with it's pseudo-serious subject matter ("don't cheat on your wife, bud."). "Conventioneers" is a great lounge tune, while "Sell, Sell, Sell" is a cha-cha poke at modern-day commercialism. This last tune is a particular treat to fans of Gordon; it has the same bouncy feel and expert lyrics.
Wallflowers fans will enjoy the track "Baby Seat" with it's excellent backbeat, while "Tonight is the Night I Fell Asleep at the Wheel" evokes the best of Billy Joel and Elvis Costello and XTC... combined.
BNL is a pop band; I don't want to give the impression that all of their work sounds derivative. But, after all, the best pop bands *are* derivative to some degree. The trick is to make what you do sound fresh. This is where BNL excels. After a couple of hit-and-miss studio albums (and one excellent concert release), I can finally look forward again to more great releases from the band.

reviewText: I listened to Radiohead in the "reverse order" so to speak, starting with Kid A, ending with Pablo Honey. Pablo Honey is their only weak album, and quite frankly I hated it, but this isn't a review of Pablo Honey... When I first got Kid A, it took me a lot of listens to even figure it out, I mean, I was exremely intrigued by this almost montrous recording, but I couldn't put my finger on exactly what made it work. Maybe it was because I had virtually no previous experience with Radiohead, Aphex Twin, or Boards of Canada ,(PS, check out Boards of Canada, they are fantastic) but it took me a while to get into it. Amnesiac is an extremely difficult album to those who only previous experience in music are Limp Bizkit or O-Town. But to those who are music afficionados, and got all the obscure band references from High Fidelity , this album is for you. Although as all radiohead records need to played as a whole, here is a little review track by track. 1) Pakt like Sardines in a Crushd Tin Box: Thom gives the impression of a paranoid, whithered old man, sulking into the corner of a dimly lit room, with his contant repeating of "I'm a reasonable man/get off my case." Not as of great of an opening track as "Everything in it's right place", but still good. 2) Pyramid Song: The album's first single and easily is seen why. The most accessible track. A constant repeating piano melody gives the sense of doom, while the strings make you feel like you are lost at sea. Fantastic. 3) Pull/Pulk Revolving Doors: Scary to fall asleep to. The random sputtering of the lyrics from what sounds like a broken down robot gives you the sense of falling through door after door until your death. 4) You and Whose Army? One of my favorite tracks. Thom's voice is utilized to the full extent, breathing life into the lyrics. His voice is so frightened, so upset, it sounds like a scared, shaking individual who is shouting out random babbelings at unknown adversaries. 5) I Might be Wrong: Blues-y, sounds almost like a normal band!(wow!) The kind-of-rock track on the record. 6) Knives out: Frightening Lyrics that suggest an unwarranted murder, without any mercy. Imagine an insane person calling for an execution, and shouting to all his friends "so...knives out!!!" as they take them out of their pockets and go in for the kill. 7) Morning Bell/Amnesiac: Same morning bell from Kid A, only with dissonant live instruments, like someone a thousand years in the future, who is extremely distraught, trying to cover the Kid a version. 8) Dollars and Cents: Another one of my favorite tracks: The main character seems to have a beyond obsession with money, an almost evil love of it. Thom shouts "All of the dollars and cents" repeatedly while on another vocal track, he mutters under his breath "We are going to CRACK your little souls" 9) Hunting Bears: instrumental, all guitars. I haven't really gotten an image out of it, like I did with Treefingers. Maybe it will just take more time. 10) Like Spinning Plates: My second favorite track. a whirring techno sound makes me imagine the character in a dark futuristic city, with towers that have spinning plates on top, as the character jumps in the "muddy river" and tries to float away from this society he hates so much. I personally think they perfect the whole soundscape idea on this song. 11) Life in a Glass House: My favorite track. Uses aleatoric jazz elements not unlike from "The National Anthem." Gives the impression that the paranoid/skitzophrenic character believes everyone can see through the walls of his house, as he hides his head in the corner of the damp basement, with his head exploding from all the images and thoughts contained in his brain. His memory cannot take anymore. Five Stars.

reviewText:
Kate Royal seems to quietly have it all - a voice of great beauty over a broad range, musicality, intelligence, communication skills, physical beauty and stage presence, and taste!  For those who have heard these attributes blossoming in her first recordings (a very fine recital with Edward Gardner conducting the Academy of St. Martin in the Fields and in the chamber orchestra version of the Mahler 4th with the Manchester Camerata conducted by Douglas Boyd), this recording will come as no surprise.  Royal not only is in fine voice for this very interesting collection of songs referencing the spell of Midsummer Night, but she also adds excerpts from operas - arias rarely taken out of context (Hermann's 'Wuthering Heights', Alwyn's 'Miss Julie', and three Britten arias that are not the usual selections chosen by sopranos for recital.

Royal combines beauty of tone with involvement in the text (her enunciation is close to perfect).  She shares some well known arias such as the Dvorak's 'Song to the Moon' and Korngold's 'Marietta's Lied' on the same level of commitment as she offers some rarely performed works.  For this listener one of the most successful songs on this generous album is the 'How beautiful it is' from Britten's 'Turn of the Screw'.  How often do we hear the wondrous orchestral introduction to this aria?

Edward Gardner conducts the Orchestra of English National Opera and the Crouch End Festival Chorus and is a sensitive collaborator.  Kate Royal is becoming one of our more important soprano artists of the time.  Now is her time.  Grady Harp, June 09

This is the CD to put all others to shame. In my humble opinion, that is.
Nothing calms your frazzled nerves, lift your spirits and takes you away quite like Enigma Mxmxc a. D. can.

I have yet to find anyone with the skills that Michael Cretu possesses. I have been enjoying Enigma for 23 years. In those years, I have listened to others. While beautiful in their own right, it still doesn't quite reach the brilliance of Cretu's style.  I see him as the true pioneer that others have tried to follow but haven't quite found the recipe as Cretu has. He mixes music from different genres, countries and cultures with sultry sounds, thought provoking lyrics in different languages and Gregorian chants like a true musical alchemist.  His music has managed to break the boundries in order to create his own genre. Not New Age, Rock, Spiritual or Classical but a combination of sounds, voices and lyrics that pull in bits and pieces of these genres into a truly seamless and unique sound.  Each song melts into another without breaking rhythm so the CD ends up sounding like it's playing just one complete song.

This 23 year old CD manages to stay high in the rankings which should indicate at what kind of musical genius Cretu is. As of today, 7/24/13, it is #1 in World Dance.

This CD starts with 'The Voice of Enigma', a kind of prologue to the rest of the 'story'.  Already, we are given an idea of what to expect from this album. "Turn off the lights, take a deep breath and relax".  Exactly.

'Principles of Lust: Sadeness/Find Love/Sadeness (Reprise) (Medley)' contains some of the most beautiful chants in Latin, highly erotic sound of whispers, sensual beats and French lyrics sung with amazing vocal ability. 'Sadeness': This song refers to the Marquis de Sade, a Frenchman who thought that sex had to be painful if it was to be pleasurable. Hence the term 'Sadism'.  Lyrics:  "Sade dit moi pourquoi le sang pour le plaisir ?  Le plaisir sans l'amour.  N'y a t'il plus de sentiment dans le culte de l'homme?  Sade tell me why blood for pleasure?  Pleasure without love.  There is no longer any sense in the cult of man?"

"Sade dis moi, qu'est ce que tu vas chercher ? Le bien par le mal,  Sade dit moi pourquoi l' 'evangile du mal ? Quelle est ta religion ou` sont tes fide`les?  Si tu es contre Dieu, tu es contre l'homme."  "Sade. tell me, what do you seek?  Good with evil, the virtue of vice.  Sade tell my why the Gospel of evil?  What is your religion?  Where are your faithful?  If you are against God, you are against man."

Given the words, Sade could also be seen as the devil.  The mix of good and evil; virtue, which is a moral excellence; vice, which is immoral wickedness.  What is he looking for?  Does he think that giving pleasure in the name of virtue is acceptable?  He wonders how 'Sade' can give pleasure or give someone joy, yet be against God.  It's a struggle to fight temptation because it is around us every day.

'Callas Went Away' is about an American born soprano named Maria Callas.

'Mea Culpa',  'An acknowledgment of one's fault or error.'  I'm guilty.  I think she feels guilt because she has given herself over fully to her desires and fantasies.  She asks Christ for mercy.  She feels like she is going crazy for letting herself go  la fin de ses fantasmes--to the end of her fantasies.  She knows it's forbidden but the temptation is very powerful.

'The Voice and the Snake'. This is based upon 'Revelations' from the Bible. Each sentence is a clear link to each angel and their trumpet and what will happen after each one sounds. "The Earth turned grey". Read Revelations 8:7.  And so on.  This is the one and only song that gives me chills.  It's about how the world will end and this song definitely has a bone chilling sound.
Cretu: 'And when the Lamb opened the 7th seal, silence covered the sky'.  Revelations 8:1 "And when he had opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven about the space of half an hour".

I'm not a Sinatra fan, but this is one of the very best CDs I own. I've listened to it since I was 17 and bargained for it at a Roman flea market...no Sinatra recording I've heard since has topped it. It's sublime. The Nelson Riddle arrangements are extraordinary, lush, and achingly sad...the instruments seem to be sighing and weeping at times.
Sinatra is perfection in this one...if you're in a downhearted mood, he'll take you to the depths, and perhaps to a good healing cry...these songs about lost love are here sung at the slowest tempi, with every word given the intensity of its full meaning.
Recorded in '58, the remastered sound is excellent, and the CD includes 2 songs that weren't in the original LP, but were recorded in the same year, "Sleep Warm", and "Where or When". In my opinion, this is a real case of "less is more", as the mood of these 2 songs is slightly different...they should have left it ending with the heartbreaking "One for my Baby".
One of my favorite songs ever written is "Angel Eyes" and strangely, considering its loveliness, not that many recordings have been made of it, and here's the rendition that's hard to top...the entire CD is full of "definitive versions", and it's probably one the most melancholy ever made too...and at the same time, so exquisitely beautiful.

reviewText: "The Virgin's Lament" is some of the most beautiful Irish traditional and modern music ever heard. It is largely 'a capela' and shows the full range of the human voice. Most of the singing is by a lady in ancient Irish Gaelic. The songs are very beautiful, pure sounding, spiritually moving (even if you don't speak Gaelic), and sorrowful and uplifting at the same time. Definitely good music for meditation, healing, relaxing, Christmas (Yule), Easter (Ostara). The music and language seem to bridge the gap between ancient Irish culture and the takeover of Ireland by the Romans, and the imposition of the Christian religion over the religion of the triple Goddess Brighid - she of the smith's forge, grain, and poetry. Listening to the music, it's not hard to feel that the original traditional songs were in part inspired by (and possibly about) Brighid Herself.

reviewText: The biggest difference in the Symphony X sound is that on "Paradise Lost" they have gone straight Progressive Power Metal and have dumped the Neo-Classical side of their sound for a more in-your-face Metal approach.  However, they do incorporate symphonic arrangements and choirs in an exemplary, bombastic production sound.  From the Progressive Metal "Domination", the driving "Serpent's Kiss", or the absolutely gorgeous title track with its glorious chorus, there is something for everyone who wants something different from Symphony X.  Those wanting more of the Neo-Classical sound Symphony X actually helped create may be disappointed.  From what I can hear, having painted themselves into a corner with "The Odyssey", a change in direction was necessary for the band to remain vital.  "Paradise Lost" has the most creative guitar work I've heard so far; while some of their albums contain flashier guitar shredding, no other has this much variation in texture and style.  I've rated many of their past albums highly, but "Paradise Lost" is certainly the most interesting and creative excursion in their already impressive catalog.

The bands first single now begins. The song prooves to be intense, touching many people. The song became an instant hit. It's no surprise, because it kicks ...! Score 5/5

reviewText:
At long last, Mercury Records has seen fit to release a pretty comprehensive single disc anthology of one of America's all-time favorite groups.  From the very beginning the Statler Brothers did it their way.  In an era when many artists found it necessary to poke fun at the values and institutions that many Americans hold near and dear the Statler Brothers were a welcome alternative. They sang songs that told a story and the stories were often about our heroes, the communities  where we live and work, the loves of our lives and cherished memories of days gone by.  Some might find that a bit corny but the Statler Brothers struck a chord with many of us and were a consistent force in American popular music for nearly four decades.

Released in April 2005, "The Definitive Collection" features 25 of the Statler Brothers biggest and most memorable hit records. The remastering job is first rate and I was very pleased to discover that the original Columbia recording of the Lew Dewitt penned "Flowers On The Wall", the groups first big hit from 1965, is included here.  I also enjoyed the newly remastered versions of the early '70s hits "Do You Remember These?" and "Class of '57".  It was these two records that turned me on to the group and made me a fan for life.  While perusing the 12 page booklet you might be surprised to learn that with the exception of a handful of "oldies but goodies" that the group decided to cover, just about all of the other tunes were written by members of the group.  Enjoy Don Reid's handiwork on "Bed of Roses", "I'll Go To My Grave Loving You" and the 1984 smash "Atlanta Blue".  Don and Harold Reid collaborated on a number of hits including "I'll Be The One", "Do You Know You Are My Sunshine?" as well as the aforementioned "Do You Remember These?"  When long time member Lew Dewitt was forced to retire with painful Krohn's disease in 1982, the group tapped 25 year old Jimmy Fortune to fill the void.  It was a stroke of genius!  Jimmy was not only a talented vocalist, he was also a gifted and prolific songwriter.  In fact, several of the Statlers' biggest tunes were penned by Jimmy including "Elizabeth", "My Only Love", "Too Much On My Heart" and the moving "More Than A Name On A Wall" from 1989.

In the final analysis reviewer PD Harris is correct.  This is "not quite a definitive" collection.  After all, the group had a total of 66 charted hits on Billboard's "Top  Country Singles" chart.  At least 10-12 of their Top 10 hits are not included here. But I am not going to quibble about it.  Those who desire more can always grab the 3 disc "30th Anniversary" box set.  It seems to me that "The Definitive Collection" is the right choice for most collectors and fans of the group.  The music is timeless and eternally uplifting.  Very highly recommended!

reviewText:
J. Cole is probably the most skilled "new generation" Hip Hop artist we've had since Lupe Fiasco, and it's very rare for me to be a fan of a new rapper. J. Cole has been around for at least 3 years mainstream wise, but I've only been a real fan when he dropped his Friday Night Lights mixtape. Since then I've checked out his earlier material from The Warm Up mixtape (which I love). J. Cole is one of very few emcees to capture the essence of the lyrical conscience rappers and also have mainstream appeal which is what makes him very versatile.  In the age of club rap records, and declining quality in lyricism nowadays thanks to the crappy Lil Waynes and his Young Money camp who only care about punch lines, and stupid gimmicks of Lil B (Based God) who do stupid s*** just to get famous,  J. Cole finds a way to bring back REAL rapping and good storytelling to Hip Hop and keep it real being true to himself. J. Cole's voice contains raw emotion and you can feel it when you listen to his songs whether it be an aggressive anthem, a painful story about struggling troubled youth or even sensual cuts about his love for women, J. Cole can pretty much convey all these kinds of emotions with ease.

With all that positivity said, Cole is nowhere near perfect. J. Cole has the inability to make  catchy memorable hooks and when he sings, sometimes it can be disastrous, but sometimes it's a fresh air. Another flaw he has is his productions. In the past J. Cole's beats sound more a less the same and boring at times. His beats always seem to have the same ambiance and same 808 drum backdrops. BUT, J. Cole has come a long way since 3 years ago, he learned a few new tricks along the way and he clearly shows them on this album. This album shows the maturity of Cole as an artist and even if the flaws still reoccur at times, J. Cole picks up the pace and learned from his mistakes on this album.

1) Intro - Nice instrumentals that leads directly into Dollar and a Dream III

2) Dollar and A Dream III - The definitive track of the entire album. J. Cole goes in heart and soul of what his third Dollar and a Dream installment. J. Cole has come a long way and this track is a good example. His storytelling and witty lyrics goes perfectly with the production which keeps on building as the song goes on full of strings and a hard hitting base thanks to the clever sampling of Kingdom Hearts 2. Perfect introductory track. 10/10

3) Can't Get Enough feat. Trey Songz  - The thought of Trey and Cole did not seem very fitting to me for some reason, but once again J. Cole proved his versatility. This song is about girls in a more negative manner but clever lyrics and punch lines sells this record. Trey is a little bit out of his comfort zone which makes him sounds like he's talking rather than singing but it's very catchy. This song also heavily samples the song Paulette by Balla Et Ses Balladins which creates a nice African/island groove. Great commercial record. 10/10

4) Lights Please - For people that don't know, this song was actually released back 2009 on his mixtape The Warm Up. The reason why this song is on the album makes sense, but honestly it should have stayed on the Warm Up. This song is almost 3 years old, but don't get me wrong, the subject matter and overall message is universal and still an overal great song. I'm just going to knock off a point for being old. Sorry. 9/10

5) Interlude - A funny little interlude where J. Cole tells a story of when he was signed to Roc Nation and got arrested all in the same day. The track's beat leads directly into the next song.

6) Sideline Story - A great laidback song, where J. Cole raps about his position as of right now in the music industry. Not being the star player, J. Cole makes it known that he is working hard and doing everything he humanly can to show he is a star player and deserves to be known for it. The one thing I never liked about Cole up until this day is his singing voice when he does his hooks. It's admirable that he does everything entirely on his own, but as a singer his voice is a hit or miss depending on the beat. Luckily J. Cole saves himself by at least writing a good hook regardless of baritone sounding hook. 10/10

7) Mr.  Nice Watch feat. Jay-Z - J. Cole is known for emotion driven storytelling so whenever he shifts his styles it's really a weird transition. This song is a braggadocios song but J. Cole provides a sick bass cracking beat and J. Cole sounds hungry. This may not be his most memorable track nor does it really showcase Cole's lyrical ability, but I have a feeling I'm going to be hearing this track a lot in the near future as entrance songs at football and basketball games, this song goes hard. 8/10

9) In The Morning feat. Drake - Once again, J. Cole puts another song on the album from his old mixtapes, this time from his recent mixtape Friday Night Lights. This song in particular was actually what made J. Cole known in 2010. A lot of people (especially the girls) started to notice J. Cole more once this song came out and ever since, his group of fans dramatically increased. This is once again almost a 3 year old song, the original version only having J. Cole himself on the track without the addition of Drake, but in my opinion this version is the superior version, even if a lot hardcore fans dislike the Drake verse, I believe it adds an extra kick. Once again I'm going to knock a point off for being a little old. Sorry...again. 8.5/10

10) Lost Ones - J. Cole has a gift in the rap game and that is his storytelling. This song tells the dramatic story of a young couple consummating there love and one day finding that the girl is pregnant. The main conflict between the couple is whether they should have an abortion or not. The 1st verse has Cole taking the role of the man in the relationship, the 2nd verse Cole takes the role of the pregnant girl, and the 3rd verse Cole is the conscience contemplating on both decisions. It's a very deep song and deserves to be recognized. 10/10

11) Nobody's Perfect feat. Missy Elliott - Here is an example of Cole's potential of creating hit singles. This song has one of the best beats on the album. Yet another song that is primarily about women and about accepting people for who they are despite of how famous they are or not. Missy Elliot drops a nice hook (I forgot that she can sing) that is catchy and sensual. The problem with this song however is that it's way too short, J. Cole could have easily added another verse or at least extended his 2nd verse. What's up with that? It could have been a classic but it's just too short. 8/10

12) Never Told - While the majority of the production on this album is credited to J. Cole (13 out of 16 to be exact) it's nice to hear a different sound from a more established veteran producer. No I.D.  made his contribution to the album with this song and you can tell right away the difference between a good producer (J. Cole) and a great producer (No I.D.) . A great song about a young boy growing up and then later becoming a man. This song isn't as straight forward, but the message is there. 9/10

13) Rise and Shine - This is Young Simba in his rawest form. Letting everyone know that Cole has arrived and everybody better beware and get ready for him because this boy ain't stopping. Not much I can say about this song except if you're listening to this album and haven't been enlightened by this man's talent by the end of this song....then I'm sorry you don't love Hip Hop. The beat on this song just gets you soooo HYPE!!! 10/10

14) God's Gift - If I would have to pick a personal favorite from this album, it would probably be this song. This is the BEST song on the album and I will tell you why; there is no other song on this album that fully demonstrates Cole's talent than this one right here. In this song we have J. Cole's most intricate beat he has ever created, as well as him pulling off an almost perfect delivery in lyrics and also providing a well written hook. This is J. Cole at his best and fully shows what J. Cole is capable of. 10/10

15) Breakdown - The last song on the album is actually the most touching song on the album. After all the songs he has ever done in the past (this album and previous mixtapes), you rarely hear J. Cole let you inside his past life from his own personal perspective. All his songs in the past are based on what he has seen and been through or him telling a story with him speaking in 3rd person, but this song is the first where he talks about his family. This song is the first time I heard J. Cole be vulnerable, speaking about his opinions about his dad who hasn't been around as often, as well as his mother which we rarely hear about in his songs and also his thoughts about past friends. This kind of vulnerability is really heartwarming if you know what J. Cole is about and a nice way to end the album 10/10

16  Bonus Track) Work Out - Besides Who Dat which was known to be the street single of Cole World first incarnation, this song was the first official single. At first listen, this song did not impress me whatsoever; his lyrics were mediocre and very mainstream, and the beat left a lot to be desired with the Kanye West sample. But as time went on, this song grew on me, but this song is aimed towards the ladies which makes it to get into unless you're at a party. I'm glad this ended up being a bonus track because it does not flow well with the rest of the album, but I hate the fact that this is the last song you hear before the CD ends; terrible decision. 6.5/10

Cole World: The Sideline is an incredible debut by North Carolina's rising star. After 2 critically acclaimed mixtapes and now a very diverse accessible debut album, J. Cole is now at the start of his legendary career. What's amazing is that J. Cole is only getting warmed up. Once J. Cole steps out of the sideline we will fully see what J. Cole is capable of. reviewText:
Inception is one of the best and most original movies to come out in the last 10 years. The film is also kind of revolutionary and blew the minds of all who saw it. The soundtrack also blew my mind, but because it expertly blended adventure and emotion into a smoothie that still tries to bring me to tears every time I listen to it.

Highlights Include:
Dream Is Collapsing
528491
Mombasa
Time

Of course, the soundtrack may be most famous for its trailer music, but strangely enough, it only appears for a few seconds at the end of "528491." There's hints of it elsewhere, but not in its true form. Not surprisingly though, the soundtrack works best when stuff is happening. Specifically, when the worlds and dreams are collapsing. Sure, when there's chase scenes too, but mostly when stuff is coming apart.

Then there's "Time." This is the track that makes me teary-eyed. Why? It's the music that accents the final scene, and incredibly emotional ones just like it. This is simply one of the best tracks from a score I've heard in YEARS. It starts soft, and then it builds. It builds for a good 3 minutes, getting louder each time, conveying a sense of escalating emotion or despair. It's a simple tune, repeated over and over, but it's highly effective. But then it crescendos, and gets softer with only a piano, highlighting the meaning of the spinning top and everything that has just happened and/or been experience. It's simply magnificent. Heck, my iPod says I've listened to it 72 times since I saw the movie, and it never gets old.

Of course, there are negatives to the soundtrack though. There seems to be a lot of dead air, particularly in "Waiting for a Train." It may work in the movie, but it's frankly a bit boring listening to it on its own, since there's really 9 minutes of nothingness going on here. Also, and this is a little nitpicky, but it kind of bugs me that the soundtrack isn't in order. That may just be me, but "We Built Our Own World" happens late in the movie. Not towards the beginning. Sure, they may be just themes of the movie, and not really scene specific, but it would be nice to have a little of this.

Overall, Hans Zimmer crafts another winner here that perfectly accents a near-perfect movie. It may have a few problems, but it makes up for it out of its moments of sheer brilliance. If you liked the movie, or you're just a soundtrack fan, I highly recommend you at least have a listen.

reviewText:
This is one of those incredibly under-appreciated albums that shows that true art and poetry are still being created.  Suzanne proves that love songs can be incredibly mysterious with the use of strange settings and metaphors.  "Honeymoon Suite" has a haunting tone, which is so rare in more recent pop music.  "World Before Columbus" is my personal favorite (and one of my all-time favorite songs).  With wonderful metaphors, it deals with everything from world history and greed to love and a desire to live and feel more deeply.

Other passages delve into fears, darkness, and issues of mortality (e.g. "Birthday," "Headshots," and "Tombstone").  "Thin Man," I discovered, refers to the skeletal "figure of death" (i.e. the Grim Reaper) mentioned in the liner notes.  The song is remarkably similar in imagery to Emily Dickinson's "Because I Could Not Stop for Death."  These themes are balanced, though, by periodically upbeat and jazzy songs, some with racy overtones (e.g. "Caramel" and "Stockings.")  As always, Mike Visceglia's base-playing and the other instrumentation are as good as it gets.  It is difficult to imagine a more beautifully written and arranged single-disc album.

There are several great songs on this 1998 collection from the American singer-songwriter Jewel Kilcher, and it is my favourite of her five albums to date. Jewel is a special artist for me and for many others who admire her blend of heartwarming, tuneful soul poetry and rocking , semi-country stylings. Her rags-to-riches story of conquering the pop world despite penury after leaving her Alaskan home for a tilt at singing stardom in the early 90's is now well-known, but I like the way that she remains a songwriter and poet at heart. On this collection, the magical songs are the intimate ballad Absence Of Fear, which beautifully summarises the feelings of being in love, the soulful Life Uncommon, the tender tune Enter From The East, the lovely choruses of Kiss The Flame , and of course the hit single Hands . "We are God's hands..." This song has some beautiful lines in it that still touch me : "Poverty stole your golden shoes, but it could not steal your laughter..." These soft, enchanting songs are good for the Spirit.

Jewel's earthier side can also find expression here on songs like Down So Long, Fat Boy and Jupiter. Fans of Jewel's current offering 0304 unfamilar with Spirit may enjoy hearing a more reflective artist on this album with fewer of the pop stylings that characterised her latest album.

Highly recommended.

This is one of the broadest and grandest recordings of this symphony in the catalogue. The sound is very fine if occasionally just a little coarse and tubby but it captures the concentration of a life performance and the balance of instruments is excellent. There is virtually no extraneous or audience noise, apart from a little grunting from the Maestro. This was a favourite symphony for Bernstein and he chose it for his farewell concert 25 years after his debut as Music Director of the orchestra here.

It is weighty but never ponderous; the Scherzo is especially released and exuberant and the Brooklyn Boys' Chorus is almost unruly in its attack, which creates a robust effect far preferable to the prissiness which affects some renderings. The playing of the New York Philharmonic is especially commendable and if anything superior to the earlier, 1961 recording, just as Christa Ludwig is preferable to Martha Lipton.

Bernstein's noble restraint in the opening of the finale pays off as he keeps his powder dry for the cataclysmic climax; this builds and builds through 28 minutes. Only Maazel takes as long in what is for me an almost equally recommendable recording with the VPO and certainly other outstanding performances are less overtly affectionate, starting with Tennstedt's searing, but comparatively brisk live account, Sinopoli in Stuttgart, Mehta and Abbado's earliest recording with the VPO. These are all wonderful recordings as this symphony has been fortunate on records but there is no denying Bernstein's ability to generate a special kind of intensity. Alongside the First and the Ninth this is probably the finest and the most typical of his recordings in the second cycle.

reviewText:
. . .I am probably the newest passenger on the John Mayer Love Train here. The first song I ever heard was "Vultures" at 4:00pm the day I saw him in concert that night with Sheryl Crow in Indianapolis, three days before "Continuum" hit the market. I got to hear him sing it live that night.  While waiting for Continuum to come out, I ordered "Try" solely to have "Vultures,"  "I Got a Woman," and "Good Love is on the Way" (I hope he'll release a studio version of this awesome rocker!) to tide me over, so to speak.  But what made me a true believer once I got this thing in my hands was hearing "Out of My Mind."  Close your eyes and you'll swear that Ray Charles is singing and Stevie Ray Vaughn is playing the guitar.  But no--apparently this is John's composition, played and sung by John with--dare it I say it?--SOUL.  And it's not even the peak of the concert.  There's lots more to come.  The encore section is 20 minutes long, including a raw rocking version of "Something's Missing."  Yes, I have to ignore the sexist lyrics of "I Got A Woman" and just listen to that blues guitar wail, but after all, he didn't write that one.  Mr. Charles did. There's a lot of variety here--a fun, funky cover of Hendrix' "Wait Until Tomorrow", "Daughters" (for those of us who can't get enough of "classic John"). The "green" song that follows "Out of My Mind" reminds me of the Beatles circa 1969.  "Vultures" rocks, of course--the only thing missing are the keyboard parts from the "Continuum" version.  I love the way he ends this one--it fades out to him and this little funky rhythmic thing.

On a live album, you're either on your game or you're not. Nothing to hid behind.  Nothing to prop you up. And it's just him and two awesome rhythm masters who, like BB King, Clapton, etc., are much too talented and busy to ever suffer fools.  Not that they have to with John. He is ON here. The crowds he played to here were much smaller and quieter than the ones on "Any Given Tuesday." There are a few times he's a bit too closer to the microphone, and you'll hear an occasionally appreciative whoop from a fan. But frankly, this captures a lot of what he's really like in concert.  No stupid mouth on this one--he banters with the crowd a little bit, but it's mostly playing and jamming and singing. For the heart and the energy that comes through here, I can put up with a little bit of crowd noise and appreciation.

If it's as well-produced as this CD, I'd love to see this on DVD with interviews and a documentary. "Continuum" will probably sell more units, but for those of us on the Love Train, this album is John's watershed album.  If he goes in this direction in the future, this is the place he began to make grown up music.  I hope his fans will be smart enough to make the journey with him from teen idol to blues master.

reviewText:
Throughout much of its period of popularity, the viola da gamba was not a professional musician's instrument. It was the dilettante's pleasure, the instrument for cultured recreational music. Such it has become again in modern times, with the "early music" movement. There are summer workshop "dude ranches" for amateur gambists all over America. Much of the music written for gambas even by the greatest composers of the late Renaissance and Baroque was written for gentlemen/patrons of perhaps limited virtuosity. Bach's gamba sonatas, for example, are less challenging in every way, including listening, than his solo cello suites.

Nonetheless, the Bach gamba sonatas are thrillingly beautiful, and Jordi Savall has lived with them until he understands them better than anyone but Bach himself. I have listened to Jordi's older recording of them so many times that I can recognize each from one random bar of music. Consequently, my first reaction to this newer performance was quizzical. Why's he playing it that way? But I've come to respect the new as much as the old. Now there are two master performances to choose from.

If you enjoy the sound of the gamba, you will be delighted to discover that Savall has a long catalogue of performances by the great French Baroque composers for his instrument: Marais, St. Colombe, Fourqueray, and others, all ravishing. No one since that era of French geniuses has made the gamba a more persuasive virtuoso's instrument than Jordi Savall.

reviewText: I love this disk, but the title and jacket may mislead. This is not a CD full of salsa/samba/mambo music. It has some elements of those, but most of the music selections have more European influence (think Villa-Lobos, although he is not represented on this disk). The opening number is very evocative of modern Amazonian music (Uakti in particular) and is both engaging and disturbing at the same time. Considering that it based on a poem entitled "Chant to Kill A Snake", the music is indeed a tone poem straight from the jungle. It made my cats, who are otherwise blase about music, run around the living room and act crazy. The other selections, as noted, have more European influence, with nods to Gershwin, Ravel and Debussy. I'm not being ethnocentric here, but just trying to present some comparisons that will be familiar to American listeners. All of these selections made me want to hear more from these composers and the orchestra. The concluding number is a live performance of the dance "Mambo" from West Side Story. It made what's left of my hair stand on end; Somewhere,(pun intended) I know Bernstein is smiling in appreciation. Highly, highly recommended!

reviewText:
I don't really remember where I first got this, just that I first heard it when I was a teenager. Prior to this, I had only read about Clapton - the legendary British guitar slinger whose fans had spray-painted "Clapton is God" on an Underground station during his tenure with John Mayall's Bluesbreakers and who was commonly viewed as `right up there' with Jimi Hendrix and other A list guitarists.

461 Ocean Boulevard didn't really sound like that guy - or at least not like what I imagine that guy would sound like. It's groovy, funky, low-key but energetic, and it has the energy of a great ensemble record, not a self-absorbed solo effort by a guitar god. Recorded in Miami in 1974, the title refers to the address of Clapton's residence there during that period.

I think this music has held up very well over the years - it's a kind of bluesy rock masterpiece that shows Clapton's wide-ranging musical interests. Long before punk made it de rigueur to have reggae influences, this record features the famous version of "I Shot the Sheriff." Other standouts are Elmore James' "I Can't Hold Out," Robert Johnson's "Steady Rolling Man" and Johnny Otis' "Willie and the Hand Jive."

I love the subtleties in this: how Clapton's guitar is always the most tasteful thing you've ever heard - not too flashy, not too subdued, not too distorted; how Clapton's voice - often a point of discussion, but actually quite strong here - blends with Yvonne Elliman's (and the band's) background vocals. 461 Ocean Boulevard is a perfect demonstration of what was great about classic rock when it was firmly rooted in its rock `n roll and r&b roots.

Sticky Fingers is of course a Stones classic and a rock classic as well. This was the first full album featuring Mick Taylor and the sound is ragged, loose and inspired on cuts like Brown Sugar, Bitch, Sway and Can't You Hear Me Knocking. In addition, Jagger/Richards produces some really memorable ballads like Wild Horses and Moonlight Mile.

reviewText:
I first heard of Mat Kearney early in 2005 after I heard "Undeniable" on the radio.  At first, the song didn't blow me away, but I liked it and I was interested in checking out this new artist some more.  What I found was an outstanding debut album, with a perfect blend of acoustic guitars, driving beats, the occasional piano, tasteful rapping, and thoughtful lyrics.  Many of the obvious comparisons can be made about him as well, as sometimes he can remind you of Coldplay, Dave Matthews, Counting Crows, or Paul Wright.

Trainwreck - 9/10 - A hard, driving beat with lyrics that set the tone for the rest of the album, with Kearney confessing that he is a "trainwreck for you."

Undeniable - 9/10 - The first single, took me awhile to appreciate how good it was.  It would be standard CCM were it not for the rapping in the verses.

Bullet - 10/10 - My favorite from the album.  I love the guitar and drum beat.  Great lyrics and a powerful message in the chorus.  "I would take a bullet for you...I would lose it all and take my fall to show you it's for real."

Girl America - 7/10 - A good track but it doesn't really stand out among the rest.  A song that reminds me of Paul Wright's style.

In The Middle - 9/10 - Some of his vocals here really make him sound like Chris Martin of Coldplay.  Just another great track.

Renaissance - 10/10 - Powerful song about losing it all and asking for forgiveness, a second chance, and a way to heal a broken heart.  Great, comforting chorus.

Call Me - 9/10 - Comparisons to Coldplay can mount here.  A nice, mellow acoustic track.

Poor Boy - 9/10 - Great beat, wish more hip-hop would sound like this.

Walking Away - 9/10 - Once again, Mat shows an ability to craft guitar riffs beautifully to complement his rapping/singing.

Tomorrow - 8/10 - Another great track, piano based beat, very cool sounding.

Won't Back Down - 9/10 - An end album piano ballad.  I just love the chorus and the feel of the song about not giving in and backing down no matter all of the chaos in your life.

Some of the best Christian music that has come out recently, it's a shame that he won't get any mainstream recognition, but there really isn't a market for am artist like him anyway.  Mat's strongest points are his guitar/piano riffs, vocal/rapping style, and his thoughtful and relatable lyrics.  I look forward to more music from him in the future.

reviewText:
What's really interesting about Psycho Circus is a lot of fans slag it off because it wasn't a "band effort" but at the same time they praise Creatures of the Night which was made under similar circumstances and recorded in a much similar manner.

I can understand why some fans don't like this album because it was suppose to be their big comeback after their highly successful 1996-1997 Reunion tour and first studio album together in almost twenty years and all that B.S. but what I care most about is the songs and Psycho Circus really delivers in that area.  Paul's lead off track and the album's title track is a skull crushing, ear bleeding rock and roll masterpiece.  It doesn't really get any better than that.  Gene surprisingly has an amazing showing on this album.  Mr. $immons really hits it out of the park every time at bat.  Within, We Are One and Journey of 1,000 Years are all awesome songs and could fit just about on any album in the band's history.  They are very timeless songs.  Gene's only misstep is You Wanted The Best but it's far from a throw away or piece of crap.  It has kind of a weak chorus but the verses are a rocking with contributing vocals by all the band members and the guitar solo is great and harkens back to classic KISS albums from the 70s.  Some people are overly critical of Paul's songs on Psycho Circus but they are much better songs that what Paul has done in the past on albums like Unmasked, Music From The Elder, Hot In The Shade, Revenge and Carnival of Souls.

Into The Void is the only real weak song on the album.  It's too bad that the band couldn't work out their differences and make it a real team effort but this is a practice that started with this very lineup twenty years before in the late 70s and continued on for the next two decades so fans really can't knock the band for that.  That's just how they record albums.  It would have been nice to hear about them getting along and recording the album together but they stopped getting along during the Reunion tour and I have to commend Gene and Paul for trying to make it work with an addict like Ace was at the time, but that's not their fault.  Sometimes, you just have to cut your losses.

reviewText:
Janet Jackson's sixth studio album, "The Velvet Rope," was released around the time of her battle with depression. By far the most difficult record of hers to complete, Janet is all the more better for it, and it shows through in the music on this excellent album. She was fighting her inner demons, and for the first time, came forward and revealed her emotional problems and proving that even the biggest superstars have their ups and downs. Her emotive feelings reflect immensely in her work on "The Velvet Rope," as she covers a wide variety of subjects contained within these emotional problems from discrimination and violent relationships, while still managing to keep things hot with her own sexual fantasies. Granted, these 'fantasies' aren't as far-fetched as those on "Would You Mind," taken from 2001's "All For You," but they are much more listenable and interesting.

"The Velvet Rope" begins with an Interlude - Twisted Elegance, before moving onto the album's explosive title-track, "Velvet Rope." Perhaps the most instantly listenable song on the album, this is a stunning song which covers the actual materials contained within this album, and how we all have needs that bring out the best in us and also, consequently, the worst in us. Janet addresses the subject with amazing confidence, and the violin break towards the end by the stunning Vanessa Mae makes this one of Janet's greatest-ever songs. "You" is another great R'n'B style song with great, almost scary, low vocals from Janet in the verses, before spicing things up in the choruses with a full-on assault on those who go around stirring trouble. "Got 'Til It's Gone" is by far one of Janet's career-highlights. The song, which samples Joni Mitchell's classic "Big Yellow Taxi," was a UK Top 10 smash in October 1997. The beat is superb, and the muffled effect enhances this while the rap by Q-Tip just elevates this to an all-time classic R'n'B tune. "Interlude - Speaker Phone" is a rather boring interlude, while "My Need" is another album highlight. Janet sings of her lover, and what she needs from him - sexually. She began the album saying "We have a special need." She's just expressing one of these many needs through sexual intimacies, and the result is brilliant.

"Interlude - Fasten Your Seatbelts" is the best interlude on the album with a feeling of joy. This feeling on happiness is only strengthened with the explosive single "Go Deep." In my opinion, it's the best song to be released as a single from the album. The beat is similar to that of her brother's "Billie Jean." "Free Xone" is a great song which tackles the difficult (in society's terms) subject of homosexuality, or more bluntly, homophobia. Janet's vocals sound a little distracted, but the instrumental beats that contrast and develop throughout the song make up for it. The pointless "Interlude - Memory" at a mere four seconds long is followed by the amazing "Together Again." Released way back in December 1997, this brilliant dance tune peaked at No. 4 in the UK. The song is a dedication to friends that Janet has lost to AIDS, and her often-criticised vocals are amazing.

"Interlude - Online" is followed by the light-hearted "Empty." The song tells the story of an online romance, with an incredibly speedy beat, yet mellow and slow background. The two work well, and the lyrics from the man, "One! Two! One! Two! Three! Four!" add to the melodic joy. Things go dark with "Interlude - Full" before the disturbing "What About." An album highlight for many, the song tells the tale of a violent relationship - with subdued verses, and explosive and angry choruses. The way the song is arranged is genius - one thinks upon first listen that as Janet describes all the good things about her man in the verses that it's a typical love song, but this is turned on its head in the choruses.

"Every Time" and "Tonight's The Night" are two great ballads which, while not the best songs on this album, are some of Janet's best slow jams. "I Get Lonely" is another album highlight. Released as a single in April 1998, this superb R'n'B hit bounces along with it's deep bassline and isolated lyrics. "Rope Burn" is another one of Janet's sex-songs, and not quite up to the rest of the standard on the album. "Anything" is a brilliant mid-tempo song to chill to, which features a great beat and soft gentle lyrics. "Interlude - Sad" is followed by "Special." This is one of those typical mid-tempo songs about inspiration - and how everyone needs to feel special. "Can't Be Stopped" is a superb hidden track that should've really been added to the tracklisting. The beat is great, and the lyrics are more of the "You can achieve anything if you want to" type.

OVERALL GRADE: 10/10

The Velvet Rope is easily Janet Jackson's most personal and emotional record to date. Some may say this is an incorrect statement and that "Rhythm Nation" was more personal and emotional, but Rhythm Nation was more of a record about world issues and not inner feelings, violence, discrimination and sexual fantasies. The question lies herein, is The Velvet Rope Janet's best record? The answer is a simple yes. The album may not have been the most talked-about and biggest selling of her career, but it definitely stretched the boundaries on what was considered acceptable amongst today's society. And just for that little point, that minor matter yet major issue, The Velvet Rope is Janet Jackson's career-defining record.

reviewText:
You, yes YOU, should get this. It's a really awesome album, and it should really be getting more attention that it has been (limited to fans of Living Legends, Definitive Jux, and Justus League.) Murs, lyrically, is more straightforward than most of his Def Jux labelmates (Aesop Rock, Cannibal Ox), which, to me, is a good thing. I like Aesop and Ox but most of the time I'd rather not have to decipher everything the rapper says. Murs has a nice unique flow and his style is pretty original compared to most rappers, mainstream and underground. And 9th Wonder earns the hype that he received as a member of Little Brother, bringing constant hot beats to the entire album.

One thing that stands out about the album is the variety of topics Murs covers. Few rappers are more realistic, honest, and personal about getting ladies (Bad Man, Freak These Tales, The Pain). Murs also talks about hard work (H-U-S-T-L-E), and the state of race in hip-hop (And this is for...). That track in particular stands out, as Murs condemns the black community, white poseurs, and white rappers taking over the business. This may sound racist to some (white people such as myself), but it really is a justified argument. It's about time somebody admits that Eminem only sells so well because he's white (even if they don't mention his name).

Murs also brings the battle tracks, like 3:16, and The Animal (featuring Phonte of Little Brother in the well-deserved only guest spot). Murs can spit the battle rhymes with the best of them. I've never heard or seen him battle but I'd be interested to hear something he did. The main standouts of the album (which says a lot) are the storytelling raps. Trevor an Them is a minute and a half, and not too eventful or compelling, but it's got some good rhymes. But the standout track is Walk Like a Man, a gripping narrative about guns, the murder of a best friend and the subsequent vengeance. I generally tend to dislike storytelling raps, as they tend to sound forced and the rhymes tend to suffer, but the way Murs pulls it off is incredible. It's the lyrical highlight of the album for me, and it's incredibly supplemented by 9th wonder, who provides a different sample for every verse, to match the tone of Murs' lyrics. I'd love to know who originally recorded the sped-up sample in the middle verse as it really elevates the track.

Speaking of 9th, this is my favorite of his works that I've heard. (The Chittlin Circuit 1.5, Minstrel Show, and Buckshot's Chemistry). He brings hot beats the whole time. The samples are perfect and the drum loops are much more varied than those on Little Brother albums (a constant complaint is that 9th always uses the same drum patterns, which this album proves is a fruitless argument). If there's a single reason Murs increases his fanbase after this album, it's 9th Wonder. And power to both of them. I know it's a long shot that they'd work together for a whole album again, but I'd love to see it. All in All, this album is worth your time.

Chapman's guitar is blazing, the rest of the band sounds tight as hell, and the production will blow you away.  On this album in particular, which has always had an impressive and rich production, the details are jaw-dropping.  You will hear elements you never noticed before, and you will hear the familiar with a refreshing clarity and intensity.  If you like UFO (and if you don't, what's wrong with you?) buy these remasters!  Oh, man, they sound SO good!

reviewText:
It may take Trent four or five years to get new product out, however, he rarely disappoints on whole.  With Teeth is by far his most consistently enjoyable album in years.  I loved big chuncks of The Downward Spiral and The Fragile but felt he copped out on some songs by repeatedly making "noise" songs that were heavy on guitar, angst and pounding drums but had very little melody.  I just didn't like his turns into that area.

This album sees him return to a more melodic approach where the song is first and foremost rather than technique.  It has all the elements that made his debut the incredible masterpiece it was and at this very moment I would rank them darn near equal.  He may never truly top that album but not because he can't, he simply isn't allowed to by his core fans.  They either want him to stay hard or go back to his original sound, which limits what he can experiment with.  However, he has achieved a balance on this album that was not present on his last two releases.

It took me a few listens to fully embrace it but once I did I was completely converted.  All in all its one of the best releases of the last year.

Great guitar/piano driven melodic soft rock from UK quintet The Feeling. `Twelve stops from home' is their debut disc and if you like The Beatles, Supertramp, ELO, or even Keane, then you'll love this.

The album's already had 3 hit singles in the UK: the ornate ballad `Sewn', and the sunnier, more upbeat pair of `Fill my world' and `Never be lonely'.

Other standouts are `Helicopter' (very ELO), the soaring ballads `Blue Piccadilly' (a dramatic waltz-like song with lead vocalist Dan Gillespie-Sells really stretching his vocal chops), the beautiful `Rose', and `Strange', and the rocky, incredibly catchy `Love it when you call' (lovely harmonies). There's also a beautiful piano ballad hidden at the end.

Very simple songs, well written, with fun, hummable killer hooks, and very British sounding. Great!!

Metal Church has been overlooked for its unique contribution to the Hard Metal of the mid-80s. Hard metal along the lines of Metallica and Megadeth with the raspy singing style of David Wayne who sounds kind of like AC/DC's Brian Johnson. If you like dynamic drum riffs, Kirk Arrington is up there with Lars Ulrich without a doubt. The guitar work of Craig Wells and Kurdt Vanderhoof is quite unique, crisp, and clear. A very tight band where none of the members get muffled through the songs. Definitely a band to check out if you like Megadeth and/or Metallica. Along with the latter, this is by far the best band in that style that came out of the 80's.

This debut album along with their second one, "The Dark", have to be their best work. The band changed singer and lead guitarist on the third album "Blessing in Disguise" and it's just not as good. Very original and intriquite guitar solo on "Gods of Wrath" and guitar intro on "Beyond the Black." Throughout the album, Kirk Arrington dishes out his drum genius. Definitely a band worth hearing and an album worth owning. I've been listening to this band since 1985 and I've never been sick of them.

reviewText:
Just look at the personnel here and know that this side swings from the first to the last note.
Super hip compositions from Trane and Donald Byrd, with a nice little ballad thing and a hip bass melody blues from PC.  Philly Joe's intro to Omicron will keep drummers up at night for centuries.  I love Donald Byrd on minor tunes and he doesn't disappoint me here.  Trane lays out for two measures in one of the tunes as though he is thinking about what to play next.  That pause in itself is a rare enough occurrence.  When he comes back in he lays down what he had been contemplating and we find it was worth the wait. I dig the silence that preceded it as much as the phrase itself, just because it so rare.
Horace and Kenny do a great job of staying out of each other's way and all pianists and guitarists should be made to listen to how they do so.  Far too often the two gang up on the soloist and bury him/her with accompaniment.
My personal favorite on the record is Omicron, a line based on the changes to Dizzy's "Woody'n You".  Trane only plays one chorus!  It is a very nice, concise chorus, but i have been listening to this record for 25 years wishing he had taken at least two more on these deceptively challenging changes.
Great music.

reviewText:
So I bought this album about 2 years ago and hated it.  Talentless, overrated, sophomoric, and juvenile would have been words I might have used to describe the Ramones.  Then about a year later something in my head snapped, and I realized just how impressive and important this album is.

It's not just amazing for historical value, but shamelessly enjoyable and life affirming... even if the subject matter is pretty nihilistic at it's core (solvent abuse, prostitution, murder by chainsaw).  Somehow Joey can sing about even the most depressing subjects and make you want to sing along not for catharisis, but just for pure enjoyment!

I don't know if they were really punk... upon first listen, I thought more of a juvenile and visceral Beach Boys.  Classic rock, sort of like those "Nuggets" bands, but just way better.  When I heard they covered Surfin' Bird and California Sun everything just made sense all of a sudden.  The Ramones reminded people again in those days of what was cool about Rock & Roll.  Two chords (MAYBE three), or better yet 1 chord, a catchy chorus and a whole lot of distortion.

Sure, they're lo-fi and by most conceptions of art appreciation they're just TERRIBLE, but that's also what makes them cool.  At the same time, the Ramones "shtick" doesn't sound calculated or forced.  My initial ignorance to the genius of this band completely bears out the course of their career.  Don't feel sorry for them though... history will be kind to the Ramones.

This album is so good!
It's a shame it was virtually slept upon here in the states!
But back in 1994, while over in the U.K., I went to see
the Brand New Heavies featuring N'dea Davenport
(another fave of mine from that era!)and a freind
told me that if I loved them, I was sure to love this almost new group at the time..Jamiroquai.

Well, we went to catch them in concert as well and WOW!
I was hooked by their sound, style and Jay-Kay's vocalizations.
Now I don't agree or understand about the comparisons that
some make between Jay and Stevie Wonder, because they
sound nothing alike, but I guess because the Jamiroquai
sound was so retro with the heavy fender rhodes, clavinet,
arp, moog & oberheim synths, etc. (circa 1970's)
that some had to make the comparison
to categorize what they were hearing!---
This album is the first Jamiroquai album that
I bought and it's great from start to finish!
"Space Cowboy", "Stillness In Time", "Half The Man",
"Manifest Destiny" "Journey To Arnhemland" & "Morning Glory"
all still stand the test of time!
Stuart Zender is an absolutely incredible bassist!
It's like the late Bernard Edwards of CHIC, Verdine White of E,W&F
and Larry Graham of Sly & The Family Stone / Graham Central Station
morphed and merged into the body of a young white kid!
Then, I went back and bought their debut
"Emergency On Planet Earth", which I also love, and then
of course, there is "Traveling Without Moving" which gave
them their crossover hit "Virtual Insanity" and finally got
them love here in the states outside the small but
loyal ultra-hip fan base they have here!
If you buy either 3 of the aforementioned albums,
you can't go wrong!

**ADDENDUM** I wish they would re-master and tweek this album though,
because the mix and sound quality was kind of sub-standard to my ear at that time and though I loved the songs,
I always felt that way in the back of my mind.

reviewText: I love the music of Ennio Morricone, but I usually am dissatisfied with the results when others arrange and play his music.  Mr. Morricone's music is quite idiosyncratic; thus, it is extremely difficult to capture the special elements that set his music apart.  Yo Yo Ma's playing is always stunning.  It is to his great credit that he actually chose to work with "the maestro" in creating this wonderful work.  The selection of these specific melodies is a stroke of genius.  While the result is very true to the original intent of the composer, the great cellist works wonders within that framework.  A purchase of this fine recording will immensely reward the listener.

reviewText: It is unnanimous, up to this point everyone here has given this disc five stars! Tito Puente was a pioneer who started the first wave of Latin music to capture attention worldwide. One of his signature songs, "Oye Come Va" was made popular by Santana Oye Como Va. I was lucky enough to have seen him perform live in a little Hermosa Beach auditorium many years before his death; he was amazing even at his than advanced age. He could wail on the timbales and work his band into a frenzy. The performance here is taken from the early fifties when he was in his prime and the result is an awe-inspiring blend of soulful vocals, horns, rhythms and percussion that results in pure dance music or as the title indicates, dance mania. This disc captures the dance crazes taht were prevelant than like the cha-cha-cha, mambo and salsa. The latin jazz influences and salsa vibe are spread throughout this winner. Everything but one song, "Estoy Siempre Junto a Ti," which is a bolero, or ballad is a cooker; this is the only song where the tempo is slowed down. A very good tune is "Hong Kong Mambo"(love the title)that features some great vibe(vibraphones)work that finishes with crashing high hat and Asian sounding vibe rhythms. If you are a DJ these are some great riffs to work into your creations. There are many good Tito Puente discs including but not limited to The Mambo King: His 100th Album,Out of This World,King of Kings: The Very Best of Tito Puente which are all highly recommended. Flat out, this one is the goods.
